title: Yachtmaster Offshore
note: Scenario questions written for study, close to the Yachtmaster Offshore syllabus. Not official exam content. figure is a spec for docs/design/figures.js (null = text question). Pass mark, exam size and time are app defaults to verify.

topics.title: Dead reckoning, EP & course to steer

questions.q: Your mate lays the Breton plotter along the leg on the passage chart and calls out 058°. You glance at the chart. What true course goes in the plan?

figure.title: Laying off the leg
lines: Plotter grid lined up on a meridian

questions.why: The arrow must point the way you go: reversed, it reads the reciprocal, 058° + 180° = 238°T — and the leg runs SW.

questions.q: You set the variation on your Portland plotter and lay it along the leg, so that it reads the magnetic course directly. What should it read?
questions.why: Set 4°W and the plotter adds it for you: 112°T + 4°W = 116°M. Set to E it gives 108°; adding 4° again by hand gives 120°.

questions.q: You are laying off the next 40 M leg on a big passage chart at sea. The nearest rose is a hand's span away and the parallel rules slip on every roll. What do you do?

figure.title: Chart table, force 6 on the beam
lines: Parallel rules slip on every roll

options: Judge it by eye against the nearest rose
Take the course from the plotter screen
Use a Breton plotter lined up on a meridian
Walk the rules anyway, in shorter steps
questions.why: A Breton-type plotter needs only a meridian or parallel under it — no rose, no walking; each slip of the rules shifts the line.

questions.q: You want hand-bearing compass bearings of three headlands for a fix from your 22 m motor yacht. Where do you take them?

figure.title: Your motor yacht
lines: Aft deck: stainless davits, the tender

options: On the flybridge, for the highest view
Beside the steering compass at the helm
Anywhere aft, well away from the engines
At a spot you have checked on a transit
questions.why: Steel, speakers and electronics deflect a hand-bearing compass; take bearings where a transit has shown it reads true.

questions.q: Your mate measured tonight's leg on the small-scale passage chart, reading the dividers on the latitude scale at the bottom edge. What is the leg's true length?
questions.why: Mercator minutes of latitude grow as sec lat: 66.0 × cos 50° ÷ cos 45° = 60.0 M. Measure beside the leg.
questions.ref: Charts — distance on the latitude scale

questions.q: At 0300 your relief navigator plots the EP on the passage chart in ballpoint, in heavy lines across the next day's legs. What do you tell him?

figure.title: Night watch, chart table
lines: Same chart for the return passage

options: Use a red pen so it shows under red light
Soft pencil, light short lines — it must rub out
Use a hard pencil and press hard to last
Fine — ink won't smudge in a wet cockpit
questions.why: Plot in soft pencil (2B), lightly and only where needed: lines must rub out without spoiling the chart for later fixes and voyages.

questions.q: Your planning chart of the north-east Atlantic covers 40°N to 60°N. You set the dividers to 10 M on the latitude scale at 40°N, then again at 60°N. How do the two spans compare on the paper?

figure.title: Planning chart, Mercator
lines: 10 M set on the latitude scale at 40°N

options: The 60°N span is about 1.5 times shorter
The two spans are exactly the same length
The 60°N span is about 1.5 times longer
The 60°N span is about twice as long
questions.why: Mercator scale grows as sec lat: sec 60° ÷ sec 40° = 2.00 ÷ 1.31 ≈ 1.5. The same mile is drawn longer nearer the pole.

questions.q: Planning a 1,200 M delivery leg to the Azores, you draw a straight line from departure to destination on a gnomonic chart. What do you do next?

figure.title: Gnomonic chart, North Atlantic
lines: It cuts the meridians at changing angles
Aboard: Mercator charts of the route

options: Measure its distance on the gnomonic's border
Lay the line's first course on the Mercator rose
Steer the course the line shows at its middle
Take off points every 5° of longitude onto the Mercator
questions.why: A great circle is a straight line on a gnomonic chart; transfer its points to the Mercator and sail rhumb lines between them.
questions.ref: Charts — gnomonic charts and great circles

questions.q: Your 140 M overnight leg runs due east along 50°N. Your crew wants to plan it as a great circle on a gnomonic chart to save distance. What do you decide?

figure.title: Tomorrow's leg
lines: Crew: 'Plot the great circle — it's shorter'

options: Rhumb line — the great circle saves under 0.1 M
Rhumb line — great circles only pay going south
Great circle — any leg over 100 M needs one
Great circle — it saves about 5 % going east–west
questions.why: On 140 M the great circle is only 0.01 M shorter; it pays on long ocean legs, mostly east–west in high latitudes.
questions.ref: Charts — gnomonic charts and great circles

questions.q: A crew member lays a plotter on the straight line drawn on the gnomonic chart to read the course. What do you tell her?

figure.title: Gnomonic chart on the table
lines: Great circle drawn as a straight line
Crew lays the plotter on the line

options: Fine — but add the variation from its rose
The course changes along the line — use the Mercator
Read it at the end of the line, not the start
Fine — read it once and steer it all the way
questions.why: A gnomonic chart doesn't keep angles: a great circle cuts each meridian at a different angle, so courses come off the Mercator.
questions.ref: Charts — gnomonic charts and great circles

questions.q: You check the plotter's figures for tonight's Channel crossing against the chart. What course and distance do you lay off?
Tonight's leg runs due north along a single meridian. How long is it?
questions.why: Along a meridian each minute of latitude is a mile: 50°47' − 48°52' = 1°55' = 115'.

questions.q: Overnight you run due east for 60 M along the parallel from this position. What longitude do you reach?
questions.why: d.long = departure ÷ cos lat = 60.0 ÷ cos 49° = 91.5' = 1°31.5' E; going east, west longitude falls: 003°28.5'W.

questions.q: From the log book you work out the boat's mean speed through the water over the night. What was it?
options: 7.8 kn
7.5 kn
2.8 kn
7.3 kn
questions.ref: Distance, speed and time — the log

questions.q: You leave Falmouth at 2050 for a Breton harbour, 121 M by the plan. The French marina wants your ETA in its local time. What do you give?
In slack water you time your 20 m motor yacht between two buoys charted 2.35 M apart. What is her speed?
options: 5.3 kn

questions.q: Your guests ask what the motor yacht's cruising speed of 25 knots is in kilometres per hour. What do you tell them?
options: About 46 km/h
About 13.5 km/h
About 29 km/h
About 40 km/h
questions.why: A knot is one nautical mile, 1852 m, per hour: 25 × 1.852 = 46.3 km/h.

questions.q: Bound for the next waypoint in the Aegean, the plotter shows BRG 209° while your plan says 214°T. What do you make of it?

figure.note: Plotter: Magnetic

options: Wrong — 214°T should show as 219°M
Nothing wrong — 214°T is 209°M
Wrong — you are 5° off the planned track
Wrong — the GPS has lost its fix
questions.why: The plotter is set to magnetic: 214°T − 5°E = 209°M. East is least — subtract it going true to magnetic.

questions.q: Your passage chart and the older approach chart of your landfall both note that their datum differs from WGS84. Where does it matter on tomorrow's 130 M passage?

figure.title: Chart notes
lines: Landfall: rocks either side of the entrance

options: Nowhere — 0.08' is under 150 m
Equally on both charts, all the way
At the landfall, on the approach chart
Offshore, where you fix every hour
questions.why: 0.08' ≈ 150 m: 0.2 mm on the 1:750,000, below plotting accuracy; 6 mm on the 1:25,000 — enough to put you on the rocks.

questions.q: Your landfall harbour's plan comes from an old foreign survey, its soundings to a different datum from your chart's. What least depth do you expect at the visitors' berth this week?

figure.title: Harbour plan, old survey
lines: Visitors' berth: 2.5 m on the plan
Lowest tide this week: 0.2 m above LAT

questions.why: Below LAT the bed is 2.5 − 0.6 = 1.9 m; the lowest tide adds 0.2 m: 2.1 m. The plan's datum sits 0.6 m above LAT.

questions.q: Your passage chart shows 8 m over a bank near your landfall; the approach chart shows a 4.2 m patch on it. Which depth do you plan on?

figure.title: Two charts, one bank
lines: Both corrected to the same week

options: 4.2 m — the larger scale shows more
8 m — the passage chart is for passage
8 m — small scales are more up to date
About 6 m — the mean of the two
questions.why: A small-scale chart leaves out detail; the larger scale shows the shoal patches. Plan on the least depth shown.
questions.ref: Charts — scale and the chart folio

questions.q: Mid-way across a 120 M crossing you plot hourly fixes. Which chart of your folio do you plot them on?

figure.title: Chart folio
lines: B: 1:325,000 — the crossing on one sheet

options: D — so the arrival plan is ready
B — the passage chart of the crossing
A — it shows the whole route at once
C — the largest scale gives the best fix
questions.why: Plot on the largest-scale chart that covers the leg: B. A is for planning; C and D don't reach mid-channel.
questions.ref: Charts — scale and the chart folio

questions.q: You check the chart folio for a 120 M night crossing to Brittany against your passage plan. What is missing?

figure.title: Folio and plan
lines: Plan B: a refuge port 25 M east
Plotter: vector charts of the area

options: Nothing — the plotter covers the refuge
Nothing — enter on the passage chart
Large-scale charts of the refuge port
A second copy of the passage chart
questions.why: A port of refuge is entered at night in bad weather: carry its approach chart and plan on paper, not only on the plotter.
questions.ref: Charts — scale and the chart folio — the passage folio

questions.q: Your planned track runs down the lane marked on the chart. What do you do?

figure.title: On the chart along your route
lines: A lane with magenta arrows and DW
Your yacht: 24 m ketch, draught 3.2 m

options: Cross it diagonally to save distance
Use it at night only, when it is quieter
Use it — its depths are the best surveyed
Replan to keep out — it is for deep ships
questions.why: A deep-water route is kept for deep-draught ships; vessels that don't need it should avoid it.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — traffic separation schemes — deep-water routes

questions.q: Your route crosses the area shown where three traffic schemes meet. What do you expect there, and how do you cross it?

figure.title: Chart where three schemes meet
lines: A magenta circle with a '!' symbol

options: Ships turning every way — cross fast, watch hard
Ships hold set lanes — cross at right angles
A closed area — re-route outside it
A slow-speed area — drift through under sail
questions.why: In a precautionary area ships converge and turn, with at most a recommended flow: navigate with particular caution.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — traffic separation schemes — precautionary areas

questions.q: On a night passage across the North Sea you see these lights ahead, about 8 M off. What are they?

figure.note: Night · white light · · — every 15 s

options: A safe-water buoy — Morse is its sign
An offshore platform — Mo(U) marks them
A lightvessel at the end of a lane
A wind turbine on a farm's corner
questions.why: Offshore platforms show a white light Mo(U), · · —, usually every 15 s; safe-water marks use Mo(A), · —.

questions.q: Your 24 m ketch's route crosses this offshore wind farm. What does the note mean for you?

figure.title: Wind farm on your route
lines: Chart note: small craft may transit
Lowest blade tip: 22 m above HAT
Your ketch: masthead 29 m above water

options: 7 m clear at HAT, more at lower tides
The blades are stopped for yachts in transit
Your mast can reach the blades — keep clear
Clear at any tide except at HAT
questions.why: Blades sweep down to 22 m above HAT, lower than your 29 m masthead: keep outside the swept circle of every turbine.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — offshore areas — wind farms

questions.q: Your night route crosses this area. What do you do?
options: Nothing — submarines keep clear of yachts
Re-route — yachts may not enter at night
Keep radio silence while in the area
Get the broadcast, show lights, keep a sharp lookout
questions.why: Exercise areas are not closed; know the broadcast of submarine activity and keep a good lookout — a dived submarine may not see you.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — offshore areas — submarine exercise areas

questions.q: 60 M offshore at night you pick up this light where the chart shows a buoy marked ODAS. What is it?

figure.note: Chart: ODAS, 60 M offshore

options: A data buoy — a special mark; pass clear
A new wreck — report it to the coastguard
A safe-water mark on the route's fairway
A lightvessel dragged off its station
questions.why: ODAS buoys gather ocean and weather data; they are yellow special marks, often Fl(5) Y 20s — give them a wide berth.

questions.q: You anchored in the dark off an open coast to wait for the stream and find you lie in a cable area. Weighing, the anchor brings up a heavy cable. What do you do?

figure.title: Anchored to wait for the stream
lines: Chart: you lie in a magenta cable area
Windlass stalls; a thick cable comes up
It lies across the anchor's fluke

options: Go hard astern to break the anchor out
Lower it, slip the anchor on a buoy, report
Lift the cable aboard and unhook it
Cut the cable free with the bolt cutters
questions.why: Never cut or force a submarine cable — power cables kill; slip the anchor and chain on a buoyed line and report the position.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — offshore areas — submarine cables

questions.q: You want to anchor overnight off this coast to wait for a fair stream. The best depth for your chain lies inside the box. What do you do?

figure.note: Chart extract

options: Anchor, with a tripping line on the anchor
Anchor — 'disused' means it was cleared
Anchor elsewhere — not in a dumping ground
Anchor — the munitions lie too deep to matter
questions.why: A disused explosives dumping ground may still hold live munitions: never anchor, trawl or dive there.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — offshore areas — dumping grounds

questions.q: Your route runs against one of the arrows beyond the end of the scheme. What does that arrow tell you?

figure.title: On the chart near the scheme
lines: Your route runs against a pecked arrow

options: A lane — you must not sail against it
A separation zone — keep out of it
A recommended track for small craft
A recommended flow — not binding, but expect ships
questions.why: A pecked-outline arrow is a recommended direction of traffic flow: no lane rule, but ships will be coming the other way.

questions.q: Your night track runs north past the rig in this warning. How far off it do you pass, and what do you do?
options: About 480 m — inside the zone; re-route
About 260 m — inside the zone; re-route
About 740 m — outside it; carry on
About 1150 m — well clear; carry on
questions.why: 0.4' of longitude × cos 50° = 0.26 M ≈ 480 m, inside the 500 m zone. A minute of longitude is not a mile.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — offshore installations — safety zones

questions.q: Your night landfall plan picks up this lightvessel 20 M out as the first mark. What changes?

figure.title: T&P notice, this week
lines: Lightvessel at the TSS end withdrawn
Replaced by a light buoy, same character
Range reduced from 24 M to 8 M

options: You see it at 20 M as before, but dimmer
You see it far later — fix on other lights first
Nothing — the character is still the same
Only its colour changes, so re-check it
questions.why: A light buoy of 8 M can't be your 20 M landfall mark: run the approach on other lights, radar and depth until it shows.
questions.ref: Offshore buoys and lightvessels — T&P notices

questions.q: Tomorrow's route crosses the area in this coastal warning. What do you do?

figure.title: Coastal navigational warning
lines: Area: four positions, in the warning

options: Wait for the range to call you on VHF
Cross it at full speed, keeping a lookout
Plot the area and route round it while firing
Nothing — warnings are for big ships
questions.why: A navigational warning defines its area by positions: plot it on the chart and keep out of it at the times given.

questions.q: You plan a first landfall on a foreign coast that your yachting almanac covers in one paragraph. Where do you find its look from seaward, its dangers, local rules and port details?

figure.title: Planning the landfall
lines: Almanac: one paragraph on this coast
Need: the view from seaward, dangers,

options: The List of Lights and Fog Signals
The List of Radio Signals
The weekly Notices to Mariners
The Admiralty Sailing Directions
questions.why: Sailing Directions describe the coast, its dangers, regulations and ports in detail, for all shipping.

questions.q: At night you time the light on your landfall headland, and it does not match the chart. What do you do?

figure.title: Light on the headland
lines: Aboard: List of Lights, corrected weekly

options: Check the corrected List of Lights
Take it for another light and stand off
Trust the chart — lights rarely change
Take it as a fault and report it
questions.why: Lights do change; the List of Lights, kept up by the NtMs, is the latest record — then correct the chart too.

questions.q: For a passage to a coast beyond your almanac's area you need the NAVTEX stations and their times and the coast stations' weather schedules. Which publication do you open?

figure.title: Beyond the almanac
lines: Destination coast: not in your almanac

options: The Admiralty Sailing Directions
The List of Radio Signals
The List of Lights and Fog Signals
The routeing chart for the month
questions.why: The List of Radio Signals covers radio stations, NAVTEX, safety and weather broadcasts worldwide, corrected weekly.
questions.ref: Nautical publications — List of Radio Signals

questions.q: Your almanac is the main publication aboard for this passage. How do you bring it up to date?

figure.title: Your almanac
lines: Now: July, before a 130 M passage

options: No need — an almanac is valid all year
Buy next year's edition when it appears
Apply the publisher's supplements, check NtMs
Rely on the plotter's chart updates
questions.why: An almanac is fixed at printing: its publisher issues corrections, and the charts and lights it lists change by NtM.

questions.q: Your NAVTEX was off while you were in harbour. How do you know the navigational warnings for your route before you sail?

figure.title: Before an overnight passage
lines: NAVTEX off for two days in harbour
Route: 140 M, open sea and a TSS

options: Wait for them to be repeated on Ch 16
Read last week's Notices to Mariners only
Check the plotter's latest chart update
Read the NAVAREA and coastal warnings in force
questions.why: Navigational warnings stay in force until cancelled, and the lists in force are published: read them before you go.

questions.q: Planning an offshore passage for next May, you want the month's gale frequency, wind roses and mean currents for the sea area. What do you consult?

figure.title: Planning for May
lines: Need for the month: gale frequency,

options: The routeing chart for May
The tidal stream atlas
The weekly Notices to Mariners
The List of Radio Signals
questions.why: Routeing charts give each month's winds, currents, gale and fog frequency, ice limits and the usual routes.

questions.q: Off the headland the tidal stream atlas page shows this arrow. What rate do you use today?
options: 2.3 kn
0.8 kn
8 kn
1.5 kn
questions.why: Atlas figures are the neap and spring rates in tenths of a knot: 08,15 is 0.8 kn at neaps, 1.5 kn at springs.

questions.q: This preliminary notice covers an area your route crosses in July. What do you do?

figure.title: Weekly NtMs, (P) notice
lines: Area: four positions; to be marked
by cardinal buoys when work starts

options: Wait for a new edition to show it
Ignore it until the buoys are charted
Pencil it in and route round the area
Cross it — 'preliminary' means not yet real
questions.why: A (P) notice gives early warning of work or change: pencil it on the chart now and plan round the area.
questions.ref: Notices to Mariners — keeping charts corrected — T&P

questions.q: Your plotter and your paper chart disagree on the fairway buoy's position. Which do you believe, and what do you do?

figure.title: Approach, the evening before
lines: Paper chart: last corrected in March

options: Neither — wait to see the buoy at dawn
The midpoint between the two positions
The paper — only paper charts are official
The ENC — then bring the paper up to date
questions.why: The freshly updated ENC likely carries a notice the paper lacks: find the NtM and correct the chart before you rely on either.
questions.ref: Notices to Mariners — keeping charts corrected

questions.q: You want the plotter to warn you before you stray into shallow water. Which chart must it be using?

figure.title: Plotter, chart menu
lines: Chart 1: RNC, a scanned paper chart
Chart 2: ENC, vector cells, same area

options: The ENC — it holds depths as data
The RNC — it is the exact paper chart
Either — both carry the same depths
The RNC, zoomed to its largest scale
questions.why: An RNC is a picture: the plotter can't read its depths. Only an ENC's vector depth data can drive a safety-contour alarm.

questions.q: On the ENC with these settings, which spot soundings are drawn bold as a danger to you?
options: 3 and 4.8 m only
3, 4.8 and 5 m
None — the contour does that job
questions.why: Soundings equal to or shallower than the safety depth show bold; the safety contour is a separate line.
questions.ref: Electronic charts — ENC and RNC — safety depth

questions.q: You set the plotter's look-ahead (anti-grounding) zone for tonight's run at cruising speed. What distance do you enter?

figure.title: Motor yacht, night passage
lines: Look-ahead is set as a distance

questions.why: 22 kn × 10/60 h = 3.7 M. Ten minutes is 0.167 h, not 0.1 h.
questions.ref: Electronic charts — ENC and RNC — look-ahead

questions.q: The plotter's route check has passed your route. What do you do before relying on it?

figure.title: Route check: no dangers found
lines: Cross-stream on leg 4: set up to 0.4 M

options: Nothing — the check has passed the route
Trust it — the rock is three corridors away
Move leg 4 another 0.05 M off the rock
Re-run it with a corridor as wide as your likely set
questions.why: A route check looks only inside its corridor: at 0.05 M it misses a rock 0.15 M off, well within the 0.4 M you may be set.
questions.ref: Electronic charts — ENC and RNC — route check

questions.q: Your mate keeps the paper plot like this on a 130 M night passage. What is wrong with it?

figure.title: Paper plot at 2300
lines: Hourly positions copied from the plotter
No DR, no bearings, no depths logged
One GPS antenna feeds plotter and AIS

options: It is no check — a GPS error is copied too
Nothing — the plotter is more exact anyway
The positions should be inked to last
It needs fixes every half hour, not hourly
questions.why: A paper backup must be independent: log course and distance for a DR, and cross-check the GPS by bearings, depth or radar.
questions.ref: Electronic charts — ENC and RNC — the paper backup

questions.q: Checking the plotter before a 120 M crossing, you find this. What do you do?

figure.title: ENC on your plotter
lines: Not bought: approach and harbour cells
At the landfall the screen shows 'overscale'

options: Switch on the satellite-photo overlay
Get the approach and harbour cells before sailing
Nothing — zoom in on the coastal cell
Nothing — the coastal cell has the same detail
questions.why: Each usage band carries the detail for its scale; a coastal cell blown up to harbour scale lacks the shoals and marks you need.
questions.ref: Electronic charts — ENC and RNC — usage bands

questions.q: Before a three-day passage you check the chart-table kit and find this. What do you do before sailing?

figure.title: Chart-table kit check
lines: Dividers: the span closes as you walk them
Breton plotter: left in the sun, now bowed

options: Keep both — re-check each course on the rose
Keep both — a GPS fix will catch the error
Tighten the dividers; replace the bowed plotter
Oil the dividers; press the plotter flat
questions.why: A creeping span falsifies every distance, a bowed plotter every course: fix or replace them in harbour.

questions.q: Your mate lays off tonight's 60 M leg with the plotter's grid squared to the chart table's edge instead of a meridian. How far from the leg's end could the boat arrive?

figure.title: Laying off the 60 M leg
lines: Plotter grid lined up on the table edge
The chart lies 3° askew on the table

questions.why: A 3° course error over 60 M: 60 × tan 3° = 3.1 M off. Line the grid up on a meridian or parallel of the chart itself.

questions.q: The new chart folio for a 140 M passage has arrived from the chart agent with this stamp. What do you do before sailing?
options: Apply Weeks 19–27 to each chart and log them
Nothing — the agent has corrected them
Correct only the two landfall charts
Apply only this week's notices to each
questions.why: The stamp dates the last correction: every later weekly notice for each chart must be applied and entered in its log.
questions.ref: Notices to Mariners — keeping charts corrected

questions.q: Checking the folio against the latest cumulative list of notices, you find this for your landfall chart. What do you do?

figure.title: Cumulative list, this month
lines: Your copy: 2019 edition, all NMs applied

options: Apply the New Edition notice as a correction
Replace it — no notice brings an old edition up
Keep it — every notice has been applied
Keep it, and note the new edition's date
questions.why: A New Edition carries changes never issued as notices and cancels the old one: buy the new chart.
questions.ref: Notices to Mariners — keeping charts corrected — new editions

questions.q: Preparing the passage chart, you find three temporary notices pencilled on it and check them against this month's list in force. What do you do?
options: Keep all three until a new edition
Ink in all three as permanent changes
Rub out 1104 and 0388; keep 2012
Rub them all out — T notices last a year
questions.why: A T notice stands until it is cancelled: the list in force shows which still apply; rub out the rest.
questions.ref: Notices to Mariners — keeping charts corrected — T&P notices

questions.q: Besides the charts, you carry these publications for the passage. How do you keep them up to date?

figure.title: Publications aboard
lines: List of Lights and Fog Signals
Charts: corrected from the weekly NMs

options: From the almanac's supplements only
No need — they change only with a new edition
Buy new editions at the start of each season
From the same weekly NMs — their later sections
questions.why: The weekly Notices to Mariners carry corrections to Sailing Directions, Lights and Radio Signals as well as charts.
questions.ref: Notices to Mariners — keeping charts corrected

questions.q: Your landfall is covered only by this cell, and you have zoomed in on a rock 300 m off your planned track. How far from where the screen draws it may the rock really lie?

figure.title: ENC at the landfall
lines: Drawing accuracy: about 0.5 mm at that scale

options: Up to about 175 m — 300 m is too close
Up to about 10 m — 300 m is ample
Up to about 1,750 m — 300 m is too close
Up to about 18 m — 300 m is ample
questions.why: The error follows the source scale, not the zoom: 0.5 mm × 350,000 = 175 m. Zooming in only magnifies it.
questions.ref: Electronic charts — ENC and RNC — over-zoom

questions.q: At 32 kn at night your mate has zoomed the plotter right in for detail, with the boat at the screen's bottom edge. How much warning does the screen give of what lies ahead?

figure.title: Fast motor yacht, night
lines: Zoomed in: 0.8 M from the boat to the top
Boat icon at the bottom edge

options: 40 min
1.5 min
0.9 min
2.5 min
questions.why: 0.8 ÷ 32 = 0.025 h = 1.5 min (90 s). At speed, zoom out until the screen shows several minutes ahead.
questions.ref: Electronic charts — ENC and RNC — zoom at speed

questions.q: You work the first leg of the Biscay crossing by Mercator sailing with the meridional parts from the tables. What course and distance do you lay off?
On the Ionian crossing you run this course and distance overnight. By mid-latitude sailing, what is your EP at dawn?
questions.ref: Charts — latitude and longitude — mid-latitude sailing

questions.q: At 0400, eight hours after your last fix, the EP on the passage chart sits 4 mm outside the 20 m contour of an offshore bank. How far off is that, and what do you make of it?

figure.title: Passage chart, 0400
lines: Natural scale 1:500,000 at the bank's latitude
EP 4 mm outside the bank's 20 m contour
Last fix 2000; DR and EP since

options: About 1.1 M — less than the EP's likely error
About 0.1 M — alter away at once
About 10.8 M — plenty of sea room
About 2.0 M — a safe margin offshore
questions.why: 4 mm × 500,000 = 2,000 m = 1.1 M. Eight hours of DR can be out by more than that: give the bank a wider berth.
questions.ref: Charts — scale and the chart folio — small-scale chart error

questions.q: Your crew transferred the great circle for this 300 M delivery leg from the gnomonic chart to the Mercator. At mid-leg, how far is it from the rhumb line, and what does it save?
options: About 3.9 M north of it; saves about 3.9 M
About 3.9 M north of it; saves about 0.1 M
About 0.1 M north of it; saves about 3.9 M
About 3.9 M south of it; saves about 0.1 M
questions.why: Vertex: tan lat = tan 49.67° ÷ cos 3.86° → 49°43.9'N, 3.9 M north; the great circle is 299.9 M vs 300.0. Not worth it.
questions.ref: Charts — gnomonic charts and great circles

questions.q: You set the safety contour for tonight's run on your 2.4 m draught motor yacht by the rule on this card. Which line does the plotter then draw bold?

figure.title: Safety contour, tonight
lines: Draught 2.4 m; squat and trim at 20 kn 0.5 m
Swell 2.0 m: allow half its height

options: A new line drawn at 4.9 m
The 2 m contour — the nearest one
The 10 m contour — the next deeper one
A new line drawn at 3.4 m
questions.why: 2.4 + 0.5 + 1.0 + 1.0 = 4.9 m. The plotter can bold only a contour the cell holds: the next deeper, 10 m.
questions.ref: Electronic charts — ENC and RNC — safety contour

questions.q: Closing the coast at night, you pass from the general cell into the approach cell, and the bold safety contour suddenly jumps 2 M closer to the shore. Why?
options: The tide has risen since you set it
The plotter has lost its depth settings
The approach cell's depths are in feet
It now bolds the 5 m line — this cell has one
questions.why: The bold line is the cell's shallowest contour at or deeper than your setting: 10 m in the general cell, 5 m in the approach cell.
questions.ref: Electronic charts — ENC and RNC — safety contour

questions.q: On a night passage the crew complains that the plotter's grounding alarm keeps sounding in open water and asks you to switch it off. You check the settings. What do you do?
options: Set the contour for your draught; keep the alarm on
Leave it as it is and keep acknowledging
Turn the volume down so the saloon can sleep
Switch it off for the night — it is a nuisance
questions.why: A factory 30 m contour cries wolf until nobody listens. Set it from draught and margin, so the alarm means something.
questions.ref: Electronic charts — ENC and RNC — alarms

questions.q: The plotter's route check for tomorrow's 130 M passage reports this. What do you make of leg 3?

figure.title: Route check: no dangers found
lines: Leg 3: crosses an area with no cell —

options: Clear — a blank area is open, deep water
Unchecked — check it on the paper chart
Clear — the route check has passed it
Clear — but re-run it with a wider corridor
questions.why: A route check can only test the data it has: where no cell is loaded it finds nothing, so it reports nothing.
questions.ref: Electronic charts — ENC and RNC — alarms

questions.q: On autopilot at night, your watchkeeper wants to wait in the saloon and come up only if an alarm sounds. What do you tell him?

figure.title: Night watch, 18 kn on autopilot
lines: Plotter alarms on: grounding, XTE, AIS CPA

options: Fine — the alarms cover every danger out there
Fine — but he checks the screen every hour
No — keep the lookout on deck; alarms miss a lot
Fine, if he sets the radar guard zone wider
questions.why: Alarms miss unlit craft, fishing gear, boats without AIS and uncharted dangers: Rule 5 needs a lookout by sight and hearing.
questions.ref: Electronic charts — ENC and RNC — alarms

questions.q: You sit down to plan tomorrow's 130 M route on the plotter and find it set like this. What do you change first?

figure.title: Plotter display
lines: Spot soundings and some symbols hidden
Planning a 130 M route for tomorrow

options: Nothing — the basic display shows the dangers
Zoom in further to bring the soundings back
Switch on the satellite-photo overlay
Switch to the full display to plan and check
questions.why: A basic display hides soundings and objects to declutter the screen: plan and check a route with everything shown.
questions.ref: Electronic charts — ENC and RNC — display levels

questions.q: Mid-crossing, your route passes over this shoal, and the plotter shows it as an ordinary sounding with no danger symbol. Is it a danger to you at speed?

figure.title: Shoal on the route, 20 kn
lines: Least depth 3.8 m, in deep water
Safety contour set to 2.4 m (your draught)
Swell 2.6 m; squat and trim 0.5 m

options: Yes — about 2.5 m in the troughs; she needs 2.9 m
No — 2.5 m in the troughs clears 2.4 m
Yes — 1.2 m in the troughs, under 2.4 m
No — 1.4 m spare under the 2.4 m draught
questions.why: Troughs take half the swell: 3.8 − 1.3 = 2.5 m vs 2.4 + 0.5 = 2.9 m. Set at the draught, the contour flags no isolated danger.
questions.ref: Electronic charts — ENC and RNC — alarms — isolated dangers

questions.q: You check the folio for a Falmouth–Brest–La Coruña passage against the route in your plan. What is missing?

figure.title: Folio and route
lines: Brest; Biscay passage; La Coruña, Ferrol
Leg 2: leave Brest by the Raz de Sein,
then cross Biscay to La Coruña

options: Nothing — the Biscay chart covers the Raz
A large-scale chart of the Raz de Sein
Nothing — the plotter has the Raz in detail
A second copy of the Biscay passage chart
questions.why: A tidal race among rocks needs its own large-scale chart; a passage chart's scale is far too small for that pilotage.
questions.ref: Charts — scale and the chart folio — the passage folio

questions.q: At 0300 on the Ionian crossing your EP nears the edge of the Italian chart, and the Greek chart takes over. No land is in sight. How do you carry the plot across?

figure.title: Changing charts mid-crossing
lines: Both on WGS84; no lights in sight

options: Measure its distance from A's edge onto B
By bearing and distance from a coast light
Plot the EP on B by its latitude and longitude
Leave B blank until the next GPS fix
questions.why: Offshore, transfer by latitude and longitude: the charts differ in scale, so a distance off an edge does not carry.
questions.ref: Charts — scale and the chart folio — the passage folio

questions.q: Before a Falmouth–Brest–La Coruña passage you go through the navigational warnings in force. Whose NAVAREA warnings do you need?
options: NAVAREA II only — both ports lie in it
NAVAREA I only — you sail from the UK
NAVAREA II and III — France and Spain
NAVAREA I and II — the route crosses 48°27'N
questions.why: Falmouth lies in NAVAREA I; Brest and La Coruña, south of 48°27'N, in NAVAREA II. Check both lists in force.

questions.q: This NAVAREA III warning covers part of your Ionian crossing. You expect to cross the area at 1830 Greek summer time. What do you do?

figure.title: NAVAREA III warning
lines: Live firing; area as given in the text
Your ETA at the area: 1830 local (UTC+3)

options: 1530 UTC — inside the window; route round
1630 UTC — just after it; carry on
1830 UTC — after the firing; carry on
2130 UTC — long after it; carry on
questions.why: 1830 local − 3 h = 1530 UTC, inside 0700–1600 UTC. Warnings run in UTC: convert before you compare.

questions.q: Your NAVTEX prints this NAVAREA III warning while you are on passage. What do you do on the chart?

figure.title: NAVAREA III 0517/26
lines: 0489 (a rig tow) is pencilled on your chart

options: Keep 0489 too until you reach port
Rub out 0489; pencil in 0517 with its number
Ink 0517 in, as it is the latest
Note 0517 in the log, not on the chart
questions.why: Plot each warning in pencil with its number, to be rubbed out when cancelled: the chart shows what is in force.

questions.q: At 0230 in thick fog, crossing an oil and gas field, you hear this ahead. What is it, and what does it tell you?

figure.title: Fog, visibility 200 m
lines: Chart: gas field, platforms 4–8 M ahead

options: A lightvessel's horn, some 10 M off
A ship at anchor sounding her signal
A platform's fog signal — likely within 2 M
A safe-water buoy's horn — the fairway
questions.why: Offshore structures sound Mo(U), · · —, usually every 30 s and audible about 2 M: slow down and pass it on the radar.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — offshore installations — fog signals

questions.q: At night your route runs along the edge of this wind farm. Which lights mark its outline for you?

figure.note: Night · wind farm ahead · the yellows flash together

options: White Mo(U) lights on every tower
The red lights high up on the turbines
None — only the radar shows the farm
The yellow lights that flash together
questions.why: Corner and edge turbines carry synchronised flashing yellow lights; the red lights high up are for aircraft, not for you.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — offshore areas — wind farms — lights

questions.q: Your night track passes 0.2 M from this offshore buoy, and AIS shows a tanker heading for it. What do you do?

figure.note: Chart extract

options: Re-route well clear — a tanker moors, hoses float
Pass between the buoy and the tanker
Hold on — a big mark is easy to pass close
Hold on — 0.2 M is outside the 500 m area
questions.why: A single buoy mooring holds a loading tanker and floating hoses; 0.2 M is 370 m, inside the 500 m area: keep well off.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — offshore installations — single buoy moorings

questions.q: Your track crosses this charted symbol, and later you plan to anchor near it to wait for the stream. What do you do?

figure.note: Chart extract

options: Go round — a well flares gas at the surface
Cross it, but anchor well away from it
Anchor beside it — it gives a lee
Stop and report it to the coastguard
questions.why: A suspended wellhead stands on the seabed, here 14 m down: no danger to your keel, but anchors and nets snag on it.

questions.q: Your route crosses this wind farm, and your ETA at its edge is 2215. What do you do?

figure.title: Wind farm: the national rules
lines: Transit: vessels under 24 m, daylight only
No anchoring or fishing inside the farm

options: Go through slowly, with a radar watch
Go through, keeping 50 m off each turbine
Go round it — transit is by day only
Go through — you are under 24 m
questions.why: The farm's own rules govern here: a vessel under 24 m may transit only in daylight, so at 2215 you go round.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — offshore areas — wind farms — the rules

questions.q: Tonight your route runs between two rows of this wind farm. How wide is the clear lane, and what do you do?

figure.title: Wind farm under construction
lines: Safety zone: 500 m round each turbine

options: 1,200 m — ample room; go through
700 m — room enough with care; go through
1,700 m — wide open; go through
200 m — too narrow at night; go round
questions.why: Each row's zone takes 500 m of the 1,200 m gap: 1,200 − 2 × 500 = 200 m — about a cable, at night, with a cross-set.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — offshore areas — wind farms — the rules

questions.q: Fog closes in by day as you transit a wind farm, and your crew suggests anchoring between two turbines to wait. The chart shows the farm like this. What do you do?

figure.title: Chart: the wind farm
lines: Turbines in a grid, depths 20–25 m
Magenta cable lines between all turbines
Export cable to the shore from the south

options: Not here — cables run between the turbines
Anchor with a tripping line on the anchor
Anchor midway, where the cables lie deepest
Anchor next to a turbine, out of the traffic
questions.why: Inter-array cables link every turbine, and an anchor can foul or cut them: leave the farm or wait under way.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — offshore areas — wind farms

questions.q: Your passage plan must cross this deep-water route on the way out. How do you plan the crossing?

figure.title: Deep-water route on your route
lines: Bends 90° at a junction 6 M to the north
Deep-draught tankers use it day and night

options: At right angles, at the bend, to see both arms
At right angles, briskly, clear of the bend
Diagonally, at the bend, to save distance
Along it for a while, with the traffic
questions.why: Ships in a DW route can hardly alter: cross on a heading at right angles, quickly, away from the bend where they turn.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — traffic separation schemes — deep-water routes

questions.q: Tonight you are watching from the deck for this landfall light. At about what range do you expect to pick it up?

figure.title: Landfall light, tonight
lines: Luminous range diagram: 9 M · eye 3 m

options: About 22 M — the nominal range
About 16.1 M — the light's height alone
About 9 M — the luminous range
About 19.7 M — the geographical range
questions.why: Geographical 2.08 (√60 + √3) = 19.7 M, but tonight's haze lets the light carry only 9 M: you see it at the lesser.
questions.ref: Nautical publications — List of Lights — luminous and geographical range

questions.q: The foreign list of lights for your landfall gives this. From your cockpit, at what range should the light rise above the horizon?

figure.title: Foreign list of lights
lines: for a height of eye of 5 m

options: About 21.0 M
About 16.3 M
About 22.7 M
About 19.3 M
questions.why: Take out the list's 5 m eye and put in yours: 21 − 2.08 (√5 − √2) = 21 − 1.7 = 19.3 M.
questions.ref: Nautical publications — List of Lights — geographical range

questions.q: At 2330 on a clear night, with your EP 30 M off the cape, you see this where the light should be. What is it?

figure.title: Approaching the cape at night
lines: EP 30 M off; the light: range 23 M
A beam sweeps the sky above the horizon

options: Its loom — good for a rough bearing only
Another light, further along the coast
Lightning from a storm over the cape
The light itself — your EP must be wrong
questions.why: A powerful light's loom shows in the sky well beyond its range; the light itself rises later — fix on it then.

questions.q: Your plan for tonight keeps 5 M off this coast. You read this in the Sailing Directions' passage notes. What do you do?

figure.title: Sailing Directions, passage notes
lines: 'In W winds an indraught sets onto
this coast at up to 1.5 kn'
Chart: no current shown · Forecast W 6

options: Ignore it — the chart shows no current
Allow for it — more offing and frequent fixes
Ignore it — the tidal atlas covers it
Close the coast to get inside it
questions.why: Sailing Directions record what the chart cannot: an onshore set of 1.5 kn eats 5 M of offing in about 3 h.
questions.ref: Nautical publications — Sailing Directions — passage notes

questions.q: After the crossing you plan a 0300 arrival at a Greek Ionian anchorage. The chart shows clear water in the approach, but the pilot says this. What do you plan?

figure.title: Sailing Directions, Ionian coast
lines: Fish farms lie off many coasts and bays,
often unlit or poorly lit; positions change,
and they are not always charted

options: Trust the chart — it shows clear water
Follow the depth contour close inshore
Time the arrival for daylight
Go in at speed on the plotter's track
questions.why: Where the pilot warns of unlit, uncharted fish farms, a chart's clear water means little at night: arrive in daylight.
questions.ref: Nautical publications — Sailing Directions — passage notes

questions.q: Your log has been found to read high. How far through the water have you actually run since the 2000 fix?

figure.title: Log calibration
lines: Log run since the 2000 fix: 126.0 M

questions.why: True = log ÷ 1.05 = 126.0 ÷ 1.05 = 120.0 M. Multiplying by 1.05 applies the error the wrong way.
questions.ref: Distance, speed and time — the log

questions.q: You take this bearing of the landfall light with the hand-bearing compass. In which of its sectors does the boat lie?
options: Red — you are on 130°T
Obscured — you are on 310°T
White — you are on 127°T
White — you are on 124°T
questions.why: 127°M + 3°E = 130°T, inside R 128°–140°. Sector limits are true bearings from seaward, so convert first.
questions.ref: Charts — true, magnetic and compass — light sectors

questions.q: A NAVTEX warning gives a drifting container's position in decimal degrees. What do you plot on the chart?
questions.why: Minutes = decimal × 60: 0.2058° × 60 = 12.35'; 0.4625° × 60 = 27.75'. Decimals of a degree are not minutes.

questions.q: Tonight's track runs through this area to be avoided on the passage chart. Does it bind your 21 m yacht?

figure.title: On the passage chart
lines: Magenta pecked line: 'Area to be avoided'
Note: by ships over 400 GT and
by all tankers laden with oil

options: Yes — but only at night
No — such areas apply only in fog
No — its note names the ships it applies to
Yes — no vessel may enter such an area
questions.why: An area to be avoided binds the ships named in its note; a yacht under 400 GT may pass with care — read the note first.
questions.ref: Chart symbols — traffic separation schemes — areas to be avoided

questions.q: On the routeing chart for May you look at the wind rose for the square your passage crosses. What does the figure in its centre tell you?

figure.title: Routeing chart, May, one square
lines: Wind rose: arrows from eight points

options: The mean wind force there is 4
A 4 % chance of fog in that square
Four gales a month in that square
4 % calms, light airs and variables
questions.why: On routeing charts the figure in the rose's centre is the percentage of calms, light airs and variable winds.

questions.q: Range control has asked you to be out of the danger area by 1100. At what time do you cross its edge?
Your Falmouth–Brest route runs through the Ushant VTS area. The List of Radio Signals says this. What do you do?

figure.title: List of Radio Signals: Ushant VTS
lines: Mandatory reports: ships of 300 GT and over
All vessels: listening watch on Ch 13

options: Nothing — the VTS is only for ships
No report — keep a listening watch on Ch 13
Report on entry, as the ships do
Call the VTS on Ch 16 at the scheme
questions.why: The reporting rule binds ships of 300 GT and over; you still listen on the VTS channel and answer if called.
questions.ref: Nautical publications — List of Radio Signals

questions.q: Your mate has loaded the almanac's waypoints for the La Coruña approach straight into the plotter route. What do you do before using them?

figure.title: Route for the landfall
lines: Waypoints typed in from the almanac's list
Not yet checked on the chart

options: Nothing — almanac waypoints are checked
Check only the last one, at the entrance
Check each one on the chart, and the legs between
Nothing — the route check will do that
questions.why: A published waypoint can be mistyped, on another datum or across a danger: plot each one and check every leg.

questions.q: Your tablet backup shows an old raster chart of a remote anchorage on your route, and its title panel says this. What depth is the sounding over the shoal?
questions.why: 7₃ is 7 fathoms 3 feet: 7 × 1.83 + 3 × 0.30 = 13.7 m. It is neither metres nor feet.

questions.q: Off Brittany you use a French tidal stream atlas whose pages are referenced to HW Brest. It is now 1150. Which page do you open?
options: HW Brest +3
HW Dover −2
HW Brest +2
HW Dover −1
questions.why: 1150 − 0915 = 2 h 35 min after HW Brest: the nearest page is HW +3, each page serving half an hour either side.

questions.q: On a night passage across an oilfield you see these lights on a large structure ahead. What do the two red lights show you?

figure.note: Night · a large structure about 3 M ahead

options: Supply vessels moored at each side
The ends of the structure — pass outside them
A tug towing it — keep clear astern
Aircraft warning lights — ignore them
questions.why: Besides its main white Mo(U) light, a large platform shows red Mo(U) lights at its ends to mark its extent.

questions.q: Your passage chart's title panel gives its scale like this. Near La Coruña, how much ground does 1 mm on this chart cover?
options: About 363 m
About 500 m
About 532 m
About 470 m
questions.why: Mercator scale holds only at the stated latitude: 500,000 × cos 43.5° ÷ cos 47° = 1:531,800, so 1 mm ≈ 532 m.

questions.q: Crossing Biscay, you will reach the edge of the continental shelf tonight with this forecast. What does the Sailing Directions' note mean for your plan?

figure.title: Sailing Directions and forecast
lines: 'Steep, heavy seas build in SW gales where
the shelf rises from 4,000 m to 200 m'

options: Heave to on the edge until the gale passes
Nothing — 200 m is far too deep to matter
Run along the shelf edge to stay in deep water
Cross the shelf edge before the gale, at right angles
questions.why: Seas steepen where the depth shoals sharply: cross that zone early and quickly, not along it and not in the gale.
questions.ref: Nautical publications — Sailing Directions — passage notes

questions.q: You are taking over a 22 m motor yacht whose flybridge compass sits 1.2 m to starboard of the centreline. What must be true for it to read her heading?

figure.title: Flybridge steering compass
lines: Compass 1.2 m to starboard of the centreline
Lubber line: to be checked before sailing

options: Its lubber line is parallel to the fore-and-aft line
It is moved onto the centreline before you sail
A small offset is added to every heading read
Its lubber line points straight at the stem head
questions.why: A compass reads the heading anywhere aboard if its lubber line is parallel to the keel; aiming it at the bow from off-centre builds in an error.

questions.q: You find this in the steering compass at 0300, 60 M from land. What do you do?

figure.title: Steering compass, 0300
lines: Bubble about 2 cm across under the glass
Card sticks, then jumps, in a turn

options: Carry on — a bubble does not affect the card
Cross-check it with another compass; refill it ashore
Top up the bowl at sea with the fresh water aboard
Steer by the GNSS COG alone until you reach port
questions.why: A big bubble makes the card stick and jump; refill with the maker's fluid ashore, and check headings against another compass meanwhile.

questions.q: On a two-day beat you check the steering compass against the satellite compass, upright in harbour and now heeled at sea. What do you do for the rest of the beat?
options: Apply the 090°C error to every heading you steer
Steer by the hand-bearing compass from the cockpit
Use the deviation found heeled on this tack
Use the upright card — heel does not change deviation
questions.why: Heeling error comes from iron below the compass tilting with the boat: it is largest on N and S headings, so check the deviation heeled.

questions.q: You are fitting these at the new helm console, with the steering compass in the middle. Which must go furthest from the compass?
options: The radar display
The autopilot control head
The plotter display
The VHF loudspeaker
questions.why: Each maker states a compass safe distance; the loudspeaker's magnet needs the most, 1.4 m here.

questions.q: You make this alteration at night and read the steering compass for the log. When do you write down the new heading?
options: Once the card has settled on the new course
At once, while the card is still turning
Never — log the plotter's COG instead
After taking 20° off for the overshoot
questions.why: After a fast turn the damping liquid keeps swirling and drags the card; wait until it settles on the new course.

questions.q: Your Biscay crossing runs between these two compass roses on the passage chart. Which variation do you use halfway across?
questions.why: Update each rose: 12 years × 10'E = 2° less west, so 2°20'W and 0°20'W; halfway, 1°20'W.
questions.ref: Compass — variation and its annual change

questions.q: You are halfway across on this small-scale passage chart. Where do you take the variation from?

figure.title: Passage chart 1:1 000 000
lines: No compass rose on this sheet
Your position: midway, 70 M from land

options: The plotter's value for the departure port
The rose on the departure harbour's chart
The isogonic line at your position, updated
Nowhere — it is only shown near the coast
questions.why: Small-scale charts give variation as isogonic lines with a year and an annual change; read the one at your position and update it.

questions.q: You use this rose on an old Channel chart in 2026. Which variation do you apply?
questions.why: 15 years × 8'E = 2°00' less west: 1°45'W − 2°00' = 0°15'E — the variation has passed through zero.
questions.ref: Compass — variation and its annual change

questions.q: Forty miles offshore you check the steering compass with the sun's bearing over its shadow pin. What is its deviation on this heading?
questions.why: Sun 227°T + 3°W = 230°M; the compass reads 228°, 2° low, so deviation is 2°E (C + dev = M).
questions.ref: Compass — deviation by the sun's azimuth

questions.q: The compass swing before a 400 M passage gives this card. What do you do?

figure.title: Swing results, steering compass
lines: Passage next week, much of it at night

options: Sail on the card — 7° is fine if you apply it
Have a compass adjuster correct it with magnets
Steer by the GNSS COG and ignore the compass
Correct it yourself with the magnets at sea
questions.why: Deviation this large comes from the boat's own magnetism; an adjuster reduces it with corrector magnets, then swings again for a new card.

questions.q: These changes were made since last season's compass swing. Which one means the deviation card can no longer be trusted?

figure.title: Since the last swing
lines: A: new anchor chain, forepeak, 14 m away
C: helm rewired, new instruments by it

options: A — the new anchor chain in the forepeak
D — the new set of sails
C — the new wiring and instruments at the helm
B — the new antifouling on the hull
questions.why: Deviation comes from iron and current near the compass; new wiring and instruments beside it change it, so swing again.

questions.q: You take the sun's bearing over the steering compass between two tabled times. What deviation do you write down for this heading?
questions.why: At 1022 the azimuth is 140° + 12/20 × 5° = 143°T, 145°M; the compass reads 148°, 3° high: deviation 3°W.
questions.ref: Compass — deviation by the sun's azimuth

questions.q: On this passage the steering compass disagrees with the card after the alteration. What is the likely cause?

figure.title: 24 m steel motor yacht
lines: Compass 3° off the card for some hours
Calm, no heel; checked by sat compass
Variation from the chart for here

options: Retained magnetism from long on one heading
Variation changing along the passage
Heeling error on the new heading
A fault in the satellite compass
questions.why: Steel held long on one heading picks up magnetism that lingers for hours after a turn; recheck the deviation until it settles.

questions.q: You swing the compass in a slow circle off the coast, sighting this distant peak on each heading. What deviation do you find on 090°C?

figure.title: Swing on a distant peak
lines: Magnetic bearing of the peak unknown

questions.why: Deviation averages out round the circle: the mean of the eight bearings, 104°, is the magnetic bearing; 101° on 090°C reads 3° low — 3°E.
questions.ref: Compass — swinging on a distant mark

questions.q: You are fitting the autopilot's fluxgate sensor on a 22 m sailing yacht. Where do you put it?
options: At the masthead, far from all the iron below
In the engine room, where it is out of the way
Low, near the middle, away from iron and cables
On the stern arch, beside the radar scanner
questions.why: A fluxgate is magnetic and feels motion: mount it low near the centre of pitch and roll, clear of iron, motors and cables.

questions.q: You set up the radar overlay and MARPA like this, and the targets plot in the wrong places. What do you fix?
options: Set the plotter display to north-up
Slow down so that the COG steadies
Turn up the radar gain until they settle
Fit a heading sensor — COG is not the heading
questions.why: Overlay and MARPA need the boat's heading; COG is her track over the ground, here 25° off the bow in the cross-tide.

questions.q: The owner of this yacht wants one heading source for the autopilot, radar and AIS. Which do you fit?

figure.title: 24 m steel motor yacht
lines: Often at slow speed or stopped

options: A satellite compass on the radar arch
The plotter's GNSS COG output
A second magnetic compass on the mast
A fluxgate sensor inside the wheelhouse
questions.why: A satellite compass takes true heading from two GNSS antennas: no deviation from the steel, and it works when stopped.

questions.q: You are about to enter the area in this warning. Which heading can you still trust inside it?

figure.title: NAVAREA warning
lines: Radius 120 M round the position given

options: The autopilot's GNSS heading
The magnetic steering compass
The plotter's COG readout
The satellite compass
questions.why: Jamming knocks out every GNSS-based heading; the magnetic compass needs no signal and no power.

questions.q: You check the steering compass against the satellite compass on a steady heading. What is its deviation on this heading?

figure.note: Sat compass 210°T

questions.why: Satellite compass 210°T + 4°W = 214°M; the steering compass reads 217°, 3° high, so deviation is 3°W.

questions.q: Making a night landfall, this bearing of the light ahead is your only position line. What does it give you?
options: Nothing until a second light comes up
How far to go, not whether you are on track
A fix, once you add the log reading to it
Whether you are on track, not how far to go
questions.why: A bearing along your track checks the cross-track error only; distance to go needs a line that cuts across it.

questions.q: Northbound across the Bay, the sounder first finds the bottom at 190 m at 0420. Which part of your DR does this check?
options: The distance run — the edge lies across the track
Neither — depths this great are not charted
Both — a single sounding is a full fix
The cross-track error — the edge runs along it
questions.why: A contour is a position line; this one cuts your track at right angles, so it checks the distance run (log and along-track stream).

questions.q: Seventy miles off, over charted depths of 4,200 m, the sounder shows this at night. What is it?

figure.title: Sounder, 0130
lines: A soft, fuzzy trace at 380 m
It rises and falls slowly over the hour

options: The bottom — the chart is in fathoms
A deep scattering layer, not the seabed
A double echo of the real seabed
An uncharted bank — alter course at once
questions.why: At night plankton and fish form a layer a few hundred metres down that gives a soft, moving echo; it is not the bottom.

questions.q: The racon on the offshore light float shows like this on your radar. Which range do you plot?

figure.title: Racon on the radar
lines: Inner end of the flash: 16.0 M

options: 17.5 M — the outer end of the flash
16.8 M — the middle of the flash
16.0 M — the inner end of the flash
14.5 M — the inner end less its length
questions.why: A racon replies as soon as it is triggered: its code starts just beyond the float, so take the range to the inner end of the flash.

questions.q: These two lighthouses come in transit at dawn. How good is the transit as a position line?

figure.title: Transit at dawn
lines: In line when 15 M off the front one

options: Better than near in — the further, the finer
Useless — a transit needs daymarks, not lights
Exact — a transit has no error at any range
Weak — they barely open as you move off it
questions.why: A transit is sensitive only while you are within about three times the distance between the marks; here you are fifteen times it.

questions.q: Your radar is head-up and you read the lightvessel's bearing from it. Which true bearing do you plot?
questions.why: True heading 212° + 2°E − 3°W = 211°T; add the relative bearing 047°: 258°T.

questions.q: You take a radar bearing of this headland's edge for a fix. How do you correct it?

figure.title: Radar bearing of a headland
lines: EBL set on the echo's eastern edge
Land lies to the west of the edge

options: Move it 1° towards the sea
Move it 1° towards the land
Move it 2° towards the land
Leave it — EBL bearings are exact
questions.why: The beam paints an echo half a beamwidth wider each side, so a land edge shows 1° too far out to sea; correct towards the land.

questions.q: At 20 kn at night you want a three-light fix with the hand-bearing compass. In which order do you take the bearings?

figure.note: Night · three charted lights

options: B, A, then C
A, B, then C
A, C, then B
C, B, then A
questions.why: Take the lights ahead and astern first — their bearings change slowly — and B, nearest the beam, last; then note the time and log.

questions.q: You take a hand bearing of this light in these conditions. How do you get a bearing you can use?

figure.title: Hand bearing at night
lines: Light 12 M off, flashing every 5 s

options: Take the largest reading of the swing
Take the first reading when the card stops
Add 8° to the reading for the swing
Take several readings and use their mean
questions.why: In a seaway the card swings about the true bearing; several readings, averaged, give the best value.

questions.q: You can take only two of these bearings before the haze closes in. Which pair gives the best fix?
options: B and C
C and D
A and C
A and D
questions.why: B and C cut at 81°, nearest 90°; A and D are 178° apart — almost the same line, the worst cut of all.

questions.q: In this sea your hand-bearing compass can be 3° out. How far can the position line from this light be off?

figure.title: Bearing of a distant light
lines: Light 20 M off by the DR

questions.why: 1 in 60: 3° at 20 M is 20 × 3 ÷ 60 = 1.0 M either side of the line.

questions.q: Your fixes keep coming out like this. What is the likely cause?

figure.title: Three fixes, 2100–2140
lines: Each cocked hat 0.4 M, same size and side
Taken within a minute each time

options: Random errors — take the centre each time
The stream setting you between bearings
The same error in every bearing, such as deviation
One of the three lights wrongly identified
questions.why: A cocked hat that keeps its size and side although the marks are right points to a constant error; one correction to all three closes it.

questions.q: You work a running fix on one light from 2200 to 0100 in this stream. How do you transfer the 2200 position line?

figure.title: Running fix, 2200 to 0100
lines: Water track 250°T at 9.0 kn, no leeway

options: 27.8 M along 248°T
27.0 M along 250°T
25.4 M along 257°T
26.2 M along 252°T
questions.why: Water track 27.0 M on 250°T plus three hours of stream (010° 1.2, 030° 0.8, 200° 0.6) gives the ground run: 26.2 M on 252°T.

questions.q: You doubled the angle on the bow of this light from 22½° to 45°. How far off will you pass it abeam?

figure.title: Doubling the angle
lines: No stream, no leeway, course steady

questions.why: Doubling the angle: the distance off at 45° equals the run, 6.0 M; abeam it is the run × sin 45° = 4.2 M.
questions.ref: Position fixing — doubling the angle on the bow

questions.q: You took this four-point bearing with the stream dead astern. How far off the light are you now it is abeam?

figure.title: Four-point bearing
lines: 0212 light 45° on the port bow, log 31.4

questions.why: The distance abeam equals the run over the ground: log 3.8 M + 1.5 kn × 24 min (0.4 h) = 4.4 M.

questions.q: You take a four-point bearing of this light with the stream across your track. How far off are you when it is abeam?

figure.title: Four-point bearing, 0300–0330
lines: Light 45° on the bow, then abeam
Stream 2 kn, setting you towards the light

options: 5.0 M — the log run, as the rule says
4.0 M — the run less the 1.0 M set
Plot it — the rule fails in a cross-set
6.0 M — the run plus the 1.0 M set
questions.why: The four-point rule needs the stream along the track; a cross-set skews the triangle, so plot both bearings and the ground track.

questions.q: After this strike you need a fix at dawn. Which method does not rely on either compass?

figure.title: After a lightning strike, 0200
lines: Steering and hand compass differ by 20°
Three charted lighthouses in sight at dawn

options: A running fix on the nearest lighthouse
Three bearings with the hand-bearing compass
A radar range and EBL bearing of one light
Horizontal sextant angles between the three
questions.why: Two horizontal sextant angles between three charted marks fix you with no compass at all; every bearing needs a compass you trust.

questions.q: You want a radar fix off this oilfield. Which echo do you use?

figure.title: Radar, 0350
lines: Echo X, 11 M: charted production platform
Echo Y, 9 M: nothing charted there
NAVAREA: a drilling rig working in the area

options: X — a fixed platform at its charted position
Y — the nearer echo gives a better range
Y — it is named in the NAVAREA warning
Both, then average the two positions
questions.why: A production platform is fixed and charted; a drilling rig moves between sites, so its position is only as good as the latest warning.

questions.q: As these two lights come in transit you want a second position line. Which do you take?

figure.title: 0420: lights A and B in transit
lines: C: a hand bearing would cut it at 25°
A's radar range would cut it at 90°
Depths all round: a flat 70–75 m

options: None — the transit alone is a fix
The radar range of A
A sounding with the echo sounder
The hand bearing of C
questions.why: A's range cuts the transit at 90° and radar ranges are accurate; C's bearing cuts it at only 25°, and the depth tells nothing here.
questions.ref: Position fixing — transit and a second line

questions.q: You are on this bearing of the light; the sounder reads below its transducer. Where on the line are you?
options: D — at the 49 m sounding
A — at the 42 m sounding
B — at the 43 m sounding
C — at the 46 m sounding
questions.why: Charted depth = sounding 45.0 + transducer 1.0 − tide 3.0 = 43.0 m, so you are at B.
questions.ref: Position fixing — depth and a bearing

questions.q: You want an independent fix as you pass this wind farm. What do you use?

figure.title: Offshore wind farm
lines: Corner turbines lit and marked singly
AIS shows each turbine as a virtual aid
Radar: a dense block of echoes

options: A hand bearing of the nearest unlit turbine
The centre of the farm's block of radar echoes
The AIS turbine symbols round you on the plotter
Radar ranges of two charted corner turbines
questions.why: AIS targets are drawn relative to your own GNSS position, so they cannot check it; ranges of charted, lit corner turbines can.

questions.q: At night, 20–25 M off, you can see these lights. Which do you take bearings of?

figure.title: Lights in sight, 0130
lines: B: Aero Al Fl WG, 12 M inland
C: glow of a flare stack, uncharted

options: A and D — the two lighthouses
B and D — the brightest pair
B and C — the nearest to the track
A and C — they cut nearest 90°
questions.why: Use lights charted and kept for mariners; an aero light is not maintained for you, and a flare stack is not charted at all.

questions.q: You have these four positions for 0300, a few cables apart. Which do you trust most?

figure.title: Four fixes, 0300
lines: B: radar ranges of 2 cliffs, 8 M, cut 80°
C: running fix on one light, 3 h run

options: C — one light, so no misidentification
B — ranges of steep cliffs, cutting well
D — its HDOP is excellent
A — three lines beat any two
questions.why: Ranges of steep cliffs are accurate and cut at 80°; bearings at 20 M err 0.3 M a degree, a 3 h run piles up errors, and the depth rules out D.
questions.ref: Position fixing — which fix to trust

questions.q: You are watching for this light from the cockpit of a 22 m sailing yacht. At what distance do you expect it to rise?
questions.why: 2.08 × (√64 + √3.0) = 2.08 × (8 + 1.73) = 20.2 M, inside the 24 M nominal range, so it rises there.

questions.q: Closing this light, the flybridge watch saw it rise at 2310. When will it rise for the helmsman at the lower helm?

figure.title: Landfall light, 2310
lines: Light height 49 m; nominal range 25 M
Eye: flybridge 7 m, lower helm 3 m
Heading straight for it at 15 kn

questions.q: On this night the light rises much further off than the formula says. What do you make of the rising distance?

figure.title: Landfall, 0140
lines: Warm air over a cold sea, flat calm
Formula gives 20 M for your eye

options: Abnormal refraction — do not use it as a range
The charted height of the light is wrong
Use the formula's 20 M; it overrides radar
The radar range must be 6 M out
questions.why: Warm air over a cold sea bends light down and lets it be seen far beyond the computed range; rising ranges hold only in normal conditions.

questions.q: At 0240 these all agree on your position, but the depth does not. Why is their agreement no cross-check?

figure.title: 0240, 90 M offshore
lines: Plotter, AIS and DSC radio: same lat/long
Sounder 112 m; charted depth there 160 m
DR from 2200 puts you 6 M south

options: AIS and DSC are less accurate than the plotter
They all take their position from one GNSS receiver
The sounder cannot be trusted at these depths
The chart was surveyed by GNSS, so it must agree
questions.why: Plotter, AIS and DSC are fed by the same receiver: if it is wrong they are all wrong together. Check with depth, DR, radar or lights.

questions.q: Your GNSS behaves like this at 0315. What do you do?

figure.title: GNSS, 0315
lines: SOG reads 0.0 kn; the date shows 2019

options: Restart the receiver and use what it gives
Steer for the new position to check it
Go back to DR from the last good fix
Trust the plotter — it shows many satellites
questions.why: Jumps, a frozen speed and a wrong date point to spoofing; plot from the last good fix and fix by depth, radar and lights.

questions.q: You fix your position by three lights at 0300 on an offshore passage. What do you enter in the log?
options: Position and course — the time is on the plot
Time and lat/long — the plotter keeps the rest
The position and the watch leader's name
Time, position, how it was fixed and the log
questions.why: The log must let anyone rebuild the plot: the time, the position, how it was fixed and the log reading.

questions.q: This warning comes in at 0230. Which entry in your log do you restart the plot from?
options: 0130 — the last fix before the spoofing
0200 — the latest GNSS fix in the log
Now — the plotter's position at 0230
0000 — only a visual fix can be trusted
questions.why: GNSS fixes after 0145 are worthless; because the log records how each fix was made, you can see 0130 was the last good one.

questions.q: You plot your 0400 position from the 0300 fix, the log and the compass, allowing for the stream and leeway. How do you mark it and log it?
options: A short cross line, logged as a DR
A triangle, logged as an EP
A circle with a dot, logged as a fix
A square, logged as a waypoint
questions.why: A position from log, compass, stream and leeway is an estimated position: a triangle on the chart, 'EP' in the log.

questions.q: Before an Atlantic passage you swing the compass of your 24 m motor yacht against her satellite compass. Which deviation do you apply on the night course?
questions.why: M = T + 2°W: 138°M on 135°C is 3°E, 177°M on 180°C is 3°W; a third of the way, 150°C: 3°E − 2° = 1°E.
questions.ref: Compass — deviation card from a swing

questions.q: Your helmsman has steered 210°C since 0200 by the card from last month's swing. Which true heading do you use for the 0300 EP?
questions.why: Two-thirds of the way from 180°C to 225°C: 1°E − 4° = 3°W, so 207°M; + 2°E variation = 209°T.

questions.q: At midnight you take the helm on the flybridge after a day at the lower helm. Which deviation card do you use now?

figure.title: Two steering compasses
lines: Lower helm: card from the swing in May
Flybridge: its own card, same swing

options: The flybridge compass's own card
The lower helm's card — it is the master
The mean of the two cards
None — the flybridge compass needs none
questions.why: Each compass sits in its own spot among the iron and wiring, so each has its own deviation and its own card.

questions.q: Before a night passage the crew stow the tender as shown. What do you do before relying on the flybridge compass?

figure.title: Tender stowage tonight
lines: Steel-hulled tender with a 60 hp outboard
Card swung with the tender on the foredeck

options: Nothing — the card covers any stowage
Check its deviation again on the night course
Add the card's largest error to every course
Apply the lower helm's card to it instead
questions.why: A steel hull and an engine 2 m from the compass change its deviation; the card was made without them there, so check it again.

questions.q: You are taking two yachts out after the winter. Which compass must be swung again before the first offshore passage?

figure.title: After the winter
lines: A: GRP sloop, ashore, nothing changed aboard
B: steel motor yacht, 5 months in a shed
B: bow north all winter, hull welded

options: A — a GRP hull loses its card in winter
Neither — nothing near either compass moved
B — her hull's magnetism has changed
Both — every card expires in a year
questions.why: A steel hull long on one heading, and hammered or welded, takes on new permanent magnetism, so her deviation changes; GRP has none.

questions.q: The compass adjuster fits these to the binnacle of your steel motor yacht. What are they for?

figure.title: Fitted to the binnacle
lines: A soft-iron Flinders bar in front

options: To shield it from the radar's signal
To correct the heeling error alone
To steady the card in a seaway
To cancel the deviation from the steel hull
questions.why: The spheres and the Flinders bar offset the magnetism induced in the hull's soft iron; the magnets offset its permanent part.

questions.q: You need bearings of three lights for a fix from your steel motor yacht. What do you take them with?

figure.title: Steel motor yacht, 0130
lines: Hand-bearing compass: 6–15° out about the decks
Azimuth ring aboard for the steering compass

options: The steering compass, with its azimuth ring
The hand compass at the bow, clear of the bridge
The hand compass, adding 10° for the steel
The plotter, as bearings to the light symbols
questions.why: On steel the hand compass is deflected everywhere; the adjusted steering compass, with its card, gives bearings you can trust.
questions.ref: Compass — bearings on a steel yacht

questions.q: You have run the new fluxgate compass's calibration circles, then check it on a transit. What do you do?

figure.title: Fluxgate check on a charted transit
lines: Steering compass agrees with the transit

options: Use it as it is — fluxgates need no card
Set a 4° heading alignment offset
Move the sensor further from the steel
Run the calibration circles again
questions.why: The same error on every heading is the sensor's alignment, not magnetism; calibration cannot see it, so set the offset.

questions.q: At 25 kn the autopilot's fluxgate heading does this in every fast turn. What is happening?

figure.title: Fluxgate heading, fast turns
lines: Swings 15° past the new course in the turn
Settles about 10 s after she steadies
Steady course: agrees with the steering compass

options: Its deviation card is out of date
The variation changes as she turns
The turn swings its sensor off the level
The engines' current deflects it at speed
questions.why: In a fast turn the sensor's gimbal swings off level and picks up the field's vertical part; trust the heading once she is steady.
questions.ref: Electronic compass — heading error at speed

questions.q: The new satellite compass is wired to the autopilot. Which compass still needs a deviation card?
options: Neither — the plotter corrects both
The satellite compass
Both of the compasses
The magnetic steering compass
questions.why: A satellite compass measures true heading from GNSS signals and has no deviation; the magnetic compass still has its own.

questions.q: You take a range and an EBL bearing of the same headland for a fix. How far off could each position line be?
options: Arc ±0.05 M; EBL line ±0.3 M
Arc ±0.3 M; EBL line ±0.05 M
Arc ±0.05 M; EBL line ±1.5 M
Arc ±0.05 M; EBL line ±0.4 M
questions.why: Across the EBL line: 12 M × 1.5° ÷ 60 = 0.3 M, six times the range arc's 0.05 M — trust the range more.

questions.q: The radar ranges of the two islands cross at X and Y. Which is your position?

figure.note: Range arcs dashed · rough EBL ±5°

options: Midway between the two crossings
X — the rough bearing of A fits only X
Y — ranges beat a rough bearing
Either — two ranges always fix you
questions.why: From X, island A bears about 333°T; from Y it would bear 290°T. Even a rough EBL tells the two crossings apart.

questions.q: Between bearings of the same light at 2200 and 0000 you alter course at 2300. By what do you move the first position line?
options: 12.1 M along 070°T
13.2 M along 056°T
11.9 M along 086°T
12.0 M along 052°T
questions.why: Add both water legs and both hours of stream: 7.0 M 040° + 7.0 M 100° + 1.4 M 160° + 2.0 M 180° = 11.9 M on 086°T.

questions.q: You work this running fix on a single light. How far could the transferred line be out from the stream alone?

figure.title: Running fix, 2130 to 0000
lines: Bearings of one light, 2.5 h apart
Atlas rate here good to ±0.4 kn

questions.why: An error of 0.4 kn for 2.5 h moves the transferred line up to 1.0 M either way, and the fix with it.

questions.q: Closing the coast in the morning, you measure the vertical sextant angle of this lighthouse. How far off is it?

figure.title: Vertical sextant angle, 0710
lines: MHWS 4.6 m; height of tide now 1.6 m

questions.q: You check the sextant's index error, then take a vertical sextant angle of this light. How far off are you?

figure.title: Vertical sextant angle, 0640
lines: MHWS 4.4 m; height of tide 0.8 m
Sextant reads 0°42.0'; IE 3.0' on the arc

questions.why: IE on the arc is subtracted: 39.0'. Height now 88 + 3.6 = 91.6 m; 1.854 × 91.6 ÷ 39.0 = 4.4 M.

questions.q: You want a distance off this lighthouse by vertical sextant angle. Which angle do you measure?

figure.title: Lighthouse on a cliff top
lines: Cliff foot 3 M off, well inside your horizon

options: From the tower's foot up to its top
From the cliff top down to the shoreline
From the light down to the shoreline below it
From the light down to your sea horizon
