questions.why: The charted elevation runs from MHWS to the light, so measure from the light to the waterline at its foot, inside your horizon.

questions.q: You are closing the Brittany coast at low water springs, watching for this light from the flybridge. At what distance do you expect it to rise?

figure.title: Light list and almanac
lines: Light 38 m above MHWS, nominal 23 M
MHWS 12.2 m; height of tide now 2.2 m

questions.why: At low water the light stands 38 + (12.2 − 2.2) = 48 m up: 2.08 × (√48 + √4) = 18.6 M, inside its 23 M range.

questions.q: Your EP puts this light 31.0 M dead ahead at 0200. When do you tell the flybridge lookout to expect it?

figure.title: Landfall light, 0200
lines: Light 52 m above MHWS, nominal 24 M
MHWS 4.8 m; height of tide 1.6 m
Flybridge eye 5.0 m; 11 kn straight at it

questions.q: Northbound in fog over the shelf, you log these soundings every 2 M. Which track have you been on?

figure.note: Soundings every 2 M, from the south

options: None of them
Track B
Track C
Track A
questions.why: Only on B does the canyon fall on the third sounding: 142, 148, then 405 m, then back to 155 and 160 m.

questions.q: Out of sight of land, you have a line of soundings taken at equal distances along a steady course. How do you get a position from them?

figure.title: Line of soundings
lines: Passage chart of the shelf, tracing paper

options: Take the deepest one as a fix
Average them and find that depth on the chart
Draw them to scale on tracing paper, slide to fit
Plot each on the DR and take the mean
questions.why: Mark the soundings along a course line on tracing paper at the chart's scale, then slide it over the chart, course kept, until they match.

questions.q: You have this single bearing of the light and a good sounding. How much does the sounding add?
options: A fix — where the line meets the 84 m sounding
A second line cutting the bearing at 90°
A check of your distance off the light
Little — the depth hardly changes along the line
questions.why: The contours run along this bearing, so the depth is about 84 m all along it; a sounding helps only where contours cross the line.

questions.q: 60 M offshore at 0200 the GNSS status page shows this. How do you treat the position?
options: As unchecked — cross-check it by other means
As good — an HDOP of 1.6 is excellent
As wrong — go back to DR at once
As lost — switch the receiver off
questions.why: With RAIM unavailable the receiver cannot flag a faulty satellite; a good HDOP proves nothing, so check by radar, depth and DR.

questions.q: On your steel motor yacht these two fixes disagree by 0.8 M. Which do you work from?

figure.title: Fixes at 0300
lines: GNSS: agrees with radar ranges of two cliffs
Visual: hand bearings of three lights
Small cocked hat, 0.8 M from the others

options: Neither — wait for daylight to fix
GNSS and radar — the hand bearings were deflected
The mean of the two fixes
The visual fix — its cocked hat is small
questions.why: Hand bearings by a steel wheelhouse share one deflection: a neat cocked hat in the wrong place. Two independent sources agree.

questions.q: Your three-light fix lies 0.5 M from the GNSS position. What do you conclude?

figure.title: Fix check, 0230
lines: Lights 18–22 M off, cut 60° and more
Visual fix 0.5 M from the GNSS

options: One of the lights must be misidentified
The GNSS is 0.5 M out — plot the visual fix
They agree — within the visual fix's own error
Average them: the truth lies midway
questions.why: At 22 M, ±2° is ±0.7 M across each line, so a visual fix there is only good to about that; 0.5 M is no disagreement.

questions.q: Making a night landfall with these lights ahead, you close all of them at the same rate. Which do you expect to see first?

figure.title: Lights ahead · your eye 3 m
lines: A: 85 m, nominal 14 M · 28 M off
B: 25 m, nominal 25 M · 27 M off
C: 55 m, nominal 20 M · 30 M off
D: 12 m, nominal 10 M · 24 M off

options: Light B
Light D
Light A
Light C
questions.why: Each shows at the lesser of its nominal and geographic range: A 14, B 14.0, C 19.0, D 10 M. C needs 11 M more; the rest 13–14 M.

questions.q: Closing the coast at night, you see this light change from white to red at 0215. What does it give you?

figure.title: Sectored light, 0215
lines: Seen white, then red, as you head SE

options: A position line on the sector's charted edge
Nothing — sector colours give no position
A fix — the change marks a single point
Your distance off the light
questions.why: Where the colour changes you are on the sector edge, a line from the light on a charted bearing; good to a degree or so, not a fix.

questions.q: Watching for the landfall light from the cockpit, you see this. What does it tell you?

figure.title: Landfall, 0410
lines: Light seen only on the top of each swell
Characteristic matches the light you expect

options: The light is weak — report it
You are at about its rising range
Haze is thickening between you
You are inside its obscured sector
questions.why: A light that shows only from the wave crests is on your horizon: you are at its rising distance for your height of eye.

questions.q: Before a night landfall after 140 M, you write up a card for each light you expect. What goes on it?
options: Its range and the date of its last check
Its name, its colour and the chart number
Its characteristic, rising range and expected bearing
Its height, its tower and its fog signal
questions.why: The watch must know what to look for, when it should rise and where: the characteristic, the rising range and the bearing.

questions.q: 90 M offshore in open water, your mate wants to fix every 10 minutes all night. What do you tell him?

figure.title: Night watch, 0100
lines: 90 M from land, nearest hazard 40 M off

options: Once a watch, since GNSS is on
Only when the GNSS alarm sounds
Every 10 minutes, as near hazards
Hourly is enough here; keep the lookout
questions.why: With no hazard for 40 M an hourly fix and EP keep you safe; save frequent fixes for the coast, and the crew for the lookout.

questions.q: Your EP can be out by 10% of the distance run since the last fix. How often must you fix to keep to your rule past this bank?

figure.title: Passing a bank at night
lines: Rule: fix before the error reaches half the gap

options: Every 1 h 30 min
Every 1 h 50 min
Every 9 min
Every 3 h 00 min
questions.why: Half the gap is 1.8 M; at 10% that takes 18 M of running, which at 12 kn is 1.5 h — 1 h 30 min.

questions.q: Reading the night's log to restart the plot, which entry falls short of a proper fix record?
options: A — a fix by lights is logged as an EP
C — no method and no log reading
B — GNSS fixes are not logged
D — radar fixes go on the chart only
questions.why: A fix record needs the time, position, how it was fixed and the log; C gives no method to judge it and no log to run on from.

questions.q: At 0315 you get only one bearing of a light before it is lost in rain. How do you record it?
options: Log it as a fix where it cuts the DR track
Log it as an EP with the light's name
Plot the line with its time; log the bearing and log
Leave it out — one line is no position
questions.why: A single position line is worth keeping: draw it with the time, and log the bearing and the log reading so it can be run on later.
questions.ref: Recording fixes — a single position line

questions.q: Your only position line is this bearing of the light, and your EP lies off it. Where on the line do you put yourself?
options: Nowhere — stay on the EP till a fix
Where your course line crosses it
Where it reaches the light's range
At the point on it nearest the EP
questions.why: With one line and an EP, take the point on the line nearest the EP: the smallest shift that fits both.

questions.q: You note the log as this light comes 26½° and then 45° on the bow. How far off will you pass it abeam?

figure.title: Light on the bow, steady course

questions.why: For 26½° then 45° the distance abeam equals the run between them: 46.1 − 40.3 = 5.8 M.

questions.q: Your three-light fix at 0200 gives this cocked hat. What do you make of its size?
options: Too big — the compass must be swung
About what the bearing errors give at this range
Small enough to treat as a point
Too big — one light must be wrong
questions.why: ±2° at 20–24 M is ±0.7–0.8 M across each line, so a 1.2 M hat is normal; treat it as an area, clear of danger here.

questions.q: To save time, the crew offers to swing the compass against the plotter's COG on passage. Will that give a good card here?

figure.title: Swing by GNSS COG?
lines: Plan: slow circle, compass vs COG

options: Yes — round a full circle the current cancels
Yes — at 6 kn a 1 kn current hardly shows
No — the current can put COG 10° off the heading
No — COG is true and the card is magnetic
questions.why: A 1 kn current at 6 kn turns the track up to 10° (sin⁻¹ 1/6) off the heading; a card needs heading — a transit, the sun, a sat compass.

questions.q: You hold 245°T for 150 M across these isogonic lines, deviation nil on this heading. Which compass course do you give the helm?
options: 240°C at the start, 243°C at the end
247°C at the start, 250°C at the end
250°C for the whole crossing
250°C at the start, 247°C at the end
questions.why: 245°T + 5°W = 250°C at the start; + 2°W = 247°C at the end — ease the course a degree as each isogonic line is crossed.

questions.q: After 140 M on EP you sight a light ahead with the right characteristic, but off its expected bearing. Is it your light?

figure.title: Landfall, 0350
lines: EP could be 7 M out after 140 M

options: Likely — a 7 M error can swing it up to 20°
No — a 7 M error moves it 7° at most
No — the bearing should agree within 3°
No — 17° off puts you 17 M from the EP
questions.why: From 20 M off, a 7 M error in the EP can shift the light's bearing by up to sin⁻¹(7/20) ≈ 20°; 17° fits, so confirm it by timing it.

questions.q: 100 M offshore, beyond soundings and out of sight of lights, how do you check each hourly GNSS fix?

figure.title: Mid-Biscay, 0200
lines: Depth 4,500 m; no lights in sight
Log, compass and the stream known

options: There is no check — accept the GNSS
Against the EP worked from the last fix
Against the AIS position of a passing ship
Against a second reading of the same receiver
questions.why: Offshore the cross-check is the EP from the last fix by log, compass and stream; a gap that grows means find out why.

questions.q: On a clear night you check the steering compass on the Pole Star. What is the deviation on this heading?
questions.why: Polaris 359°T + 3°W = 002°M; the compass reads 004°, 2° high, so the deviation is 2°W.
questions.ref: Compass — deviation by the Pole Star

questions.q: Three lights are in sight for a hand-bearing fix as you run at 18 kn. Which do you take first, second and last?
options: C, A, then B
A, C, then B
A, B, then C
B, C, then A
questions.why: B is nearly ahead and C on the quarter: their bearings change slowly. A is nearly abeam and changes fastest, so take it last.

questions.q: You can take radar ranges of any two of these. Which pair gives the best fix?
options: A and C
A and D
A and B
B and D
questions.why: Range arcs cut at the same angle as the targets' bearings differ: A and C are 90° apart; A–D and B–D are near-reciprocal, A–B 15°.

questions.q: At 0100 you had only a radar range of an island; at 0230 you take a bearing of a light. How do you run the 0100 range on?

figure.title: Running fix with a range
lines: Ground track and run for 1.5 h known

options: Move the arc's nearest point along the track
Move the island by the run; redraw the arc
Add the run to the 8.0 M range
You cannot — wait for two lines at once
questions.why: A transferred circle keeps its radius: move its centre by the ground run since 0100 and draw the 8.0 M arc again from there.

questions.q: Closing the coast on this bearing of the light, you see nothing well after its rising time. Why?
options: Haze has cut its luminous range
The light is out — report it and carry on
You are inside its obscured sector
Its rising range is less than you worked out
questions.why: Light-list bearings are from seaward: on 238°T you are in the 210°–255° arc where the land hides it.

questions.q: Your noon sun check finds 4°W on 200°C, where the card says 1°W. What do you do with it?
options: Apply 3°W extra on every heading
Ignore it — an adjuster made the card
Average the two and use 2½°W
Log it and use 4°W on this heading for now
questions.why: A fresh check beats an old card on that heading: log it, use it and check again; a gap that stays means a new swing.

questions.q: Your helmsman wants to apply the deviation card to the COG on the plotter. What do you tell him?
options: The card is for the magnetic compass only
Apply it, then add the variation
Apply it only when the GNSS is weak
Apply it twice for the plotter's error
questions.why: COG comes from GNSS and has no deviation; the card corrects only the magnetic compass it was made for.

questions.q: The headland's echo lies between the 4 M and 6 M rings. How do you get its range for the fix?

figure.title: Radar, 6 M scale
lines: Headland echo between the 4 and 6 M rings

options: Estimate it by eye between the rings
Put the VRM on the echo and read it off
Take it as 5 M, midway between
Take the nearer ring, 4 M, to be safe
questions.why: Fixed rings give only a rough guide; the VRM set on the echo measures the range to the radar's full accuracy.

questions.q: You take radar ranges of two charted rocks. The arcs cross twice; which crossing is your position?

figure.title: Radar ranges, 0420
lines: Rock B lies 10.0 M due east of rock A
Range of A 6.0 M · range of B 8.0 M
Sounder 85 m: south of AB 80–90 m

options: 6.0 M from A on 037°T
8.0 M from A on 127°T
6.0 M from A on 143°T
6.0 M from A on 323°T
questions.why: A 6-8-10 triangle: the crossings lie 3.6 M east of A and 4.8 M either side of AB. The 85 m sounding picks the south one: 143°T from A.

questions.q: At 0100 you crossed the 200 m shelf edge; at 0300 a light bears 040°T. How do you run the 200 m line on for the fix?

figure.title: Contour and bearing, 0100–0300
lines: Water track 180°T at 8.0 kn, no leeway

options: 16.0 M along 180°T
16.0 M along 176°T
16.0 M along 182°T
16.0 M along 184°T
questions.why: A contour runs on like any position line: 16.0 M on 180° by log plus 1.0 M on 270° of stream = 16.0 M along 184°T.

questions.q: Your GNSS failed at 1800 halfway across Biscay. From the log book, where is the 0600 DR from the 1800 fix?
questions.why: 37.5 M on 210°T, then 52.5 M on 235°T, added as vectors: 87.9 M on 225°T. Not the mean course and the summed log.

questions.q: Crossing the western Channel southbound in your 24 m sloop, you work up the 0700 EP from the 0100 fix. Where do you plot it?
options: 151°T, 48.0 M from the fix
147°T, 49.9 M from the fix
155°T, 49.4 M from the fix
155°T, 46.3 M from the fix
questions.why: Water track 151°T (the W wind sets you east of the heading) for 48.0 M, then the six streams summed, 4.0 M toward 088°T: 147°T, 49.9 M.

questions.q: You are bound south off Portugal on a steady northerly. Where do you plot today's noon EP from yesterday's noon fix?

figure.title: Noon to noon
lines: Yesterday's noon fix 30 M W of Finisterre

questions.why: 24 h × 6.5 kn = 156.0 M on 205°T, then 24 h of current: 14.4 M toward 190°T. EP 204°T, 170.0 M.

questions.q: On a night passage your GNSS has failed and you are on EP. The track ahead passes a shoal. What do you do?

figure.title: Night, GNSS down since 1600
lines: Rule aboard: EP good to 10% of the run
Shoal 6 M to port of the planned track

options: Alter to clear it by 1 M more than planned
Hold on and sound all the way past it
Hold on: 6 M off the shoal is a safe margin
Alter to clear it by over 8.5 M until you fix
questions.why: 85 M since the fix × 10% = 8.5 M of doubt: a 6 M margin is not enough until you get a fix.
questions.ref: DR — error growth on a long passage

questions.q: Offshore in Biscay your passage chart is too small a scale to plot on, so you work the DR by calculation. What is the 0200 DR?
questions.why: d.lat = 140 cos 35° = 114.7' S; departure 140 sin 35° = 80.3 M W; ÷ cos 47°23' (mid-lat) = 118.6' of d.long W.

questions.q: Before a five-hour night leg you sum the streams at the diamond on your track. What net stream do you lay off?
questions.why: Five hourly vectors head to tail: 5.4 M west-going, less 0.7 M east-going in the last hour — 4.7 M toward 268°T.

questions.q: You cross for these four hours as the flood runs at the diamond. How far does the stream carry you along 055°T?

figure.title: Diamond C, flood 055°T
lines: Mean ranges: springs 5.6 m, neaps 2.6 m

questions.q: Your 22 m motor yacht cruises at 14 kn with a F5 wind on the beam. What leeway do you allow in the EP?
options: 5°, as for a sailing yacht on a reach
Half a sailing yacht's, about 3°
10°, for her high topsides and flybridge
None: under power she makes no leeway to allow
questions.why: A motor yacht under power is taken to make no leeway; any wind drift shows up when you fix.

questions.q: Offshore on a reach in deep water, you use the GNSS to find this large yacht's real leeway. What is it?

figure.title: Leeway check, deep water
lines: Heading 300°T · log 8.0 kn · wind NE F6

options: 5° to port: water track 295°T
5° to starboard: water track 305°T
19° to port: water track 281°T
12° to port: water track 288°T
questions.why: Water vector = ground less current: 288°T 7.6 kn minus 180°T 1.0 kn = 295°T 8.0 kn; heading 300°T, so 5° to port.

questions.q: After 12 hours on the wind you find the leeway in the EP was overstated. Where is the yacht against the EP?

figure.title: Leeway check
lines: Crew used 8°, from their 9 m yacht
Close-hauled, 90 M since the last fix

options: 4.5 M to windward of the EP
7.5 M to windward of the EP
12.0 M to windward of the EP
7.5 M to leeward of the EP
questions.why: 5° too much leeway over 90 M: 5 × 90 ÷ 60 = 7.5 M. She went less to leeward than plotted.

questions.q: Your 20 m motor yacht crosses at 10 kn and you want one course for the whole six hours. Which course do you steer?
questions.why: Streams summed: 6.1 M toward 091°T. One 6-hour triangle on 60 M of water track: aim off 6° up-tide, 009°T.
questions.ref: Course to steer — one course for the crossing

questions.q: You plan one heading for the whole 13-hour crossing in your 24 m sloop. Which heading do you give the helm?
questions.why: Net stream 2.4 M toward 279°T: water track 189°T. The W wind sets you east, so head 4° up into it: 193°T.
questions.ref: Course to steer — one course for the crossing

questions.q: You draw a five-hour course-to-steer triangle for an offshore crossing. What sets the radius of the arc you swing?
options: Log speed × 5 h: the distance through the water
Plotter SOG × 5 h: the distance over the ground
SOG less the stream × 5 h, net of the tide
Log speed × 1 h, as the triangle is hourly
questions.why: The arc is the water distance — boat speed through the water for the whole time; the stream is its own vector.
questions.ref: Course to steer — one course for the crossing

questions.q: On passage you compare two GNSS fixes with the log. What speed have you made good between the fixes?

figure.title: Fixes
lines: 1445 fix, 54.0 M on from the first
Log over the same time: 58.5 M

options: 7.8 kn
7.2 kn
7.4 kn
7.7 kn
questions.why: 0715 to 1445 is 7 h 30 = 7.5 h; 54.0 ÷ 7.5 = 7.2 kn over the ground. Not 7.30 h, not the log.

questions.q: It is noon on Tuesday. What have you made good towards the destination, and when do you arrive if it holds?

figure.title: Noon positions
lines: Mon noon: 312 M to go · log 2046
Tue noon: 168 M to go · log 2242
The two fixes are 152 M apart

options: 6.3 kn — Wednesday 1432
8.2 kn — Wednesday 0834
6.0 kn — Wednesday 1600
7.0 kn — Wednesday 1200
questions.why: Distance to go fell 144 M in 24 h: 6.0 kn towards it. 168 M ÷ 6.0 = 28 h: Wednesday 1600.

questions.q: You look back over the day's run along the coast. What speed have you made good over the whole run?
options: 7.0 kn
4.0 kn
5.5 kn
5.6 kn
questions.why: 62 M in 11 h = 5.6 kn. The mean of 7.0 and 4.0 ignores that the legs took different times.

questions.q: You head for the race, where the stream turns fair at 1330. Working the streams hour by hour, when do you reach its entrance?
questions.why: Hourly SOG 5.5, 6.2, 7.3, 8.2, 9.0, 9.6 kn: 45.8 M in 6 h; the last 0.2 M at 10 kn takes a minute — 1401.

questions.q: You must reach the race before its fair stream ends. What speed through the water must you hold?

figure.title: The gate
lines: Mean foul stream on the way: 1.2 kn

options: 7.6 kn
8.8 kn
9.1 kn
6.4 kn
questions.why: 1215 to 1745 is 5.5 h: 42.0 ÷ 5.5 = 7.6 kn over the ground, plus 1.2 kn of foul stream = 8.8 kn.

questions.q: A 90 M passage ends at a tidal gate with six hours of fair stream. When do you plan to arrive at the gate?
options: On the first estimate, with no margin
In its last hour, to carry the most fair tide
Early in the fair stream, with time in hand
At the turn to foul, when it is slack
questions.why: ETA errors grow over 90 M: arrive early and you can wait; arrive late and the foul stream costs you hours.

questions.q: On a 120 M leg you find the log over-reads like this. Where is the yacht against the DR along the track?

figure.title: Log calibration
lines: Measured run: true 4.0 M, log 4.2 M
Log since the last fix: 120.0 M

options: 5.7 M beyond the DR
6.0 M short of the DR
6.0 M beyond the DR
5.7 M short of the DR
questions.why: The log reads 1.05 for 1: true run 120 ÷ 1.05 = 114.3 M, 5.7 M short. 5% of 120 = 6.0 uses the wrong base.
questions.ref: DR — error growth on a long passage

questions.q: Your EP for a 20-hour crossing allowed the weaker current. Where is the yacht against the EP?
options: 6.0 M east of it
12.0 M east of it
0.3 M east of it
6.0 M west of it
questions.why: 0.3 kn too little current for 20 h: 0.3 × 20 = 6.0 M further east than the EP.
questions.ref: DR — error growth on a long passage

questions.q: Planning a 100 M crossing, you list what could go wrong. Which error could move your EP furthest by the far side?

figure.title: Errors on a 100 M crossing
lines: Stream rates may be 0.3 kn out (14 h)

options: The steering: up to 3.3 M
The stream: up to 4.2 M
The steering: up to 2.0 M
The log: up to 3.0 M
questions.why: Stream 0.3 kn × 14 h = 4.2 M; steering 2° × 100 ÷ 60 = 3.3 M; log 3% of 100 M = 3.0 M.
questions.ref: DR — error growth on a long passage

questions.q: Your 22 m steel motor yacht has two night legs to run. Which compass courses do you give the helm?
options: 087°C, then 255°C
077°C, then 253°C
077°C, then 261°C
070°C, then 253°C
questions.why: 082°M, deviation 5°E: 077°C. 258°M, deviation 3°W: 261°C. Each heading takes its own deviation.

questions.q: For the 0300 DR you need the true heading the helmsman held. Which do you lay off?
questions.why: Deviation at 157°C, between 4°E and 1°E, ≈ 3°E: 160°M; with 1°W variation, 159°T.

questions.q: You tack at 0400 onto the new heading. Which deviation do you use in the DR for the next leg?
options: 2°W, read from the card for 310°C
1°W, read from the card for 330°C
3°E, kept from the last tack
None: the compass was swung last year
questions.why: Deviation changes with the heading: after the tack read the card at 310°C, about 2°W between 300° and 330°.

questions.q: You have worked out the course to steer for the night. Which compass course do you write up for the helm?
questions.why: 244°T + 5°W = 249°M; the card gives about 3°W there, so add it again: 252°C.

questions.q: On the night watch you work up the 0300 EP from the 0200 position. Where do you plot it from there?
questions.why: 064°C + 2°E − 3°W = 063°T; wind on the port bow, water track 068°T for 8.4 M; add the stream: 077°T, 7.4 M.

questions.q: At 0300 the GNSS fix lies 1.8 M from the EP you worked from the 0200 fix. What do you do?

figure.title: Skipper's night orders
lines: Plot the GNSS fix each hour
Work the EP from the last fix as well
Log: time, log, heading, wind, barometer

options: Trust the EP and leave the fix off the chart
Trust the GNSS and stop working the EP
Plot the midpoint of the two and carry on
Call the skipper and find why they differ
questions.why: Over one hour they should agree closely; 1.8 M points to a GNSS, heading, log or stream error — find it now.

questions.q: The GNSS drops out at 0240 and you work an EP for that moment. Where is it from the 0200 fix?
questions.why: 5.6 M on 220°T by log, then 40 min of stream: 1.0 M toward 300°T. EP 230°T, 5.9 M.

questions.q: Your motor yacht has a 180 M passage ahead. What is the fastest speed on the curve that keeps the reserve?
options: 9 kn: uses 1100 l
15 kn: uses 2760 l
12 kn: uses 1800 l
18 kn: uses 3400 l
questions.why: Usable 4000 − 800 = 3200 l. 15 kn: 12 h × 230 = 2760 l, it fits; 18 kn: 10 h × 340 = 3400 l eats into the reserve.
questions.ref: Motor yacht — fuel, speed and range

questions.q: Into a steady foul current, which speed carries your motor yacht furthest over the ground, and how far?

figure.title: Range against the current
lines: Foul current 2.0 kn all the way

questions.why: 10 kn: 1500 ÷ 80 = 18.75 h at 8 kn over the ground = 150 M. 16 kn: 7.5 h at 14 kn = 105 M.
questions.ref: Motor yacht — fuel, speed and range

questions.q: Your owner must average over 15 kn but wants the least fuel used. Which speed do you run?
options: 24 kn: the fewest engine hours
8 kn: 4.0 l per mile
16 kn: the least fuel per hour
20 kn: 11.5 l per mile
questions.why: Per mile: 16 kn 12.8 l, 20 kn 11.5 l, 24 kn 12.5 l. Over the hump and on the plane, 20 kn burns least per mile.
questions.ref: Motor yacht — fuel, speed and range

questions.q: How far can your motor yacht go at 10 kn and still arrive with the reserve kept?
questions.ref: Motor yacht — fuel, speed and range

questions.q: Your destination lies dead to windward. Which way is faster towards it, and what do you make good?

figure.title: Into wind and sea
lines: Wind dead ahead F5, short head sea

options: Motor straight: 6.0 kn beats 3.2 kn
Motor-sail and tack: 7.0 kn made good
Motor-sail and tack: 7.4 kn made good
Motor-sail and tack: 8.5 kn made good
questions.why: Water track 34° off the wind (30° plus 4° leeway): 8.5 × cos 34° = 7.0 kn made good, better than 6.0.

questions.q: On this passage, about how much fuel does motor-sailing save over motoring alone?
options: About 84 l
About 192 l
About 90 l
About 102 l
questions.why: Motor-sailing: 96 ÷ 8.5 = 11.3 h × 9 = 102 l. Motoring: 12 h × 16 = 192 l. Saved: about 90 l.

questions.q: Bound west across the Seine Bay overnight, you time your arrival off Barfleur for the turn of the stream. When do you sail?

figure.title: Timing the point
lines: Off Barfleur at 1340, as it turns fair
Mean fair stream on the way 0.5 kn

questions.q: To make the gate you must pass the waypoint at 1500. Which course and speed through the water do you need?

figure.title: 1030: waypoint 32.0 M on 250°T
lines: Pass it at 1500 for the gate

options: 261°T at 7.3 kn
250°T at 7.1 kn
239°T at 7.2 kn
261°T at 7.6 kn
questions.why: Streams 1030–1500 sum to 6.5 M toward 159°T. Water vector = 32.0 M on 250°T less that = 32.8 M on 261°T, in 4.5 h: 7.3 kn.
questions.ref: Course to steer — a waypoint at a set time

questions.q: You must pass the waypoint on time to meet the gate beyond it. What speed through the water must you make?

figure.title: Against the stream
lines: Waypoint 27.0 M ahead, due in 3 h

options: 7.5 kn
9.0 kn
questions.why: 27.0 M over the ground plus 4.5 M of foul stream = 31.5 M through the water in 3 h: 10.5 kn.
questions.ref: Course to steer — a waypoint at a set time

questions.q: Your track was laid 2 M off this wind farm. At night you find yourself 1.5 M off the track towards it. What do you do?

figure.note: Sketch, not to scale

options: Head straight for B: it is the shortest way
Slow down and pass at this distance
Regain the track: it holds the planned margin
Hold the heading: 0.5 M off is enough
questions.why: The track was set for a 2 M margin; a new course for B from here keeps you nearer the farm. Get back on the line.

questions.q: With no stream offshore you find yourself off the track, as shown. How much do you alter to head straight for B?

figure.note: Sketch, not to scale

options: 4° to starboard
10° to port
6° to starboard
10° to starboard
questions.why: 1 in 60: 5 M over the 75 M run is 4° of track error; 5 M over the 50 M to go is 6° more to close: 10° in all.

questions.q: Far offshore on a night watch the plotter shows you off the track to a distant waypoint. What is the sound plan?

figure.title: Open sea
lines: No dangers anywhere near the track

options: Steer straight for the waypoint from here
Turn back at right angles onto the track
Hold the old heading: the error averages out
Steer 45° towards the track until on it
questions.why: In open water with nothing near the track, a new course from where you are is shortest; regaining the line gains nothing.

questions.q: You want to regain the planned track within the next 15 M. What do you do?

figure.title: Rejoining the track
lines: XTE 2.5 M to port of the track
Plan: back on the track within 15 M

options: 10° towards the track, and hold it
10° towards the track, back 10° on it
6° towards the track, back 6° on it
2.5° towards the track, back 2.5° on it
questions.why: 1 in 60: 2.5 M back over 15 M is 2.5 × 60 ÷ 15 = 10°. On the line, turn back 10° onto the track's course.

questions.q: To be sure which way to turn when you raise the coast, you aim off deliberately. How much do you alter from the direct course?

figure.title: Landfall plan
lines: Harbour 100 M ahead on a low coast
Arrive 5 M east of it, then run west

options: 3° to the west
5° to the east
3° to the east
20° to the east
questions.why: 1 in 60: 5 M off over 100 M is 5 × 60 ÷ 100 = 3°, to the side you want to be.

questions.q: At dawn a compass check shows an error you did not know about. How far off the intended track could it have put you?

figure.title: Compass check at dawn
lines: Steering compass 3° out on this heading
Run since the last fix: 140 M

questions.why: 1 in 60: 3° × 140 ÷ 60 = 7.0 M off the track — not a mile per degree.

questions.q: Offshore you compare the noon fix with the noon DR worked from the 0600 fix. What current set you over the six hours?

figure.title: Noon
lines: 0600 fix · DR worked on from it

questions.why: The fix is 6.0' S and 6.0' of longitude E of the DR (× cos 48.6° = 4.0 M): 7.2 M toward 147°T in 6 h = 1.2 kn.

questions.q: You want to use the gap between this fix and the EP as the current for the next six hours. What does the gap measure?

figure.title: 0400: fix against EP
lines: 0400 fix lies 3.2 M SE of the EP

options: The GNSS error: keep the EP, drop the fix
Every error since 2200, the current only in part
The current alone: apply it in full next leg
The leeway alone: double it on the next leg
questions.why: Fix minus EP sums all the errors — leeway, log, steering and stream. Use it with care, not as a measured current.

questions.q: Over three hours your fixes show you set off the water track. What current has been running?
options: Set 004°T, 1.5 kn
Set 272°T, 0.2 kn
Set 184°T, 1.5 kn
Set 184°T, 4.5 kn
questions.why: Current = ground vector − water vector: 21.0 M on 092°T less 21.6 M on 080°T = 4.5 M toward 184°T, over 3 h = 1.5 kn.

questions.q: A night squall made you run off for 40 minutes. Where is your 0300 DR from the 2200 fix?
You give the helmsman a compass course from the true course on the rose. Which compass course do you give?

figure.note: T → M → C

questions.why: True to compass: add west, subtract east. 080°T + 5°W = 085°M; − 3°E = 082°C.

questions.q: Your 22 m motor yacht crosses at 20 kn on one course. Which course do you steer?

figure.title: Fast crossing
lines: Streams over the 3 h: 5.4 M toward 270°T

questions.why: 3 h at 20 kn is 60 M of water track: aim off asin(5.4 ÷ 60) ≈ 5° up-tide, 005°T. Not 5.4 M against one hour's 20 M.
questions.ref: Course to steer — one course for the crossing

questions.q: Beating north-east overnight in your 24 m ketch, you work up the 0400 EP. Where is it from the 2200 fix?

figure.title: Night beat from the 2200 fix
lines: 0100 wind veers E: tack to 045°T · 7.0 kn

questions.why: Port tack: water track 096°T, 19.5 M. After the tack the leeway goes to port: 039°T, 21.0 M. Add 4.2 M toward 250°T: 066°T, 31.4 M.

questions.q: At the 0300 change of watch you see how the relief is working the EP after the tack. What do you tell them?

figure.title: 0300 handover
lines: Relief: still adds 6° to the heading

options: Leave it out: on a beat it cancels from tack to tack
Carry on: leeway is always added to the heading
Add 12° now to make up for the last tack's error
Take it off the heading now: the wind is on the other side
questions.why: Leeway is to leeward: added on port tack, subtracted on starboard. After a tack it changes side.

questions.q: Headed by a wind shift at 0230, the helmsman bears away on the same tack. Where do you plot the 0300 EP from the 0200 position?
questions.why: Water tracks 009°T for 3.6 M and 344°T for 3.4 M (leeway to port on starboard tack), plus 1.3 M toward 100°T: 008°T, 6.7 M.

questions.q: After tacking onto port at 0300 the helmsman steers this compass course. Which water track do you lay off for the next hour?
questions.why: Deviation at 128°C ≈ 4°W: 124°M; + 2°E = 126°T. Port tack, leeway to starboard: 133°T water track.

questions.q: A head sea slowed your 22 m motor yacht at 1700. Where is the 0800 DR, 24 hours after the last fix?

figure.title: 24 hours since the 0800 fix
lines: 1700: sea gets up, slowed to 11 kn
No current, no leeway under power

questions.why: 144 M on 245°T (9 h at 16 kn), then 165 M on 230°T (15 h at 11 kn), added as vectors: 237°T, 306.4 M.

questions.q: Your motor yacht runs fast until the forecast head sea arrives. When do you reach the destination?

figure.title: Motor yacht, 300 M passage
lines: Then a head sea: 10 kn the rest of the way

questions.q: You run fast first, then slow down to arrive with the reserve intact. How long can you run at 14 kn?

figure.title: 260 M passage
lines: Plan: fast first, then 9 kn to arrive

questions.why: 160x + 60 × (260 − 14x) ÷ 9 = 2600 gives x = 13 h: 182 M fast, then 78 M at 9 kn.
questions.ref: Motor yacht — fuel, speed and range

questions.q: Under storm jib and trysail in a NW gale you take a bearing of the wake. Which water track do you plot?
options: 251°T: leeway 9°
245°T: leeway 15°
248°T: leeway 12°
275°T: leeway 15°
questions.why: Wake 068°M astern: water track 248°M = 245°T with 3°W. The heading is 260°T, so 15° of leeway, to port.

questions.q: You lay hove-to through the worst of the night. Where is the 0600 EP from the 0000 fix?
questions.why: 6 M on 040°T forereaching, 9 M of drift toward 130°T and 3 M of current toward 090°T: 095°T, 13.8 M.

questions.q: On a moonless night in a gale you cannot see the wake to judge the leeway. What do you allow in the EP?

figure.title: 0200, gale
lines: Wind W F8, rough sea, no moon
Storm jib and trysail, close reach

options: Your usual 5°: storm sails are set flat and hard
Plotter COG less the heading, the current and all
None: under storm sails she makes no way to leeward
A generous 15° or more, and keep the sea room
questions.why: Leeway grows sharply in heavy weather with little sail; overstate it and widen the margin from the lee shore.

questions.q: You run off before the storm towing a drogue. How far off the coast will you be at 0600?

figure.title: Running off under a drogue, 2100
lines: Coast 40.0 M to the NE, running NW–SE

questions.why: 31.5 M on 050°T toward the coast; the current's 5.4 M on 160°T takes 1.8 M off that: 29.7 M run, 10.3 M left.

questions.q: In light airs you motor-sail across at 5 kn, and in hour 2 the stream runs faster than you. Which one heading do you steer for the crossing?
questions.why: Net stream 3.5 M east over the 4 h; 20 M of water track: aim off asin(3.5 ÷ 20) ≈ 10° west, 350°T. One hour's stream needs no answer alone.
questions.ref: Course to steer — one course for the crossing

questions.q: The wind will ease halfway, so you plan 7 kn then 5 kn under engine. Which heading do you steer for the four hours?

figure.title: Four-hour leg, one heading
lines: Streams over the 4 h: 8.0 M toward 260°T
Wind easing: engine on at 1400 rpm

questions.why: Water distance 14 + 10 = 24 M; with 8.0 M of stream toward 260°T the triangle gives 359°T. 28 M (7 kn × 4) gives 356°T.
questions.ref: Course to steer — one course for the crossing

questions.q: Your yacht and the owner's motor yacht cross the same 48 M track together from 0800. Which heading does each steer?

figure.title: Track 000°T, 48 M, from 0800
lines: Yacht 6 kn: 8 h · motor yacht 24 kn: 2 h

options: Yacht 002°T · motor yacht 002°T
Yacht 358°T · motor yacht 005°T
Yacht 355°T · motor yacht 002°T
Yacht 002°T · motor yacht 355°T
questions.why: Yacht: 8 h of stream, net 1.5 M west: aim 2° east. Motor yacht: only h1–2, 4.5 M east: aim 5° west. Each takes its own hours.
questions.ref: Course to steer — one course for the crossing

questions.q: Your destination lies 120 M dead to windward and you will tack all the way. What do you make good, and when do you arrive?

figure.title: Beat offshore
lines: Tacking 42° off the true wind · leeway 5°

options: 5.1 kn — Wednesday 0528
5.5 kn — Wednesday 0353
5.6 kn — Wednesday 0332
7.5 kn — Tuesday 2200
questions.why: Water tracks 42° + 5° leeway = 47° off the wind: 7.5 × cos 47° = 5.1 kn. 120 M ÷ 5.1 = 23 h 28: Wednesday 0528.

questions.q: The wind is not quite on the nose of your destination. Which tack do you sail first, and what do you make good on it?

figure.title: Beat to a destination 010°T, 90 M
lines: Water tracks 50° each side of the wind

options: Port: 2.5 kn towards it
Starboard: 6.4 kn towards it
Starboard: 7.4 kn towards it
Either: 4.5 kn on average
questions.why: Starboard tack tracks 340°T, 30° off the course: 7.4 × cos 30° = 6.4 kn. Port tracks 080°T, 70° off: 2.5 kn. Take the making tack.

questions.q: Beating to a waypoint far upwind, you read the plotter. Which figure do you use for the ETA?

figure.title: Beating, 80 M to the waypoint
lines: Plotter: SOG 7.4 kn · VMG to WPT 5.0 kn

options: SOG: 7.4 kn over the ground
The mean of SOG and VMG: 6.2 kn
VMG: 5.0 kn towards the waypoint
Log: 7.0 kn through the water
questions.why: Only the speed towards the waypoint closes the distance: 80 M at 5.0 kn VMG is 16 h, whatever the SOG along the tack.

questions.q: You cross the Channel overnight on one course to steer. When do you make your landfall, and is it light?
options: 0906, after sunrise
0840, after sunrise
0625, before sunrise
0824, after sunrise
questions.why: One triangle: the arc of 6.0 kn × T meets B when T = 10 h 24, with streams summed to that time: 0824. The first hour's SOG gives 0625.

questions.q: On your first night landfall on this coast, the ETA comes out before dawn. What do you do?
options: Slow down or heave to, and close the coast at first light
Close it on the plotter alone: the chart is good
Speed up to be in before the wind gets up
Hold on and feel your way in with the echo sounder
questions.why: A strange, unlit, rocky coast is no place to arrive in the dark: time the landfall for daylight.

questions.q: It is 2200 and you will be off the entrance far too early. What speed through the water do you slow to?

figure.title: 2200: entrance 35.0 M ahead
lines: Fair current 1.0 kn all the way

options: 5.1 kn
3.1 kn
3.3 kn
4.1 kn
questions.why: 2200 to 0630 is 8 h 30: 35.0 ÷ 8.5 = 4.1 kn over the ground, less the 1.0 kn fair current = 3.1 kn through the water.

questions.q: At noon you find the navigator applied the deviation the wrong way when setting the course yesterday. Where is the yacht?

figure.title: 24 h on one course
lines: 6.5 kn for 24 h · open sea, no current

options: 10.4 M south of the track
4.0 M north of the track
10.4 M north of the track
5.2 M north of the track
questions.why: Right was 271°C; 275°C steered gives 274°T, 4° to starboard. 1 in 60: 4° × 156 M ÷ 60 = 10.4 M north.
questions.ref: DR — error growth on a long passage

questions.q: At 0200 the skipper of your 24 m motor yacht moves from the flybridge to the lower helm. Which compass course do you give below?

figure.title: Changing helm stations, 0200
lines: Lower helm compass: dev 2°W on this heading

questions.why: Each compass has its own deviation: 214°C + 3°E = 217°M; below, 2°W deviation: 217° + 2° = 219°C.

questions.q: The autopilot steers by its fluxgate, which reads magnetic and was calibrated to no deviation. The rose shows the steering compass's deviation. Which heading do you set?

figure.note: Autopilot: °M

questions.why: True to magnetic: subtract east variation, 156°T − 3°E = 153°M. The steering compass's deviation is not the fluxgate's.

questions.q: You plan a 20-hour offshore leg on one course. Which compass course do you give the helm?
questions.why: 20 h of current, 10 M toward 160°T: water track 239°T; NW wind, leeway to port: head 243°T; + 5°W = 248°M; + 2°W dev = 250°C.
questions.ref: Course to steer — one course for the crossing

questions.q: The forecast gives a head sea for the whole leg. Which speed keeps your reserve, and what is left on arrival?

figure.title: Motor yacht, 160 M leg
lines: Tank 3000 l · keep 600 l in reserve
Flat water: 12 kn 130 l/h · 15 kn 210 l/h
Head sea: +30% fuel per hour, same speed

options: 15 kn: 760 l left
12 kn: 1267 l left
12 kn: 747 l left
15 kn: 88 l left
questions.why: Head sea: 130 × 1.3 = 169 l/h at 12 kn × 13.3 h = 2253 l; 747 l left keeps the 600 l. At 15 kn: 273 l/h × 10.7 h = 2912 l.
questions.ref: Motor yacht — fuel, speed and range

questions.q: Into this head sea your motor yacht makes only 11 kn at her usual 1800 rpm. Do you have the fuel to run the leg at those revs?

figure.title: Leg 132 M into a head sea
lines: 1800 rpm: 14 kn, 160 l/h in flat water
Head sea: 1800 rpm gives only 11 kn

options: Yes: it needs 1509 l of 1900 usable
Yes: it needs 1140 l of 1900 usable
Yes: it needs 1920 l of 2200 aboard
No: it needs 1920 l of 1900 usable
questions.why: The revs burn 160 l/h whatever the speed: 132 M ÷ 11 kn = 12 h × 160 = 1920 l, over the 1900 l above the reserve.
questions.ref: Motor yacht — fuel, speed and range

questions.q: A light breeze forward of the beam lets you set the main for a long calm-weather passage. How much further can you go motor-sailing?
options: About 94 M
About 392 M
About 151 M
About 245 M
questions.why: Motor-sailing: 280 ÷ 8 = 35 h × 7 kn = 245 M. Engine alone: 280 ÷ 13 = 21.5 h × 7 kn = 151 M. The gain: about 94 M.

questions.q: Your motor yacht must clear the gate before it closes. Which speed on the curve do you run, and what fuel does the leg take?

figure.title: 0800: gate 66.0 M ahead, closes 1500
lines: Mean foul stream on the way 1.0 kn

questions.why: 66 M in 7 h needs 9.4 kn over the ground, 10.4 kn through the water: run 12 kn. SOG 11 kn: 6 h × 110 l/h = 660 l.

questions.q: Your sister yacht, 30 M due east, must transfer an injured crew member to you and holds her course. Which course do you steer to meet her soonest?

figure.note: Sketch, not to scale

questions.why: Collision course: sin A = 6 × sin 90° ÷ 8, A = 49° off her bearing towards her course: 090° + 49° = 139°T. 127°T aims where she is in 3 h 45.
questions.ref: Course to steer — a rendezvous at sea

questions.q: Offshore, you have agreed to meet the crew boat at W at 0600 for a crew change. What do you steer, and at what speed through the water?

figure.title: 2330: meet the crew boat at W at 0600

options: 306°T at 7.4 kn
292°T at 5.8 kn
300°T at 6.5 kn
292°T at 5.6 kn
questions.why: Water vector = ground less current: 42.0 M on 300°T less 7.8 M toward 340°T = 36.4 M on 292°T, in 6 h 30: 5.6 kn.
questions.ref: Course to steer — a rendezvous at sea

questions.q: Port rules make your 24 m yacht take a pilot, who boards at the fairway buoy at 0800. When must you leave?

figure.title: Pilot boards at the fairway buoy, 0800
lines: Foul stream 1.5 kn all the way

questions.ref: Course to steer — a rendezvous at sea

questions.q: You must catch up with the sister yacht ahead to pass her a spare part. How long until you are alongside?

figure.title: Sister yacht 24.0 M ahead, same course
lines: Open sea, the same current for both

questions.why: Same course, so you close at 8.5 − 6.0 = 2.5 kn: 24.0 ÷ 2.5 = 9.6 h = 9 h 36.
questions.ref: Course to steer — a rendezvous at sea

questions.q: Your sister yacht radios her position for a night rendezvous. Which course and distance close her?

figure.title: Rendezvous by radio
lines: She lies hove-to, waiting for you

questions.why: d.lat 30.0' N; d.long 45.0' E × cos 46°25' = 31.0 M of departure: 046°T, 43.2 M. Not 45 M of d.long as miles.
questions.ref: Course to steer — a rendezvous at sea

questions.q: At night in the north-east-bound lane, the plotter shows you set towards the separation zone, with the bend ahead. What do you do?

figure.note: Night · XTE 0.6 M towards the zone · sketch

options: Reset the route so that the XTE reads zero
Hold the heading: 0.6 M is still inside the lane
Steer straight for the next waypoint from here
Regain the lane's track and follow it round the bend
questions.why: In a lane a new course to the waypoint cuts the corner through the separation zone; get back on the planned track.
questions.ref: Cross-track error — in a TSS lane

questions.q: The stream is setting you across the lane towards the separation zone. Which heading regains the lane's track within 3 M?

figure.title: NE-bound lane, 0300
lines: XTE 0.6 M to port, towards the zone

questions.why: Close 0.6 M in 3.0 M: ground track 045° + 11° = 056°T. Against 1.2 kn toward 315°T at 7.5 kn, head 9° more to starboard: 065°T.
questions.ref: Cross-track error — in a TSS lane

questions.q: In the lane, with a strong stream across it, you engage the autopilot's track mode on the route. What does it do?

figure.title: TSS lane, night
lines: Route leg runs down the lane centre

options: Switches itself off once the XTE grows
Heads up into the stream to hold the track line
Points the bow at the waypoint, stream or not
Holds the heading it had and lets her drift off
questions.why: Track mode steers to keep the XTE near zero, so it crabs into the stream; heading and COG differ.
questions.ref: Cross-track error — in a TSS lane

questions.q: You compare six hours of GNSS track with the log and the heading. What current has set you?

figure.title: Six hours, 0000–0600
lines: GNSS fix to fix: 51.0 M toward 228°T

options: Set 166°T, 1.8 kn
Set 351°T, 1.5 kn
Set 171°T, 1.5 kn
Set 171°T, 8.7 kn
questions.why: Water track 237°T (leeway 3° to port), 46.8 M. Ground 51.0 M on 228°T less that: 8.7 M toward 171°T in 6 h = 1.5 kn.

questions.q: Mid-ocean, the GNSS and the log disagree steadily along your heading for six hours. What can you conclude?

figure.title: Six steady hours
lines: Log last calibrated at the start of the season

options: A fair current of 1.0 kn, for certain
A GNSS error: trust the log instead
The log over-reads by 1.0 kn
A fair current, a log that under-reads, or both
questions.why: A difference along the heading can be current or log error; you can't split them without a log check or a cross-track sign.

questions.q: You stop the engines of your motor yacht to change a fuel filter in a flat calm. What current is running?

figure.title: Engines stopped 0300–0340
lines: Flat calm, no wind on the hull

questions.why: Stopped in a calm, the drift is the current: 0.9 M in 40 min = 0.9 ÷ 0.67 h = 1.4 kn toward 075°T.

questions.q: After 15 hours the current turns out to have run in a different direction from the one in your EP. Where is the yacht against the EP?
options: 6.0 M W of it
6.2 M WNW of it
12.0 M W of it
6.2 M ESE of it
questions.why: Real minus used: 12 M on 210°T less 12 M on 180°T = 6.2 M toward 285°T. The same rate still moves you 2 × 12 × sin 15°.
questions.ref: DR — error growth on a long passage

questions.q: You crossed on one course worked from the spring rates, but today is neaps. If all else is right, where do you end up?

figure.title: Crossing to B, 8 h, one heading
lines: Today is neaps: rates 55% of springs
No leeway, log and steering good

options: 5.3 M west of B
4.3 M east of B
4.3 M west of B
9.6 M west of B
questions.why: You aimed off for 9.6 M of east-going stream; neaps gave only 55%, 5.3 M. The other 4.3 M of aim-off leaves you west, up-tide.
questions.ref: DR — error growth on a long passage

questions.q: Your ETA is worked from the log speed, but the log was found to under-read. When do you really arrive, if the speed holds?

figure.title: Log check on a measured run

questions.ref: DR — error growth on a long passage

questions.q: After 144 M of open sea your EP will be rough, so you plan to hit the low coast well north of the harbour. What do you lay off from the direct line?

figure.title: Landfall plan
lines: Harbour 144 M ahead on a low coast
EP doubt ±6 M across the track
Plan: strike the coast 9 M north of it

options: 4° to the north
4° to the south
9° to the north
3° to the north
questions.why: 1 in 60: 9 M off over 144 M is 9 × 60 ÷ 144 ≈ 4°, to the side you chose. The 6 M of doubt alone gives too little.

questions.q: You want to strike the coast 6 M north of the harbour, with this current across your track all the way. Which heading do you steer?

figure.note: Sketch, not to scale

questions.why: The current sets you 12 M north in 20 h; you want only 6 M: 6 M to cancel, 6 × 60 ÷ 120 = 3° south of 090°T, 093°T.

questions.q: Your passage runs well outside the area of the tidal stream atlas. What stream data do you use out there?

figure.title: 120 M west of the shelf edge
lines: The tidal stream atlas ends 40 M offshore

options: The arrows from the atlas's nearest page
None: there is no stream at all offshore
The current from the routeing chart, checked by fixes
The plotter's tidal arrows from the coast
questions.why: Offshore the tidal streams are weak and rotary; the routeing (pilot) chart gives the mean current. Check it by fixes.

questions.q: At 0215 the whole electrical system dies. From the paper log, where is your DR from the 2300 fix?

figure.title: Rebuilding the DR · var 7°W
lines: Running before the wind · no stream

questions.why: 205°C + 2°E − 7°W = 200°T for 15.6 M; 228°C + 6°E − 7°W = 227°T for 9.7 M: 210°T, 24.6 M. Each heading has its deviation.

questions.q: With the electrics dead you need a speed for the DR, so you time a chip of wood along the deck. What speed do you log?

figure.title: No log, no GNSS
lines: Two marks on deck 22.0 m apart
A chip thrown at the bow passes them

options: 8.6 kn
2.3 kn
4.4 kn

questions.q: At 0240 every instrument and the autopilot go dark. What gives you the heading for the DR from now on?

figure.title: 0240: total electrical failure
lines: Steering by hand from now on
Handheld GNSS on its own batteries

options: The heading the plotter showed before it died
The magnetic steering compass, read by torchlight
The autopilot's last fluxgate heading
The COG of a handheld GNSS, taken as the heading
questions.why: The magnetic compass needs no power; steer and log by it, applying its deviation. COG is not heading.

questions.q: Your motor yacht lay stopped for repairs after the fix, beam-on to the wind. Where is the 0400 EP from the 0130 fix?
questions.why: 2 h 30 = 2.5 h: windage 3.0 M toward 110°T plus current 1.5 M toward 200°T: 137°T, 3.4 M. 2 h 30 is not 2.3 h.

questions.q: You run due west along the parallel for a day with no current. What is tomorrow's noon DR longitude?
You are working the height of tide at Dover for 1400 on the standard port's curve. Which high water do you write in the box under the curve?
options: 1638 — then 1400 is HW−2 h 38 min
Either HW — the curve is the same both sides
0412 — the higher HW, 1400 is HW+9 h 48 min
1105 — curves start at LW: LW+2 h 55 min
questions.why: Enter the HW nearest the time you want: 1400 is 2 h 38 min before the 1638 HW, on the rising side of the curve.

questions.q: You are bringing your 24 m motor yacht into Plymouth Sound and will cross the charted 2.1 m patch at 1220. What depth of water will you have over it?

figure.title: Plymouth — standard port curve
lines: Charted depth on the patch: 2.1 m

questions.why: 1220 is HW−3. Height = LW + factor × range = 0.8 + 0.46 × 4.4 = 2.8 m; plus 2.1 m charted = 4.9 m.

questions.q: You will anchor off at 1215 to wait for your berth and want the height of tide then from the curve. What is it?
questions.why: 1215 is HW+3 on the ebb to the 1530 LW: 1.2 + 0.52 × 4.6 = 3.6 m. The 0250 LW belongs to the flood before.

questions.q: You are leaving the marina on the ebb for an overnight passage. What is the latest time you can cross the sill?
You need the height of tide at 0820 on the flood, and today's range falls between the spring and neap curves. What is it?

figure.title: Standard port — two curves
lines: Mean ranges: springs 5.6 m · neaps 2.4 m

questions.why: Range 4.8 m is ¾ of the way from neaps to springs: factor 0.34 − ¾ × 0.12 = 0.25; 0.6 + 0.25 × 4.8 = 1.8 m.

questions.q: Today's range at the standard port is bigger than the mean spring range on the curve diagram. Which curve do you read?

figure.title: Curve diagram — today
lines: Mean ranges: springs 5.9 m · neaps 3.1 m
Spring curve solid · neap curve dashed

options: The neap curve, the one drawn dashed
The spring curve, without going beyond it
Halfway between the two curves
Beyond the spring curve, in proportion
questions.why: Interpolate between the curves only for a range between them; above the mean spring range, use the spring curve.

questions.q: You are bound for a small secondary port that has no tidal curve of its own in the almanac. How do you find the height of tide there at 1500?

figure.title: Almanac — secondary port
lines: No curve printed for this port

options: The rule of twelfths — curves are for standard ports
A nearby port's curve, with that port's own heights
Plymouth's curve, with this port's times and heights
Plymouth's curve and heights, shifted by the time difference
questions.why: Correct the HW and LW times and heights to the secondary port, then work them on the standard port's curve.

questions.q: You are anchored off the secondary port and need the time of this afternoon's low water there. Interpolating the difference, when is it?
You will lie at anchor off the secondary port over tonight's low water. What is the height of that low water there?

figure.title: Secondary port — LW height
lines: LW diff: MLWN +0.5 m · MLWS −0.1 m

questions.why: 1.5 m is halfway between MLWS and MLWN: difference −0.1 + ½ × 0.6 = +0.2 m, so 1.5 + 0.2 = 1.7 m.

questions.q: You plan an early-morning arrival at the secondary port. Interpolating both differences, when is high water there and how high?
questions.why: Time: 0300 is halfway, −0025 → 0235. Height: 5.6 m is ⅔ of the way to MHWS: −0.3 − ⅔ × 0.6 = −0.7 → 4.9 m.

questions.q: You are working tides for Yarmouth, Isle of Wight, and the almanac's curve is drawn in hours from low water, not high water. Why?
options: LW is when the Solent streams all turn
HW times there are kept in local time
HW there is a long stand or double — LW is sharp
These ports have only one LW each day
questions.why: Between Swanage and Selsey HW is flat or double, so its time is vague; the curves use the well-defined time of LW.

questions.q: You want to enter Lymington at 1610 over the shallow approach. What is the height of tide then by the port's curve?
questions.why: 1610 is LW+3. Height = LW + factor × range = 0.7 + 0.62 × 2.2 = 2.1 m.

questions.q: You plan to leave Yarmouth at 1505 and need the height of tide then. Interpolating the port's curves, what is it?
questions.why: 1505 is LW+4. Portsmouth's 3.0 m is halfway between its ranges: factor 0.80; 0.8 + 0.80 × 1.8 = 2.2 m.

questions.q: You are taking the yacht into a Solent river on the flood. What is the earliest time you can cross the bar at its entrance?
Your 24 m motor yacht needs near-HW depth to reach a berth in Southampton, and you are running late: you will be there at 1235. What do you find?

figure.title: Southampton — today
lines: Double HW: the almanac gives the first
Second HW about 2 h after the first

options: No second HW — that comes only at neaps
The ebb running hard since the first HW
Still near the top, between the two HWs
About 0.7 m lower, as the twelfths give
questions.why: With a double HW the level stays near the top for about 2 h after the first HW; the rule of twelfths does not fit here.

questions.q: You plan to scrub the hull on the grid at Portland over low water. The port's curve in the almanac shows a long stand at low water. What does that give you?

figure.title: Portland — curve
lines: Long stand at LW (a double LW)
Plan: scrub on the grid at LW

options: A lower LW than the tide table shows
Stronger streams over the grid at LW
A shorter time on the grid than usual
Longer at the bottom of the tide to work
questions.why: A stand holds the level near LW for longer, so the grid stays dry longer than a normal curve would suggest.

questions.q: You are anchoring off Lundy for the night in your 24 m motor yacht, open to the swell. What is the least depth from the surface at which you let go now?

figure.title: Lundy — anchoring now
lines: Now HW+1: tide 6.5 m · next LW 0.9 m
Want 1.0 m under the keel in the troughs

questions.why: At LW you need 2.0 + 1.0 + ½ × 1.2 swell = 3.6 m; the tide falls 6.5 − 0.9 = 5.6 m, so 3.6 + 5.6 = 9.2 m now.

questions.q: You plan to anchor off Herm for the night in your 24 m motor yacht. What is the least charted depth you can anchor in?

figure.title: Off Herm — overnight
lines: Want 1.5 m under the keel at LW

questions.why: Charted depth + LW height must give draught + clearance: 2.2 + 1.5 − 1.1 = 2.6 m charted.

questions.q: You are entering a marina over its sill in your 24 m motor yacht. The tide gauge at the sill shows the depth over it. Can you go in?

figure.title: At the sill
lines: Draught 1.9 m · squat at 5 kn 0.2 m

options: No — 1.3 m short of water
Yes — 2.3 m under the keel
Yes — 0.5 m under the keel
Yes — 0.7 m under the keel
questions.why: The gauge already reads the depth over the sill: 2.6 − 1.9 − 0.2 squat = 0.5 m. Don't take off the drying height again.

questions.q: You come alongside the harbour wall at high water to dry out for a scrub. When does the keel take the ground?

figure.title: Drying out at the wall
lines: Foot of the wall dries 1.2 m

questions.why: She touches when the tide is down to 1.2 + 2.1 = 3.3 m: factor (3.3 − 0.7) ÷ 5.2 = 0.50, which is HW+3 = 1230.

questions.q: You are drying out a fin-keeled yacht against the wall tonight. How do you make sure she leans onto the wall as the water leaves her?

figure.title: Against the wall tonight
lines: Fender board rigged on the wall side

options: Weight to the wall side, a halyard to the quay
Fenders only, keeping her bolt upright
Weight to the outboard side, to spare the wall
Breast lines slack, letting her lie off the wall
questions.why: Give her a slight heel inwards: move weight to the wall side and take a halyard to a strong point ashore.

questions.q: You plan to dry out against an unfamiliar harbour wall on tonight's low water. What do you do first?

figure.title: Strange harbour
lines: Drying berth along the old wall
Plan: dry out on tonight's LW

options: Rig fenders to keep her well off the wall
Sound along the berth for level, firm ground
Lay out an anchor to hold her off the wall
Check the depth at the wall at HW only
questions.why: The keel must land on level, firm ground free of debris: sound or look at the berth near LW before you use it.

questions.q: You are waiting off a river bar with a heavy swell running in. By the pilot's rule, from what time on the flood does the bar stop breaking?
After 130 M across Biscay you arrive off the river bar at 0230 with a tired crew. What do you do?

figure.title: Off the bar, 0230
lines: Ebb over the bar 3 kn until 0500
Swell 2 m from the W · wind W F5
Pilot: breaks on the ebb in a W swell

options: Cross now at full power, before it gets worse
Cross at LW slack, 0500, before the flood starts
Anchor just off the bar and wait for daylight
Stand off in deep water; cross on the flood after dawn
questions.why: The ebb against the swell makes the bar break; wait in deep water and cross on the flood, in daylight, well before HW.

questions.q: You plan to leave a river over its bar on tomorrow's ebb, after two days of heavy rain inland. What do you expect at the bar?

figure.title: River bar — after rain
lines: Two days of heavy rain inland
Pilot: ebb up to 3 kn in normal flow
Plan: out over the bar on the ebb

options: A stronger, longer ebb and a weaker flood
No ebb at all until the river drops
A weaker ebb and a stronger, longer flood
The same streams — the tide ignores rain
questions.why: Flood water coming down the river adds to the ebb and holds back the flood: expect a harder ebb and steeper seas on the bar.

questions.q: You will go through the Alderney Race with the fair stream this afternoon. What rate do you plan for at its strongest?

figure.title: Alderney Race — atlas
lines: St Helier ranges: sp 9.6 m · np 4.8 m

options: 7.0 kn
4.7 kn
3.6 kn
5.9 kn
questions.why: 6.4 m is a third of the way from neaps to springs: 3.6 + ⅓ × (7.0 − 3.6) = 4.7 kn.

questions.q: It is a very small neap tide, and you are plotting the next hour of a night crossing from the atlas. What rate do you use by your position?

figure.title: Atlas — small neaps
lines: Mean ranges: sp 5.2 m · np 2.6 m
Almanac: extend the line beyond neaps

options: 0.7 kn
1.5 kn
0.5 kn
1.1 kn
questions.why: Extend the line below neaps: 0.7 − (0.6 ÷ 2.6) × 0.8 = 0.5 kn. The stream is weaker than the neap figure.

questions.q: You are working out the tidal offset for a 4-hour leg from the atlas, interpolating each hour for today's range. What net offset do you lay off?
options: 5.2 M to the east
2.6 M to the east
5.1 M to the east
3.9 M to the east
questions.why: Today is halfway: E 1.2 + 1.8 + 1.5 and W 0.6 — net 4.5 − 0.6 = 3.9 M to the east.

questions.q: You in yacht A (8 kn) and a fast motor yacht B (24 kn) make the 24 M crossing to Alderney together, with a steady beam stream. How far is each set off her line if neither allows for it?

figure.title: Crossing — two yachts
lines: Stream steady for the next 3 h+
Yacht A 8 kn · yacht B 24 kn

options: A and B 7.5 M each
A and B 2.5 M each
questions.why: Set = stream × time in it: A takes 3 h (7.5 M), B 1 h (2.5 M). The slow yacht feels the stream three times as much.
questions.ref: Tidal streams — slow and fast boats

questions.q: Your 8-knot displacement motor yacht reaches the Alderney Race two hours late, and the stream there has turned foul. How long will the 8 M through the Race take?

figure.title: Alderney Race — late
lines: Your speed through the water: 8 kn

options: About 1 h 00 min
About 2 h 40 min
About 1 h 36 min
About 37 min
questions.why: Over the ground 8 − 5 = 3 kn: 8 M ÷ 3 kn = 2 h 40 min. A slow boat has to keep the tidal gate.
questions.ref: Tidal streams — slow and fast boats

questions.q: Your crew opens the Channel Islands tidal stream atlas at the page for HW Dover +2 to plot the next hour. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Atlas — Channel Islands
lines: Pages in hours from HW St Helier

options: Fine — Dover and St Helier are the same
Take the page before, to be on the safe side
Work the hour from HW St Helier instead
Add an hour for summer time and go on
questions.why: An atlas is used with the port its pages are referenced to; HW Dover and HW St Helier are hours apart.

questions.q: You are on a 24-hour passage 100 M west of Ushant, out of the Channel streams. What offset do you allow for in your DR over the day?

figure.title: Offshore, 100 M W of Ushant
lines: Tidal streams: rotary, up to 0.8 kn

options: About 26 M to the NE
About 19 M to the NE
Nothing — it all cancels out
About 7 M to the NE
questions.why: Rotary streams nearly cancel over whole cycles; the steady 0.3 kn current adds up: 0.3 × 24 = 7 M.

questions.q: You are crossing Biscay from Brest to A Coruña. Once you are off the continental shelf, the chart shows no tidal diamonds. What do you allow for?

figure.title: Biscay crossing
lines: Shelf edge: 6 h out from Brest
Beyond it: no diamonds, depths 4,000 m

options: The routeing chart's weak current, checked by fixes
Nothing — deep water does not move
The last diamond's rates, hour by hour
The Channel atlas pages for HW Dover
questions.why: Over the deep ocean tidal streams are weak; plan with the mean current from routeing charts or the pilot, and confirm by fixes.

questions.q: In July you plan to take the yacht north along the Portuguese coast from Lisbon to Baiona. What do you have to plan against?
options: Southerly winds on the edge of the high
Northerly winds and a south-going current
Strong tidal streams to time, as in the Channel
A north-going current that offsets the wind
questions.why: In summer the Portuguese trades blow from the north and the Portugal Current sets south: both are foul going north.

questions.q: You are motoring west out of the Mediterranean through the Strait of Gibraltar. What does the mean surface current mid-strait do to you?
options: Sets N across, onto the Spanish shore
Nothing — the Med has no tides
Sets E into the Med, against you
Sets W out of the Med, with you
questions.why: Evaporation draws Atlantic water in: the surface flow sets east into the Med, while the outflow runs deep.

questions.q: Bound west from Gibraltar to Cádiz in your 7-knot motor yacht, you are at Europa Point as the W-going inshore stream begins. Which way do you go to Tarifa, and how long will it take?

figure.title: Europa Point → Tarifa, 20 M
lines: Your speed through the water: 7 kn

options: Inshore — about 3 h 38 min
Mid-strait — about 4 h 00 min
Mid-strait — about 2 h 13 min
Inshore — about 2 h 21 min
questions.why: Inshore: 7 + 1.5 = 8.5 kn over the ground, 20 ÷ 8.5 = 2 h 21 min. Mid-strait: 7 − 2 = 5 kn, 4 h.

questions.q: On your night watch the plotter shows your track crossing this patch 15 M offshore. What do you expect there?

figure.title: Passage chart — night watch
lines: Overfalls symbol over a 30 m ridge
Spring stream 3 kn across the ridge

options: Steep, breaking seas, even in light wind
Smooth water in the lee of the ridge
Nothing at 30 m — overfalls need shallows
An eddy, but a flat sea surface
questions.why: A strong stream over an uneven bottom throws up overfalls in deep water too; at springs they can be dangerous in a calm.

questions.q: You are passing Portland Bill on the E-going spring stream. Where does the race lie now?

figure.note: Spring stream · depths in metres

options: West and SW of the Bill, upstream
East and SE of the Bill, downstream
Due south, the same on every stream
Close under the Bill on both sides
questions.why: A race forms where the stream sweeps past the headland and spreads downstream: on the E-going stream, E and SE of the Bill.

questions.q: You are taking your 15 m sailing yacht west round Portland Bill in daylight at neaps, in a light breeze, at the time the pilot gives for the inshore passage. Which way is quickest and safe today?

figure.note: Neaps · daylight · inshore passage time

options: Any of them — the race is weak at neaps
C — 5 M off, the long way outside the race
A — the inshore passage, a few cables off
B — 1.5 M off, outside the inshore passage
questions.why: In settled weather, at neaps and at the right time, the inshore passage close off the Bill avoids the race at its shortest.

questions.q: You are rounding Portland Bill eastbound at night with a spring stream, keeping outside the race. How far off do you pass?

figure.title: Portland Bill — night
lines: Pilot: race up to 3 M off the Bill

options: About 1 M — just outside the inshore passage
2 M — between the race and the Bill
3 M — right on the race's limit
5 M or more — clear of the race's edge
questions.why: Give the race its full width plus a margin: with the race up to 3 M off, pass 5 M or more off the Bill at night.

questions.q: You are heading west past St Alban's Head on the W-going spring stream, with the wind W F6 against it. Which track do you take?

figure.note: Race up to 3 M off · rough inshore in strong wind

options: C — 4 M off, outside the race
B — 1.5 M off, through the middle
A — close in, the inshore passage
A or C — either side of the race will do
questions.why: Wind against a spring stream makes the race and the inshore passage rough; keep well outside, or wait for the stream to turn.

questions.q: You are bound south from Camaret through the Raz de Sein and want to arrive just as the S-going stream begins. When do you leave Camaret?
options: About 1500
About 1040
About 0040
About 1250
questions.why: The S-going stream starts at 0750 + 5 h = 1250; 13 M at 6 kn takes 2 h 10 min, so leave about 1040.

questions.q: You are bound west through the Pentland Firth with a heavy westerly swell outside. When do you plan to clear the western exit?

figure.title: Pentland Firth — westbound
lines: Merry Men of Mey: on the W-going stream
They lie across the western exit

options: On the E-going stream, punching through it
At the height of the W-going, to rush through
At the end of the W-going stream, near slack
Any time — the swell cannot reach the Firth
questions.why: The race at the western exit builds on the W-going stream against the W swell; time the exit for slack as it dies away.

questions.q: You are motoring west into the wind with the spring stream running west under you. What wind speed does the sea surface feel as it builds the waves?
options: About 19 kn
About 25 kn
About 16 kn
About 22 kn
questions.why: The water moves 3 kn into the wind, so the wind over it is 19 + 3 = 22 kn — that is what steepens the seas.

questions.q: You are approaching a tide race at speed in your planing motor yacht, with the wind against the stream. How do you take it?
options: Slow right down, or route outside the race
Speed up to skim the crests on the plane
Keep 22 kn — you are through in minutes
Trim the bow down and hold full speed
questions.why: Short, steep seas slam a fast hull and can injure the crew; come off the plane or go round outside the race.

questions.q: You lie alongside a low quay in a North Sea port with a deep low passing. What height of high water do you plan for tonight?
questions.why: The surge forecast already includes the low pressure: 4.6 + 0.9 = 5.5 m. Adding 0.34 m for 979 hPa counts it twice.

questions.q: You plan to take your 24 m motor yacht through a swatchway across the Thames Estuary sands at low water. What depth do you expect there?
options: 3.1 m — 0.7 m under the keel
0.7 m — hard aground
2.3 m — under your 2.4 m draught
3.9 m — 1.5 m under the keel
questions.why: A negative surge lowers the tide: 1.5 + 1.6 − 0.8 = 2.3 m, less than the draught. Wait for more tide.

questions.q: Your yacht lies at a low quay in a southern North Sea port for the week. Which forecast should worry you most about a big positive surge?
options: A slow high over Scandinavia, light winds
A thundery trough with squalls inland
A SW gale ahead of a warm front, with rain
A deep low tracking SE, a N gale behind it
questions.why: A deep low moving SE drives a northerly gale down the shallow, narrowing North Sea: the classic big positive surge.

questions.q: You are leaving the Solent for Guernsey and want to carry the Race's fair stream from its start on to St Peter Port. When do you leave the Needles?

figure.title: Needles → Alderney Race
lines: Then St Peter Port, 25 M beyond

options: About 0740
About 0400
About 1340
About 0700
questions.why: 62 M at 7 kn takes 8 h 51 min: 1630 − 8:51 = 0739. You also pass the Needles inside its fair window.

questions.q: You are planning the passage east from Dartmouth to the Solent. You will meet one foul tide whatever you do. Where do you want to take it?

figure.title: Dartmouth → Needles, 85 M at 6 kn
lines: Portland Bill: race, streams to 7 kn

options: In the Needles Channel, at the very end
Across Lyme Bay, where it is weakest
Spread out — it makes no difference
Off Portland, to have it over early
questions.why: Spend the foul stream where it is weak, in the open bay, and carry the fair stream through the headlands and narrows.

questions.q: You are waiting off St Helier in your 24 m yacht to enter the marina over its sill on the flood. Reading the curve between the hours, what is the earliest time you can cross?
You are taking your yacht up a North Brittany river under a fixed bridge. Between which times today can you not pass under it?

figure.title: River bridge — chart and almanac
lines: Clearance 12.4 m above HAT 6.2 m · MHWS 5.3

questions.why: Underside 12.4 + 6.2 = 18.6 m; you need tide ≤ 18.6 − 15.8 = 2.8 m, factor (2.8 − 0.6) ÷ 5.0 = 0.44: from HW−3 to HW+4.

questions.q: You anchored at high water in a sound in the Isles of Scilly at the end of a night passage. By the curve, by what time must you move to keep your margin under the keel?

figure.title: St Mary's, Scilly — at anchor
lines: Anchored at HW 1105 (5.8 m) in 6.7 m
Draught 2.2 m · want 1.0 m under the keel

questions.q: You are anchored in Braye Harbour, Alderney, over a charted 2.4 m for the night. What will you have under the keel at tonight's low water?

figure.title: Braye — secondary on St Helier
lines: St Helier: MLWN 4.0 m · MLWS 1.4 m
Braye LW diff: MLWN −1.5 · MLWS −0.5 m

questions.why: 2.7 m is halfway from MLWS to MLWN: −0.5 + ½ × (−1.0) = −1.0, so LW 1.7 m; 2.4 + 1.7 − 2.6 = 1.5 m.

questions.q: You are timing your arrival off Paimpol, a secondary port on St-Malo, for this morning's high water. Interpolating the time difference, when is it?
You will enter Douglas, Isle of Man, at 0830 after a night passage across the Irish Sea. What is the height of tide there then?
questions.why: Douglas: HW 1130 6.8 m, LW 0500 0.7 m. 0830 is HW−3: 0.7 + 0.42 × 6.1 = 3.3 m on Liverpool's curve.

questions.q: You want to enter the drying harbour at Minehead on this morning's flood. Working its tide from Avonmouth, what is the earliest time you can reach your berth?

figure.title: Minehead — on Avonmouth
lines: Berth dries 4.2 m · draught 2.0 · want 0.4 m

questions.q: You planned to leave a drying berth near Avonmouth at HW+2 on the ebb, and you are an hour late. How much less water do you have than you planned?
questions.why: On the curve the factor drops from 0.80 to 0.58 in that hour: 0.22 × 11.6 m = 2.6 m. Twelfths (2.9) or an average (1.9) don't fit.

questions.q: You want to cross the shallow patch off Swanage at LW+3. What height of tide do you have then?
questions.why: Swanage has a young flood stand: the curve gives 0.30 at LW+3, so 0.3 + 0.30 × 1.8 = 0.8 m — not the twelfths' 1.2 m.

questions.q: You are leaving Cowes on the last of the ebb at 1250, two hours before low water. What is the height of tide then by the Cowes curve?
questions.why: 1250 is LW−2, on the left of the curve: 0.9 + 0.30 × 3.2 = 1.9 m. The LW+2 factor belongs to the flood after.

questions.q: You will leave Bembridge Harbour tonight on the ebb, over the drying approach, for an overnight passage. What is the latest time you can cross it?
You are leaving Southampton in your 24 m motor yacht after the second high water. Compared with the flood, what do you expect of the ebb?

figure.title: Southampton — the curve
lines: Rise about 7 h, with a double HW

options: The same as the flood, mirrored
Shorter and stronger — the fall is squeezed
Weak until LW, then a sudden rush
Longer and weaker, after the long stand
questions.why: The double HW stretches the rise to about 7 h, so the fall comes in about 5 h: the ebb runs harder than the flood.

questions.q: You will take your yacht up the river at a secondary port, under an overhead power cable, at this evening's high water. Can you pass?

figure.title: Power cable — secondary port
lines: Chart: safe clearance 21.5 m above HAT 6.5 m
Std port HW 5.0 m · MHWS 5.6 · MHWN 4.4
HW height diff: MHWS +0.4 · MHWN +0.2 m
Mast and aerials: 20.8 m above the water

options: Yes — 2.2 m to spare
No — 4.6 m short
Yes — 1.9 m to spare
Yes — 0.7 m to spare
questions.why: 5.0 m is halfway: +0.2 + ½ × 0.2 = +0.3, HW 5.3 m. Clearance 21.5 + 6.5 − 5.3 = 22.7 m, less 20.8 m: 1.9 m to spare.

questions.q: Approaching a power cable over a river, your crew says the wires look well above the charted figure and wants to add the difference to your margin. What do you tell them?
options: Go under near the pylons, where it is highest
Add it — the chart is always conservative
Judge the sag by eye and use that
Use the charted safe clearance — it allows for arcing
questions.why: A power cable's charted safe clearance already keeps you out of the arcing zone; never eat into it by judging the wire.

questions.q: You want to scrub on the harbour grid this week, going on at one high water and off at the next, with the tides building from neaps. Which is the first day it works?

figure.title: Harbour grid — neaps to springs
lines: Mon HW 4.7 LW 2.4 · Tue HW 4.9 LW 2.2
Wed HW 5.2 LW 1.9 · Thu HW 5.5 LW 1.6
On and off with 0.3 m · LW 0.5 m below the grid

options: Wednesday
Monday
Thursday
Tuesday
questions.why: You need HW ≥ 2.6 + 2.0 + 0.3 = 4.9 m and LW ≤ 2.6 − 0.5 = 2.1 m: Wednesday (5.2 m, 1.9 m) is the first day with both.

questions.q: You go onto the grid on Friday morning's spring high water for a job that needs two low waters, and the tides are now taking off. Which is the last high water you can float off on?

figure.title: On the grid — Fri 0630, HW 5.7 m
lines: Float off with 0.3 m under the keel

options: Friday 1900
Saturday 2000
Sunday 0830
Sunday 2100
questions.why: She floats off with 2.6 + 2.0 + 0.3 = 4.9 m: Saturday 2000 (5.1 m) is the last HW above that. Miss it and she is neaped.

questions.q: You are on the grid at a secondary port and want to float off on this evening's high water. Can you?

figure.title: On the grid — secondary port
lines: Float off with 0.3 m under the keel

options: Yes — 0.4 m to spare
Yes — 0.9 m to spare
No — 0.1 m short
Yes — 0.2 m to spare
questions.why: HW here is 5.0 − 0.5 = 4.5 m; you need 2.4 + 1.9 + 0.3 = 4.6 m — 0.1 m short. Wait for a bigger tide.

questions.q: You are bringing the yacht onto a harbour grid to scrub her. At what state of the tide do you arrive?

figure.title: Harbour grid
lines: Grid dries 2.2 m · posts to lie against

options: On the young flood, for the most time
At LW, to see the grid clearly first
At half-ebb, so she dries out quickly
Shortly before HW, to settle as it falls
questions.why: Arrive near the top of the tide, secure her over the bearers and to the posts, and let her settle as the ebb leaves her.

questions.q: You are drying out against a harbour wall overnight, with low water at 0300. What do you arrange for the night?

figure.title: Against the wall tonight
lines: Halyard to the quay · fenders and a board

options: Someone aboard to tend the lines as she settles
All crew ashore until she floats again
Breast lines only, with the springs taken off
Lines made fast tight at HW and left alone
questions.why: As the tide falls the lines need easing to keep her leaning on the wall, and taking in as she lifts: someone stays on watch.

questions.q: Your night crossing of the western Channel takes six hours, and the diamond on the track gives spring and neap rates. Interpolating each hour for today's range, what total tidal offset do you plot?

figure.title: Diamond, sp/np kn — 2200 to 0400
lines: Ranges: sp 5.6 m · np 2.8 m · today 4.2 m
