options: 5.5 M towards 076°T
4.1 M towards 076°T
2.8 M towards 076°T
7.4 M towards 072°T
questions.why: Today is halfway: 1.35, 1.95, 1.65 and 0.9 M, then 0.45 and 1.2 M back; head to tail they give 4.1 M towards 076°T.

questions.q: You are crossing the Irish Sea from Holyhead to Dublin Bay, seven hours across the north–south streams. Interpolating each hour for today's range, where does the stream leave you?

figure.title: Irish Sea crossing, 7 h — sp/np kn

options: 9.9 M to the north
3.4 M to the north
5.1 M to the north
6.8 M to the north
questions.why: Today is halfway: 1.5 + 2.1 + 1.8 + 1.5 + 0.6 = 7.5 M north, less 0.9 + 1.5 = 2.4 M south — 5.1 M to the north.

questions.q: You in an 8-knot yacht and a 20-knot motor yacht both start a 40 M crossing with a beam stream that turns after three hours. If neither allows for it, how far off the line does each end up?

figure.title: Crossing — 40 M
lines: Beam stream E-going 2 kn for 3 h

options: Neither — the stream cancels out
Slow 4 M, fast 2 M
Slow 10 M, fast 4 M
Slow 2 M, fast 4 M
questions.why: Slow: 3 h at 2 kn E, then 2 h at 2 kn W — 2 M net. Fast: 2 h, all in the E-going stream — 4 M. The turn helps the slow boat.
questions.ref: Tidal streams — slow and fast boats

questions.q: Your displacement motor yacht has a 60 M leg to run at 10 kn, and the stream will be foul all the way. How much fuel do you plan for the leg?

figure.title: Fuel for the leg
lines: Leg 60 M · foul stream 2.5 kn on average
At 10 kn through the water: 36 l/h
At 7.5 kn through the water: 24 l/h

options: About 290 l
About 220 l
About 170 l
About 190 l
questions.why: Over the ground 10 − 2.5 = 7.5 kn: 60 ÷ 7.5 = 8 h at 36 l/h = 288 l. The burn follows the speed through the water.
questions.ref: Tidal streams — slow and fast boats

questions.q: You will cross diagonally from Dartmouth to Guernsey, about eight hours under way, with the Channel stream running along your track. To carry the fair stream for longest, when do you leave?

figure.title: Stream along your track (kn, + fair)
lines: Hours from HW Dover 1120 · 8 h under way

questions.why: 0720 covers the hours HW−4 to HW+3: −0.2 + 0 + 0.6 + 1.4 + 1.8 + 1.6 + 1.2 + 0.4 = +6.8 M, more than any other start.

questions.q: Your 24 m motor yacht will cross from the Solent to Cherbourg at 22 kn, about three hours, with a fresh westerly forecast. What should decide your departure time?

figure.title: Solent → Cherbourg at 22 kn
lines: Spring streams 3–4 kn at each end

options: Arriving at slack water, to save the most fuel
Carrying a fair stream for the whole crossing
Avoiding wind against the spring stream at each end
Leaving at LW, when the Needles Channel is calmest
questions.why: At 22 kn the stream adds little to the time or the fuel; wind against a spring stream off the Needles and the Cotentin makes the seas that hurt.
questions.ref: Tidal streams — slow and fast boats

questions.q: You are taking the yacht up the Bristol Channel from Swansea to Portishead, about 45 M at 7 kn. When do you leave?
options: Near HW, for the deepest water
Any time — the streams there are weak
At half-flood, with the strongest stream
Near LW, to carry the whole flood up-channel
questions.why: Up-channel streams reach 4–5 kn at springs: leave about LW so the flood carries you most of the way before it turns.

questions.q: Leaving Cherbourg for St Peter Port at 7 kn through the water, you want the Race and then the Little Russel with the stream. What is the latest you can leave?

figure.title: Cherbourg → St Peter Port
lines: To the Race 14 M, little stream
On to the Little Russel 14 M: fair 2 kn

options: About 1230
About 1130
About 1340
About 0850
questions.why: 2 h + 10 M ÷ 11 kn (55 min) + 14 M ÷ 9 kn (1 h 33 min) = 4 h 28 min before 1700: 1232, inside the Race's window too.

questions.q: You are bound from Cherbourg to Guernsey overnight and will pass Alderney at about 0200. Which route do you plan?

figure.title: Alderney — passing at 0200
lines: Race: about 8 M wide, overfalls at springs

options: The Race, close along the Alderney shore
The Race, mid-channel, on the fair stream
The Swinge at slack, on the plotter
The Swinge, shorter and out of the Race
questions.why: The Race is 8 M wide, with room to keep clear of its rocks and overfalls; the narrow, rocky Swinge is no place to be at night.

questions.q: You will go through the Raz de Sein at 0300 on the fair stream. What do you do before you reach it?

figure.title: Raz de Sein — tonight
lines: Through the Raz at 0300 · fair stream
Wind NW F4 · swell W 1.5 m
Crew of four, two on watch

options: Reef only once the seas build in it
The crew below, the skipper alone on deck
Harnesses on, hatches shut, the crew briefed
Lifejackets stowed, ready to hand
questions.why: A race can throw up steep, breaking seas with little warning, worst at night: secure the boat and the crew before you enter, not in it.

questions.q: You are rounding Pointe de Barfleur eastbound in fog on the spring stream, and you can hear nothing of the race. Which track do you take?

figure.note: Fog · spring stream · race up to 4 M off

options: B — 2 M off, between the two
A or B — the fog means a calm sea
A — close in, the inshore passage
C — 6 M off, outside the race
questions.why: In fog you can neither see the race nor pilot the inshore passage by eye: pass well outside the race's charted limit and fix often.

questions.q: Weather holds you in port for five days, and your planned Alderney Race passage moves from neaps to springs. What changes?

figure.title: Alderney Race — the plan
lines: Fair stream: the same hours from HW

options: Stronger streams, shorter slacks — re-plan the timing
Longer slacks, so the timing is easier
Nothing — the Race times are fixed by HW
Weaker streams, as the moon is new
questions.why: From neaps to springs the Race's rate about doubles and the turn comes quicker: recheck the timing, the rate and wind against tide.

questions.q: You plan to take your 6-knot yacht west through the Gulf of Corryvreckan at slack water. On which tides can you do it?

figure.title: Gulf of Corryvreckan — the pilot
lines: Narrows 2.5 M · streams to 8.5 kn at springs
Slack: about 15 min springs, 1 h neaps
Whirlpool and overfalls on the W-going

options: On the W-going stream, riding it through
At neaps, when slack lasts long enough
On any tide, if you arrive on time
At springs, when slack comes at a fixed time
questions.why: The narrows take 2.5 M ÷ 6 kn = 25 min, longer than the 15 min of slack at springs: only a neap slack gives you the time.

questions.q: Bound east through the Pentland Firth in your 6-knot yacht, you reach the western entrance an hour after the fair stream has turned foul. What do you do?

figure.title: Pentland Firth — eastbound
lines: Streams to 10 kn and more at springs
Races and eddies at both ends

options: Go north of Stroma, where it is weaker
Anchor in the Firth until the stream eases
Wait at Scrabster for the next fair stream
Push on — the foul stream is only an hour old
questions.why: The foul stream builds to many knots, with races at both ends: a 6-knot yacht cannot stem it. Go back and wait for the E-going stream.

questions.q: After 30 hours from Baiona you reach Figueira da Foz at 0100, and the port radio says the bar is closed to small craft. What do you do?

figure.title: Figueira da Foz, 0100
lines: Port radio: bar closed to small craft
Swell NW 3.5 m · wind NW F5
Pilot: Nazaré, 35 M S, no bar

options: Anchor just off the bar until it opens
Follow a fishing boat in over the bar
Enter at HW, when the bar is deepest
Go on to Nazaré, an all-weather harbour
questions.why: A closed bar is closed for a reason, and crossing it may break the law: go on to a harbour without a bar, or stand off in deep water.

questions.q: You are waiting off Póvoa de Varzim with a long-period swell running in. By the pilot's rule, from what time on the flood can you cross the bar?

figure.title: Póvoa de Varzim — bar
lines: Bar charted 2.5 m · swell 2.0 m at 14 s
Pilot: over 12 s, keep depth ≥ 2 × swell

questions.why: Depth needed 2 × 2.0 = 4.0 m, so tide 4.0 − 2.5 = 1.5 m: factor (1.5 − 0.6) ÷ 3.0 = 0.30, which is HW−4 = 1240.

questions.q: Your chart shows 3.5 m on a river bar on the Spanish Atlantic coast, but this spring's port notice gives 2.0 m after the winter storms. What do you plan with?

figure.title: River bar — two sources
lines: After a winter of W gales

options: The chart's 3.5 m — the official survey
The notice's 2.0 m — bars shift
The mean of the two, 2.8 m
The chart, less 10 % for its age
questions.why: Bars move with storms and river floods: plan with the latest survey or notice, and watch the sounder on the way in.

questions.q: You must pass under a bridge on tonight's equinoctial spring high water, with a positive surge forecast. How much room will you have under it?
options: 15.5 m — 0.9 m to spare
14.6 m — nothing to spare
14.9 m — 0.3 m to spare
15.2 m — 0.6 m to spare
questions.why: The surge lifts HW to 6.0 + 0.6 = 6.6 m, above HAT: 15.2 + 6.3 − 6.6 = 14.9 m. The surge already includes the low pressure.

questions.q: Your yacht is in a low-lying east-coast marina for the week, and a surge of +0.8 m is forecast with a deep low. When is it most dangerous?
options: Whenever it comes — the timing does not matter
If it peaks near a neap high water
If it peaks near low water
If it peaks near a spring high water
questions.why: A surge adds to the tide: on a spring HW it gives the highest levels, over pontoon piles and quays; near LW it does little harm.

questions.q: At high water your mast will clear the bridge by 0.6 m at the predicted height, but wind against tide is raising a 1.2 m chop under the span. What do you do?

figure.title: Under the bridge at HW
lines: Room at the predicted height: 0.6 m

options: Wait — the crests and the pitching eat the 0.6 m
Go — the troughs give back what the crests take
Go — 0.6 m is over the usual 0.5 m margin
Go fast, so that the mast lifts less
questions.why: In waves the mast rises with the crests, about half the wave height, plus the pitching: the 0.6 m is gone. Wait for a smoother sea.

questions.q: After three days of westerly gales you set out across Biscay from A Coruña to Brest. Which way does the wind-driven surface current set you?

figure.title: Biscay after the gales
lines: W gale F8–9 for three days, now W F5
Pilot: wind drift up to 0.5 kn

options: Towards the N–NE — left of downwind
Towards the E–SE — right of downwind
Nowhere — the rotary streams cancel it
Towards the W — back into the wind
questions.why: In the northern hemisphere a wind drift sets to the right of downwind: after westerly gales it runs E–SE, towards the French coast.

questions.q: On day two of the Biscay crossing, over 4,500 m of water, your fixes show a steady set of about 0.4 kn for the last 12 hours. How do you carry it in your DR?

figure.title: Mid-Biscay, day two
lines: Depth 4,500 m · far off the shelf
Fixes: set 120°, about 0.4 kn, 12 h steady
Pilot: streams here under 0.2 kn, rotary

options: From the Channel atlas pages, hour by hour
As a tidal stream that will turn in 6 h
As a steady current, applied every hour
Not at all — it will average out over the day
questions.why: Over the abyssal plain the tidal streams are weak; a set that holds for 12 h is current: keep applying it and recheck at each fix.

questions.q: In December you take the yacht north from Lisbon to Baiona. Where do you route to get the most help from the current?

figure.title: Lisbon → Baiona, December
lines: Pilot: winter N-going current over the slope
Tidal streams on this coast: weak

options: Close inshore, in the tidal streams
Anywhere — the current is the same all year
50 M offshore, in the Portugal Current
Over the shelf edge, in the N-going current
questions.why: In winter a N-going current runs along the shelf edge, while the Portugal Current further out sets S: keep over the slope.

questions.q: You need the height of tide at HW+2 at the standard port on a very small neap tide. What is it?

figure.title: Standard port — small neaps
lines: Mean ranges: springs 5.4 m · neaps 2.6 m

questions.why: The 2.0 m range is below the mean neap range: read the neap curve, not beyond it — 1.6 + 0.75 × 2.0 = 3.1 m.

questions.q: You have marked HW 6.1 m and LW 1.3 m on the scales of the standard port's curve diagram. What do you draw next?

figure.title: Curve diagram — setting up
lines: HW 6.1 m marked on the top scale
LW 1.3 m marked on the bottom scale

options: A line from the HW height to the HW time
A line joining the two heights
A line along the mean spring range
A line up from the time you want
questions.why: Join HW on the top scale to LW on the bottom one; from the curve you then go across to that line and read the height off the scale.

questions.q: You anchor off Sark at high water in 12.0 m for a few hours. What will you have under the keel at low water?

figure.title: Sark — on St Helier
lines: St Helier HW 10.6 m · LW 1.2 m
Sark diffs: HW −1.1 m · LW −0.2 m

options: Aground — 0.3 m short
0.6 m under the keel
1.5 m under the keel
3.5 m under the keel

questions.q: You anchored in 8.0 m at HW+1 this evening to wait two nights for the weather, with springs coming. What will you have under the keel at tomorrow night's low water?

figure.title: At anchor — two nights
lines: Anchored at HW+1 in 8.0 m · tide 5.0 m
LW tonight 0.9 m · tomorrow night 0.4 m

questions.why: Tomorrow's LW is lower: 8.0 − (5.0 − 0.4) = 3.4 m of water, less the 2.4 m draught = 1.0 m. Tonight's 0.9 m LW leaves 1.5 m.

questions.q: Your 24 m motor yacht is crossing an offshore bank at 18 kn with a swell running. What do you have under the keel in the troughs?
questions.why: 6.2 m charted + 1.0 m tide = 7.2 m; less half the 2.0 m swell, 0.4 m of squat and the 2.4 m draught: 3.4 m in the troughs.

questions.q: In a Brittany port, the inner basin's gate is worked only on tides of coefficient 60 or more. Today's coefficient is 48 and rising towards springs. When can you go in?

figure.title: Inner basin — capitainerie
lines: Gate worked at coefficient 60 and over

options: Tomorrow
In two days
In a week, at springs
Today, near HW
questions.why: Rising about 7 a day: 55 tomorrow, 62 the day after — the first tide of 60 or more is in two days.

questions.q: You will go through the Chenal du Four at its strongest today. The French atlas gives rates for coefficients 45 and 95. What rate do you plan for?
options: 2.4 kn
4.2 kn
3.5 kn
5.2 kn
questions.why: Coefficient 65 is 20 ÷ 50 = 0.4 of the way from 45 to 95: 2.4 + 0.4 × 2.8 = 3.5 kn.

questions.q: You are passing Arklow on the Irish coast, where the almanac shows a spring range of under a metre. Your crew says the streams must be weak. What do you plan for?

figure.title: Off Arklow — the almanac
lines: Atlas: streams up to 3 kn offshore

options: Streams of a few tenths of a knot
Streams at HW only, none at LW
No streams — the tide hardly rises
Streams of up to 3 kn despite the small range
questions.why: Near an amphidromic point the range is small, yet the water still runs hard past it: take the rates from the atlas, not the range.

questions.q: Your 24 m ketch must pass under the river bridge on her way up to the yard. Can you go under now, and with what margin?

figure.title: River bridge, 1530
lines: HAT 6.1 m; height of tide now 3.5 m
VHF aerial and light 1.5 m above that

options: Yes — 1.4 m to spare
Yes — 2.3 m to spare
Yes — 2.9 m to spare
No — 3.8 m short

questions.q: You are bound for a harbour with a dredged entrance after a night at sea. What height of tide do you need before you go in?

figure.title: Night entry — pilot book and plan
lines: Entrance dredged to 3.2 m below CD
Swell running in the entrance: 1.6 m
Your rule: half the swell + 0.5 m clear

questions.why: You need 3.6 + 0.8 (half the swell) + 0.5 = 4.9 m of water; 4.9 − 3.2 dredged = 1.7 m of tide.

questions.q: You are bringing your 24 m yacht into a strange marina at dusk. How do you plan the berthing?

figure.title: Marina plan (pilot book)
lines: Dead end; berth on the last finger
Your yacht: 24 m LOA, bow thruster

options: Go in briskly so the wind cannot set you down
Turn in the fairway on the bow thruster alone
Reverse down the fairway so you never turn in it
Go in bow first and turn at the end of it
questions.why: A 24 m yacht cannot safely turn in 30 m with a crosswind; reversing in from the open end needs no turn and keeps a way out.

questions.q: Your 23 m ketch is off the entrance at night when the signal mast shows this. What do you do?

figure.note: Signal mast · pilot book: yellow exempts vessels under 20 m

options: Go in outside the main channel, keeping clear
Go in — the yellow light exempts small craft
Go in — the reds are for ships over 50 m
Wait outside — the exemption is for under 20 m
questions.why: Three reds: no entry. The yellow exempts only the vessels the port names — here under 20 m, so not your 23 m yacht.

questions.q: Your 23 m yacht will pass reporting point ALPHA in ten minutes on a night arrival. What do you do?

figure.title: Port VTS — pilot book
lines: Vessels of 20 m LOA and over:
report at point ALPHA and the breakwater
and keep watch on ch 14 inside the area

options: Report to VTS on ch 14 at ALPHA, then listen there
Stay silent — VTS reports are for ships only
Report once you are inside the breakwater
Call on ch 16 only if you need assistance
questions.why: The port rule turns on length: at 23 m you report at each point and keep a listening watch on the VTS channel.

questions.q: You reach the fairway buoy in fog and call VTS, which tells you this. What do you do?

figure.title: 0555, fog, visibility 0.1 M
lines: You: fairway buoy, 24 m motor yacht
Wait area: south of the fairway buoy

options: Enter now and pass her port to port inside
Hold in the wait area until the ferry is out, then enter
Enter fast to be through before she sails
Anchor in the channel until she has passed
questions.why: Meeting a ferry in a narrow channel in 0.1 M visibility is the risk to avoid: wait clear, then go in on radar with VTS informed.

questions.q: You are closing this point at night, and your plan offers three clearing bearings on the light. Which do you use?

figure.note: Depths below CD

options: B — the 5 m line leaves 1.6 m under the keel
A — the 2 m line, the shortest way round
C — the 10 m line, for the draught in a swell
Any of them — the sounder will warn you
questions.why: On the 5 m line a 3 m swell takes 1.5 m off your 1.6 m: almost nothing. At night with a deep draught, clear the 10 m line.

questions.q: You are rounding a cape at night on a parallel index line. What do you change?

figure.title: Radar, 0310, rounding the cape
lines: Index line set 1.2 M to starboard
Yacht yawing ±15° in a quartering sea
The cape's echo jumps on and off the line

options: Use the EBL instead and stay head-up
Move the index line to 1.5 M for a margin
Alter away each time the echo jumps inside
Feed in a heading and set the display north-up
questions.why: Head-up and unstabilised, every yaw swings the picture under a fixed index line; a stabilised north-up display holds it still.

questions.q: Your plan turns you onto a transit in a narrow approach. When do you start the turn?

figure.title: Pilotage plan, leg 3
lines: Course 040°M until the beacons are in transit
then turn to 125°M along the transit
Your yacht: 24 m, 10 kn, turns slowly

options: A little before the marks come into line
When the marks have opened past the line
When the plotter shows you on the line
Exactly as the marks come into line
questions.why: A 24 m yacht carries her way through a big turn: start the wheel early so she settles on the transit, not past it.

questions.q: You have spent the evening on the pilot book, the tidal atlas, the forecasts and the crew list for a 140 M crossing. What is the next stage of the plan?

figure.title: Passage: 140 M crossing
lines: Drawn on the chart: nothing yet

options: Appraisal — reading the sources once again
Planning — tracks, waypoints, timings and plan B
Execution — the final go and the crew briefing
Monitoring — checking progress against the plan
questions.why: Appraisal (gather and weigh), planning (draw it all), execution (decide and brief), monitoring (check it on the way).

questions.q: The owner asks which SOLAS chapter V carriage rule applies to his yacht. What do you tell him?
options: A voyage data recorder
An ECDIS with a paper backup
A radar reflector, if practicable
An AIS Class A transponder
questions.why: SOLAS V/19 asks every ship under 150 GT, if practicable, for a radar reflector; AIS A, a VDR and ECDIS are for larger ships.

questions.q: You plan a 135 M crossing ahead of a gale front, and two models disagree on its timing. What is your latest departure?

figure.title: Planning on Thursday evening
lines: Gale front: model A Sat 2000, B Sat 1000
Your rule: in 6 h before the earlier one

options: Friday 2000
Friday 1600
Friday 2200
Friday 1000
questions.why: 135 ÷ 7.5 = 18 h. Earlier model Sat 1000 − 6 h margin − 18 h = Fri 1000.

questions.q: You want to reach gate B just as its fair stream begins, having left through gate A. When do you pass gate A?

figure.title: Two tidal gates
lines: Gate B, 115 M on: fair from 0230 next day
Planned speed over the ground 7 kn

questions.q: A new forecast reaches you halfway across. What do you do?

figure.title: 1400, 55 M out on a 140 M crossing
lines: Home, N: 55 M, 8.5 kn, entrance open to SW
Refuge E: 38 M, beam reach, 8 kn, all-tide
Destination S: 85 M upwind, 5.5 kn, bar

options: Press on for the destination — about 0527
Bear away for the refuge — in by about 1845
Turn back for home — in by about 2028
Heave to and let the gale pass over you
questions.why: Refuge: 38 ÷ 8 = 4.75 h → 1845, sheltered; home 55 ÷ 8.5 → 2028, entrance open to SW; on: 0527, in the gale.

questions.q: You are choosing the departure time for an overnight passage to this coast. Which arrival do you plan?

figure.title: Landfall after 130 M
lines: Coast low and featureless for 20 M
Harbour: unlit buoys, reef 1 M off

options: Arrive at 2300, to enter on the light
Arrive at 1500, to see the coast by day
Raise the light before dawn, enter after 0640
Arrive at dusk, as the light comes on
questions.why: A low coast is hard to identify by day; a light’s characteristic identifies it at night. The unlit entrance then needs daylight.

questions.q: Your night route north must get past the end of this scheme. Which crossing do you plan?

figure.note: Ships converge and turn in the area

options: B — through the precautionary area
Along the separation zone to its end
B — it keeps clear of the lanes
A — across both lanes at right angles
questions.why: Ships converge and turn in a precautionary area, with no set direction; a right-angle crossing of the lanes meets predictable traffic.

questions.q: The plotter flags this on the route for tonight’s passage. What do you do?
options: Move the leg — 0.2 M is inside the 500 m zone
Accept it, and call the standby vessel
Accept it — 0.2 M is outside a 500 m zone
Keep the leg and pass at reduced speed
questions.why: 0.2 M = 370 m, inside the 500 m zone, which no yacht may enter; re-route with a mile or more to spare.

questions.q: Your crew want to take the short cut through the wind farm tonight, keeping a radar watch. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Wind farm on the route
lines: Transit allowed; fishing boats, few on AIS
You would pass through at night, in rain

options: Radar works best among turbines: go through
The turbines mask small echoes: go round it
Go through on autopilot, radar on 24 M
Go through — AIS shows all the traffic there
questions.why: Turbines return strong echoes, side lobes and shadows that hide small craft; with rain and fishing boats without AIS, pass outside.

questions.q: You lead the watch on the second night of a 30-hour passage. What do you do?

figure.title: 0310 — the skipper is asleep
lines: Ship on the starboard bow, bearing steady
Orders: call me if a CPA is under 1 M

options: Slow down a little and watch the bearing
Hold on — the ship will see you on radar
Alter boldly to starboard now, then call the skipper
Call the skipper and wait for his orders
questions.why: With 9 min to go the watch acts at once under Rules 15 and 16, then calls: standing orders never delay avoiding action.
questions.ref: Passage planning — watches and night orders

questions.q: Your passage reaches the shipping lanes 21 hours after you leave. Which departure do you plan?
options: 0600 — a fresh crew for the busy lanes
0600 — ships’ lights show their aspect best
Either — the watches keep everyone rested
1800 — the lanes fall in daylight, not at 0300
questions.why: At 0300, 21 h after an early start, a crew is at its lowest ebb; at 1500 the lanes are crossed in daylight with the watches settled.

questions.q: Your watermaker may fail, so you carry sealed drinking water. How much do you take?

figure.title: Provisioning for the crossing
lines: Rule: 3 L per person per day, bottled
plus 3 days' reserve in case of delay

questions.why: 7 people × 3 L × (2 + 3) days = 105 L.

questions.q: You plan the fuel for the run and a possible diversion to the port of refuge. How much does your rule ask you to carry?

figure.title: Motor yacht, 120 M passage
lines: Twin engines, each 55 L/h at 12 kn
Generator 8 L/h, running all the way
Port of refuge 40 M beyond, at 12 kn

options: About 1,570 L
About 1,890 L
About 1,760 L
About 1,010 L

questions.q: Your crew asks how the radar measures range. The echo of a ship comes back as on the card. How far off is she?

figure.title: How far is the echo?
lines: Echo returns 74.1 µs after the pulse

questions.why: The pulse goes out and back: 300,000 km/s × 74.1 µs ÷ 2 = 11.1 km = 6.0 M.

questions.q: You are closing a high coast at night after 140 M. When do you expect the cliffs to paint on the radar?

figure.title: Landfall by radar, 2200
lines: Your scanner 9 m above the sea
Radar range ≈ 2.2 (√h₁ + √h₂) M, h in m

questions.q: You are taking a radar range and bearing of a small islet for your offshore plot. Where do you take them?

figure.title: Radar, 12 M range
lines: Islet 8 M off paints as an arc 0.6 M wide
You want its range and bearing to plot

options: Range to the near edge, bearing to the arc’s centre
Range and bearing both to the left end
Range to the far edge, bearing to the centre
Range to the centre, bearing to one end
questions.why: Range is sharp at the echo’s leading edge; the beam width smears bearing both ways, so take the centre of a point target.

questions.q: You switch the radar on for the night watch and see this. What do you adjust first?

figure.title: Radar switched on at dusk
lines: Screen clean: only the coast shows
Sea and rain controls at zero

options: Turn the rain clutter control up full
Tune, then raise the gain to a faint speckle
Turn the sea clutter control to maximum
Lower the gain further to keep it clean
questions.why: A clean screen usually means too little gain or poor tuning: tune for the strongest echoes, then gain up to a light background.

questions.q: The AIS shows a yacht close on the bow, but the radar shows nothing there. Why?

figure.title: Radar, rough sea
lines: Screen clear right up to own ship
AIS: yacht 0.8 M on the port bow

options: Her AIS is wrong — trust the radar
Yachts never show on radar in a seaway
The sea clutter control has wiped out her echo
She is inside the radar’s minimum range
questions.why: Sea clutter (STC) cuts close-range gain; at maximum it removes small echoes too. Set it to leave a little clutter showing.

questions.q: A ship on AIS is inside the squall ahead, but the radar shows only rain. What do you do?

figure.title: Radar, 0140
lines: Rain squall 3 M ahead: a solid patch
AIS: a ship inside it, heading your way

options: Rely on the AIS — radar cannot see in rain
Turn up the sea clutter control instead
Raise the gain until the patch is solid
Use the rain control to break up the rain and find her
questions.why: The rain control (FTC) keeps only the leading edges of echoes, thinning the rain so a ship’s echo inside it can stand out.

questions.q: Your motor yacht’s radar has a blind sector dead ahead. How do you keep watch on passage?
options: Yaw the bow now and then to look into the sector
Rely on the radar — 8° is too narrow to matter
Turn up the gain to see through the mast
Use a longer range scale to see past it
questions.why: A ship can hide in a blind sector for many minutes; alter 10–15° from time to time and keep a visual lookout ahead.

questions.q: On an overnight passage a ship tells you this on VHF. What improves your echo most?

figure.title: VHF call from a ship, 0300
lines: Ship: 'we saw you only at 2 miles'
Your reflector: small, on the pushpit

options: Your own radar left on transmit
An active radar target enhancer, mounted high
A brighter tricolour at the masthead
A second small reflector beside the first
questions.why: A ship sees only what comes back to her: an active enhancer (RTE) high up returns her pulse amplified, clear of the clutter.

questions.q: You pick up an offshore light float’s racon like this. Where do you measure its range?

figure.title: Racon on the light float
lines: Echo of the light float 9 M ahead
Racon paint: Morse T ( — ) beyond it
You want a range for your offshore fix

options: To the end of the dash, less a mile
To the far end of the racon paint
To the near end of the racon paint
To the middle of the racon paint
questions.why: The racon paint starts just beyond the beacon’s own echo: its near end gives the range, the line’s direction the bearing.

questions.q: On watch you see this on the X-band radar. Where is the survival craft?

figure.title: Radar, 0420, 12 M range
lines: A line of 12 dots on bearing 040°T

options: 1 M beyond the farthest dot
At the farthest dot, at the screen’s edge
Midway along the line of dots
At the nearest dot, 7.2 M on 040°T
questions.why: A SART answers the radar with 12 dots running outward; the casualty is at the dot nearest you. Alert the MRCC and head there.

questions.q: You are plotting a ship crossing ahead of you at night. What CPA and time of CPA does the plot give?
options: CPA 0.9 M at 0334
CPA 0.9 M at 0322
CPA 0.9 M at 0325
CPA 1.1 M at 0327
questions.why: The echo’s 0300–0312 track, extended, passes 0.9 M from you; at its relative speed CPA comes 22 min after 0312: 0334.

questions.q: To give the crossing ship more room you turn 60° to starboard at 0312. What CPA does the new plot give?

figure.title: Same plot, at 0312
lines: You alter now to 060°T, still 10 kn

options: About 5.7 M
About 3.4 M
About 0.9 M
About 0.7 M
questions.why: New relative motion = her 270° 12 kn minus your 060° 10 kn; drawn from 042°, 5.9 M it passes about 3.4 M off.

questions.q: You want to know what this ship is really doing before you decide. What are her course and speed?
options: About 190°T at 14 kn
About 317°T at 20 kn
About 010°T at 14 kn
About 339°T at 15 kn
questions.why: True vector = relative motion in 6 min plus your own vector: the echo’s shift plus 0.8 M on 090° gives about 010°T, 14 kn.
questions.ref: Radar plotting — true and relative motion

questions.q: Your crew says the ship’s vector crosses well ahead of you, so all is well. What do you tell them?

figure.title: ARPA, true vectors, 12 min
lines: Target's vector ends 1 M ahead of your bow

options: They are right — she will cross a mile ahead
Only once the bearing is steady for 20 min
Only if her true vector meets our own
There is a risk of collision — read the CPA, not the vector
questions.why: A true vector shows where she goes, not how close she passes; a CPA of 0.1 M and a steady bearing mean risk of collision.

questions.q: A minute after your alteration the ARPA shows a comfortable CPA. How far do you trust it?
options: Not yet — give it a few minutes to settle
Fully — the alteration was a large one
Fully — the ARPA updates every scan
Not at all — ARPA fails after a turn
questions.why: ARPA averages over several minutes, so just after your own alteration its vectors lag. Watch the bearing open; recheck at 3–4 min.

questions.q: At dawn you find that the heading sensor feeding your MARPA was in error all night. Which of its outputs were wrong?

figure.title: MARPA on your yacht
lines: Heading from a fluxgate reading 6° high
Own course and speed from GPS
Radar north-up, stabilised by that heading

options: Only the targets’ ranges, by 6 %
Targets’ true courses and speeds; CPA and TCPA held
CPA and TCPA; the true vectors held
Nothing — MARPA does not use the heading
questions.why: A heading error turns every echo 6° about you: relative motion keeps its CPA and TCPA, but adding the GPS vector skews true vectors.

questions.q: You assume the ship can see you on her AIS. Why may she not?

figure.title: 0230, AIS
lines: Your set: AIS Class B, 2 W
Ship 6 M off, Class A, closing
No reply to your VHF call yet

options: Class A sets cannot show Class B targets
Class B only receives; it sends nothing
Class B sends less often, weaker, and may be filtered
AIS shows only ships over 300 GT
questions.why: Class B (2 W, every 30 s at speed, lower priority for slots) may be weak, late or filtered off a busy bridge display.

questions.q: You compare the radar with the AIS overlay. What do you make of this echo?

figure.title: 0350, radar and AIS
lines: Radar: echo 4 M on the port bow

options: A false echo — a ship would be on AIS
A buoy — only buoys go without AIS
A second-trace echo from the far coast
A vessel without AIS — plot it like any other
questions.why: Many fishing boats, yachts and warships send no AIS; a steady bearing on any echo means risk of collision.
questions.ref: AIS — what it does not show

questions.q: Your AIS alarm sounds for this target. What is it?

figure.title: AIS alarm, 0115
lines: Symbol: a circle with a cross

options: An AIS MOB beacon — a person in the water
An AIS EPIRB — a vessel in distress
A virtual aid marking a new danger
An AIS-SART — a liferaft or survival craft
questions.why: MMSI 972 is an AIS MOB device (970 an AIS-SART, 974 an EPIRB-AIS): someone is in the water — go to them and alert the MRCC.

questions.q: You read this warning before a night passage. What do you do?

figure.title: NAVTEX, before sailing
lines: New wreck 3 M off your track near WP4
Marked by a virtual AIS aid only
No buoy in the water yet

options: Look out for the buoy’s light on the way
Plot the wreck on the paper chart and the plan
Nothing — the plotter will show the mark
Watch for its echo on the radar
questions.why: A virtual aid exists only on AIS: no light, no echo, and gone if your AIS fails. Put the danger on paper as well.

questions.q: You check the GNSS page before the approach. What does the change mean?

figure.title: GNSS status, 0230
lines: Landfall in 3 h on a rocky coast

options: The fix is better — fewer satellites, less noise
The chart datum has changed overnight
The fix is far less accurate: cross-check it
Nothing — HDOP only matters in harbour
questions.why: A high HDOP means poor satellite geometry and a much bigger error; check the GNSS position against radar ranges and depth.

questions.q: Your crew says that with SBAS showing, the GPS cannot be wrong now. What do you tell them?
options: SBAS only shifts the chart datum
SBAS gives a fix with no satellites
They are right — SBAS cannot be jammed
It sharpens the fix and flags faults, but can be jammed
questions.why: SBAS (EGNOS, WAAS) sends corrections and integrity warnings by satellite — it still rests on weak signals that can be jammed.

questions.q: You are 60 M offshore when the plotter shows this. What do you do?

figure.title: Eastern Med, 0215
lines: SOG 0.0, then 41 kn; clock 3 min out
Radar, log and compass: all normal

options: Treat GNSS as jammed: radar, compass and DR
Restart the plotter and carry on with it
Stop the boat until the position settles
Steer back towards the GPS track line
questions.why: Jumps, a wild SOG and a wrong clock while the other sensors are steady mean interference: go by DR and radar, and report it.

questions.q: Your crew on watch trusts the autopilot to hold the course. What happens?

figure.title: 0300, autopilot in wind mode
lines: Shipping lane 4 M to the north

options: She follows the wind 25° to starboard, away
She follows the wind 25° to port, towards the lane
She tacks herself onto port tack
She holds 090°T and the sails begin to luff
questions.why: Wind mode holds the wind angle, not the heading: a 25° back takes her from 090° to about 065°, towards the lane. Watch the compass.

questions.q: You want to check the sounder against the charted depth plus the tide. What depth of water does it show?

figure.title: Echo sounder
lines: Offset set to show depth below the keel

questions.why: A below-keel reading + draught = depth of water: 3.4 + 2.6 = 6.0 m, the figure to compare with charted depth + height of tide.

questions.q: Your log under-reads, so you checked it at slack water. What distance through the water do you use for the night’s DR?

figure.title: Log check
lines: 1 h run at slack water, no current

questions.why: Log factor 8.4 ÷ 7.8 = 1.077, so 62.4 × 1.077 = 67.2 M through the water.

questions.q: The antenna cable chafes through at 0200, 100 M offshore. What loses its position?

figure.title: Your installation
lines: One GNSS antenna on the arch, feeding:
and the radar overlay over NMEA 2000

options: Everything on the list, the DSC alert position too
Only the plotter — the rest have their own
Only the AIS — it alone uses satellites
Nothing — NMEA 2000 keeps the last fix
questions.why: One antenna is a single point of failure: plotter, AIS, the DSC distress position and track steering all go. Carry an independent GNSS.
questions.ref: Integrated electronics — single point of failure

questions.q: The owner of the 22 m yacht says the plotter’s saved track is the log now, so the paper log can go. What do you tell him?
options: Keep it, but only while in harbour
Keep it — the track has no decisions, weather or crew
Agree — the track is a full legal record
Agree — a paper log is only for ships
questions.why: A track shows where you went, not the weather, watches, checks and decisions — and it dies with the power. Keep a written log.

questions.q: You are entering tonight with both these aids ahead of you. Which do you steer by?

figure.title: Night entry — pilot book
lines: Leading lights 152°T: axis of the dredged cut
Cut 60 m wide, dredged to 4.5 m
Dir light W sector 148°–156°T: depths to 3.0 m

options: The white sector, using the sounder for its edges
The white sector — it is the brighter of the two
The leading lights — the white sector is wider than the channel
Either — both mark the same safe water
questions.why: The 8° white sector spans water of 3.0 m, too shallow for 3.8 m; only the leading lights hold you in the 60 m dredged channel.

questions.q: You must anchor in this unlit bay tonight. How do you find the planned spot?

figure.note: Depths in metres; dashed arcs: ranges

options: By radar bearings of the beach, the nearest echo
By following the 15 m depth in until you arrive
By the plotter’s position, zoomed in on the spot
By two radar ranges off the steep points, checked by the sounder
questions.why: Ranges off steep points are the sharpest radar fix in the dark; the sounder confirms the depth. Bearings smear by the beam width.
questions.ref: Pilotage — an unlit anchorage by radar

questions.q: Fog closes in as you round this cliff on radar. Outside what VRM ring do you keep the cliff’s echo?

figure.note: Plan: round the cliff, reef to starboard

questions.why: The low reef gives no echo, so measure from the cliff: 0.7 M of reef + 0.5 M margin = keep the cliff outside 1.2 M.

questions.q: You are taking your 24 m motor yacht into the outer harbour in fog. What is the highest speed your rule allows?

figure.title: Fog, entering the outer harbour
lines: Your rule: stop within half the visibility

options: 12 kn
6 kn
9 kn
4 kn
questions.why: Half of 2 cables is 1 cable: at 6 kn she stops in 0.9 cable, at 9 kn she needs 2.0. So 6 kn is the most the rule allows.

questions.q: You are writing the plan for this entry. Where does it put the abort point?

figure.title: Entry plan — narrow harbour, 0300
lines: Entrance 40 m wide; inner basin 90 m across
Your yacht 24 m; turning circle about 60 m
The plan needs an abort point

options: At the heads, once you can see inside
Wherever the helmsman starts to feel unsure
Outside the heads, while you can still turn away
In the basin, where she has room to turn
questions.why: With the swell from astern a 24 m yacht is committed once past the heads; decide go or no-go where you can still turn and stand off.

questions.q: You reach the reporting point and call VTS, as the pilot book asks. What does your report give?

figure.title: Calling VTS at point BRAVO
lines: Your yacht: 23 m, inbound at night
Pilot book: report at BRAVO on ch 12
Then keep watch on ch 12 to the berth

options: Your crew list and last port, as for customs
Only your name, and that you will keep clear
Nothing until VTS asks you for details
Name, position, intentions and ETA at the berth
questions.why: VTS fits you into its traffic picture: who you are, where, where bound and when. Then keep watch on its channel.

questions.q: Inbound in fog, you hear VTS give this. What do you do with it?

figure.title: VTS, 0420, fog
lines: You: inbound, 1.5 M from the entrance

options: Find her on radar and plot her as any other ship
Ignore it — VTS messages are for ships
Ask VTS to give you a course to steer
Hold your course — VTS will keep you apart
questions.why: Traffic information is not traffic control: it tells you she is coming. The lookout, the plot and the Rules stay with you.

questions.q: Your 24 m yacht must turn onto the leading line tonight. How far short of the point where the two tracks meet do you put the wheel over?

figure.title: Night entry — onto the leading line
lines: Turn 70° to starboard onto the line
Turning radius at your helm angle: 200 m
Ignore her delay in answering the helm

options: About 110 m
About 140 m
About 550 m
About 200 m
questions.why: Wheel-over distance = radius × tan(half the turn) = 200 × tan 35° = 140 m before the tracks meet.

questions.q: You are finishing the contingencies of your plan for a 140 M crossing. What does its medical line list?

figure.title: Passage plan — contingencies
lines: Ports of refuge: listed for each stage
Weather: plan B for a gale

options: Only the contents of the first-aid kit
The nearest airports for flying crew home
Ports with a hospital on each stage, and the radio medical route
The crew’s next of kin and their home phones
questions.why: A casualty 100 M out needs a plan: which ports on each stage have a hospital, and how to reach radio medical advice via the MRCC.

questions.q: A crew member is hurt halfway across, as on the card. Which way gets him to a hospital soonest?

figure.title: 0100, 70 M out of 130: crew member hurt
lines: Radio medical: ashore to a hospital, soon
A: 30 M upwind at 5 kn; hospital 2 h by road
B: 50 M on a reach, 8.5 kn; hospital there
Home 70 M at 9 kn; destination 60 M at 7.5 kn

options: Home — back alongside by about 0847
Port A — the nearest, in about 0700
On to the destination — about 0900
Port B — in about 0653, the hospital at the port
questions.why: B: 50 ÷ 8.5 = 5.9 h → 0653, hospital there. A is in at 0700 but 2 h from one (0900); home 0847; on, 0900.

questions.q: Your night orders set the fixing routine as on the card. When does the watch change to 6-minute fixes?

figure.title: Night orders — fixing
lines: Within 3 M of any danger: every 6 min
0215: 10.5 M from the bank, 10 kn, closing

questions.why: Six-minute fixes start 3 M from the bank: 10.5 − 3 = 7.5 M to run at 10 kn = 45 min after 0215 → 0300.

questions.q: Your 0300 fix lands well away from the EP, as on the card. What does your monitoring routine say now?

figure.title: 0300 — the fix and the plan
lines: 0230 fix on the track; 0300 EP on the track
0300 radar fix: 1.5 M east of the EP
Orders: a fix every 30 min offshore

options: Steer back to where the EP put you
Find the cause, and fix more often until it is clear
Ignore it — one odd fix is just an error
Accept the fix and keep to the 30-minute routine
questions.why: A 1.5 M jump in 30 min means a stream, a sensor or the plot is wrong; tighten the routine until you know which.

questions.q: You fly home tonight, and a relief skipper takes the yacht on, as on the card. What do you hand over first?

figure.title: Halfway port — you leave tonight
lines: Sails at 0600 for the second 120 M leg
Watermaker weak; one crew new to nights

options: The plotter route — it holds all he needs
The keys, the ship’s papers and the fuel receipts
The plan and its changes, the defects and the crew
Nothing formal — he can read the log
questions.why: The new skipper takes on the plan: what has changed, what is broken and who is fit for what. Papers and keys come after.

questions.q: Your night route crosses the traffic lanes in the conditions on the card. How do you plan the crossing?

figure.title: Crossing the lanes, 2300
lines: 24 m ketch; the lanes 9 M across in all
Under sail alone: 3–5 kn, heading wanders

options: Sail across slowly — a sailing yacht stands on
Sail along the lane until the wind fills in
Wait in the separation zone for more wind
Motor-sail across at a steady speed and heading
questions.why: At 3 kn on a wandering heading you spend 3 h in the lanes and confuse the ships; motor-sail for a steady heading and speed.

questions.q: Checking tonight’s route, you find WP4 here. What do you do?

figure.note: Ship routes from the routeing guide

options: Move it clear of the point where the ships turn
Keep it, and cross the point at full speed
Keep it, and call each ship on VHF
Keep it — ships keep clear of a yacht there
questions.why: Ships converge and alter at the same point off a cape; a yacht turning there meets them all, mid-turn. Put WP4 clear of their routes.

questions.q: It is the second afternoon at sea, as on the card. What do you do now to be ready for the landfall?

figure.title: 1500, the second day
lines: Landfall on a rocky coast at about 0400
Crew of five, all short of sleep

options: Give everyone coffee at 0300, before you close
Send half the crew to sleep now, by turns
Keep everyone up — the landfall needs all hands
Let them rest once the landfall is made
questions.why: Rest is part of the plan: crew who sleep this afternoon and evening are fresh at 0400; coffee at 0300 does not undo 20 hours awake.

questions.q: You check the fuel before the run, as on the card. Which figure does your fuel plan use?
options: The gauge — a dip is spoilt by heel
The gauge — it is the newer reading
The dip — half, so you take on fuel first
The mean of the two, about five-eighths
questions.why: A gauge sender sticks and drifts; the dip measures the fuel. Half is less than your plan needs, so fill up before you go.

questions.q: It is the morning of departure, as on the card. What is left to do before you slip?

figure.title: Departure morning, 0600
lines: Plan made and checked last night

options: Nothing — the plan was finished last night
Draw the whole route again on the chart
Let the crew vote on whether to go
Check the new forecast against the plan, then brief the crew
questions.why: Execution: confirm the plan still fits the latest forecast and the boat, decide, then brief everyone on the plan, watches and plan B.

questions.q: You take the motor yacht across ahead of the wind on the card. When do you expect to arrive?

figure.title: Motor yacht, 140 M, leaving 0600
lines: From 1400: NE 6 on the nose; 10 kn at best
Your rule: in before 1700, when F7 arrives

options: About 1512
About 1646
About 2000
About 1445
questions.why: 0600–1400 at 16 kn = 128 M; the last 12 M at 10 kn take 1 h 12 min → 1512, before the 1700 limit.

questions.q: You are setting up the night watches on your motor yacht, as on the card. What do you add for the lone watchkeeper?
options: The autopilot’s off-course alarm, nothing more
A watch alarm that must be reset every few minutes
A radar guard zone to stand in for the lookout
Longer watches, so there are fewer handovers
questions.why: Alone at night with the autopilot steering, a watchkeeper can doze off unseen; an alarm that sounds unless reset catches it early.

questions.q: You plot this echo on the night watch. If neither of you alters, when does she reach you?

figure.note: Relative motion, north-up

options: About 0257
About 0234
About 0248
About 0236
questions.why: Steady bearing, CPA nil: 2.0 M closed in 12 min = 10 kn, so the 6.0 M left take 36 min from 0212 → 0248.

questions.q: Two echoes close on you at once. Which is the more urgent, and when is her CPA?
options: A — CPA nil at about 0336
B — CPA 0.3 M at about 0312
A — CPA nil at about 0342
B — CPA 0.3 M at about 0318
questions.why: A: steady bearing, nil CPA, but 36 min off (0342). B passes 0.3 M off in 12 min (0318): deal with B first, without closing A.

questions.q: You alter now to starboard for the CPA your orders ask. To what course do you alter?

figure.title: Radar plot, own ship 000°T 10 kn
lines: Alter at 0142 to starboard, still 10 kn
Orders: a CPA of at least 2 M

options: About 046°T
About 314°T
About 024°T
About 028°T
questions.why: From 040°, 5.0 M lay the line tangent to the 2 M ring (23.6° off); with her vector 261°, 9.8 kn the triangle gives 046°T.
questions.ref: Radar plotting — the alteration for a CPA

questions.q: Rather than turn, you slow down as on the card. What CPA does the new plot give?

figure.title: Radar plot, own ship 000°T 12 kn
lines: At 0406 you slow to 6 kn (take it as at once)

options: About 1.6 M
About 2.4 M
Nil, as before
About 4.2 M
questions.why: Her true vector 300°, 12 kn minus your 6 kn north gives relative motion 270°: from 060°, 4.8 M she passes 2.4 M ahead.

questions.q: The third plot of this echo falls off the line of the first two. What CPA does she now give?

figure.note: Relative motion, north-up

options: CPA 1.3 M at 0526
CPA 2.1 M at 0519
CPA 2.1 M at 0525
CPA nil at 0523
questions.why: The bend at 0506 shows she has altered: plot afresh from 0506 and 0512 only. That line passes 2.1 M off, CPA at 0525.
questions.ref: Radar plotting — a target that alters

questions.q: Your route crosses a fast-ferry route tonight. At what range must the radar first show a ferry to give the warning your orders ask?

figure.title: Night orders, ferry route ahead
lines: Orders: 20 min warning of any ferry

questions.why: Relative speed = her 225°, 30 kn less your 000°, 12 kn = 39.4 kn; × 20 min = 13.1 M — beyond 12 M, so watch on the 24 M scale.

questions.q: You hand over the radar watch for the night, as on the card. Which range scales does the watch use?
options: A long one for early warning, a short one for small craft
The 24 M scale only, for the earliest warning
The 3 M scale only, for the finest detail
Whichever scale shows the most echoes
questions.why: Long scales give early warning of ships; small craft and buoys show only on a short scale. Switch between them on every look.

questions.q: This yacht’s echo appears 2 M off, and the guard zone never sounded. Why not?

figure.note: Radar, 12 M range

options: A guard zone works only on AIS targets
Her echo first showed inside the zone’s inner edge
The alarm waits until an echo has stayed 5 min
The zone filters out echoes as small as hers
questions.why: A small echo may first paint at 2–3 M; a ring from 6 M out never sees it. A guard zone helps the lookout, it does not replace one.

questions.q: You are closing the coast at night in heavy rain, and the radar shows this. Why is there nothing behind the squall?

figure.title: Radar, 0200, heavy rain ahead
lines: Squall 2–4 M ahead; rain control set
Coast at 9 M paints either side of it
Behind the squall: no coast, no echoes

options: The rain control wipes out all echoes behind it
Nothing is there — the coast has a gap
The rain soaks up the pulse, so echoes beyond it fade
X-band sees through rain; the coast there is low
questions.why: Heavy rain absorbs and scatters X-band energy, so targets beyond a squall fade or vanish. Slow down and look round its side.

questions.q: You set a parallel index line to pass the cape, as on the card. Which way do you draw the line?

figure.title: Parallel index past the cape
lines: Stream on the beam: heading 033°T holds it
Pass the cape 1.5 M off to port

options: Along the bearing of the cape now
Parallel to the heading, 033°T
Parallel to the cape’s coastline
Parallel to the ground track, 045°T
questions.why: A fixed echo moves across the screen opposite to your motion over the ground, so the index line runs parallel to the track, not the heading.
questions.ref: Radar — parallel indexing with a stream

questions.q: A ship passes close and the radar paints this arc around her. What is it?

figure.note: A ship passes 0.4 M off

options: Side lobes from her strong echo, not real targets
Second-trace echoes from far off
Her wake and the broken sea behind her
A fleet of small craft around her
questions.why: A big echo close by returns energy through the scanner’s side lobes, painting an arc at her range. Turn the gain or sea clutter down a touch.

questions.q: You are tracking a ship on MARPA when this happens. What is the likely cause?

figure.title: MARPA, 0330
lines: Acquired: ship A, CPA 1.8 M, 14 kn
Her echo passes close to a fishing boat
Now: vector swings, CPA 0.2 M, 3 kn

options: The MARPA has found her real CPA at last
The tracker has jumped to the fishing boat’s echo
The fishing boat’s AIS has been fed into it
Ship A has slowed and turned towards you
questions.why: When two echoes pass close, MARPA may swap them and its data jump. Re-acquire both and check each by compass bearing and by eye.

questions.q: You switch the radar to true trails, as on the card. What do you make of the echo with no trail?

figure.title: Radar, true trails (ground-stabilised)
lines: Ships’ echoes: trails behind each one
One echo 3 M ahead: no trail at all

options: It is a false echo — real ones leave trails
It is on your course and at your speed
It is stopped — a buoy or a ship at anchor
It is closing you head-on at speed
questions.why: Ground-stabilised true trails show movement over the ground, so no trail means stopped. In relative trails, an echo keeping pace with you has none.

questions.q: In a strong cross-stream the ARPA and the ship’s lights disagree, as on the card. Why?

figure.title: 0215, strong tidal stream across
lines: Ship ahead, steady 10 min: vector crossing
Her lights: masthead lights in line, red

options: Her navigation lights are set for a tow
Her lights are wrong — trust the vector
The ARPA has lost her and is guessing
The vector shows her track over the ground, not her heading
questions.why: In a cross-stream a ship crabs: ground-stabilised vectors show her course over the ground, her lights her heading. Sea-stabilise to judge aspect.

questions.q: The AIS shows a tanker 28 M away, but the radar shows nothing on her bearing. Why?

figure.title: 0100, AIS and radar
lines: Radar on 24 M: no echo on her bearing
Your scanner 8 m up; her bridge about 30 m

options: She is beyond your radar horizon; her AIS reaches further
Her AIS is false — trust the empty radar
The radar needs a 48 M scale to show her
Large ships paint only inside 12 M
questions.why: Radar sees to its horizon: about 2.2 × (√8 + √30) ≈ 18 M to her bridge, while VHF from her high aerial carries further. Expect her echo later.

questions.q: The radar and the AIS tell you different things about this ship, as on the card. Which do you believe?

figure.title: 0330, radar and AIS
lines: AIS: cargo ship, status "moored", SOG 11.8 kn
Radar: her echo closing, bearing steady
Lights: masthead, sidelight, no anchor light

options: The AIS SOG alone — she is only drifting
The plot and her lights — the status is typed in by hand
Neither — call her and wait for a reply
The AIS status — she is moored, so ignore her
questions.why: Navigational status is set by her crew and often left wrong; her SOG, the plot and her lights say she is under way. Act on the risk.
questions.ref: AIS — what it shows and what it does not

questions.q: The radar shows two echoes in step, but the AIS shows one vessel, as on the card. What is the second echo?

figure.title: 0130, radar and AIS
lines: Radar: her echo, and another 0.4 M astern
Second echo: same course and speed, no AIS

options: A false echo from the tug’s own hull
A yacht in her wake — pass between the two
Her tow — and you keep clear of the gap between them
A second-trace echo from far astern
questions.why: A tow often sends no AIS of its own. Two echoes in step with one AIS: treat it as a tow and never pass between them.

questions.q: GNSS is lost mid-crossing, as on the card. What still works as before?

figure.title: 0130, 60 M from landfall: GNSS lost
lines: AIS, DSC VHF, autopilot in track mode

options: The AIS and DSC, with fixes of their own
The autopilot, still steering the route
Everything but the plotter’s position
Radar, compass, log and sounder; the pilot on compass
questions.why: Without GNSS the AIS sends no position, DSC alerts carry none and track mode stops. Radar, compass, log and sounder carry on: DR and radar.
questions.ref: GNSS — failure and what is left

questions.q: The GNSS fails on passage at night, as on the card. What do you do first?
options: Write down the last fix and time, and start a DR
Wait — the satellites will soon come back
Restart the plotter until it finds a fix
Head for the nearest land to get a fix
questions.why: The last good fix with its time and log reading starts your DR; write it down before it scrolls off a screen.

questions.q: Approaching the strait, you find this. What do you trust?

figure.title: 0400, approaching the strait
lines: GNSS: steady fix, HDOP 0.8, SOG 9 kn
Radar ranges put you 2.5 M north of it
Two ships on AIS show inland, at an airport

options: The GNSS — an HDOP of 0.8 shows it is sound
The radar ranges — the GNSS may be spoofed
The mean of the two positions
The GNSS, after retuning the radar
questions.why: Spoofing gives a smooth, confident and false fix with a good HDOP. Radar ranges and depths are independent: trust them, and report it.

questions.q: The autopilot’s off-course alarm keeps sounding, as on the card. What do you do?

figure.title: 0230, off-course alarm
lines: Autopilot on compass, close reach, F6
Heading swings 25° up in each gust
Full main, no reef; rudder hard over

options: Turn the autopilot’s gain up to its maximum
Widen the off-course alarm to 30°
Reef or ease the main to take off the weather helm
Switch to wind mode to follow the gusts
questions.why: No pilot beats the weather helm of an over-pressed yacht; balance her — reef, ease the main — and it will steer again.

questions.q: At speed on the flybridge, the autopilot alarm shows this. What do you do first?

figure.title: Flybridge, 0100, 18 kn
lines: Rudder angle shows hard over to port

options: Reset the autopilot and engage it again
Look up the fault code in the manual
Call the skipper, and wait at the helm
Take the helm in hand steering and slow down
questions.why: A drive fault can leave the rudder over at 18 kn: take hand steering at once and slow down, then look for the fault.

questions.q: Far offshore at night the sounder shows this. What do you make of it?

figure.title: 0300, 70 M offshore
lines: Sounder: 14 m, then 22 m, then nothing
No shoal on the chart or in the Notices

options: False echoes — fish, a layer in the water, or wake
An uncharted shoal — stop and sound around it
A seamount: the chart datum must be wrong
The sounder is right; the chart is out of date
questions.why: Beyond its range a sounder can show fish, plankton layers or wake as depths; jumpy readings in 2,000 m are not a shoal.

questions.q: Your log is out of action, so you work the plot from the GNSS, as on the card. How do you find the next hour’s position?

figure.title: Log out of action
lines: Paddlewheel fouled by weed: reads 0.0 kn

options: From heading and SOG, then apply the stream
From COG and SOG alone — they hold the stream already
Wait — with the log at 0.0 you have no plot
From COG and SOG, then apply the atlas stream
questions.why: GNSS COG and SOG are over the ground, so the stream is in them. Laying the atlas stream on top counts it twice.

questions.q: The log has failed, so you time a chip of wood along the deck. What is your speed through the water?

figure.title: Log fouled — checking the speed
lines: Marks on deck 22 m apart, bow to stern
The chip passes from mark to mark in 4.0 s

options: 5.5 kn
questions.why: 22 m ÷ 4.0 s = 5.5 m/s; × 3,600 ÷ 1,852 = 10.7 kn through the water.

questions.q: On the approach the radar overlay sits off the chart, as on the card. What do you navigate by?

figure.title: Radar overlay on the plotter
lines: Coast echo 0.3 M east of the charted coast
The same offset all round, steady
Radar ranges to the cliffs agree together

options: The charted coastline — echoes always lie off it
The mean of the chart and the echoes
The overlay — the radar is 0.3 M out
Radar ranges — the plotter’s position may be off
questions.why: A steady, uniform offset means the plotter’s position (the GNSS or the chart datum) is wrong, not the radar. Fix by radar ranges near the coast.
questions.ref: Radar and the plotter — overlay offset

questions.q: The plotter shows this alarm, but the radar shows no line of dots on that bearing. Why not?

figure.title: Plotter, 0510
lines: Radar on 12 M: no line of dots there

options: An AIS-SART sends AIS only — there is no radar reply
The survivors are below the radar horizon
On test the dots are switched off
Your radar gain is too low to show them
questions.why: An AIS-SART (MMSI 970) reports its GNSS position by AIS; only a radar SART paints dots. Head for the AIS position and alert the MRCC.

questions.q: The plotter sounds an alarm for this AIS target. What do you do?
options: Switch the AIS alarms off for the day
Note it in the log — someone is testing a SART
Head for it and send a MAYDAY RELAY
Alert the MRCC — a liferaft is out
questions.why: An AIS-SART on test sends "SART TEST"; in distress it sends "SART ACTIVE". Log it and carry on; act at once on ACTIVE.

questions.q: You are fitting out for a 150 M crossing, as on the card. Which backup do you add?

figure.title: Fit-out for a 150 M crossing
lines: All navigation on one NMEA 2000 network
One battery bank, one GNSS antenna

options: A larger house battery bank
A second plotter on the same network
A handheld GNSS and VHF on their own batteries
A spare display for the main plotter
questions.why: A backup is a backup only if it shares nothing: its own aerial, power and screen. A second plotter on the same network fails with it.
questions.ref: Integrated electronics — single point of failure

questions.q: The GNSS fails 45 M from a low coast, as on the card. How do you plan the landfall now?

figure.title: GNSS lost, 0130 — 45 M to the landfall
lines: Harbour on a low coast; streams uncertain
Light on the point 3 M W of it: Fl(2) 10s 20M
Radar, sounder and DR all good

options: Follow a ship’s AIS track towards the coast
Wait offshore until the GNSS comes back
Steer straight at the harbour on the DR
Aim off to one side, so you know which way to turn
questions.why: After 45 M of DR the error may lie either side. Aim off on purpose; at the coast the radar, sounder and light tell you to turn one way.

questions.q: Your watch leader says Rule 17 leaves you nothing to do but hold on. What does Rule 2 add?

figure.title: Night, 120 M offshore, under sail
lines: You: 22 m sloop, the stand-on vessel
Ship 40° on your port bow, 4 M
Bearing steady, no sign of altering

options: Precautions too — call her, light up your sails
Fire a red flare so that she cannot miss you
Nothing — holding on is all a stand-on vessel does
Turn to port now and cross well ahead of her
questions.why: Rule 2(a): no rule excuses neglect of good seamanship — a VHF call, a light on the sails (Rule 36); a red flare means distress.

questions.q: You must give way to A, but B is close on your starboard quarter. What do you do?

figure.title: Clear night, open sea
lines: A: ship on your stbd bow, 2.5 M
B: overtaking on stbd quarter, 3 cables

options: Turn hard to starboard to pass astern of A
Slow right down or stop and let A pass ahead
Turn to port — the only side that is open
Hold on — B being there makes you stand-on
questions.why: Rules 2(b), 8(e) and 16: a starboard turn closes B; to port you cross A's bow — taking off speed keeps you clear of both.

questions.q: Your crew switches on the anchor light. Are you a vessel at anchor under the Rules?

figure.title: Gale, 130 M offshore, night
lines: Lying to a parachute sea anchor

options: Yes — you are held by it and not making way
Yes — a sea anchor is an anchor under Rule 3
No — you are not held to the ground: under way
Neither — a drifting yacht is outside the Rules
questions.why: Rule 3(i): under way means not at anchor, made fast to the shore or aground — a sea anchor holds you to the water, not the seabed.

questions.q: Under sail at night, you are converging with this warship as a helicopter lands on her flight deck. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Night · warship, helicopter landing aft

options: She does — RAM covers only buoys and cables
You — any warship has the right of way
She does — power keeps clear of sail
You — recovering aircraft makes her RAM
questions.why: Rule 3(g)(iv): launching or recovering aircraft is restricted in ability to manoeuvre — red-white-red; Rule 18(b): sail keeps clear.

questions.q: Which part of the Rules governs you and this ship?

figure.title: Clear where you are, 0300
lines: Fog bank 1 M to the east
Radar: a ship inside it, 4 M, closing

options: Rule 19 — you are near an area of fog
Rule 19 for her, the steering rules for you
None until her lights come into sight
Rules 11–18 — your own visibility is clear
questions.why: Rule 19(a): it applies to vessels not in sight of one another when navigating in or near an area of restricted visibility.

questions.q: Your mate says the alarms make this a proper look-out. What does Rule 5 say?

figure.title: Night watch, 140 M offshore
lines: Watchkeeper below, out of the rain
Radar guard zone 3 M, AIS alarm on
A look round on deck every 20 min

options: Enough offshore — Rule 5 is for coastal waters
Not enough — a look-out on deck at all times
Enough if the guard zone is set out to 6 M
Enough — radar and AIS are 'all available means'
questions.why: Rule 5: a proper look-out at all times by sight and hearing as well as radar and AIS — small craft and debris raise no alarm.

questions.q: Your 22 m motor yacht has plotted this target in fog. What CPA would a 10° turn to starboard now give?
options: About 1.1 M — enough to pass clear
About 0.1 M — it brings her closer
About 0.6 M — far too small a turn
About 0.2 M — the turn changes nothing
questions.why: Her true vector 271°T 15 kn less yours 010°T 12 kn gives CPA 0.6 M. Rule 8(b): one large alteration — 60° gives 2.4 M.

questions.q: Your 22 m motor yacht is closing this small target. From the plot, what are her true course and speed, and so the situation?

figure.title: Clear night · you 270°T, 12 kn
lines: No lights seen yet, no AIS

options: About 090°T, 8 kn — head-on, both turn starboard
About 090°T, 20 kn — head-on, both turn starboard
About 090°T, 4 kn — head-on, both turn starboard
About 270°T, 4 kn — you are overtaking her
questions.why: Relative motion 090°T 8 kn plus your own 270°T 12 kn gives her 270°T 4 kn: once in sight, Rule 13 — you keep clear.

questions.q: You decide to give way by slowing your 22 m motor yacht to 4 kn now. What CPA will that give?
options: About 3.9 M — she passes well ahead
About 5.9 M — she passes far ahead
About 1.7 M — she passes ahead
About 0.5 M — no better than now
questions.why: New relative vector: her 280°T 12 kn minus your 000°T 4 kn; from 040°T 6.0 M its CPA is 3.9 M — Rule 8(e), taking off way.

questions.q: Your mate wants to stand the crew down. What does Rule 7(c) say?

figure.title: Fog, 0310
lines: Your yacht yawing ±10° in the swell

options: Not yet — first turn to port to open the CPA
Not yet — one minute of data is scanty
Stand down — 2.5 M is a safe passing
Stand down — MARPA counts as radar plotting
questions.why: Rule 7(c): no assumptions on scanty radar information — a vector a minute after acquisition, with the yacht yawing, is not yet steady.

questions.q: You take bearings of this 330 m tanker's bridge, right aft. They draw slowly aft, about 1° a minute. Is there a risk of collision?

figure.note: 1.0 M · bearing of her bridge draws aft

options: No — the bearing is changing, so she passes clear
Only if her AIS shows a CPA under 0.5 M
It may still exist — her bow is 300 m ahead of it
No — a steady bearing is the only sign of risk
questions.why: Rule 7(d)(ii): risk may exist despite a bearing change with a very large ship at close range — her bow passes far closer than her bridge.

questions.q: Your mate wants to come back to the old course at once. What does Rule 8(d) say?

figure.title: AIS, 1420
lines: You turned 50° to starboard for ship A
A now: CPA 2.0 M, TCPA 9 min

options: As soon as she is abeam, at any range
Now — and alter again if the CPA closes
Now — the CPA already shows 2.0 M
Not until she is finally past and clear
questions.why: Rule 8(d): the action must result in passing at a safe distance, its effect checked until the other vessel is finally past and clear.

questions.q: Motoring up a narrow channel in your 23 m motor yacht, you meet this tanker coming down. Which rules govern you?

figure.note: Narrow channel · you: 23 m motor yacht

options: Rules 9(a) and 14 — keep to starboard, port to port
Rule 18 — a power vessel gives way to a larger one
Rule 9(b) — as a small craft you must not impede her
Rule 9(d) — you must not cross ahead of her bow
questions.why: Rule 9(b) covers vessels under 20 m and sailing vessels; at 23 m under power you keep to starboard (9(a)) and meet her as Rule 14 says.

questions.q: Motoring up a narrow channel at night in your 22 m motor yacht, you meet this vessel working in the fairway. What do the Rules say?

figure.note: Night · narrow channel, ahead, coming down

options: Neither — Rule 9 suspends Rule 18 in a channel
She must not impede you, but if risk arises you keep clear
She must keep clear of you — fishing has no rights here
You keep clear, and she may work wherever she likes
questions.why: Rule 9(c): fishing must not impede vessels navigating in the channel; Rule 8(f)(iii): once risk exists, Rule 18 still binds you.

questions.q: Your passage runs past this traffic separation scheme without using it. How do you plan the route?

figure.note: Traffic separation scheme · north up

options: Cut across its end, where the lanes meet
Anchor near its end to wait for daylight
Keep clear of it by as wide a margin as you can
Run along the edge of the separation zone
questions.why: Rule 10(h): a vessel not using a scheme avoids it by as wide a margin as practicable; 10(f), (g): care near its ends, no anchoring.

questions.q: You are bound along this coast, past the scheme. May you use the inshore traffic zone?

figure.note: Traffic separation scheme · north up

options: Yes — any yacht may use the inshore zone
Only by night — by day, use the lane
Yes — every vessel under 50 m may use it
No — at 22 m under power you must use the lane
questions.why: Rule 10(d): the inshore zone is for vessels under 20 m, sailing and fishing vessels, or to reach a place in it — not a 22 m motor yacht passing by.

questions.q: Crossing a scheme at night, you see these lights in the separation zone ahead. What is she, and may she be there?

figure.note: Night · inside the separation zone, ahead

options: Fishing, not trawling — she may fish in the zone
Not under command — drifted in; call the VTS
Fishing — not allowed there; report her
A pilot vessel on station — the zone is hers
questions.why: Red over white all-round, no sidelights: fishing other than trawling, not making way; Rule 10(e)(ii) lets her fish in the zone.

questions.q: Risk of collision now exists. Who has a duty to act?

figure.title: Crossing the westbound lane
lines: Your 22 m sloop, under sail, 4 kn
Ship following the lane, 1.2 M off
Bearing steady — you left it late

options: Only you — Rule 10(j) puts it all on you
Both — you not to impede, she to keep clear
Neither — hold on, and she will pass
Only she — you are the sailing vessel
questions.why: Rule 8(f): your duty not to impede stands at close range too, and the ship, once risk exists, must still follow Rule 18 and keep clear.

questions.q: Your 23 m motor yacht is crossing the eastbound lane at right angles. This ship, following the lane, is on your port bow on a steady bearing. Who gives way?

figure.note: Eastbound lane · bearing steady, 3 M

options: You do — vessels crossing a lane always give way
Neither — Rule 10 replaces Rule 15 in a scheme
She does — Rule 15; you stand on and watch her
You do — Rule 10(j) puts you at the bottom
questions.why: Rule 10(j) binds vessels under 20 m and sailing vessels only; Rule 10(a) leaves Rule 15 in force — she has you on her starboard side.

questions.q: Later you see her crossing the lane against the flow of traffic. Is she breaking Rule 10?

figure.title: NAVTEX, 0600
lines: Keep 2 M clear; RAM signals shown

options: Yes — every vessel in a lane must follow its flow
No — but she must give way to you under sail
Yes — she may cross only at right angles
No — cable work exempts her; keep clear of her
questions.why: Rule 10(l): a vessel restricted in ability to manoeuvre laying cable in a scheme is exempt from Rule 10 as far as the work needs; Rule 18 applies.

questions.q: You take over the watch and check the lights. What is wrong?

figure.title: Your 22 m ketch, 0100
lines: Main and mizzen up, engine at 1,800 rpm

options: The red-over-green — it says you are under sail
The steaming light — with sail up you show none
Nothing — the extra lights only add a warning
The sidelights — show the tricolour instead
questions.why: With the engine driving you are power-driven (Rule 3(b)); Rule 25(c) red-over-green is for sailing vessels only — and no tricolour over 20 m.

questions.q: Your 24 m motor yacht is closing this coaster from her starboard side. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: You 020°T 20 kn · she 045°T 12 kn · bears 345°T

options: She does — she is on your port bow
You — you are coming up from abaft her beam
You — but only until you are abeam of her
She does — the slower vessel gives way
questions.why: From her you bear 165°T, 120° from her bow — over 22.5° abaft her beam: Rule 13, you keep clear until finally past and clear.

questions.q: From your 22 m motor yacht you see these lights on your port bow, on a steady bearing. What do you do?

figure.note: Night · on your port bow, bearing steady

options: Turn to port to pass ahead of her bow
Treat her as power-driven — you stand on
Treat her as under sail — keep clear, early
Stand on, and sound five short blasts
questions.why: Red-over-green with a steaming light below: in doubt (Rules 2 and 7(a)) take the worse case — a sailing vessel you must keep clear of.

questions.q: Under sail at night, you are converging with this vessel on a steady bearing. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Night · on your starboard bow, closing

options: You do — she is at work and has priority
Neither — both of you turn to starboard
You do — a pilot vessel on duty is RAM
She does — power keeps clear of sail
questions.why: White over red is a pilot vessel on duty — a power-driven vessel with no special place in Rule 18: she keeps out of your way.

questions.q: Who keeps clear now that risk of collision exists?

figure.title: Off Corfu at dusk, under power
lines: A seaplane on the water, taxiing

options: You — Rule 15 then binds her as it would a ship
You — aircraft always have the right of way
She does — she is on your starboard side
She does — a seaplane always keeps clear
questions.why: Rule 18(e): a seaplane on the water keeps well clear in general, but where risk of collision exists she follows Part B — she is to starboard.

questions.q: Offshore at night, you see these lights moving at great speed just above the water. What is she, and who keeps clear?

figure.note: Night · very fast, just above the water

options: A hovercraft — you keep clear of her
A WIG craft in flight — she keeps clear of you
An aircraft in distress — call MAYDAY RELAY
A fast patrol boat — stop until she passes
questions.why: Rule 23(c): a WIG craft taking off, landing or flying near the surface adds a flashing red; Rule 18(f): she keeps well clear of all vessels.

questions.q: Annex I sets the spacing for a vessel of your length. What is the least height for the upper red light?

figure.title: Engine dead, 90 M offshore
lines: Your 22 m motor yacht, not under command
Rigging two all-round reds on the mast

options: 3 m — 1 m apart, the lower at least 2 m up
4 m — the height the lower light needs
6 m — 2 m apart, the lower at least 4 m up
8 m — 2 m apart, the lower at least 6 m up
questions.why: Annex I 2(i): from 20 m, lights in a vertical line are at least 2 m apart, the lowest at least 4 m above the hull: 4 + 2 = 6 m.

questions.q: In fog you are catching up this radar target fine on your starboard bow. May you alter to port to pass her?

figure.note: Fog · radar: 1.5 M, same course, 4 kn; you 12 kn

options: Yes — in fog any alteration is allowed
No — sound two prolonged, two short and wait
No — never to port for a target ahead of the beam
Yes — she is a vessel you are overtaking
questions.why: Rule 19(d)(i): avoid turning to port for a vessel forward of the beam — other than for a vessel being overtaken.

questions.q: Which action keeps within Rule 19?

figure.title: Fog · you 000°T, 10 kn
lines: A: 30° on stbd bow, closing, CPA 0.2 M
B: on stbd quarter, overtaking, CPA 0.3 M

options: Slow to bare steerage way, or stop
A bold turn to port, away from B
Speed up to draw ahead of them both
A bold turn to starboard, for A
questions.why: Rule 19(d): no turn to port for A, forward of the beam; none towards B, abaft it — so 19(e): cut speed to steerage way, stop if need be.

questions.q: Your crew wants to sail on the masthead tricolour. May you?
options: Yes — with the red-over-green above it
No — the tricolour is only for yachts under 20 m
Yes — but only offshore, away from traffic
Yes — any sailing yacht may use it
questions.why: Rule 25(b): the combined masthead lantern is for sailing vessels under 20 m; at 22 m you show separate sidelights and a sternlight.

questions.q: What is the least height above the hull at which Annex I lets you place the masthead light?

figure.title: Your new 22 m motor yacht
lines: One masthead light, on the radar arch

options: 12 m — the upper limit in the rule
2.5 m above the gunwale
6.4 m — her breadth, as it is over 6 m
6.0 m — the fixed minimum
questions.why: Annex I 2(a)(i): from 20 m, the masthead light is at least 6 m above the hull, or the breadth if greater — never more than 12 m needed.

questions.q: What is the highest above the hull that Annex I lets you fit the sidelights?

figure.title: Your 22 m motor yacht
lines: Masthead light 7.2 m above the hull
Sidelights to go on the wheelhouse sides

options: 3.6 m — half of the masthead height
6.2 m — 1 m below the masthead light
4.0 m — the least height for lights in a line
5.4 m — three-quarters of the masthead height
