questions.why: Annex I 2(g): a power vessel's sidelights are no higher than three-quarters of the forward masthead light: 0.75 × 7.2 = 5.4 m.

questions.q: If neither alters, how long does the ship have from first seeing your lights to meeting you?

figure.title: Clear night, reciprocal courses
lines: You: 22 m sloop under sail, 8 kn
Ship: 16 kn, keeping a good look-out
Your lights carry their rule ranges

options: About 5.0 minutes
About 15 minutes
About 2.5 minutes
About 12.5 minutes
questions.why: Under sail you show no masthead light; Rule 22(b): sidelights of 12–50 m carry 2 M; closing at 24 kn: 2 ÷ 24 h = 5.0 min.

questions.q: Which of this ship's lights can you see?

figure.note: At night · she bears 300°T, heading 160°T

options: Both masthead lights and her green sidelight
Both masthead lights and her red sidelight
Only her sternlight
Both masthead lights and both sidelights
questions.why: You bear 120°T from her, 40° on her port bow: inside her masthead and red sectors (to 112.5° on each side), outside her sternlight's.

questions.q: Strictly, what does Rule 24 ask your yacht to show while she tows the RIB?

figure.title: Your 22 m motor yacht, at night
lines: Towing your 5 m RIB, 30 m astern
No vessel in distress — just the tender
Lifting it means a stop at sea

options: Your usual lights — a tender is not a tow
Your usual lights, with a torch shone on the RIB
Two masthead lights in a line, sides, stern, towing light
Towing lights only once the tow is over 200 m
questions.why: Rule 24(a): two masthead lights in a vertical line, sidelights, sternlight and a yellow towing light; 24(i) relief is for a tow in distress.

questions.q: What should the tug show, by night and by day?

figure.title: Tug and tow, crossing ahead
lines: Towline 180 m, tug's stern to barge

options: Two masthead lights — the towline is under 200 m
Two masthead lights, as she is under 50 m
Three masthead lights in a line; a ball by day
Three masthead lights in a line; a diamond by day
questions.why: Rule 24(a): the tow is measured from the tug's stern to the after end of the tow: 180 + 60 = 240 m, over 200 m.

questions.q: Is she lit correctly, and what will she sound in fog while making way?

figure.title: Night, 2 M off
lines: A ship's lights: two masthead lights,
AIS: tug pushing a barge, 160 m

options: Yes — lit as one power vessel; one prolonged
No — the barge needs its own lights; 1 long, 3 short
Yes — but in fog she sounds 1 long, 2 short
No — she needs towing lights; 1 long, 2 short
questions.why: Rule 24(b): a rigidly connected composite unit is lit as one power-driven vessel; Rule 35(f): she sounds as one — one prolonged blast.

questions.q: How many all-round white lights should the pipeline show along its length?

figure.title: Tow at night, from NAVTEX
lines: Pipeline section 230 m long, 2 m wide
Partly submerged, towed by a tug
Low in the water, hard to see

options: Two, one at each end
Four, about 77 m apart
Three, about 115 m apart
Five, about 58 m apart
questions.why: Rule 24(g): a light at each end and more between, so none is over 100 m apart: 230 m needs 3 gaps — 4 lights, 77 m apart.

questions.q: You come up on this vessel working among a fishing fleet at night. What is she doing?

figure.note: Night · among a fleet, no sidelights

options: Trawling with her net fast on a wreck
Fishing with gear out over 150 m
Trawling and hauling her nets
Trawling and shooting her nets
questions.why: Annex II: below green over white, white over red means hauling nets; two whites, shooting; two reds, the net fast on an obstruction.

questions.q: Motoring at night off the Spanish coast, you see these lights ahead. What is she, and what do you do?

figure.note: Night · the yellows flash in turn, once a second

options: A tug with a tow over 200 m — pass astern of it
A hovercraft under way — treat her as power
A trawler shooting her nets — pass close astern
A purse seiner hampered by her net — keep well clear
questions.why: Annex II 3: two yellow lights flashing alternately every second, below the fishing lights, mark a purse seiner hampered by her gear.

questions.q: You see these lights ahead on a dark night. What is she, and what does it mean for you?

figure.note: Night · not moving, no sidelights

options: A trawler with her net fast — she cannot move off
A trawler shooting nets — she will soon get under way
A trawler not under command, drifting
A trawler at anchor, fishing through the night
questions.why: Annex II 2(a)(iii): two reds below the trawling lights mean the net is fast on an obstruction; two reds alone would mean NUC.

questions.q: This dredger is at anchor. Is she showing the right lights?

figure.note: Night · not moving; no anchor light seen

options: No — she must add her anchor lights
Yes — at anchor these replace her anchor lights
Yes — and you may pass her on either side
No — at anchor she shows anchor lights only
questions.why: Rule 27(d)(iv): a dredger at anchor shows red-white-red and the red and green pairs instead of anchor lights; pass on the green side.

questions.q: What does this tell you?

figure.title: Calm day, 2 M off Gozo
lines: A 6 m RIB stopped, bubbles nearby
On her: a rigid board of code flag A,

options: She has a pilot on board and is on duty
She is in distress and needs assistance
Divers down — keep well clear, at slow speed
She is fishing with long lines astern
questions.why: Rule 27(e): a small vessel engaged in diving shows a rigid replica of code flag A at least 1 m high — she cannot get out of your way.

questions.q: What is she doing?

figure.title: By day, off a naval area
lines: A grey warship, under way, slow
Three black balls: one at the foremast
head, one at each end of the fore yard

options: Restricted — towing a sonar body astern
Aground — the three balls are her signal
Not under command, with divers down
Clearing mines — do not approach her
questions.why: Rule 27(f): three balls (by night three greens) at the foremast head and the yardarms mark mine clearance; aground is three in a line.

questions.q: Which fog signal do the Rules ask of you?

figure.title: At anchor, 0400, fog rolls in
lines: Your 22 m yacht, off a strange coast

options: Ring the bell rapidly for 5 s every minute
Any efficient sound signal every 2 minutes
One prolonged, two short every 2 minutes
The bell, then a gong aft, every minute
questions.why: Rules 33 and 35(g): at 20 m or more you carry a bell and ring it at anchor; 'some other efficient signal' is allowed only under 20 m.

questions.q: How long from first hearing her whistle until you meet?

figure.title: Fog, head-on, neither alters
lines: Her whistle carries its Annex III range

options: About 2.1 minutes
About 4.3 minutes
About 3.2 minutes
About 10 minutes
questions.why: Annex III: the whistle of a vessel of 200 m or more carries 2 M; closing at 20 + 8 = 28 kn: 2 ÷ 28 h = 4.3 min.

questions.q: What is she?

figure.title: Fog, in an anchorage
lines: a bell rung rapidly for 5 s, forward,
then a gong rung rapidly, aft

options: A vessel of 100 m or more, aground
Two vessels at anchor, one astern of the other
A vessel of 100 m or more, at anchor
A vessel under 100 m, at anchor and fishing
questions.why: Rule 35(g): a vessel of 100 m or more at anchor rings the bell forward, then the gong aft; aground adds three strokes either side.

questions.q: This ship, 3 M away, gives one flash of an all-round white light above her masthead lights. What does she mean?

figure.note: Night · ship 3 M off · you hear nothing

options: I am altering my course to port
I am operating astern propulsion
I am in doubt about your intentions
I am altering my course to starboard
questions.why: Rule 34(b): a light signal of one flash, about a second long, means 'I am altering my course to starboard' — seen up to 5 M.

questions.q: What is she telling you?

figure.title: Night, 110 M offshore, calm
lines: A yacht 1 M off sounds her horn
without stopping, and flashes a light:

options: She is in distress — go to her aid
She is testing her horn — no action needed
She doubts your intentions — keep clear
She warns you off — she is fishing
questions.why: Annex IV: a continuous sounding of any fog-signal apparatus and SOS by any signalling method are both distress signals.

questions.q: What is the orange sheet for?

figure.title: In the liferaft, 140 M offshore
lines: A search aircraft expected at dawn
In the grab bag: an orange sheet
with a black square and a black circle

options: To mark divers down near the raft
To be seen and recognised from the air
To show you are at anchor or aground
To ask ships to keep well clear of you
questions.why: Annex IV 3(a): orange canvas with a black square and circle helps identification from the air — as does a dye marker.

questions.q: Your crew wants to show the not-under-command lights. Are they right?

figure.title: Dismasted, 110 M offshore
lines: Rig cut away, engine running well
Motoring at 6 kn for the nearest port

options: Yes — a dismasted yacht is not under command
Yes — and add sidelights while making way
No — under engine you can manoeuvre: power-driven
No — show the RAM lights, red-white-red
questions.why: Rule 3(f): NUC means unable to manoeuvre as the Rules require through an exceptional circumstance — under engine you can: power-driven.

questions.q: Are you and this ship 'in sight of one another' as the Rules mean it?

figure.title: Fog, 0500, visibility 1 cable
lines: Ship on radar and AIS, 2 M, closing
You have spoken to her bridge on VHF

options: Yes — radar contact counts as being in sight
Yes — AIS has identified her by name
Yes — once you have spoken on VHF
No — only when one can see the other by eye
questions.why: Rule 3(k): vessels are in sight only when one can be observed visually from the other — so Rule 19 governs you both, not Rules 11–18.

questions.q: Your crew says this ship is lit against the Rules. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Night, off a naval exercise area
lines: Her masthead lights stand on an

options: Rule 1(e) lets her state set the closest compliance
Warships are outside the Rules altogether
They are right — report her to the coastguard
She must be NUC — the lights mark damage
questions.why: Rule 1(e): a vessel of special construction complies as closely as her Government decides — warships are still bound by the Rules (1(a)).

questions.q: The mate argues that with ARPA running, 22 kn is a safe speed. What does Rule 6 weigh against him?

figure.title: Fog, 0300, 80 M offshore
lines: Your 24 m motor yacht planing, 22 kn
Radar on the 12 M range, ARPA on

options: Only visibility — radar is not a Rule 6 factor
Small craft lost in clutter, the long range scale
Only traffic density, and it is light out here
Nothing — with ARPA any speed is safe offshore
questions.why: Rule 6(b): radar's limits, the range scale in use, sea clutter and small craft it may miss all count — with 2 cables' visibility as well.

questions.q: The AIS and the radar disagree about this ship. Which do you go by?

figure.title: Night, 2200, clear
lines: AIS: ship A, CPA 1.8 M, TCPA 14 min

options: The AIS — its CPA comes from her own GNSS
The AIS — 1.8 M is a safe passing distance
The steady bearing — risk of collision exists
Neither — call her and agree how to pass
questions.why: Rule 7(a), (d)(i): a steady compass bearing means risk, and if in doubt risk is deemed to exist — AIS is one means, not the judge.

questions.q: Your mate says her bearing has drawn 20° left since the turn, so she will pass clear. Will she?
options: Yes — a 20° change of bearing is plenty
No — but only because she is now inside 3 M
Yes — once her bearing moves, risk is gone
No — her compass bearing is still 040°T
questions.why: Rule 7(d)(i): judge by compass bearing — 020°T + 20° relative = 040°T, unchanged: risk still exists, and your turn was too small.

questions.q: Your 23 m motor yacht is about to cross this dredged channel. A deep-draught ship coming down it bears steady on your port bow. What do you do?

figure.note: Dredged channel · ship 1.5 M, bearing steady

options: Wait — do not cross if it would impede her
Cross now, sounding five short to warn her
Cross now — only boats under 20 m must wait
Hold on — she has you on her starboard side
questions.why: Rule 9(d): no vessel of any size may cross a narrow channel if that impedes one that can navigate only within it — 9(b)'s 20 m limit isn't here.

questions.q: Your 22 m motor yacht is bound for Port A, inside this inshore traffic zone. May you leave the lane and use the zone to get there?

figure.note: Traffic separation scheme · north up

options: Only by day — at night you must use the lane
Yes — you are bound for a port within the zone
No — at 22 m under power you must stay in the lane
Only under sail — power must keep to the lane
questions.why: Rule 10(d)(ii): any vessel may use an inshore traffic zone when en route to or from a port, installation or place situated within it.

questions.q: You must cross this scheme to the north under sail, but the wind blows straight down the right-angle heading. What do you do?

figure.note: Traffic separation scheme · north up

options: Tack across in short boards up the lanes
Wait in the separation zone for a shift
Motor-sail across on a heading of 000°T
Sail across close-hauled on 045°T
questions.why: Rule 10(c): cross on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the flow — with an engine aboard, 000°T is practicable.

questions.q: You are sailing east along this lane at night in your 22 m sloop. Where in the lane do you keep?

figure.note: Traffic separation scheme · north up

options: Inside the separation zone, out of the way
Down the middle, where the ships expect you
Close along the edge of the separation zone
Near its outer edge, well clear of the zone
questions.why: Rule 10(b)(ii): keep clear of a separation line or zone; near the outer edge you also impede the ships least (10(j)).

questions.q: Your 22 m motor yacht is joining the eastbound lane from its side, at the small angle Rule 10 asks for. This ship in the lane is closing on your port quarter, bearing steady. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Night · joining the lane at 15° · you 10 kn, she 16 kn

options: She does — she is overtaking you
You do — a vessel joining gives way to the lane
Neither — Rule 10 replaces the steering rules
You do — she is the larger, less handy vessel
questions.why: She is 150° from your bow, over 22.5° abaft your beam, seeing your sternlight: Rule 13 — she keeps clear; 10(a) keeps every other Rule in force.

questions.q: You must stop to change the impeller. Where may you do it?

figure.title: 0230, crossing a scheme
lines: Your 22 m motor yacht, one engine
Overheating: 20 min left at low revs
You are in the eastbound lane

options: Anywhere — once stopped, Rule 10 stops applying
In the separation zone — an emergency allows it
In the lane, showing NUC lights while you work
At anchor near the end of the scheme
questions.why: Rule 10(e)(i): a separation zone may be entered in an emergency to avoid immediate danger; 10(g) bars anchoring near a scheme's ends.

questions.q: Crossing a lane under sail in your 22 m ketch, you see these lights on your port bow. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Night · crossing the lane · on your port bow, steady

options: Neither — three reds mean she is aground
She does — power keeps clear of sail
You — avoid impeding her: she's constrained by draught
She does — she has you on her starboard side
questions.why: Rules 18(d) and 28: three all-round reds mark a CBD vessel — all but NUC and RAM avoid impeding her, as 10(j) also asks of you.

questions.q: Which of you must avoid impeding the tanker?

figure.title: Westbound lane, clear night
lines: Tanker: in the lane, CBD lights
You: 23 m sloop under sail, close by

options: Neither — in a lane Rule 10 replaces 18
Only you — a fishing vessel is exempt
Only the trawler — you are under sail
Both — the trawler as well as you
questions.why: Rule 18(d)(i): every vessel but NUC and RAM avoids impeding a CBD vessel — fishing included; in a lane 10(i) and 10(j) say it again.

questions.q: Close-hauled at night, you see this yacht's masthead tricolour showing red, the bearing steady. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Wind N · you 045°T, port tack · she bears 330°T

options: You — you cannot tell which tack she is on
She does — her red shows she is on port tack
She does — she is the yacht to windward
Neither — both of you bear away to starboard
questions.why: Her red puts her heading between 150° and 262°T — either tack in a north wind; Rule 12(a)(iii): on port tack, you keep clear.

questions.q: Your 24 m motor yacht is overtaking this sailing yacht on her port side. Your harbour lies to the east. When may you turn across her bow?

figure.note: You 24 kn · she 6 kn · your harbour lies east

options: Now — she must hold her course and speed
Only when finally past and clear, well ahead
Once ahead — then she must keep clear of you
As soon as you are abeam of her
questions.why: Rule 13(d): a later change of bearing doesn't make you a crossing vessel — keep clear until finally past and clear; Rule 18 says the same.

questions.q: Your 22 m motor yacht at 15 kn and this ship at 15 kn are closing almost end-on. What do you do?

figure.note: 6 M, 3° to starboard · AIS CPA 0.3 M, stbd to stbd

options: A small turn to starboard, then watch her CPA
Hold on — green to green, she will pass you clear
A bold turn to starboard, early — pass port to port
A small turn to port to open the green-to-green pass
questions.why: Rule 14(c): in doubt, assume head-on and turn to starboard, boldly — a small turn cuts the 0.3 M CPA, and a port turn can cancel hers.

questions.q: What do the Rules ask of you with these two ships?

figure.title: Three ships converging, 0100
lines: A: ship 40° on your port bow, 3 M
B: ship 40° on your stbd bow, 3 M

options: Wait for A to act first, then deal with B
Turn to port to pass astern of A, clear of B
Hold on — A gives way to you, so you stand on
Keep clear of B, boldly — and keep watching A
questions.why: Rule 15: B has you on her port side — keep clear of her (16); you remain stand-on for A, so watch her under Rule 17 as you turn.

questions.q: Your 22 m motor yacht is the stand-on vessel. When may you first act on your own to avoid this ship?

figure.title: Clear night, you stand on
lines: Ship on your port bow, bearing 300°T
0310: no reply to your five short

options: Now — it is apparent she is not keeping clear
Only when she is too close to avoid you alone
Never — the stand-on vessel holds on to the end
Only once she has answered your five short
questions.why: Rule 17(a)(ii): you may act as soon as it is apparent she is not taking appropriate action; 17(b) makes it a duty only at the last stage.

questions.q: You are the stand-on vessel in your 22 m motor yacht. How do you answer her?

figure.title: Night, 4 M apart, closing
lines: Ship on your port bow, bearing steady
VHF: 'Motor yacht, I am keeping my
course — alter to port, green to green'

options: Agree, and sound two short blasts as you turn
Refuse the port turn — slow down or turn to starboard
Agree — a VHF agreement replaces the Rules
Ignore her — the Rules forbid passing deals by VHF
questions.why: Rules 17(a)(ii) and 17(c): acting as stand-on, don't turn to port for a ship on your port side — a VHF deal doesn't override the Rules.

questions.q: Both radar targets are closing. Which way may you turn to avoid them?

figure.title: Fog · you 090°T, 8 kn
lines: A: 20° on your port bow, 3 M,
B: on your port quarter, 1.5 M,

options: Neither way — Rule 19 allows only slowing
To port — to pass astern of A
To starboard — away from both of them
To port — but only once B has passed
questions.why: Rule 19(d): no turn to port for A, forward of the beam, and none towards B, abaft it — a bold turn to starboard breaks neither.

questions.q: On watch in your 22 m motor yacht, you are coming up on these lights from astern at 6 kn more than her. What is she, and who keeps clear?

figure.note: Night · fine ahead · radar: she makes 3 kn, you 9 kn

options: Aground, with her anchor light — pass wide
Fishing, not trawling — her gear is astern
NUC and stopped — the white is her anchor light
NUC and making way — you keep clear of her
questions.why: Rule 27(a): two all-round reds; making way she adds sidelights and a sternlight — the one you see from astern. Rules 13 and 18: you keep clear.

questions.q: Your radar shows this vessel moving with exactly the set and rate of the current. She shows only these two reds. Is she lit correctly?

figure.note: Radar: she moves 070°T 2.0 kn · current 070°T 2.0 kn

options: Yes — drifting, she makes no way through the water
No — two reds alone need an anchor light too
Yes — a NUC vessel never shows sidelights
No — she is moving, so she must show sidelights
questions.why: Rule 27(a)(iii): NUC adds sidelights and a sternlight only when making way through the water — drifting with the stream, she isn't.

questions.q: Which day shapes does Rule 27 ask your yacht to hoist now?

figure.title: By day, 90 M offshore
lines: Your 22 m motor yacht: rudder jammed
You cannot steer or keep clear

options: Ball, diamond, ball in a vertical line
Two black balls in a vertical line
Three black balls in a vertical line
One black ball where it can best be seen
questions.why: Rule 27(a)(ii): not under command — two balls in a vertical line; one ball means at anchor, three aground, ball-diamond-ball RAM.

questions.q: Motoring at night, you are catching up these lights from right astern. Can you tell from them whether the tow is over 200 m long?

figure.note: Night · ahead, you catching up · radar: two echoes in line

options: Yes — the tow's diamond is lit at night
Yes — a tow over 200 m shows two yellows
No — from astern no masthead lights show
Yes — the tow then shows a second sternlight
questions.why: Rule 24(a): the length shows in two or three masthead lights, seen from ahead and abeam; from astern, only the towing light and sternlights.

questions.q: This tug, towing a barge astern, is on your starboard bow at night. Which of the tug's own lights face you?

figure.note: Night · she bears 050°T, heading 100°T, towing astern

options: Her masthead lights and her green sidelight
Her white sternlight alone — no yellow
Her masthead lights and her red sidelight
Her yellow towing light over her sternlight
questions.why: You bear 230°T from her, 130° from her bow — inside the 135° astern arc her sternlight shares with the yellow towing light above it.

questions.q: Overtaking at night, you see these lights ahead; the low white on the left is the sternlight of her tow. What is she?

figure.note: Night · ahead, you are catching up

options: A tug whose tow severely restricts her turning
A tug whose tow is over 200 m long
A pilot vessel towing a disabled yacht
A tug towing a vessel not under command
questions.why: Rule 27(c): a tow that severely restricts her from deviating from her course adds red-white-red to the 24(a) lights — yellow over the sternlight.

questions.q: You are slowly catching up this dredger, working under way. On which side do you overtake her?

figure.note: Night · dredging under way · you are right astern

options: On neither — no one may overtake a RAM vessel
On your left — her port side, by the greens
On either side — under way the pairs lapse
On your right — her starboard side, by the reds
questions.why: Rule 27(d): the greens mark the side to pass, the reds the obstruction — from astern her port side is on your left; Rule 13: you keep clear.

questions.q: Motoring along the coast at 2200, you see these lights on a small boat 4 cables ahead, beside a charted dive site. What do you do?

figure.note: Night · a small boat, not moving, by a dive site

options: Stand by her — these are her distress lights
Pass close — she is only a boat at anchor
Slow down and pass wide — divers may be down
Stand on — a small boat must keep clear of you
questions.why: Rule 27(e)(i): a vessel too small for all the RAM lights shows red-white-red when diving — divers may be in the water round her.

questions.q: Your crew says the extra white light on this anchored buoy tender is a mistake. Are they right?

figure.note: Night · buoy tender at anchor, servicing a buoy

options: Yes — a white there means she is making way
Yes — anchor lights are for ships over 50 m
Yes — at anchor the RAM lights replace it
No — RAM at anchor adds her anchor light
questions.why: Rule 27(b)(iv): a RAM vessel at anchor shows her anchor light as well; only dredging and underwater work (27(d)) drop it at anchor.

questions.q: In a fishing fleet at night, you are 1 M astern of this vessel and closing. What is she doing?

figure.note: 1 M ahead, in a fleet · lower pair seen from 1 M

options: Shooting her trawl — it is going out astern
Towing another trawler a short way astern
Hauling her trawl — she is about to stop
Net fast on a wreck — she cannot move off
questions.why: Annex II 2(a)(i): two whites below the green-over-white trawling lights mean shooting nets — her trawl is paying out astern, towards you.

questions.q: Your track runs between these two vessels. What do you do?

figure.title: Night, 1 M ahead
lines: Each: green over white, all round

options: Stand on — the searchlights mean they'll give way
Go round both — one net is towed between them
Pass close astern of the nearer — gear is ahead
Pass between — 4 cables leaves you room
questions.why: Annex II 2(b): pair trawlers each direct a searchlight forward and towards the other — their net is strung between them: never pass between.

questions.q: On a night passage under power, this cluster of lights comes at you from right ahead at great speed. What is she, and what is your move?

figure.note: Night · dead ahead, closing very fast

options: A vessel towing — the yellow shows her tow
A WIG craft in flight — she keeps clear of you
A hovercraft head-on — alter to starboard
A purse seiner — keep clear of her net
questions.why: Rule 23(b): an air-cushion vessel in the non-displacement mode adds an all-round flashing yellow; she is power-driven, so Rule 14 applies.

questions.q: Your mate says this vessel must be 50 m or more, as she shows two masthead lights. Is he right?

figure.note: Night · 3 M off · no AIS

options: Yes — only ships of 50 m or more show two
Yes — under 50 m, two would mean towing
No — two masthead lights mean under 50 m
Not necessarily — under 50 m she may show two
questions.why: Rule 23(a)(ii): under 50 m a second masthead light is not required but allowed — and a tug's are in a vertical line, not like these.

questions.q: Which light falls short of Rule 22 for your length?

figure.title: Survey of your 22 m motor yacht

options: The masthead light — 5 M is needed from 20 m
The sternlight — 3 M is needed from 20 m
The anchor light — 3 M is needed from 20 m
The sidelights — 3 M is needed from 20 m
questions.why: Rule 22(b): from 12 to 50 m a masthead light carries 5 M (only 3 M under 20 m); sidelights, sternlight and all-round lights 2 M.

questions.q: How high and how far aft must that after masthead light be, at the least?

figure.title: Your 24 m motor yacht
lines: You choose to fit a second, after

options: 8.5 m up, and 6 m abaft the forward one
11.0 m up, and 12 m abaft the forward one
11.0 m up, and 6 m abaft the forward one
8.5 m up, and 12 m abaft the forward one
questions.why: Annex I 2(a)(ii), 3(a): at least 4.5 m higher than the forward light (6.5 + 4.5 = 11.0 m) and half her length, 12 m, abaft it.

questions.q: Does this light meet the Rules for the Rule 34(b) light signals?

figure.title: Refit, your 24 m motor yacht
lines: white, 2 M range, to go 1 m above it

options: No — but only the height: 4.5 m clear is needed
Yes — 2 M is the range for all-round lights
No — it must carry 5 M and sit 2 m clear of it
No — but only the range: 3 M is needed
questions.why: Rule 34(b)(iii) and Annex I 12: an all-round white seen at 5 M at least, 2 m or more vertically apart from a single masthead light.

questions.q: Your crew hoists this small ball, bought for a dinghy. Does it meet Annex I for your yacht?

figure.note: Your 22 m motor yacht at anchor · ball 0.3 m across

options: Yes — any ball seen from 1 M will do
No — at anchor you show two balls, not one
Yes — shape sizes apply only from 50 m
No — from 20 m a ball is at least 0.6 m across
questions.why: Annex I 6: a ball is at least 0.6 m in diameter; only a vessel under 20 m may use smaller shapes to suit her size.

questions.q: At 0300 off the Breton coast you round these lights 1 M off, keeping them in view. From every side you see just these three. What is she?

figure.note: Night · not moving · on a charted shoal

options: Aground — her anchor light and two reds
At anchor and fishing, with her gear out
Not under command and at anchor in the tide
Not under command, making way, seen from astern
questions.why: Rule 30(d): aground — anchor light(s) plus two all-round reds; a white seen from every side is all-round, not a 135° sternlight.

questions.q: Which signals do the Rules ask of you until you float off?

figure.title: 0200, fog, your 22 m ketch aground
lines: On a sandbank, waiting for the flood

options: Two reds only; one prolonged and two short
Anchor light and two reds; bell with three strokes
Two reds only; two prolonged blasts
Anchor light only; the bell rung rapidly, 5 s
questions.why: Rules 30(d), 35(h): anchor light plus two all-round reds; the bell rung rapidly 5 s each minute, with three distinct strokes before and after.

questions.q: With the engines dead, which fog signal does Rule 35 ask of you now?

figure.title: Fog, 90 M offshore, 0400
lines: Your 22 m motor yacht: both engines dead

options: One prolonged, every 2 min or less — you're power
Two prolonged, every 2 min or less — you're stopped
One prolonged and two short, every 2 min or less
The bell, rung rapidly for 5 s every minute
questions.why: Rule 35(c): NUC sounds one prolonged and two short, at most 2 min apart — the two prolonged of 35(b) is for a power vessel able to move.

questions.q: Creeping in at 3 kn, you hear this from the vessel ahead. What is she telling you?

figure.title: Fog, 0500, entering a roadstead
lines: Ahead, each minute: a bell rung
rapidly for about 5 s — and now also

options: She is NUC and drifting down towards you
She is a pilot boat and wants you to stop
She is aground and you are standing into danger
She is at anchor and you are standing into her
questions.why: Rule 35(g): at anchor she rings the bell each minute and may add short-prolonged-short to warn an approaching vessel of her position.

questions.q: Which of these sound signals meets Annex III for your length?

figure.title: Refit: your 23 m motor yacht
lines: C: horn, 2,000 Hz tone, heard 1 M

options: B — 400 Hz, heard at 1 M
D — 400 Hz, heard at 0.5 M
C — 2,000 Hz, heard at 1 M
A — 150 Hz, heard at 2 M
questions.why: Annex III: under 75 m the fundamental is 250–700 Hz; from 20 m the range is 1 M, set by tones up to 700 Hz — 2 kHz counts only under 20 m.

questions.q: Does this bell meet Annex III for your yacht?

figure.title: Fitting out your 22 m yacht
lines: 112 dB at 1 m, striker 4% of its mass

options: Yes — any bell will do under 50 m
No — from 20 m the mouth must be 300 mm
Yes — 110 dB at 1 m is all that is asked
No — from 20 m you need a gong as well
questions.why: Annex III 2: from 20 m the bell's mouth is at least 300 mm across and it gives 110 dB at 1 m; a gong is needed only from 100 m.

questions.q: Is that sound signal right for a yacht under sail?

figure.title: Clear day, under sail alone
lines: Your 22 m ketch bears away to
starboard to pass astern of a ship
Crew gives one short blast as you turn

options: No — only the stand-on vessel may signal
Yes — one short tells her you turn to starboard
No — those signals are for power-driven vessels
Yes — any vessel in sight signals each turn
questions.why: Rule 34(a): manoeuvring signals are given by a power-driven vessel under way, in sight of another — under sail alone you give none.

questions.q: To draw her attention, which use of your lights does Rule 36 allow?

figure.title: Night, 100 M offshore, under sail
lines: Ship 2 M on your starboard bow
Bearing steady; no answer on VHF 16

options: A red flare — the signal ships notice most
The searchlight held on her bridge until she turns
The masthead strobe, flashing until she turns
The searchlight on your own sails, not her bridge
questions.why: Rule 36: a searchlight may be directed towards the danger so as not to embarrass any vessel; strobe-like lights are to be avoided.

questions.q: Which of these sightings is an Annex IV distress signal?

figure.title: Night watch, 120 M offshore
lines: A: a green star from a fishing boat
B: flames from a barrel on a deck
C: a strobe on a racing yacht
D: a searchlight swept over a sail

options: B — the flames on the vessel's deck
D — the searchlight swept over a sail
A — the green star from the fishing boat
C — the strobe on the racing yacht
questions.why: Annex IV 1(h): flames on the vessel, as from a burning tar or oil barrel, mean distress; green stars, strobes and searchlights do not.

questions.q: What do you make of these bangs?

figure.title: Night, 100 M offshore
lines: A vessel 2 M off, hidden in rain
A gun or explosion is heard
about once a minute for 10 min

options: A fog signal — she is at anchor
A distress signal — she needs help
A salute — a warship is passing
A warning — a firing range is active
questions.why: Annex IV 1(a): a gun or other explosive signal fired at intervals of about a minute is a distress signal.

questions.q: Which yacht is NOT making an Annex IV distress signal?

figure.title: By day, 90 M offshore
lines: Yacht A: arms raised and lowered slowly
Yacht B: her ensign flown upside down
Yacht C: a square flag with a ball below
Yacht D: orange smoke from a canister

options: A — the arms raised and lowered
C — the square flag and the ball
B — the ensign flown upside down
D — the orange smoke
questions.why: Annex IV lists arms slowly raised and lowered, a square flag with a ball, orange smoke — an upside-down ensign is not among them.

questions.q: What do the Rules say about your crew's plan?
options: Yes — out-of-date flares are no longer signals
No — but hand flares are fine, rockets not
Yes — if you tell the coastguard first
No — a distress signal is for distress alone
questions.why: Annex IV 2: using or showing any distress signal except to indicate distress is prohibited — a red flare may start a search.

questions.q: You are two days out on an offshore passage, where the boat is drawn, south of the centre of this high. Where does the wind come from?

figure.note: You: south of the centre

options: From about ENE
From about ESE
From about N
From about WSW
questions.why: Round a high in the north air turns clockwise and slightly outwards: on its south side it blows from about ENE.
questions.ref: Pressure systems — wind round a high

questions.q: You are planning a passage south along Portugal, 40 M offshore, from this July chart. What wind do you plan for?

figure.title: Synoptic chart, July, 1200 UTC
lines: Azores high 1030 hPa to the NW
Isobars run N–S along the coast
You: bound S, 40 M off Portugal

options: W 5–6 onshore, a sea breeze by noon
N 5–6, fresher near the capes by afternoon
S 3–4, backing SE by the afternoon
Light and variable under the high
questions.why: High to the NW, heat low over Iberia: the summer northerly (nortada) — strongest in the afternoon and off the capes.
questions.ref: Pressure systems — Azores high and the heat low

questions.q: Your route for the next 24 hours crosses the area shown on the prognosis chart. What weather do you plan for?

figure.title: Prognosis T+24 for your route
lines: Highs to the NE and SW of you
Lows to the NW and SE of you
Isobars far apart over your track

options: Clear skies and a steady sea breeze
A steady fresh breeze from the nearest high
Light, variable wind, with fog or thunder
A gale from the deeper of the two lows
questions.why: A col between two highs and two lows has slack, shifting winds; in warm moist summer air it brings fog or thunderstorms.

questions.q: You are deciding whether to start a 3-day passage south across Biscay, and the forecaster's notes mention the jet stream. What does it tell you?

figure.title: Forecaster's notes, Monday
lines: Jet at 300 hPa: 160 kn, straight W–E

options: Gales at the surface wherever the jet blows
A blocking high will hold for the whole week
Nothing — it is too high to affect the sea
Lows will run fast along it, one after another
questions.why: A strong straight jet steers and feeds surface lows: they form, deepen and race along beneath it in a quick series.
questions.ref: Depressions — the jet stream as context

questions.q: You are in port at 50°N with a two-day passage planned, and you compare two analysis charts 24 hours apart. What is this low doing?
options: Deepening explosively — storm force near it
Filling slowly — the worst of it is over
Moving away — the fall is only diurnal
Deepening normally — a gale at most
questions.why: 28 hPa in 24 h is past the bomb rate (about 21 hPa at 50°N): an explosive low — storm-force winds round it are likely.

questions.q: You are one day out on a passage south-west of Ireland and read the latest analysis. Where do you watch for a new low that could reach you?

figure.title: Analysis, 0600 UTC
lines: Triple point 300 M W of Ireland
Pressure falling fast at the point
Your route: 150 M S of the point

options: Over Iceland, where the old low re-deepens
At the triple point, where the fronts meet
Behind the cold front, in the polar air
Along the warm front, far to the east
questions.why: A new (secondary) low often forms at the triple point of an old occluded system — here 150 M from your route.
questions.ref: Depressions — occlusion and the triple point

questions.q: You are reading the surface analysis before a two-day passage, and one front across your route is drawn like this. What do you plan for along it?

figure.title: Surface analysis, 0000 UTC
lines: on opposite sides of the line

options: A cold front — a squall line, then clear
A trough — showers, then a ridge behind
A stationary front — long rain, poor visibility
An occlusion — one sharp veer, then clear
questions.why: Triangles and semicircles on opposite sides mark a stationary front: wide cloud, long spells of rain and poor visibility.

questions.q: You are on passage in the warm sector, and you get this at 1000 UTC. At about what time does the front reach you if you hold your course?

figure.title: Analysis received 1000 UTC
lines: Cold front 150 M W of you
Now: SW 6 in the warm sector

options: About 1730 UTC
About 2043 UTC
About 1617 UTC
About 1546 UTC
questions.why: Closing speed 20 + 6 = 26 kn: 150 ÷ 26 = 5.77 h = 5 h 46 min after 1000 — about 1546 UTC.

questions.q: You are 120 M offshore when the cold front goes through and the wind veers sharply from SW to NW. What sea do you meet for the next few hours?
options: A confused cross sea — old SW on new NW
The same SW sea, simply easing at once
A smooth sea — the new wind flattens the old
A long, regular swell from the NW only
questions.why: After a big veer the old SW sea keeps running while the NW wind raises a new one across it: a confused, breaking cross sea.
questions.ref: Fronts — the sea after a veer

questions.q: You are planning which side of an approaching low's track to be on during the passage. Which of the two yachts meets the stronger wind?

figure.title: Low 975 hPa moving NE at 30 kn
lines: Its track passes between two yachts
Yacht A: 150 M NW of the track
Yacht B: 150 M SE of the track

options: A — the low's motion adds to its wind there
B — the low's motion adds to its wind there
Both the same — they are equally far off
A — it lies closer to the colder air
questions.why: On the right of a moving low's track (NH) the wind blows the way the low travels, so the two add: SE of a NE-bound low.
questions.ref: Depressions — the stronger side of the track

questions.q: You are reading this satellite image at the chart table before leaving on a two-day passage. What is forming to the west?

figure.title: Satellite image, 0600 UTC
lines: Comma-shaped cloud head to the W
A dark dry slot cutting into it

options: A dying low — its cloud breaking up
A ridge, with clearing air behind it
A rapidly deepening low
A heat low over the warm sea
questions.why: A comma-shaped cloud head with a dry slot cutting in and cooling tops is the signature of a low deepening fast.

questions.q: You plan to cross Biscay in late September, and this is in the outlook. How do you treat it in your plan?

figure.title: Outlook, late September
lines: Your area: 72 to 96 h from now

options: As a dying storm — it will be weak by then
As no risk — such storms never reach here
As a tropical storm — only its eye is a risk
As a deep autumn low — be in port by then
questions.why: Ex-hurricanes often re-deepen as ordinary lows on reaching cooler water and can bring severe gales to European waters.

questions.q: You are measuring the isobar spacing over your track on this chart. What geostrophic wind do you read?

figure.title: Chart and scale
lines: Adjacent isobars over you: 60 M apart

options: About 25 kn
About 50 kn
About 12 kn
About 17 kn
questions.why: The scale is for 4 hPa: two 2-hPa gaps make 120 M, and 120 M on the scale gives 25 kn.

questions.q: You have two synoptic charts with the same isobar spacing over your track. Which gives you more wind than the geostrophic scale shows?

figure.title: Same spacing, two charts
lines: A: isobars curving tight round a low
B: isobars curving round a high

options: Neither — the scale is the gust
B, round the high
Both alike — the scale holds
A, round the deep low
questions.why: Gradient wind: curving round a low the wind is less than geostrophic, round a high it is more, for the same spacing.
questions.ref: Synoptic charts — gradient wind and curvature

questions.q: You work out the wind for the first night of your passage from the chart and these rules. What surface wind do you plan for?
options: About 31 kn from 255° — F7
About 41 kn from 225° — F9
About 31 kn from 225° — F7
About 36 kn from 225° — F8
questions.why: 45 × 0.85 = 38 kn gradient; × 0.8 = 31 kn at the sea surface, backed 15° from 240° to 225°: force 7.
questions.ref: Synoptic charts — forecasting wind from isobars

questions.q: You have just downloaded this prognosis chart for your passage. Which time does it show?
options: 0430 UTC Tuesday
1200 UTC Monday
1200 UTC Tuesday
0000 UTC Tuesday
questions.why: A prognosis is valid at its data time plus the step: 1200 UTC Sunday + 36 h = 0000 UTC Tuesday.

questions.q: Your 24 m yacht's masthead anemometer reads 30 kn, and you log the wind against this forecast. What force do you log?

figure.title: Anemometer and forecast
lines: Masthead sensor: 28 m above the sea
At 28 m wind is ~15 % above 10 m

options: About 26 kn — F6
About 34 kn — F8
About 15 kn — F4
About 30 kn — F7
questions.why: Forecast and Beaufort wind is at 10 m: 30 ÷ 1.15 = 26 kn at 10 m — force 6, as forecast.
questions.ref: Beaufort scale — the height of the anemometer

questions.q: You are on watch in mid-Biscay at 0400 and must log the wind force from the sea alone. What do you write?
options: Force 7 — near gale
Force 8 — gale
Force 10 — storm
Force 6 — strong breeze
questions.why: Moderately high, longer waves, crests breaking into spindrift and foam in well-marked streaks: Beaufort force 8.

questions.q: You are 130 M off the coast when this warning comes in. What mean wind and what sea do you prepare for?
options: 56–63 kn, waves of 9 to 14 m
48–55 kn, waves of 4 to 6 m
48–55 kn, waves of 6 to 9 m
41–47 kn, waves of 4 to 6 m
questions.why: Storm 10 is a mean of 48–55 kn; sea state 'high' is 6–9 m (very rough 4–6, very high 9–14).

questions.q: You will spend three hours of tonight's passage in this sea. What is the biggest wave you plan for?
options: About 3.5 m
About 4.4 m
About 2.2 m
About 6.5 m
questions.why: 3 h of 8-s waves is about 1350 waves, so the 1-in-1000 wave will come: 1.86 × 3.5 = 6.5 m.
questions.ref: Sea state — significant and maximum wave height

questions.q: You must decide whether to carry on through the night in this new wind. What significant height do you plan for, and what odd wave?

figure.title: W 30 kn, after a calm, for 12 h
lines: By duration: 12 h 3.6 m · 24 h 4.6 m
By fetch: 100 M 3.3 m · 300 M 4.8 m

options: Hs 3.3 m, the odd one near 6 m
Hs 3.6 m, the odd one near 6.7 m
Hs 4.6 m, the odd one near 8.6 m
Hs 3.3 m, the odd one near 3.3 m
questions.why: The sea is limited by the smaller of fetch and duration: 100 M gives 3.3 m; 1.86 × 3.3 ≈ 6 m for the biggest of the night.
questions.ref: Sea state — fetch and duration tables

questions.q: You plan to leave a west-facing port whose entrance breaks in big swell. When does this storm's swell reach you?

figure.title: Storm in the Atlantic
lines: Monday 0000: storm 900 M W of you
Swell energy goes at half that

options: About 1200 Wednesday
About 1600 Tuesday
About 2000 Monday
About 0800 Thursday
questions.why: Wave speed 3 × 15 = 45 kn; the swell's energy travels at half, 22.5 kn: 900 M takes 40 h — Monday 0000 + 40 h.

questions.q: You are skipper of a 14 m yacht, and on the same day you could meet either of these seas. Which is the more dangerous to you?

figure.title: Two seas, same height range
lines: A: Hs 4 m, period 6 s (wind sea)

options: B — the higher sea is always worse
B — its long period hits harder
A — short and steep, its crests break
Neither — 5 m is fine for 14 m
questions.why: Steepness, not height, makes crests break: 4 m in 6 s (about 56 m long) is steep; 5 m in 13 s (260 m) is a long, safe swell.
questions.ref: Sea state — steepness and breaking waves

questions.q: You are heading E onto the continental shelf with this forecast. Where on the route will the gale's sea be worst?

figure.note: Depths in metres

options: At A — in the deep ocean
Alike — all far deeper than the waves
At C — on the shelf, nearer land
At B — over the shelf edge
questions.why: Where the bottom rises from ocean depths to 200 m the waves steepen and turn confused: cross the shelf edge before a gale.
questions.ref: Sea state — the continental shelf edge

questions.q: You are planning a 3-day passage whose middle lies out of NAVTEX range. What do you rely on for the met warnings there?

figure.title: Passage plan, communications
lines: Route up to 150 M off; 3 days

options: SafetyNET — the METAREA warnings by satellite
VHF Ch 16 — the coastguard's gale warnings
NAVTEX on 490 kHz — the national service
The GRIB you downloaded before leaving
questions.why: SafetyNET (Inmarsat EGC) broadcasts the GMDSS high seas warnings and forecasts for each METAREA, far beyond NAVTEX range.
questions.ref: Forecast products — GMDSS, NAVTEX and SafetyNET

questions.q: You are one day out on a passage south, and the NAVTEX messages are coming in garbled. What do you do?

figure.title: NAVTEX receiver
lines: Selected: the station behind you only

options: Switch the receiver off and on
Select the station ahead as well
Accept all message types instead
Wait — the station behind will clear
questions.why: NAVTEX stations reach a few hundred miles: as one fades astern, add the next one along your route to the receiver.

questions.q: You are at the chart table in the western Channel, bound south across Biscay, reading the shipping forecast. Which areas matter most for the next 24 h?

figure.title: Shipping forecast, 0520
lines: You: in Plymouth, bound S for Biscay
Low 975 in Sole, moving E 25 kn

options: Plymouth and Biscay — along your route
Plymouth only — the area you are in
Plymouth, Biscay, and Sole to windward
Shannon and Fastnet — they carry gales
questions.why: Read your own area, the ones on your route and the ones upwind where the weather comes from — here the low in Sole.

questions.q: You are checking the ensemble forecast for a waypoint you will pass on Thursday. How do you read it?

figure.title: Ensemble at the waypoint, Thursday
lines: 40 show a gale, force 8 or more

options: 20 % — the gale is unlikely
100 % — the control run shows it
50 % — the models cannot tell
80 % — plan as if the gale will come
questions.why: 40 of 50 members means an 80 % chance: treat the gale as likely and plan the passage round it.

questions.q: Your passage takes four days, and you look at the ensemble for the last day. How much do you trust the control run for day 4?
options: Little — the spread is wide; plan an escape
Fully — the control is the best single run
Fully — day 4 is inside the model's range
Little — so plan on the average, W 5
questions.why: When the members spread from NE 3 to SW 8 the forecast has low confidence: keep ports of refuge and plan for the worst case.

questions.q: You have run the weather-routing software for a 220-mile passage, and it offers two routes. Which do you take?

figure.title: Routing output, from GRIB
lines: N route: 5 h faster than S
N: 34 kn true, seas 4.5 m at 0300
S: 24 kn true max, seas 3 m

options: The N route — five hours less at sea
The S route — the N one breaks your limits
The N route — it is the router's fastest
The S route — it is shorter in miles
questions.why: The N route runs past both your limits — and the router's 34 kn is a GRIB mean, with gusts above it. Take the S route.

questions.q: You are planning the last 20 M of an offshore passage to a harbour under high mountains. Which forecast do you plan that stretch on?

figure.title: Landfall forecasts
lines: Regional model, 2 km: NE 25 kn in gaps
Harbour: below a gap in the range

options: The global GRIB — it covers the whole route
The global GRIB — its wind is the lighter
The regional model — it sees the gaps
The average of the two — about 18 kn
questions.why: A 25 km grid smooths the mountains away; a 2 km model resolves the gap winds where the harbour lies.
questions.ref: Forecast products — model resolution at landfall

questions.q: You are 100 M offshore in the western Approaches in June. Which fog do you expect out here?
options: Sea smoke — cold air over warm sea
Radiation fog — the sea cools at night
Frontal fog — rain into cold air
Advection fog — moist air cooled by the sea
questions.why: Far out at sea the water hardly cools at night: fog there is advection fog, warm moist air cooled from below by colder sea.

questions.q: You are closing the Portuguese coast after a night offshore in the August northerly. Where do you expect to meet fog?
options: Inshore, over the cold upwelled water
Offshore, over the warmer water
Only after dark, as the land cools
Nowhere — a fresh N wind keeps fog away
questions.why: The northerly lifts cold water along the coast: the sea inshore is below the 16°C dew point, the sea offshore is above it.

questions.q: You plan to cross the shipping lanes over the shelf tonight. Do you expect fog over the shelf?
options: No — dew point about 3°C, far below the sea
Yes — dew point about 15°C, above the 14°C sea
No — dew point about 1°C, far below the sea
No — the air is 4°C warmer than the sea
questions.why: 18 − (100 − 85)/5 = 15°C dew point: air cooled over 14°C water passes its dew point — fog is likely.
questions.ref: Fog — predicting it from the dew point

questions.q: You are leaving a Norwegian fjord at dawn in January. What do you see over the water?
options: Advection fog — moist air over cold sea
Haze — salt from the breaking waves
Sea smoke — steam off the warmer sea
Radiation fog — drifting off the land
questions.why: Very cold air flowing over much warmer water makes steam fog (sea smoke), thickest near the shore the air comes from.

questions.q: You are making your landfall along this straight coast at the end of a two-day passage. What wind do you expect in the last 10 M close along it?

figure.title: Landfall, northern hemisphere
lines: Coast runs SW–NE, land to the SE
Wind at sea: SW 5, along the coast
You: bound NE, 2 M off the coast

options: Less wind — divergence along the coast
The same — the coast is straight
Less wind — the land shelters you
More wind — convergence along the coast
questions.why: NH: wind blowing along a coast with the land on its right, looking downwind, converges there and blows harder than offshore.

questions.q: You are making your landfall at this high island in the trade wind after a night at sea. Where do you expect the strongest wind?

figure.note: Island 1900 m high · NE trade 20 kn

options: B — off the end, where the flow squeezes past
A — on the windward face, in the full trade
D — well out in the lee, in clear air
C — close under the lee, out of the trade
questions.why: A high island under the trade inversion turns the wind round its ends: acceleration zones off the flanks, a wind shadow in the lee.

questions.q: You are making your landfall on this cliff-bound coast at the end of a passage. How far off do you run along it to the harbour?

figure.title: Landfall, 0700
lines: W swell 4 m running onto the cliffs

options: 0.5 M off — the shortest way in
3 M off — the sea is confused close in
3 M off — the swell is smaller there
0.5 M off — the cliffs give a lee
questions.why: Swell reflected off cliffs crosses the incoming waves within a mile or so: a steep, confused sea. Keep a few miles off.
questions.ref: Local effects — reflected seas off cliffs

questions.q: You are 120 M offshore at night, and this is to windward. What do you prepare for as it arrives?

figure.title: Night watch, 0230
lines: Large Cb approaching from the W
Dark roll cloud along its base

options: A slow back to S, a steady 15 kn
A lull, then the same SW 15 kn
A sudden shift to W, gusts of 30–40 kn
A sudden shift to E, gusts of 20 kn
questions.why: The gust front ahead of a big Cb throws out cold air from the storm's side: a sharp shift and gusts of two or more times the wind.

questions.q: You are tracking a rain cell on radar on a night passage. At about what time does it reach you?

figure.title: Radar plot of a rain cell

options: About 1442
About 1323
About 1342
About 1330
questions.why: Steady bearing, range closing 4 M in 12 min = 20 kn: the last 6 M take 18 min — about 1330. Reef before it.
questions.ref: Squalls — tracking a cell on radar

questions.q: You are motoring north in the Tyrrhenian Sea, and this appears to the west. What do you do?
options: Keep going north at speed, off its track
Turn east and run ahead of it
Stop and let it pass ahead of you
Turn west to meet it and pass behind it
questions.why: A waterspout moves with its parent cloud: get out of its path at right angles to its track — here, straight on north.

questions.q: A thunderstorm will cross you tonight, 120 M offshore. Where do you put the handheld VHF and the spare GPS?
options: In a dry bag in the cockpit locker
In the oven — the metal box screens them
In the bilge, out of the way
On the chart table, switched on
questions.why: A closed metal box like the oven acts as a Faraday cage and may save the spare electronics from a strike.

questions.q: You plan an overnight crossing of the western Mediterranean in September. When are the thunderstorms most likely on your crossing?
options: Mid-afternoon, as they are over land
Never at sea — only over the hills
At night and early morning, over the sea
At sunset only, as the air cools
questions.why: Over a warm sea, storms peak at night and early morning, when cold air aloft makes the air most unstable; over land, by afternoon.
questions.ref: Thunderstorms — at sea and over land

questions.q: You are on passage with a cold front due tonight. In which air do you meet gusts past your first reef?

figure.title: Forecast for your route
lines: Behind cold front: NW 26 kn, unstable
First reef: for gusts of 30 kn

options: In the warm sector — gusts near 33 kn
Behind the front — gusts near 31 kn
In neither — both means under 30 kn
Behind the front — gusts near 39 kn
questions.why: Stable warm air gusts little: 22 × 1.2 = 26 kn. Unstable polar air gusts hard: 26 × 1.5 = 39 kn, well past 30.
questions.ref: Air masses — gusts in stable and unstable air

questions.q: You are on passage when this gale warning comes in. What do you do?

figure.title: Gale warning, 1400
lines: NW gale 8 in 6 h, onshore; 24 h
You: 25 M off, harbour 15 M away
Its bar faces NW; breaks in swell > 2 m
Swell now 2.5 m; open sea to the SW

options: Head SW now for sea room, away from the coast
Heave to here, 25 M off, and wait
Anchor off the bar and wait for HW
Run for the bar harbour before the gale
questions.why: A bar facing an onshore gale and swell will break; 25 M is too little offing for a long blow. Gain sea room while you can.
questions.ref: Heavy weather — sea room or a port of refuge

questions.q: You plan to wait out this gale hove-to where you are. Can you?

figure.title: Gale SW 8 tonight
lines: Hove-to, you drift NE at 2.5 kn
Lee shore: 40 M to the NE
No port you can enter in an onshore gale

options: Yes — about 15 M of drift; you have 40
No — about 45 M of drift; you have 40
Yes — about 18 M of drift; you have 40
Yes — about 7 M of drift; you have 40
questions.why: 2100 to 1500 is 18 h: 18 × 2.5 kn = 45 M of drift, more than the 40 M to the lee shore. Make offing first.
questions.ref: Heavy weather — sea room for heaving to

questions.q: You are planning a 270-mile passage between two gales. Do you go?

figure.title: Weather window
lines: Gale eases Tue 0600; sea big till 1200
You want 6 h in hand at the far end

options: Go at 1200 Tue — 9 h in hand
Go at 0600 Tue — 3 h in hand will do
Wait — at best you arrive 3 h before it
Go at 0600 Tue — 15 h in hand
questions.why: 270 M at 6 kn = 45 h: leaving 0600 Tue you arrive 0300 Thu, only 3 h before the earliest gale (0600) — short of your 6 h.
questions.ref: Heavy weather — the window and its margin

questions.q: You are skipper of a 22 m motor yacht planning a 160-mile run into the sea. When do you leave to keep to your limit with the most in hand?

figure.title: Motor yacht, head sea all the way
lines: Your limit: head sea under 2 m
Sea: 3 m at 0000, under 2 m by 0800
Next front: back to 2 m by 2000

options: Leave at 0400 — in by 1400
Leave at 1000 — in by 2000
Leave at 1200 — in by 2200
Leave at 0800 — in by 1800
questions.why: 160 M at 16 kn = 10 h. The sea is under 2 m from 0800 to 2000: leaving at 0800 puts you in at 1800, 2 h in hand.
questions.ref: Heavy weather — a window for a motor yacht

questions.q: You are on passage off Madeira in a steady trade wind, and you read back the barometer log. What does the fall tell you?
options: The daily pressure swing — nothing to act on
A low approaching — reef and prepare
A front within 6 h — head for port
The trade dying — start the engine
questions.why: At low latitudes pressure swings about 1–2 hPa twice a day, lowest near 0400 and 1600: a fall like this means nothing.

questions.q: You are comparing the barometer logs of two passages with your crew. Which blow do you expect to last longer?

figure.title: Two barometer logs
lines: A: 20 hPa fall spread over 36 h

options: B — the faster the fall, the longer
A — long foretold, long last
Both alike — only the fall counts
B — a short fall gives a long gale
questions.why: A slow, long fall means a big, slow system and a long blow; a fast fall means a sharp, short one — 'short notice, soon past'.

questions.q: You are in Brest planning a crossing SSW to Spain, about 36 hours at sea, from this sequence of prognosis charts. When do you leave?

figure.title: Prognoses, 0000 UTC Monday
lines: T+12: cold front through, squalls, NW 7
T+24: NW 6 easing, sea going down
T+48: ridge over Biscay, NW 3, then light
T+72: next warm front, S 6 rising 7

options: At T+48, to start in the calm of the ridge
At T+72, on the new southerly breeze
At T+24, as the NW eases behind the front
Now, to get well on before the front
questions.why: Leaving at T+24 gives a fair NW, then the ridge, and you are in by T+60 — before the next low's S wind. T+48 meets the S 6 at sea.

questions.q: You are delivering a yacht along New South Wales, 100 M offshore, where the boat is drawn, north of this low's centre. Where does the wind come from?

figure.note: You: north of the centre

options: From about N
From about ENE
From about WSW
From about WNW
questions.why: Southern hemisphere: air turns clockwise round a low, crossing the isobars inwards — on its north side it blows from about WNW.
questions.ref: Pressure systems — Buys Ballot in the south

questions.q: You are planning a three-day passage north-east up the North Sea in May, and every prognosis looks like this. What wind do you plan for?

figure.title: Prognoses T+24 to T+96
lines: It hardly moves from chart to chart
Lows steered round, N of Iceland
Your route: NE up the North Sea

options: A steady E–SE wind, day after day
A NW wind as the high drifts away E
A W wind, backing S as each low passes
A gale each day as the lows run through
questions.why: A blocking high sits for days and steers the lows round it: on its south-west flank the North Sea keeps a steady easterly.

questions.q: You are planning a three-day passage from Madeira to the Azores, with a high centred on the rhumb line. Which way do you route?

figure.title: Madeira to the Azores, 3 days
lines: High 1030 hPa centred on the rhumb line
Light airs within 150 M of the centre

options: Round its N side, on the westerly
Round its S and W sides, on the easterly
Round its E side, on the northerly
Straight through the centre — the shortest
questions.why: NH air turns clockwise round a high: its S side has an E wind, fair for a course of 300°T; the light centre means days of motoring.
questions.ref: Pressure systems — routing round a high

questions.q: You are crossing Biscay on 210°T, and this low will pass east of you, moving NE. What wind do you log as it goes by?

figure.title: Biscay, tomorrow
lines: Low 990 hPa moving NE at 25 kn
Its track: 120 M E of your route

options: Veering E, SE, then S — close-hauled at the end
Veering S, SW, then W — on the nose at first
Backing NE, N, then NW — free all the way
A steady NE — no shift as it passes
questions.why: On the left of a low's track (NH) the wind backs as it passes — NE, N, NW — and each of them is abaft the beam on 210°T.
questions.ref: Depressions — the track and the wind on board

questions.q: You are hove-to in mid-Biscay at night as this low tracks east right over you. What do you prepare for next?

figure.title: Night log, mid-Biscay
lines: Forecast: centre tracking E over you

options: Calm until dawn, as the low fills
The SE gale again, from the same side
A slow veer to S, then SW, easing
A NW gale, coming in within an hour or two
questions.why: When a centre passes right over you the wind dies at the lowest pressure, then comes back hard from the opposite side — here the NW.
questions.ref: Depressions — the centre passing over you

questions.q: You are on day two of a Biscay crossing and read back today's log. What has passed over you?

figure.title: Day log, mid-Biscay
lines: No warm, muggy spell all day

options: An occlusion — the warm sector never reached you
A warm front — the cold front is still to come
A cold front — the warm one passed in the night
A trough — the low's fronts are still to come
questions.why: One band of rain, a single veer and no warm, damp spell: the cold front has lifted the warm sector off the sea — an occlusion.

questions.q: You are 100 M out on a passage south-west when the weather turns back on you after the cold front. What is happening?

figure.title: Log after the cold front
lines: Chart: a wave on the front 200 M SW

options: The warm front again — clear skies behind
A wave low is running NE along the front
The old low filling — the rain will fade
A heavy shower — the NW will be back soon
questions.why: The front has stalled and a wave is forming on it: a secondary low runs along the front, the wind backs, rain returns, and it may deepen.
questions.ref: Depressions — a wave on the cold front

questions.q: You read this analysis, with a secondary low south of the main one, before choosing your track. At which point do you expect the strongest wind?

figure.note: Northern hemisphere · analysis 0600 UTC

options: D — at the main low's centre
A — between the two centres
B — on the far side of the secondary
C — at the secondary's centre
questions.why: On the side of a secondary away from the main low the two circulations add: the strongest wind. Between the two centres they oppose.

questions.q: You are planning a three-day passage from Lisbon to Madeira, and the forecaster's notes say this. How do you treat the low in your plan?

figure.title: Forecaster's notes, Thursday
lines: Jet stream buckled into a deep loop
A low has cut off W of Portugal
The models disagree on its track

options: Fast — the jet will sweep it NE within a day
Harmless — the jet will steer it W, away
Gone — it will fill before you sail
Slow and erratic — low confidence, keep updating
questions.why: Cut off from the jet, a low is no longer steered: it drifts slowly and erratically, the models disagree, and it can sit for days.
questions.ref: Depressions — the cut-off low and the jet

questions.q: You are planning a two-day passage north along the Norwegian coast in January, and this is in the forecaster's notes. What does it warn you of?

figure.title: Forecaster's notes, January
lines: Your passage: 2 days N along the coast

options: Small, fierce lows — gales at short notice
Large, slow lows — days of warning first
Thick fog — light winds for days
Clear, settled cold — the best of sailing
questions.why: Polar lows form fast in Arctic air over a warmer sea: small and intense, often missed by the models — gales and snow with little warning.

questions.q: You plan to cross the Ionian from Sicily to Greece late in October, and this is in the forecast notes. What do you decide?

figure.title: Forecast notes, Tuesday
lines: Sea 25°C, cold air aloft over Sicily
No port of refuge on the way

options: Go — such storms happen only in the tropics
Postpone — a small, intense storm may form
Go — it will give you a fair NW breeze
Go — it will bring only heavy rain
questions.why: A medicane is a small, tropical-like Mediterranean cyclone over a warm autumn sea: storm-force winds, and a track poorly forecast.

questions.q: You are bound for the Faroes at 60°N, and your chart's geostrophic scale was made for 40°N. What wind does the isobar spacing over you give?

figure.title: Geostrophic scale on the chart
lines: Spacing over you reads 30 kn on it

options: About 41 kn — F9
About 20 kn — F5
About 22 kn — F6
About 30 kn — F7
questions.why: Geostrophic wind goes as 1 / sin(latitude): 30 × 0.64 ÷ 0.87 = 22 kn. The same spacing gives less wind at a higher latitude.
questions.ref: Surface analysis — the geostrophic scale with latitude

questions.q: You measure the gap between two isobars along 50°N on a small-scale chart, in degrees of longitude. What geostrophic wind do you get?
options: About 16 kn — F4
About 32 kn — F7
About 25 kn — F6
About 39 kn — F8
questions.why: 2° of longitude at 50°N is 120 × cos 50° = 77 M, not 120 M: 3000 ÷ 77 = 39 kn. Distance is never measured on the longitude scale.
questions.ref: Surface analysis — measuring the isobar spacing

questions.q: You are reading the general synopsis of a high seas bulletin before leaving Falmouth for Spain. What does it say the low will do?
options: Move to Fastnet and deepen by 12 hPa
Stay where it is and deepen to 970
Move to Fastnet and fill by 12 hPa
Die out, as a new 970 low forms at Fastnet
questions.why: 'Expected Fastnet 970 by 0000' gives where the centre will be and its pressure then: 982 to 970 hPa is a deepening of 12 hPa.
questions.ref: Forecast products — the high seas synopsis

questions.q: You are bound south-west, and this is your area forecast in the high seas bulletin. Will the change head you?
options: No — it veers to SW, onto the beam
Yes — it backs to SW, onto the nose
No — 'backing' means it is easing
Yes — it veers to SW, onto the nose
questions.why: Backing is an anticlockwise shift: NW to SW is a back of 90°, and a SW wind is dead ahead on a course of SW.

questions.q: The high seas bulletin gives this for the area next to yours, and your crew is alarmed by the word. What does it mean?
options: Gusts to 64 kn round a force 10 mean
A true hurricane, eye and all
Force 12: a mean of 64 kn or more
An ex-hurricane that keeps its eye
questions.why: 'Hurricane force' is simply Beaufort 12 — a mean of 64 kn or more — and is used for deep mid-latitude storms too.
questions.ref: Forecast products — Beaufort terms in a bulletin

questions.q: You plan to cross Biscay in two days, and the synopsis says this about the low there now. What will it do?
options: Join the next low as a gale centre
Leave the bulletin's area to the E
Deepen fast — too quick to track
Fade out — no longer a low of its own
questions.why: 'Losing its identity' means the low is dying out or merging into the general pattern: it will no longer be a separate centre.

questions.q: You are in mid-passage, out of NAVTEX and VHF range, with no satellite terminal aboard. How do you get the surface analysis and the prognoses?

figure.title: Mid-passage, day 2
lines: 300 M from NAVTEX and VHF stations

options: By HF weatherfax, decoded on the laptop
From NAVTEX, set to a distant station
On VHF Ch 16, from the coastguard
From the GRIB saved before you left
questions.why: An SSB (HF) receiver picks up radiofax broadcasts of analysis and prognosis charts thousands of miles away; a laptop decodes them.

questions.q: You are ordering a GRIB by satellite phone for the next three days of your passage. Which request do you send?
options: The whole North Atlantic, 0.25°, hourly, every layer
Your route only, 0.5° grid, 3-hourly, wind and pressure
The whole ocean at 2°, wind only, 24-hourly
Your route only, but with every layer on offer
questions.why: On a slow, paid link ask only for what you need: a small box, wind and pressure, 3-hourly — a small file that is still useful.
questions.ref: Forecast products — ordering a GRIB at sea

questions.q: You download a GRIB at 1000 UTC on the morning you sail. Which model run do you get, and how old is it?

figure.title: Global model
lines: Each is ready about 4½ h after

options: The 1200 UTC run — just out
The 0600 UTC run — 4 h old
The 0000 UTC run — already 10 h old
The 1800 UTC run — 16 h old
questions.why: The 0600 run is not ready until 1030, so at 1000 the newest is the 0000 run: its data are already 10 h old.

questions.q: You must decide whether to leave on a 30-hour crossing, and your three sources disagree. Do you go?

figure.title: Go/no-go, 30-h crossing
lines: GRIB, one model run: SW 18 kn
Ensemble: 35 % chance of a gale, day 2
No port of refuge on the way

options: Yes — and steer round the gale using the GRIB
Yes — a 35 % chance means it probably won't come
Yes — the GRIB shows only 18 kn all the way
No — the bulletin and the ensemble both flag a gale
questions.why: One model run shows no gale, but a 1-in-3 ensemble chance and the forecaster's 'gale 8 later' say it may come: no-go for a 30-h leg.
questions.ref: Forecast products — GRIB, ensemble and the official forecast

questions.q: You are choosing between two routes for a two-day passage from this ensemble output. Which do you take?

figure.title: Ensemble, day 2 of your passage
lines: Chance of a mean force 7 or more:
S route: 9 h longer at sea

options: The S route — it cuts the risk to 20 %
The rhumb line — 70 % is not a certainty
The S route — there the chance is nil
The rhumb line — it saves 9 hours
questions.why: Seven in ten members give force 7 or more on the rhumb line; nine more hours at sea for a one-in-five risk is the better bet.
questions.ref: Forecast products — the ensemble for routeing

questions.q: Your routing software gives this ETA for a 210-mile passage. When do you really expect to arrive, against the front?

figure.title: Weather routing, 210 M
lines: Router ETA: 30 h, at 100 % of polars
Cold front at the destination: in 34 h

options: In about 30 h — 4 h before the front
In about 37½ h — 3½ h after the front
In about 36 h — 2 h after the front
In about 24 h — 10 h before the front
questions.why: At 80 % of the polars the passage takes 30 ÷ 0.8 = 37½ h — after the front. Multiplying by 0.8 or adding 20 % is the slip.

questions.q: You download a satellite wind pass at sea and compare it with the GRIB for the same hour. Which do you plan the next 12 hours on?

figure.title: Your area, 0945 UTC
lines: ASCAT pass: 35 kn in a band 60 M wide
You: on the band's S edge

options: The GRIB — it covers the next 12 hours
The average of the two — about 30 kn
The satellite pass — it measured the wind
The GRIB — satellites cannot see wind
questions.why: A scatterometer pass (ASCAT) measures the surface wind from the sea's roughness; when it shows more than the model, the model is low.
questions.ref: Forecast products — satellite winds and the GRIB

questions.q: You are 130 M out on the first night of a passage, and the weather is not what was forecast. What do you make of it?
options: Just a local squall — it will settle back
The barometer is faulty — sail to the forecast
The forecast is right — the wind is a gust
The low is deeper or nearer — reef and replan
questions.why: Two forces more and the glass falling fast: your own observations beat an old forecast. Assume the low is deeper or closer than shown.

questions.q: You look at the extra layers of tonight's GRIB for your route. What do they tell you?

figure.title: GRIB layers, tonight
lines: Wind: W 12–15 kn all along the route
CAPE: 1800 J/kg over the E half

options: Thunderstorms are likely over the E half
Nothing — CAPE matters only to pilots
Fog over the E half — the air is saturated
A strong, steady wind over the E half
questions.why: CAPE is the energy available to rising air: over about 1000 J/kg the air is unstable enough for big Cb — squalls and lightning.
questions.ref: Forecast products — CAPE in a GRIB

questions.q: You are running in from the deep ocean towards the continental shelf with this swell. At about what depth does it start to feel the bottom and steepen?

figure.title: Swell from the W
lines: A wave feels the bottom where
the depth is under half its wavelength

options: About 22 m
About 153 m
About 11 m
About 306 m
questions.why: Deep-water wavelength 1.56 × 14² = 306 m; a wave feels the bottom at half that, about 153 m — just inside the 200 m shelf edge.
questions.ref: Sea state — the shelf and the deep sea

questions.q: It is 2200, and you will reach your next waypoint, far out in Biscay, at 1000 tomorrow. What significant height do you plan for there?

figure.title: Wind W 8 (40 kn) since 1600
lines: Hs by duration: 6 h 3.4 m · 12 h 5.1 m
18 h 6.3 m · by fetch, 500 M: 8.3 m

options: About 3.4 m
About 8.3 m
About 6.3 m
About 5.1 m
questions.why: By 1000 the wind will have blown for 18 h: 6.3 m. The 500 M fetch would allow 8.3 m, so duration limits it; counting from now gives 5.1 m.

questions.q: You are bound north tomorrow under this forecast. From where do the big waves come?
options: From the SW, on the quarter
From the E, on the beam
From the NE, on the bow
From the W, on your beam
questions.why: Swell runs on from the storm that made it, whatever the local wind: here the 4 m comes from the W, on the beam of a northbound yacht.
questions.ref: Sea state — swell and wind sea

questions.q: Your anemometer failed overnight, 100 M offshore, and you log the wind from the sea at 1600. What force do you write?

figure.title: Log at 1600, anemometer out
lines: Foam not yet blown in streaks

options: Force 6 — strong breeze
Force 8 — gale
Force 5 — fresh breeze
Force 7 — near gale
questions.why: Large waves forming, white foam crests everywhere and some spray: Beaufort force 6, with waves of about 3 m in the open sea.
questions.ref: Beaufort scale — the sea at force 6

questions.q: You are crossing the Gulf Stream on a passage from Charleston to Bermuda. When do you cross it?

figure.title: Gulf Stream crossing
lines: Tomorrow: N 6–7 behind a cold front
Crossing the stream takes about 10 h

options: Tomorrow, on the fresh fair northerly
Today, before the northerly sets in
Any time — the current flattens the sea
Tomorrow night, once the N is steady
questions.why: A northerly against a 3–4 kn NE-going stream raises steep, breaking seas: cross while the wind still runs with the current.
questions.ref: Sea state — wind against an ocean current

questions.q: You skipper a 22 m motor yacht on a 120-mile run into the sea. Which part of this forecast sets your go or no-go?

figure.title: Forecast for the run
lines: Swell NW 3 m, 7 s, after a gale

options: The visibility — the radar needs it
The pressure — and how fast it rises
The sea — its height and period ahead
The wind force — as for a sailing yacht
questions.why: Under power the wind itself matters little; the head sea's height and steepness decide how fast — and how safely — she can go.
questions.ref: Sea state — a motor yacht's limits

questions.q: You are skipper of a 22 m planing motor yacht leaving at 0700 for a 132-mile run, and the forecast sea builds from halfway. When do you plan to arrive?

figure.title: Motor yacht, head sea
lines: Sea over 2 m from halfway on
In over 2 m you slow to 11 kn

options: About 1300
About 1500
About 1900
About 1600
questions.why: 66 M at 22 kn = 3 h, then 66 M at 11 kn = 6 h: 9 h, in at 1600. Averaging the two speeds (16.5 kn) gives 1500 — the slip.
questions.ref: Sea state — a planing yacht slowed by the sea

questions.q: You skipper a 24 m motor yacht heading into the sea, and four forecasts are possible for tomorrow. Which gives the worst pitching and slamming?

figure.title: Head sea, Hs 1.5 m in each case

options: Period 4 s
Period 6 s
Period 12 s
Period 9 s
questions.why: 1.56 × 4² = 25 m: a wavelength about her own length makes her pitch hardest. 6 s gives 56 m, 9 s 126 m, 12 s 225 m.
questions.ref: Sea state — wavelength and a motor yacht

questions.q: You and a friend cross the same beam swell — you in a 22 m motor yacht whose stabilisers have failed, he in a 15 m sailing yacht under main. Why does he roll far less?

figure.title: Beam swell, open sea
lines: Swell 2.5 m, 9 s, on the beam

options: The swell is smaller where he is
The wind in his sail damps the roll
A shorter boat always rolls less
His keel is heavier than your hull
questions.why: Wind pressure on a set sail resists every roll; a motor yacht has no such damping, so a beam swell throws her about.
questions.ref: Sea state — a motor yacht in a beam sea

questions.q: You are making a night landfall in thick fog after two nights at sea. Where, and how, do you go in?

figure.title: Landfall, 0200
lines: Advection fog, forecast to last 24 h+
Port A: 3 M, rocky entrance 1 cable wide
Port B: 15 M on, wide, deep, buoyed
Radar, AIS, GPS fine; crew tired

options: Stop off A and wait there for daylight
Into A on the plotter, at slow speed
On to B, in on radar and plotter at slow speed
Stand off and wait 24 h for it to clear
questions.why: Sea fog will not clear soon; a narrow rocky entrance in fog with a tired crew is the real risk. A wide, deep, buoyed one is the safe landfall.

questions.q: You are approaching the Channel at night in the fog of a warm sector. When do you plan to make your landfall?

figure.title: Night approach, 2300
lines: Behind it: dry polar air, clear

options: Now — the fog lifts as the wind rises
Before 0600, while the wind is still light
At dawn — the sun will burn the fog off
After 0600, in the clear air behind the front
