questions.why: Warm-sector sea fog lasts as long as the warm, moist air: it clears when the cold front brings in the dry polar air.
questions.ref: Fog — clearing behind a cold front

questions.q: You are closing Gran Canaria after a three-day passage, and the visibility is going. What is cutting it, and how long will it last?

figure.title: Canaries landfall, February
lines: Wind E 5, hot and dry, off Africa

options: Saharan dust — until the wind leaves the east
Radiation fog — until mid-morning
Sea fog — until the sun burns it off
Rain haze — until the front passes
questions.why: An east wind off the Sahara carries dust (the calima) out over the Canaries: a dry, yellow haze that lasts as long as the easterly.

questions.q: You are making your landfall to anchor at A, tucked in east of the point, out of this swell. Will A be quiet?

figure.note: Swell W 3 m, 12 s · wind E 2

options: Yes — swell runs only with the wind, now E
No — the swell bends round the point into A
Yes — A faces away from the swell
No — the light E wind raises a big sea at A
questions.why: Swell refracts as it feels the bottom and wraps round a point into the bay behind it — smaller, but still rolling, a long swell most of all.
questions.ref: Local effects — swell round a point

questions.q: You are heading east at 6 kn at night, and the radar shows this cell crossing ahead of you. What do you do?

figure.note: Radar, 2300 · cell moving S at 18 kn

options: Speed up and cross ahead of it
Turn S to run along with it
Slow down, let it cross, pass astern of it
Turn N to meet it and pass behind early
questions.why: Treat a moving cell like a ship crossing at 18 kn: you cannot outpace it, so slow down, let it cross, then pass behind it.

questions.q: Your crew want to motor east at 7 kn to outrun this squall line. When does it reach you if you do?

figure.title: Radar, 1500
lines: Squall line 15 M W of you
Gusts in it forecast to 45 kn

options: In about 36 min
In about 2 h 09 min
In about 28 min
In about 50 min
questions.why: It closes at 25 − 7 = 18 kn: 15 M takes 50 min instead of 36. You gain 14 minutes — use them to reef, not to run.

questions.q: Lightning struck the water close aboard in the night, and now the steering compass and the GPS disagree. What do you do?

figure.title: After the lightning, 0300
lines: GPS COG as a compass course: 128°C

options: Steer by GPS; check and swing the compass later
Apply the 19° as deviation, as usual
Apply the 19° as a change of variation
Trust the compass — the GPS has been hit
questions.why: A near strike can magnetise steel aboard and shift the deviation: steer by GPS, check by the sun or a transit, and have it swung.

questions.q: You are on watch at 0200, 120 M offshore under a towering cloud, and you see this. What does it tell you?

figure.title: Night watch, 0200
lines: Towering cloud overhead, no rain yet
The hair on your arms stands up

options: A masthead light shorting — check the wiring
St Elmo's fire — lightning may strike soon
Phosphorescence — plankton in the spray
The tricolour reflected in the rain
questions.why: St Elmo's fire is a glow discharge in a strong electric field: a strike is possible — keep the crew off the rig and away from metal.

questions.q: You decide to run for this refuge rather than ride the gale out off a lee shore. When are you in, and with how much in hand?

figure.title: 1400, gale warning
lines: You make 7.5 kn; stream 1 kn against
Lee shore 50 M E of you

options: In by about 2000 — 3 h 00 min in hand
In by about 1918 — 3 h 42 min in hand
In by about 2055 — 2 h 05 min in hand
In by about 2132 — 1 h 28 min in hand
questions.why: Over the ground 7.5 − 1 = 6.5 kn: 45 ÷ 6.5 = 6.92 h = 6 h 55 min from 1400 — in at 2055, two hours before the gale.
questions.ref: Heavy weather — a port of refuge

questions.q: You must ride out this gale at sea, with no port open to you. Which tactic can you keep up for the whole gale?

figure.title: SW gale 9, for 30 h
lines: Lee shore: 80 M to the NE
Running with a drogue: about 3.5 kn
No port you can enter in it

options: Run off with a drogue — about 105 M
Heave to — about 21 M of drift
Run off with a drogue — about 9 M
Heave to — about 42 M of drift
questions.why: 30 h × 1.4 kn = 42 M hove-to, inside your 80 M; running at 3.5 kn needs 105 M — more sea room than you have.
questions.ref: Heavy weather — tactics and sea room

questions.q: You get this warning 140 M offshore, and your crew want to beat for the nearest port. What do you do?

figure.title: Gale warning, 1200
lines: Coast you left: 140 M NE — a lee shore
Open, deep water all round you

options: Prepare the boat and ride it out at sea
Beat for the port before the gale arrives
Motor hard for the port, in by tomorrow
Run back downwind to the coast you left
questions.why: 90 M to windward is 18 h or more — the gale will catch you on the way, and the coast astern becomes a lee shore. Use the sea room.
questions.ref: Heavy weather — sea room or a port

questions.q: You hove-to through the night's gale and now want to resume your course to windward. When do you go?

figure.title: Morning after the gale
lines: 0800: NW 5, sea still 5 m and steep

options: In two days — a sea never eases sooner
In a few hours — the sea lags the wind
Now — the wind is down to force 5
Now — a big sea drops as fast as the wind
questions.why: The old sea takes many hours to go down after the wind eases: beating into a steep 5 m sea now risks gear and crew for little gain.

questions.q: You are 110 M offshore at night, and no warning has come in yet. What does your barometer tell you to prepare for?

figure.title: Barometer log
lines: Rule of thumb, fall in 3 h:
10 hPa or more — a storm likely

options: A near gale — one more reef
Nothing until a warning comes
A storm — force 10 is likely
A gale — force 8 at most
questions.why: 11 hPa in 3 h is past the 10 hPa rule of thumb: a storm is likely. Prepare now — a warning can lag what the barometer shows.
questions.ref: Barometer — the rate of fall and a storm

questions.q: You are driving your motor yacht towards a low, and the barometer has dropped fast. What is the real tendency, without your own run?

figure.title: Motor yacht, last 3 h
lines: Isobars: 4 hPa per 80 M on your track

options: 5.4 hPa — falling quickly
1.4 hPa — falling slowly
7.8 hPa — falling very rapidly
3.0 hPa — falling
questions.why: 48 M at 16 kn across 4 hPa per 80 M accounts for 2.4 hPa: 5.4 − 2.4 = 3.0 hPa in 3 h — 'falling', not 'falling quickly'.
questions.ref: Barometer — the tendency on a moving yacht

questions.q: You haul out a 14 m GRP yacht after six years afloat and find this below the waterline. What is it?

figure.title: Haul-out after six years afloat
lines: Blisters 5–15 mm, below the waterline only
Pricked, they weep a sour, vinegary liquid

options: Osmosis — water in the laminate behind the gelcoat
Galvanic corrosion eating into the laminate
Delamination of a balsa core under the skin
Air trapped under the last coat of antifouling
questions.why: Water diffuses through the gelcoat and reacts with the resin: acid fluid in blisters below the waterline is osmosis.

questions.q: Surveying a 16 m yacht before an offshore season, you test the foredeck round the windlass. What have you found, and what is the repair?

figure.title: Foredeck, balsa-cored sandwich
lines: Tapped round the windlass: a dull thud
Deck flexes underfoot; moisture reads high

options: Gelcoat crazing — fill, fair and polish the surface
Wet, delaminated core — re-core it, epoxy-pot the bolt holes
Osmosis in the deck — dry it out under covers
Normal deck flex — fit a bigger backing plate
questions.why: Water in through unsealed bolt holes rots the core and parts it from the skins; re-core and seal every hole in epoxy.

questions.q: Your yacht hit a rock keel-first at 5 knots last week. You have hauled her out before a 150 M passage. What do you do?

figure.title: After the grounding
lines: Crack at the front of the keel–hull joint
Inside: grid parted from hull at aft bolts
No leak so far; passage planned in six days

options: Fill and fair the joint crack, then sail
Re-torque the keel bolts and sail as planned
Have her surveyed and the grid repaired before you sail
Sail, and pump and check the bilge every watch
questions.why: The moulded grid spreads the keel's loads into the hull; once it has parted, the keel is not properly held. Survey and repair first.

questions.q: You are preparing a 20 m steel ketch for an offshore season. How do you treat this?

figure.title: Steel hull, pre-season check
lines: Bilge, where water lies: rust through paint
Waterline: paint chipped to bare steel

options: Overcoat with copper antifouling, which stops the rust
Fit an extra zinc anode inside the bilge
Wire-brush the loose rust and touch up in enamel
Blast or grind to bright steel, epoxy-prime, recoat, dry the bilge
questions.why: Steel rusts wherever its coating is broken: clean to bright metal, epoxy-prime and recoat; an anode in the bilge protects nothing.

questions.q: The yard has quoted for antifouling your aluminium yacht. What do you tell them?
options: No copper antifouling — use a copper-free one
Copper is fine below the waterline, not above
Fine, as long as the zinc anodes are renewed
Fine — copper is the best antifouling for any hull
questions.why: Copper and aluminium make a galvanic cell: copper paint on an aluminium hull eats the hull. Use a copper-free antifouling.

questions.q: On a classic wooden yacht you lift a deck fitting that has leaked rainwater all season. What have you found?

figure.title: Under the fitting
lines: Fresh water has lain here, unventilated

options: Dried-out wood — oil it until it swells
Rot — cut back to sound wood and stop the leak
Salt damage — rinse it well with fresh water
Worm — treat with insecticide and fill it
questions.why: Fungal rot needs fresh water and still air; salt water slows it. Cut out to sound timber, scarph in new wood, re-bed the fitting.

questions.q: After two days hard on the wind on starboard tack, the crew report this. Where is the water most likely coming in?

figure.title: Leak report, day 2
lines: Drips behind the headlining, all along port
Dry on port tack; windows and hatches dry

options: Condensation running down the cold hull
The port chainplates where they pass the deck
The hull-to-deck joint under the port toerail
The port windows, past their seals
questions.why: A leak along the whole lee side, only when the rail is buried, is the hull-to-deck joint working; a chainplate leaks at one spot.

questions.q: You are 40 M out on a 140 M passage, close-hauled on starboard tack in F6, when you find this. What do you do?

figure.title: Main bulkhead
lines: Tabbing cracked along the hull, starboard
Saloon door now jams on starboard tack

options: Carry on full sail and check the crack each watch
Fill the crack with sealant and carry on
Tighten the starboard cap shroud to stiffen it
Reef hard to unload the rig and divert to the nearest port
questions.why: The bulkhead carries the shroud loads into the hull; moving under load, it can let the rig go. Unload it and get in.

questions.q: Lifting the floorboards of a 22-year-old yacht before an offshore passage, you find this. What is the concern?

figure.title: Bilge check
lines: Bilge never dry; salt water round the bolts
Rust weeps from round two stainless nuts
No sign of movement at the keel joint

options: Crevice corrosion of the bolts — have them drawn and checked
Galvanic attack on the lead — fit a keel anode
Surface rust only — tighten and paint the nuts
Normal — stainless steel always weeps a little
questions.why: Stainless starved of oxygen in wet salt corrodes unseen inside the hole; weeping rust is the warning. Draw a bolt or X-ray it.

questions.q: At haul-out before a 150 M passage, you rock the blade of your spade rudder. What do you conclude?

figure.title: Rudder check, on the hard
lines: Blade tip moves 4 mm side to side by hand
It knocks underway in a seaway

options: The quadrant is loose on the stock — tighten it
Worn bearings — renew them; a spade hangs on them alone
The blade is delaminating — fill it with resin
Normal play — water fills the gap once afloat
questions.why: A spade rudder is cantilevered from its bearings with no skeg below; play hammers them apart in a seaway. Renew before you go.

questions.q: Checking the seacocks of a used yacht you are buying, you find this on the engine intake. What is it, and what do you do?

figure.title: Engine-intake through-hull
lines: Pinkish colour where it is scratched

options: Anode damage — move the hull anode nearer
Surface corrosion — fit a domestic brass valve
Dezincification — replace it with bronze or a rated composite
Normal patina — clean and grease the valve
questions.why: Salt water leaches the zinc out of brass, leaving weak pink copper. Fit bronze, DZR brass or a certified composite seacock.

questions.q: The evening before a 140 M passage, you find this on your rig check. What do you do?

figure.title: Rig check
lines: Cap shroud, 1×19 stainless wire, 11 years old
One strand broken at the lower swage

options: Tape over it and check it daily on passage
Tighten the bottlescrew a turn to share the load
Favour the other tack to spare that shroud
Replace the shroud before you sail
questions.why: One broken strand at a swage means the wire is fatigued there and more will follow; replace it, and suspect its sisters.

questions.q: On a 10-day passage, the genoa halyard has sat at the same hoist since you left. What do you do about this?

figure.title: Day 6, halyard check
lines: Cover chafed fuzzy at the masthead sheave

options: Freshen the nip — shift the wear point a little each day
Tension it harder so it stops moving on the sheave
Grease the sheave and leave the halyard as it is
Nothing until the cover parts — the core takes the load
questions.why: On passage chafe works at one spot; ease or hoist a few centimetres daily to spread it, and end-for-end the line later.

questions.q: Your 22 m motor yacht's stability booklet gives these figures. What is her righting lever GZ at 10° of heel?

figure.title: Stability booklet, loaded condition
lines: KG 2.40 m (keel to centre of gravity G)

questions.why: GM = KM − KG = 0.65 m; at small angles GZ ≈ GM × sin θ = 0.65 × 0.174 = 0.11 m.

questions.q: This is your yacht's GZ curve, as a table from her stability data. What is her angle of vanishing stability?
options: About 130°
About 60°
About 124°
About 90°
questions.why: AVS is where GZ falls to zero: between 120° (0.03) and 130° (−0.05), about 124°. 60° is only where GZ peaks.

questions.q: You plan a 140 M crossing in this yacht. The forecast is in. What do you decide?
options: Go — Category B means offshore, in any forecast
Go — STIX 28 clears the 23 that Category B needs
Go, but keep within 60 M of land throughout
Wait — day 2 is beyond what Category B is designed for
questions.why: Category B is designed for up to F8 and significant waves up to 4 m; F9 and 4–5 m seas are Category A conditions.

questions.q: A friend wants to buy this boat for regular 120 M crossings. What does her builder's plate tell you?
options: Inshore only: designed for up to F6 and 2 m waves
Sheltered waters only: up to F4 and 0.3 m waves
Ocean: unlimited, as long as 8 or fewer sail
Offshore: designed for up to F8 and 4 m waves
questions.why: RCD category C (inshore) covers up to Beaufort 6 and significant waves up to 2 m — not a 120 M crossing.

questions.q: The owner wants all four of these fitted before an offshore season. Which raises the yacht's centre of gravity the most?

figure.title: Proposed additions (height above G)
lines: Radar arch with radar: 60 kg at 2.5 m
Dinghy and outboard on davits: 90 kg at 1.4 m
Second bower anchor: 30 kg at 0.5 m

options: The second bower anchor
The in-mast furling
The dinghy on the davits
The radar arch
questions.why: G rises with weight × height: the furling's 45 × 9.0 = 405 kg·m beats 150 for the arch and 126 for the dinghy.

questions.q: Water from a burst hose is sloshing freely across your motor yacht's engine room. Using the booklet's formula, what is her effective GM now?

figure.title: Engine room flooding
lines: Displacement 40 t; GM 0.85 m before the flood
Free water 4.0 m long (l) × 3.6 m wide (b)
Rise of G = ρ × l × b³ ÷ (12 × Δ)

questions.why: Free surface: 1.025 × 4.0 × 3.6³ ÷ (12 × 40) = 0.40 m; GM 0.85 − 0.40 = 0.45 m. Pump it out and stop it spreading.

questions.q: A wide fuel tank, half full, costs your motor yacht this much GM. The yard can fit a watertight centreline division. What will the loss become?

figure.title: Main fuel tank, half full
lines: Free-surface loss of GM now 0.08 m

questions.why: Free surface goes with width cubed: two tanks of half width give 2 × (½)³ = ¼ of the loss, so 0.08 ÷ 4 = 0.02 m.

questions.q: You are delivering a 15 m catamaran offshore. Her stability data show this. What does it mean for how you sail her?

figure.title: 15 m catamaran — stability data
lines: Maximum GZ at 11°, as the windward hull lifts
GZ falls steeply beyond; AVS about 90°
Inverted, she is about as stable as upright

options: Reef by wind strength: past the peak she capsizes and stays over
Fly a hull for speed: stability grows with heel
Press on: ballast will right her beyond 90°
Reef by heel, as in a monohull: she will warn you
questions.why: A cat's form stability peaks as a hull lifts and gives little warning; once over she floats inverted. Reef for the gusts.

questions.q: You are comparing two 13 m yachts for a passage with a risk of breaking seas. If each is rolled over, which is more likely to stay inverted?
options: B — her wide beam lowers her centre of gravity
B — she is stable upside down over 64°, A over 40°
Neither — any ballasted yacht rights at once
A — her higher AVS holds her inverted longer
questions.why: Beyond its AVS a yacht is stable inverted: B's range is 180° − 116° = 64°, A's 40°. It takes a bigger wave to right B.

questions.q: Breaking seas are forecast for tonight. Going below, you find this. Why does it matter for your stability?

figure.title: Below at dusk
lines: Washboards stowed in the quarter berth
Forehatch closed but not dogged down

options: It does not — openings matter only in harbour
Open hatches let the hull vent and right faster
The GZ curve assumes a closed hull: shut and secure it all
Water below sits low and adds to her stability
questions.why: In a knockdown water floods in through any opening, adds free surface and wrecks the GZ curve: washboards in, hatches dogged.

questions.q: A travel-lift is about to lift your saildrive yacht. Where does the aft sling go?

figure.title: Haul-out
lines: Sling marks on the topsides, forward and aft
Saildrive leg just aft of the aft mark

options: Wherever she balances; check the leg later
Right aft, under the rudder, for balance
Under the saildrive, the strongest point
On the aft mark, clear of the saildrive leg
questions.why: Slings go on the builder's marks, clear of the saildrive, shaft, rudder and transducers, which a sling can crush or tear off.

questions.q: Hauled out after nine months afloat, you look at the anodes. What does the hull anode tell you?

figure.title: Anodes at haul-out
lines: Hull anode: like new, under antifouling

options: It is painted over and protecting nothing
It is fine — it can stay for another season
It is the wrong alloy for salt water
The hull is overprotected — remove the anode
questions.why: An anode works only bare and bonded: the paint cut it off, so the nearby seacock corroded instead. Never paint anodes.

questions.q: The yard has moved your yacht from the slipway to the hard. Walking round her before they leave for the weekend, you see this. What needs changing?

figure.title: On the hard, gale forecast
lines: Keel on one short block under its aft end
Stands under flat panels between bulkheads
Stands not chained to each other

options: Nothing — it is a normal way to prop a yacht
Keel blocked along its length; stands under bulkheads, chained
Take her weight on the stands, keel just touching
Add stands at the bow and stern overhangs only
questions.why: The keel carries the weight on full-length blocking; stands only steady her, under bulkheads, chained so they cannot walk.

questions.q: The slipway cannot take you, so you use the grid for 24 hours — on at one morning high water, off at the next. Which morning do you go on?

figure.title: Slipway and careening grid
lines: Slipway cradle: max 15 t — you are 19 t
To float on or off the grid: 4.3 m of tide
Morning HW: Tue 4.2 · Wed 4.4 · Thu 4.5 m

options: Tuesday, on the rising tides
Thursday, at the top of springs
Wednesday
Friday, once springs are past
questions.why: You must float on and off: Wed 4.4 m on, Thu 4.5 m off. On Thursday, Friday's 4.2 m leaves you neaped; Tuesday is too low.

questions.q: Your three-cylinder diesel uses a litre of oil a day and smokes blue under load. The mechanic gives you this. What is wrong?

figure.title: Compression test, bar
lines: Cylinder 3, a little oil squirted in: 27

options: A dribbling injector in cylinder 3
The head gasket between cylinders 2 and 3
A burnt exhaust valve in cylinder 3
Worn rings or bore in cylinder 3
questions.why: Oil seals the rings for a moment, so compression that rises with oil means ring or bore wear; a bad valve would stay low.

questions.q: At sea you have changed both fuel filters and bled the system. The engine still will not fire. What do you do next?

figure.title: After the filter change
lines: Bled at the fine filter: fuel bubble-free
Bled at the injection pump: fuel bubble-free
Engine cranks well but does not fire

options: Crack the injector pipe unions and crank until fuel spurts
Keep cranking — it will draw the air through
Change the new filters — one must be faulty
Spray start aid into the air intake
questions.why: Air is trapped between the injection pump and the injectors: slacken each union at the injector, crank, tighten as fuel comes.
questions.ref: Power plant — bleeding the fuel system

questions.q: Over three days on passage you see this at each morning check. What is happening?

figure.title: Engine oil, daily check
lines: Level above the max mark, higher each day
Oil thin and smells of diesel
No water or emulsion in it

options: It was overfilled at the last change — drain some
Fuel is leaking into the sump — a lift pump diaphragm
Coolant is getting in — the head gasket
Normal — warm oil reads higher and thinner
questions.why: A split lift-pump diaphragm (or injection-pump seal) lets diesel into the sump and thins the oil; stop, fix, change the oil.

questions.q: After 12 hours motoring into a rough sea, the panel shows this and the revs start to hunt. What do you do?

lines: Filter vacuum, inHg: 2 at the start
Duplex primary filter, standby side clean

options: Bleed the line — air is leaking in before the filter
Clean the air filter — the turbo is short of air
Switch to the clean side — the filter is clogging
Ease the revs — the injection pump is wearing
questions.why: Rising vacuum across the primary filter means it is blocking: a rough sea stirs up tank sludge and diesel bug. Change over, renew it.

questions.q: Over the last few weeks the engine has run hotter at cruising revs. You have already checked these. What is the most likely cause?

lines: Normal at these revs 82°; coolant tank full
Strong flow at the exhaust; new impeller

options: The raw-water seacock left partly closed
The thermostat stuck in the open position
A worn impeller — change it once again
Scale or impeller debris blocking the heat-exchanger tubes
questions.why: Strong raw-water flow and full coolant point to poor heat transfer: scaled or blocked heat-exchanger tubes. Rod or descale them.

questions.q: After two days hard on the wind heeled to port with the engine off, you try to start it. This happens. What do you do?

figure.title: Engine below the waterline
lines: It turns part of a turn, then locks solid
Oil on the dipstick grey and milky; level up

options: Take out the injectors and turn it by hand to clear the water
Bleed the fuel system — it is an air lock
Parallel the batteries and crank it harder
Tap the starter and keep trying the key
questions.why: A stuck anti-siphon valve let seawater siphon into the exhaust and cylinders: hydraulic lock. Cranking bends rods; clear it by hand, change the oil.

questions.q: Your steel motor-sailer has a keel-cooled engine. After six months in a warm marina it overheats at cruising revs. What is the most likely cause?

figure.title: Keel-cooled engine
lines: Coolant runs through pipes outside the hull
No raw-water pump in the engine's circuit

options: A worn raw-water impeller
Growth fouling the keel-cooler pipes outside
The thermostat stuck open
A scaled-up heat exchanger
questions.why: A keel cooler is a heat exchanger in the sea itself: weed, barnacles or thick paint on its pipes stop it shedding heat. Clean it bare.

questions.q: Before an offshore season you sent an oil sample for analysis. This comes back. What is the most likely cause?

figure.title: Oil analysis report
lines: Wear metals iron and aluminium rising

options: Coolant leaking into the oil
Seawater getting into the oil
Dirt getting past a damaged air filter or intake
Normal wear — the oil change is due
questions.why: Silicon is dust; with rising wear metals it means dirt is getting in through the intake. A coolant leak shows glycol, sodium and potassium.

questions.q: Your battery monitor logged these loads over 24 hours on passage. What is the smallest AGM house bank that lasts 24 hours without going below half charge?

figure.title: Battery monitor, last 24 h
lines: Autopilot 6 A, 24 h · instruments 3 A, 24 h
Nav lights 1 A, 10 h · radar 3 A, 10 h

options: About 400 Ah
About 320 Ah
About 860 Ah
About 630 Ah
questions.why: 144 + 72 + 60 + 10 + 30 = 316 Ah a day; using only half an AGM bank, it needs about 2 × 316 = 632 Ah.

questions.q: At a refit you replace the AGM house bank with lithium (LiFePO4). The engine's alternator charges it directly. What must you add?

figure.title: Refit plan
lines: New house bank: LiFePO4 with its own BMS
BMS cuts the bank off at a cell limit

options: Alternator protection or a DC-DC charger
A monthly equalisation charge
Nothing — lithium accepts any charge
A higher float voltage for lithium
questions.why: If the BMS cuts the bank off while charging, the alternator's voltage spikes and it can burn out; lithium also overworks a standard one.

questions.q: The engine will not crank — one click. You put a voltmeter on the circuit and read this. What is the fault?

figure.title: Voltmeter readings
lines: Key to start — at the battery posts: 12.2 V
Key to start — at the starter terminal: 8.1 V

options: A flat engine battery — charge it
A bad connection in the starter cable or its earth
A blown fuse in the ignition circuit
A seized starter motor — replace it
questions.why: The battery holds 12.2 V under load but only 8.1 V reaches the starter: 4 V lost in a corroded or loose cable, terminal or earth strap.

questions.q: Since you took a season berth on shore power, the anodes behave like this. What do you fit?

figure.title: Anode wear
lines: At anchor last year: anodes lasted 12 months
Marina, on shore power: half gone in 6 weeks
Crowded pontoon, all on shore power

options: Magnesium anodes while in the marina
Bigger zinc anodes, changed more often
A galvanic isolator in the shore-power earth
Nothing — cut the earth wire in the shore lead
questions.why: The shore earth joins your underwater metals to every boat on the pontoon; an isolator blocks that galvanic current but keeps the safety earth.

questions.q: Motoring at cruising revs, the gearbox starts to slip in ahead. You find this. What do you do first?

figure.title: Gearbox check
lines: Slips at high revs, grips at low revs
Hot, burnt smell from the box
Oil on the dipstick well below the mark

options: Top it up with whatever engine oil is aboard
Run on at high revs to bed the clutches in
Adjust the throttle cable for more revs
Top up with the specified oil and find the leak
questions.why: Low oil lets the clutch packs slip and burn: top up with the oil the maker specifies, find the leak, keep the revs moderate.

questions.q: Vibration at cruising revs has grown over the season, and the stern gland drips more. At haul-out you find this. What is it?

figure.title: Shaft check on the hard
lines: Shaft moves 3 mm up and down at the P-bracket

options: A worn cutless bearing — replace it, check the alignment
Soft engine mounts — fit harder ones
Normal play — water lubrication takes it up
A bent propeller blade — have it trued
questions.why: The water-lubricated cutless bearing wears; the shaft whips, vibrates and works the stern gland. Renew it and check alignment.
questions.ref: Power plant — shaft and cutless bearing

questions.q: You are preparing a 9-year-old saildrive yacht for a 150 M passage. The maker's manual says this. What do you do?

figure.title: Saildrive manual
lines: Rubber diaphragm seals the leg to the hull

options: Inspect it from inside; replace it only if wet
Replace the diaphragm at haul-out before you go
Leave it — rubber below water lasts decades
Replace it at the next 7-year interval
questions.why: The diaphragm is all that keeps the sea out round the leg; at 9 years it is past the maker's 7-year life. Renew it first.

questions.q: Backing into a Med berth in a crosswind, you get this from your folding propeller. What do you do?

figure.title: Going astern at tickover
lines: Very little sternway; the bow blows off
Prop clear; she drives normally ahead

options: Go ahead first — folding props drive only ahead
Stop and dive on it — something is round it
Give a firm burst of astern revs to open the blades
Stay at tickover and wait for the way to build
questions.why: Folding blades open by spin and thrust; at tickover astern they barely open. A firm burst opens them, then ease back.
questions.ref: Power plant — folding and feathering propellers

questions.q: 80 M offshore, your 22 m twin-screw motor yacht loses her port engine. The starboard one runs fine. What does she do, and what do you do?

figure.title: Port engine stopped
lines: Manual: the dead shaft may trail free

options: Bow swings to starboard — hold it with port rudder; moderate revs
Bow swings to port — open the starboard engine to full
No swing — the shafts are close together; full revs
Bow swings to port — hold it with starboard rudder; moderate revs
questions.why: The working starboard screw pushes the bow to port; steer against it, and keep the revs down: one engine is overloaded driving the hull alone.

questions.q: On passage you run the 8 kW generator three hours a day, only to power the watermaker. After a fortnight you see this. What do you change?

figure.title: Generator after 2 weeks
lines: Black, oily soot round the exhaust outlet
Runs cleanly on a full-load test

options: Load it up — run the charger and water heater with it
Change the injectors — they are dribbling
Fit a bigger generator for the watermaker
Run it longer each day at the same load
questions.why: At 15% load a diesel never gets hot: unburnt fuel glazes the bores and wets the exhaust ('wet stacking'). Give it real load.

questions.q: On passage the engine starts doing this. What is the most likely fault?

lines: Steady white smoke with a sweet smell
Coolant down a litre a day; bubbles in tank

options: Water in the fuel — drain the separator
A failed head gasket or a cracked head
A blocked exhaust injection elbow
Normal smoke from a cold engine
questions.why: White, sweet-smelling smoke with coolant loss and bubbles in the header tank means coolant is reaching the cylinders: the head gasket.

questions.q: At night you motor through a line of fishing floats. Moments later this happens. What is it, and what do you do?

figure.title: 2340, motoring
lines: Revs fall at the same throttle; black smoke

options: A slipping gearbox — top it up and slow down
A blocked air filter — clean it and carry on
A fouled prop — stop the engine, clear it at first light
Water in the fuel — drain the separator
questions.why: Sudden vibration and an overloaded engine just after fishing gear is a fouled prop: stop it, then clear it in daylight, tethered.

questions.q: You are about to leave on this passage. Which service falls due before you arrive?

figure.title: Engine log
lines: Oil & filter: done at 1,180, every 250 h
Fuel filters: done at 1,300, every 500 h

options: Nothing — every item lasts the passage
The impeller — it falls due on passage
Both the oil and the impeller
The oil and filter — change them before you leave
questions.why: 420 × 0.6 ÷ 6.5 ≈ 39 h, so about 1,449 h on arrival. The oil is due at 1,430; the impeller (1,500) and filters (1,800) are not.

questions.q: These are your displacement motor yacht's dimensions. Above about what speed does she need far more power for very little more speed?
options: About 10.5 kn
About 9.1 kn
About 5.8 kn
About 11.3 kn
questions.why: Hull speed ≈ 1.34 × √LWL in feet: 18.6 m = 61 ft, √61 = 7.81, × 1.34 = 10.5 kn. Use the waterline, not the length overall.

questions.q: This is your planing motor yacht's consumption curve. Once she is on the plane, at which speed does she burn the least fuel per mile?

figure.title: Fuel consumption, both engines
lines: On the plane from about 17 kn

options: 14 kn
24 kn
18 kn
30 kn
questions.why: Litres per mile = L/h ÷ kn: 18 kn 9.4, 24 kn 8.75, 30 kn 10.0 — least at 24 kn; 14 kn, still off the plane, is worst at 10.7.

questions.q: You are buying a 15 m GRP yacht for offshore work. The survey and the owner's offer are below. What does a lasting cure need?

figure.title: Pre-purchase survey
lines: Blisters below the waterline, many small
Moisture meter: wet across the bottom

options: Two coats of hard antifouling to seal the gelcoat
Pressure-wash, dry a weekend, then antifoul as usual
Peel the gelcoat, dry the laminate for months, then epoxy-coat
Grind out the blisters, fill them, and antifoul
questions.why: Osmosis lives in wet laminate: only peeling, drying until the meter reads dry, and an epoxy barrier stop it coming back.

questions.q: Checking the deck before an offshore season, you find this round a stanchion base. What is it, and what do you do?

figure.title: Stanchion base, side deck
lines: The stanchion rocks when you pull it
Underneath: washers only, no backing plate

options: Old gelcoat crazing — polish and wax it
Osmosis in the deck — dry it out
Sun damage — paint over the deck
Overload at the base — rebed it on a backing plate
questions.why: Star cracks radiating from fastenings mean the load is not spread: rebed on a backing plate, seal the holes, repair the gelcoat.

questions.q: The surveyor has measured your 20-year-old steel yacht's plating ultrasonically. Which plating must be renewed?

figure.title: Ultrasonic thickness survey
lines: Renew any plate below 75% of original

options: The bilge plating only
All of it — she has lost steel everywhere
The bilge and the waterline plating
None — every reading is above 4 mm
questions.why: 75% of 6.0 mm is 4.5 mm: the bilge (4.2 mm, 70%) is below it; the waterline (4.7 mm, 78%) and topsides are above.

questions.q: Your carvel-planked wooden ketch is relaunched after six dry months ashore. What do you expect, and what do you do?

figure.title: Relaunch day
lines: Six months ashore in a dry summer

options: Seal the open seams from inside with silicone
She leaks till the planks swell — keep her in the slings
The planking has failed — haul her out again at once
Nothing — a sound wooden hull never leaks a drop
questions.why: Dried planks shrink and the seams open; afloat they take up water and close in a day or two. Keep her in the slings, pumps going.

questions.q: Your rigger estimates chainplate loads this way. Close-hauled at 25° of heel, roughly what load does the windward cap-shroud chainplate carry?

figure.title: Rigger's estimate
lines: Displacement 15 t; GZ at 25° heel 0.62 m
Load ≈ RM ÷ chainplate's distance off CL

options: About 14.4 t
About 9.3 t
About 6.0 t
About 3.0 t
questions.why: RM = 15 t × 0.62 m = 9.3 t·m; ÷ 1.55 m = 6.0 t. Dividing by the full 3.1 m spread halves it; 9.3 is the moment, not a load.

questions.q: Re-torquing the keel bolts at haul-out, you reach this nut. What do you do?

figure.title: Keel bolts, re-torque
lines: Bolts 1–5 reached the torque in a few degrees
Bolt 6 has turned half a turn already
The wrench never reaches its setting

options: Tighten the other five harder to share the load
Back it off a full turn and torque it up again
Keep turning until the torque wrench finally clicks
Stop: the bolt or thread is yielding — get it checked
questions.why: A nut that turns on without the torque rising means a stretching bolt, a stripping thread or a crushing backing: stop and investigate.

questions.q: The keel builder's manual gives the bolt torque in N·m, but your torque wrench is scaled in lbf·ft. What do you set it to?
options: About 250 lbf·ft
About 460 lbf·ft
About 35 lbf·ft
About 340 lbf·ft
questions.why: 340 N·m ÷ 1.356 = 251 lbf·ft. Multiplying gives 461 — an overload that can stretch the bolt; ÷ 9.81 gives kgf·m, not lbf·ft.

questions.q: You are choosing between two otherwise similar 14 m yachts for passages far from help, through waters full of fishing gear. Which rudder do you prefer?

figure.title: Two yachts, one choice
lines: A: spade rudder on its stock and 2 bearings
B: rudder hung on a full skeg, lower pintle
Waters: pot lines, nets, floating debris

options: A's — a spade has no skeg that can be torn off
B's — the skeg supports the blade and guards it from lines
B's — a skeg-hung rudder gives more lift than a spade
A's — a balanced spade cannot jam or foul
questions.why: A skeg carries a lower bearing and fends off lines and debris; a spade hangs from its stock alone — more efficient, less protected.

questions.q: Two seacocks below the waterline need renewing before an offshore season. The yard offers these four sets. Which do you accept?

figure.title: Yard's seacock options
lines: All four sets in stock, at the same price

options: Bronze skin fitting with a 316 stainless valve
Bronze skin fitting with a brass plumbing valve
Bronze skin fitting with a bronze ball valve
Nylon garden valve on a nylon skin fitting
questions.why: Below the waterline use one metal — marine bronze or DZR — or a rated composite set: stainless crevice-corrodes, brass dezincifies.

questions.q: Close-hauled as shown, 90 M from port, you hit a floating container. A crack in the bow takes water at every wave. What do you do first?

figure.note: Crack: starboard bow, just above the waterline

options: Bear away onto a run to keep her upright
Start the engine and motor head to sea
Hold this tack so the heel presses the crack shut
Tack, so she heels to port and lifts the crack clear
questions.why: On port tack she heels to starboard and buries the damage; on starboard tack it lifts clear, to be dried and patched from inside.

questions.q: On your aluminium yacht you read the hull potential against a silver-chloride reference electrode, switching circuits on in turn. What do the readings tell you?
options: The bilge-pump circuit leaks current through the hull
The hull is overprotected — take off an anode
All is normal — the reading stays negative
The anodes are spent — renew them all
questions.why: Switching that circuit on drives the hull from −1,000 to −700 mV, out of the protected range: a DC leak is eating the aluminium.

questions.q: Your 17 m yacht has rod rigging. Before a season of 150 M passages, the rigger reports this. What do you do?

figure.title: Rigger's report, rod rigging
lines: Heads look perfect; no visible cracks
Rigger's interval: heads remade at 10 years

options: Tape the spreader bends and check them daily
Unstep the mast and have the rod heads remade
Nothing — rod shows broken strands well before it fails
Check the tension and sail — rod rarely breaks
questions.why: Rod is a single strand: it fails by fatigue at the cold-formed heads and bends, without the warning wire gives. Service it on time.

questions.q: Four months after the yard fitted Dyneema lower shrouds, a tension check on passage shows this. What do you do?

figure.title: Rig check, day 3
lines: Tension now 12% below the set-up figure
Covers sound, no chafe; caps tension normal

options: Replace them before the next passage
Check the mast step — the mast is sinking
Re-tension them — Dyneema creeps under steady load
Leave them — a little slack lets the mast flex
questions.why: Dyneema slowly creeps under constant load, more when warm: re-tension to the set-up figure and check it on a schedule.

questions.q: On your morning rig check you find this on a Dyneema cap shroud. What do you do?

figure.title: Rig check at the spreader tip
lines: Cover worn through at the spreader end

options: Re-tension it — the fuzz is only a sign of creep
Tape over the fuzz and keep an eye on it daily
Nothing — Dyneema is far stronger than steel wire
Replace it before you sail, and pad the spreader tip
questions.why: Synthetic rigging fails by chafe and UV, not fatigue: cut core fibres mean lost strength. Replace it and protect the contact point.

questions.q: You are buying a 13 m yacht for offshore passages. The haul-out survey lists these. Which do you have investigated before you agree a price?

figure.title: Pre-purchase survey, on the hard
lines: Rudder weeps water from its lower edge
Anodes half gone after a season

options: The rudder — water inside can corrode its stock and frame
The antifouling — the wear shows osmosis coming
The anodes — half gone means a stray current
The cutless bearing — it will need doing soon
questions.why: Water weeping from a rudder means a wet core; the stainless frame inside can corrode unseen. Have it opened or tested.

questions.q: Your 24 m motor yacht takes a heavier tender on her top deck. Reading the booklet's GZ curve, what is her righting lever at 30° now?

figure.title: Stability booklet and the new tender
lines: Δ 60 t with the new tender aboard
Tender 1.5 t, 4.8 m above the yacht's G
Rise of G = w × h ÷ Δ

questions.why: GG1 = 1.5 × 4.8 ÷ 60 = 0.12 m; new GZ = 0.42 − 0.12 × sin 30° = 0.36 m. Without the sine, 0.30; adding it, 0.48.
questions.ref: Stability — the GZ curve and added weight

questions.q: To clear a blocked pick-up, the engineer pumps fuel from the port tank to the starboard one. What list does it give your motor yacht?

figure.title: Fuel transfer
lines: Δ 48 t · KG 2.40 m · GM 0.80 m
Moved: 1.2 t, port tank → starboard tank
Shift of G: GG1 = w × d ÷ Δ

options: About 14° to starboard
About 4° to starboard
About 7° to starboard
About 2° to starboard
questions.why: GG1 = 1.2 × 4.0 ÷ 48 = 0.10 m; tan θ = 0.10 ÷ 0.80 → 7°. Half the distance gives 4°; counting the weight twice, 14°.

questions.q: The crane lifts your tender off its chocks to launch it. While it hangs from the crane head, what is the yacht's GM?

figure.title: Launching the tender
lines: Δ 30 t; GM 0.70 m, tender in its chocks
Tender 0.45 t; chocks 2.0 m above G
Rise of G = w × h ÷ Δ

questions.why: A hanging weight acts at the crane head: it rises 6.0 − 2.0 = 4.0 m; GG1 = 0.45 × 4.0 ÷ 30 = 0.06 m; GM 0.70 − 0.06 = 0.64 m.

questions.q: Your motor yacht leaves on a 140 M passage with four full fuel tanks; she will burn about half. The engineer plans as below. What do you tell him?

figure.title: Engineer's fuel plan
lines: Four tanks, 1,500 L each, all full
Plan: draw from all four evenly

options: Run one tank down at a time; keep the others full
Draw the two wing tanks together, then the centre pair
Draw all four, and transfer to level them each watch
Agreed — an even draw keeps her trim and list level
questions.why: Every slack tank adds its own free surface: four half-full tanks cost far more GM than one. Run them down one at a time.

questions.q: At dusk on a 130 M catamaran delivery, you set the sail plan for the night. Following the owner's manual, what do you set?

figure.title: 15 m catamaran, tonight
lines: Manual: reef 1 at 20 kn, 2 at 25, 3 at 30

options: Second reef, and ease the sheets in each gust
Third reef — for the 32 kn gusts, not the mean
Full main — she barely heels, so she is not pressed
First reef — for the top of the mean, 22 kn
questions.why: A cat gives no heel to warn you and capsizes past her peak GZ: reef for the strongest gust — 32 kn is over the 30 kn third-reef mark.

questions.q: Two days out, your motor yacht's roll has become slow and lazy. You time it and use the rule in her booklet. What is her GM now?

figure.title: Rolling period check
lines: Now, a full roll out and back: 9.6 s

options: About 0.39 m
About 0.06 m
About 0.25 m
About 0.50 m
questions.why: √GM = 0.8 × 6.0 ÷ 9.6 = 0.50, so GM = 0.25 m — about half the 0.47 m of a 7 s roll. Find the free water or weight high up.

questions.q: Running before a big following sea at night, the watch want the washboards out so they can come and go. What is her real limit of stability like that?
options: About 125° — she rights herself up to her AVS
About 90° — the moment her mast is flat
About 62° — the angle of her greatest GZ
About 105° — past it she floods and the curve fails
questions.why: The GZ curve assumes a watertight hull: with the companionway open she floods at 105°, well short of the 125° AVS. Washboards in.

questions.q: You plan a 120 M crossing in this yacht with eleven aboard. What does her builder's plate allow?
options: No more than eight aboard for the crossing
Eleven is fine — the plate allows twelve
Eleven, if you stay within 60 M of land
Eleven, if the load stays under 1,600 kg
questions.why: Her Category B rating holds only with eight or fewer; with eleven she is a Category C, inshore boat — wrong for a 120 M crossing.

questions.q: A gale is forecast for tonight. You find this on deck. What do you do with the cans?
options: Lash them higher up, on the coachroof, out of the way
Stow them low and central below, well secured
Move them all to the windward rail for the night
Leave them — the weight helps her stand up
questions.why: 160 kg at the rail raises G and cuts the stability that brings her back from a knockdown. Stow heavy gear low and central.

questions.q: The yard will haul you on their slipway today. At what state of the tide do you motor onto the submerged cradle?

figure.note: Cradle hauled up the rails by winch

options: At low water, when the cradle's blocks show
On the early ebb, so she settles onto the cradle
On the last of the flood, about an hour before HW
Any time — the winch does all the work
questions.why: Come on with the tide still rising: if she is badly placed, the flood lifts her clear to try again. On the ebb she can be left on it askew.

questions.q: Your 22 m motor yacht cruises at 28–32 kn. The yard proposes the antifouling below. What do you ask for instead?

figure.title: Yard's antifouling quote
lines: Two coats of soft self-polishing paint
Rated by the maker for up to 25 kn

options: No antifouling — her speed keeps her clean
Nothing — self-polishing lasts longest of all
A thicker coat of the same self-polisher
A hard antifouling made for high speeds
questions.why: Self-polishing paint wears away with water flow and is soon scrubbed off at 30 kn; fast boats take a hard antifouling.

questions.q: The yard aligned your new engine to the shaft before relaunch. Afloat, she vibrates at cruising revs. What do you do?

figure.title: After the engine refit
lines: Aligned on the hard, in the cradle
Propeller checked and balanced last year

options: Have the alignment rechecked afloat once she has settled
Tighten the engine mounts hard down
Fit a bigger shaft anode to damp it
Rebalance the propeller before anything else
questions.why: A hull changes shape afloat and with the rig tensioned: align at the coupling with feeler gauges after a few days in the water.
questions.ref: Power plant — shaft alignment and vibration

questions.q: On a cold spring morning the engine cranks slowly and will not fire, though fuel reaches the injectors. Why not?

figure.title: Cold start
lines: Starter turns slowly; battery 11.9 V at rest
Fuel spurts at a cracked injector union

options: Air in the fuel — it needs bleeding again
Too slow to make enough heat of compression
Water in the fuel — drain the separator
The injection pump timing has slipped
questions.why: A diesel fires on the heat of compression: slow cranking lets heat and pressure leak away. Charge or parallel the battery; use the glow plugs.

questions.q: After a filter change at sea, the engine does this. What is the most likely fault?

figure.title: Since the filter change
lines: Bled: it starts and runs sweetly
After about 20 min it falters and stops

options: An injector is dribbling in one cylinder
Diesel bug is clogging the new filter
A bad seal lets air in on the suction side
The lift pump is failing when it gets hot
questions.why: On the suction side a poor seal leaks air in, not fuel out — so no drip. Re-seat the filter bowl's seal and check the unions.

questions.q: You are preparing a yacht that has sat for two years for a 150 M passage. A sample from the bottom of the tank looks like this. What do you do?

figure.title: Fuel tank sample
lines: Taken from the tank's drain point
Water layer with black slime above it

options: Add biocide and sail — it kills the bug
Top the tank up with fresh fuel to dilute it
Change the filters and carry plenty of spares
Polish the fuel and clean the tank before you sail
questions.why: A seaway stirs the sludge into the filters within hours. Polish the fuel through a filter loop, clean the tank, then dose biocide.
questions.ref: Power plant — fuel bug and fuel polishing

questions.q: Your four-cylinder engine knocks and smokes black at idle. You slacken each injector union in turn and note the change in revs. Which injector is at fault?

figure.title: Injector cut-out test at idle
lines: Union slackened in turn — fall in revs:

options: No. 3 — cutting it off changes nothing
No. 2 — it gives the biggest drop
No. 4 — it gives the smallest drop
All four — the drops are uneven
questions.why: A cylinder that is firing loses revs when its fuel is cut; No. 3 makes no difference, so it was already not firing properly.

questions.q: Your turbocharged diesel has started to do this. What is the most likely cause?

figure.title: Blue smoke
lines: Blue at idle and light load, clears on load
Oil level correct, but using more each week
Compression even on all four cylinders
Oil film in the intake pipe after the turbo

options: A dribbling injector
Worn turbocharger oil seals
Worn piston rings in one cylinder
An overfilled sump after the oil change
questions.why: Blue smoke with even compression, the right oil level and oil in the intake after the turbo: its seals leak oil into the charge air.

questions.q: Two hours after refuelling at a remote quay, the engine does this. What is the most likely cause, and what do you do?

figure.title: 2 h after refuelling
lines: Misfiring; grey-white smoke, no sweet smell
Separator bowl: a clear layer under the fuel

options: A blocked air filter — clean it
A cold engine — let it warm up
Water in the fuel — drain the separator, change tanks
A blown head gasket — stop the engine for good
questions.why: Misfiring and grey-white smoke soon after refuelling, with water in the separator bowl: bad fuel. Drain, switch tanks, watch the bowl.

questions.q: In a Force 8 you closed the engine-room vents to keep the spray out. Since then the panel shows this. What do you do?

lines: Black smoke; engine room very hot

options: Stop and check the prop for a rope
Slow to idle — the turbo is failing
Switch fuel filters — one is clogging
Open the vents — the engine is starved of air
questions.why: A diesel needs a great deal of air: shut vents starve it, so it smokes black, loses revs and heats the room. Open them; trust the baffles.
questions.ref: Power plant — black smoke and loss of power

questions.q: Cruising at 1,900 rpm, your twin-screw motor yacht's starboard engine starts to overheat. What is the most likely fault?

lines: Stbd seacock open; little exhaust water
Stbd strainer bowl half air, not refilling

options: The starboard intake is blocked outside the hull
The starboard thermostat has stuck shut
The starboard impeller has failed
The starboard heat exchanger has scaled up
questions.why: A strainer below the waterline floods by itself even if the impeller dies; air in it that will not clear means the intake is blocked.

questions.q: Crossing at night, your twin-screw motor yacht's port engine will no longer reach its revs. What is the most likely cause?

figure.title: Port engine, 0300
lines: Port in neutral: revs freely to 2,600
Black smoke from port only, under load
Port shaft has vibrated since about 0200

options: The port turbocharger is failing
Something round the port propeller
The port gearbox is slipping
The port fuel filter is clogging
questions.why: It revs freely unloaded but smokes and labours in gear, and the shaft vibrates: the load has grown — a fouled port propeller.

questions.q: After a new propeller was fitted, the sea trial gives this. What does it tell you?

figure.title: Sea trial, new propeller
lines: Top speed 1.5 kn below the old propeller

options: Too much pitch — the propeller is too heavy
A fouled hull — scrub her and try again
Too little pitch — the propeller is too light
The governor is set too low — raise it
questions.why: Reaching rated revs at part throttle with poor speed means the prop is not loading the engine: underpropped. It needs more pitch.

questions.q: Your motor yacht, fully laden, will not reach her revs at full throttle. What do you ask the propeller shop to do?

figure.title: Full-throttle trial, laden
lines: Rated 3,000 rpm; aim 2,900 at full throttle
Yours: 2,500 rpm, black smoke, hot exhaust
Prop shop: 1 in of pitch ≈ 200 rpm

options: Leave it — lower revs save fuel
Add 2 in of pitch
Take 2.5 in of pitch out
Take 2 in of pitch out
questions.why: Overpropped: (2,900 − 2,500) ÷ 200 = 2 in less pitch. 2.5 in aims at the 3,000 maximum, not the 2,900 target.

questions.q: The charger has been on for three hours. The crew say it is failing because the current keeps dropping. What is happening?

lines: Bulk: 62 A until 14.4 V at 2 h 10 min
Now 3 h in; current still falling

options: Absorption — at 14.4 V the current falls as it fills
The charger is failing — swap in the spare one
The bank is full — switch it to float by hand
A shorted cell is refusing to take the charge
questions.why: Bulk pushes full current up to the set voltage; absorption holds that voltage while the current tapers; float follows when nearly full.

questions.q: Three weeks into a long passage, the AGM house bank holds less each day. Your routine is below. What is happening, and what do you change?

figure.title: Charging routine on passage
lines: No solar; the charger never reaches float
Week 3: lower voltage under the same loads

options: Run that hour at higher revs to finish the charge
It is sulphating, never full — give it a long full charge
Normal ageing — nothing can be done at sea
The alternator is failing — fit the spare
questions.why: An hour gets bulk done, but absorption needs hours more; a bank kept at 50–80% sulphates. Charge it to full regularly.

questions.q: Ten days out, the battery monitor and the voltmeter disagree. Which do you believe, and what do you do?

figure.title: House bank, day 10
lines: Voltage after 2 h with no load: 12.2 V
AGM at rest: 12.8 V full · 12.2 V ≈ 50%

options: Neither — an AGM bank always rests at 12.2 V
The monitor — 91% is right; the bank is ageing
The voltage — the monitor has drifted; recharge fully
The monitor — the voltmeter must be reading low
questions.why: A shunt monitor only counts amp-hours and drifts until it syncs at full; 12.2 V at rest is about half. Charge to full to resync it.

questions.q: You will replace the AGM house bank with lithium (LiFePO4). What is the smallest lithium bank that gives you the same usable amp-hours?

figure.title: House bank change
lines: Now: 600 Ah AGM, used down to 50%

options: About 600 Ah
About 960 Ah
About 240 Ah
About 375 Ah
questions.why: Usable now: 600 × 50% = 300 Ah. Lithium used to 80%: 300 ÷ 0.8 = 375 Ah. 960 inverts the ratio; 240 multiplies both.

questions.q: Your yacht will spend the winter 40 km up a freshwater river. Which anodes do you fit for those months?

figure.title: Winter plan
lines: Berth: 40 km up a freshwater river
Fitted now: zinc anodes, for the sea

options: Magnesium — zinc goes passive in fresh water
None — fresh water does not corrode metal
Keep the zinc — it works in any water
Aluminium — it is made for fresh water
questions.why: Zinc and aluminium anodes crust over in fresh water and stop working; magnesium is active enough. Back to zinc or aluminium at sea.
questions.ref: Power plant — anodes for fresh, brackish and salt water

questions.q: Your home berth is in a brackish estuary, and you sail at sea all summer. Which anodes suit both?

figure.title: Anodes for your berth
lines: Hull GRP; bronze shaft, prop and seacocks

options: Magnesium — the most active is the safest
Aluminium alloy — it works in salt and brackish water
Zinc — the standard for any sea-going boat
Zinc at sea, and nothing in the marina
questions.why: Zinc goes passive in brackish water; magnesium overprotects in salt and wastes fast. Aluminium alloy anodes work in both.
questions.ref: Power plant — anodes for fresh, brackish and salt water

questions.q: On your 24 V motor yacht at anchor, these AC loads run through the inverter each day. About how many amp-hours do they take from the house bank?

figure.title: AC loads via the inverter
lines: Induction hob 1,800 W, 45 min a day
Coffee machine 1,100 W, 30 min a day
TV and laptops 120 W, 4 h a day

options: About 100 Ah
About 230 Ah
About 110 Ah
About 90 Ah
questions.why: AC 1,350 + 550 + 480 = 2,380 Wh; ÷ 0.88 = 2,705 Wh from the bank; ÷ 24 V = 113 Ah. Ignoring the loss gives 99; 12 V doubles it.

questions.q: The crew want the aircon on. Which of the running loads can stay on while it starts, without tripping the generator?

figure.title: Generator and aircon
lines: Aircon 1.8 kW running, 3× that to start

options: None — switch everything off first
All three — the total is only 6.8 kW
The charger and the watermaker
Only the watermaker
questions.why: Starting takes 3 × 1.8 = 5.4 kW, leaving 1.6 kW: only the 1.2 kW watermaker fits. Once the aircon runs, add the others back.

questions.q: Nine days into a passage, your watermaker shows this. What do you do?
options: Divert the product overboard and clean the membrane
Change the prefilters again and carry on
Raise the pressure to force the salt back out
Drink it — at 640 ppm it is still fresh water
questions.why: Rising salinity at normal pressure with clean prefilters means a fouled membrane: dump the product and clean it by the maker's routine.

questions.q: You are leaving the yacht for three weeks. The watermaker has run daily until today. What do you do with it?

figure.title: Watermaker manual
lines: Unused over 2 weeks: pickle the membrane

options: Take out the prefilters and leave the rest
Pickle the membrane, as the manual says
Run it hard today to leave it clean
Leave it full of seawater until you return
questions.why: Left unused, a membrane grows bacteria within days: flush it every few days, or pickle it for a longer lay-up.

questions.q: Before a 150 M passage you check the engine log. Is the oil change due?

figure.title: Engine log
lines: Oil and filter: every 250 h or 12 months

options: No — it falls due at the next 250 h
No — only 80 of the 250 hours are used
Yes — the 12 months have passed
Only if the oil on the dipstick looks dark
questions.why: Intervals are 'hours or months, whichever comes first': oil ages and gathers acid and moisture even while the engine sits.

questions.q: After a diversion, fuel is short in your planing motor yacht. At which speed does she go furthest on what is left?

figure.title: Fuel curve, 20 m planing yacht
lines: On the plane from about 20 kn

options: 22 kn
26 kn
30 kn
8 kn
questions.why: Litres per mile = L/h ÷ kn: 8 kn 4.5, 26 kn 9.2, 22 kn 9.5, 30 kn 10.3. Slow, off the plane and below the hump, goes furthest.

questions.q: You are rigging a snubber for a night at anchor in your 24 m yacht, with a swell running in. Your mate offers the line in the figure. What do you say?

figure.title: The mate's offer for the snubber

options: No: it hardly stretches, so each snatch hits the fittings
Yes, if you double it so that it can never part
Yes, once each end has a good whipping on it
Yes: twice the strength means half the risk of parting
questions.why: A snubber works by stretching; Dyneema stretches about 1%, so the shock loads go straight into the chain, cleats and windlass.

questions.q: You are making up a towing bridle from 12 mm Dyneema for an offshore tow. Your crew starts tying a bowline in each end. What do you tell them?
options: Carry on, but tape the tails flat along the line
Splice the eyes: knots slip in it and halve its strength
Tie figure-of-eight loops, which hold in any rope
Carry on: Dyneema is strong enough for any knot
questions.why: Dyneema is slippery and weak in knots: a bowline can creep out and keeps about half its strength; a spliced eye keeps most of it.

questions.q: You read this note in the survey of your 20 m sloop before the season. What do you do about the runners?

figure.title: Survey before the season
lines: Cover clean, no chafe, no stiffness
Worked hard every season over 80 mm sheaves

options: Keep them: aramid does not age the way polyester does
Turn them end for end and keep them for a season
Replace them: aramid weakens with flexing and UV, unseen
Keep them and check the covers at mid-season
questions.why: Aramid loses strength from flex fatigue over sheaves and from UV with no outward sign; old aramid running rigging is replaced on age.

questions.q: You are lengthening the rode of your 20 m yacht for a season of deep anchorages. Which rope and which join?

figure.title: Lengthening the rode
lines: Windlass gypsy takes rope and 10 mm chain
50 m of chain now; adding 100 m of rope
The join must run over the gypsy

options: Dyneema braid, with a thimbled eye and a shackle
Three-strand polyester, shackled to the last link
8-plait nylon, with a thimbled eye and a shackle
8-plait nylon, spliced through the last chain link
questions.why: 8-plait nylon stretches and stows without kinking; a rope-to-chain splice runs over the gypsy, where a shackle and thimble jam.

questions.q: You will tie this line into the bridle with bowlines for a tow in a seaway. What is the most working load you should put on it?

figure.title: Line for the tow bridle
lines: 16 mm nylon three-strand, MBS 6.0 t new
Wet nylon keeps about 85% of that
A bowline keeps about 60% of the rest

options: About 0.6 t
About 3.1 t
About 0.7 t
About 1.0 t
questions.why: 6.0 × 0.85 wet × 0.6 for the knot = 3.06 t at break; ÷ 5 = about 0.6 t.

questions.q: You are buying new stern lines for a gale berth stern-to. What is the smallest size that does the job?

figure.title: Gale berth, 24 m motor yacht
lines: Stern load 6.0 t, shared by two lines
Nylon MBS: 20 mm 8.8 t · 24 mm 12.5 t

options: 36 mm
28 mm
24 mm
20 mm
questions.why: 3.0 t per line × 4 = 12 t; ÷ 0.9 for the splice = 13.3 t, so 28 mm (16.6 t). 24 mm forgets the splice.

questions.q: A surge is running into the harbour and you double up your bow lines like this. When the surge snatches, what share of the load does line A take?

figure.title: Doubling up for the surge
lines: Bow line A: 6 m from cleat to bollard
Bow line B: 12 m, to a farther bollard
Same nylon, both made just taut

options: About a third of it
All of it, until A parts
About two-thirds of it
About half of it
questions.why: A line's stiffness goes as 1/length: the 6 m line is twice as stiff as the 12 m one, so it takes 2/3. Make doubled lines the same length.

questions.q: You have cut new 24 mm three-strand mooring lines for the season. How do you finish the cut ends so they last?
options: A few turns of tape, wound tight over the end
A heat-sealed end, melted with a hot knife
A common whipping of twine round the end
A sailmaker's whipping, sewn through the strands
questions.why: A sailmaker's or palm-and-needle whipping is stitched through the rope and cannot slide off; a melted end or tape soon frays.

questions.q: You must join two lengths of 20 mm three-strand nylon into one long warp that has to run through a snatch block made for 20 mm rope. Which splice?
options: A long splice — it keeps the rope's diameter
Two eye splices, joined with a shackle
A short splice, with its fat part tapered
A short splice — the strongest join of all
questions.why: A short splice nearly doubles the diameter and jams in the sheave; a long splice keeps the diameter, so it runs through the block.

questions.q: The braid-on-braid main halyard of your 20 m sloop is furry and thin in the cover where it sits in the clutch at full hoist, but not worn through. What do you do?
options: Strip the cover off and use the core alone
Turn it end for end, moving the wear off the clutch
Nothing: the core carries all of the load
Tape over the worn part and keep it as it is
questions.why: In braid-on-braid the cover takes part of the load and protects the core; end-for-ending puts fresh cover in the clutch.

questions.q: You need to anchor for the night where the chart and the pilot book show this bottom. Which anchor do you use?

figure.title: Anchorage in a Scottish sea loch
lines: Depth 9 m at the chosen spot

options: The Bruce — its claw grips rock the best
The Danforth — its flukes bite the deepest
The fisherman — its thin fluke spears the kelp
The CQR — its plough digs in under the weed
questions.why: Broad flukes skate over kelp and rock; the fisherman's narrow arm gets through the weed and hooks a crevice.

questions.q: You anchor here for the night in your 20 m yacht. How do you lie?
options: To the Danforth: it holds the most in sand
To both in a V, spread either side of the SW
To the Danforth, with extra chain for the veer
To the Rocna: it turns and resets as she swings
questions.why: A Danforth-type holds well in a straight pull but often trips and clogs when pulled round; a roll-bar anchor turns and resets.

questions.q: The chain of your 24 m yacht is worn and the yard offers this replacement. What do you do?
options: Refuse it: buy chain made to fit the gypsy
Take it: high-test chain is stronger, so better
Take it and run it with the clutch half on
Take it: the same 13 mm fits any gypsy
questions.why: A gypsy is cut for one chain's link pitch and width; chain to another standard rides up and jumps the gypsy under load.

questions.q: You must ride out a gale at anchor here, with no tide to allow for. How much nylon do you let out after the chain?
options: About 140 m
About 60 m
About 20 m
About 46 m
questions.why: (18 + 2) × 7 = 140 m of rode; less the 80 m of chain = 60 m of nylon.
questions.ref: Anchoring — scope by depth and weather

questions.q: You are checking whether the windlass of your 24 m yacht can weigh the anchor here. What pull does it need?

figure.title: Weighing anchor in 25 m
lines: Anchor 60 kg; 80 m of 12 mm chain out
Chain 3.2 kg/m; 27 m hangs as it lifts

options: About 260 kg
About 150 kg
About 440 kg
About 950 kg
questions.why: 60 + 27 × 3.2 = 146 kg lifted; × 3 = about 440 kg. Only the hanging chain counts, not all 80 m.

questions.q: You must ride out this gale at anchor in the lee of the shore, with good sand and plenty of room. How do you lay two anchors?

figure.note: Gale SW 8 for 24 h, veering W

options: One to the SE and one to the SW, 90° apart
One to the SW and one to the NE, 180° apart
Both let go together, close under the bow
Both ahead in a V: one to the SW, one to the W
questions.why: An open moor spreads two anchors ahead across the expected wind, so both share the load as it veers; 180° apart is for a reversing stream.

questions.q: You will lie to a Bahamian moor for five days in a tidal river. How do you stop the two rodes twisting round each other?
options: Join both to a mooring swivel lowered below the keel
Lead both rodes over the same bow roller
Make both rodes fast on the same bow cleat
Lay the two anchors 90° apart, not 180°
questions.why: She turns with every tide, wrapping the rodes; a swivel joining them below the keel lets her turn without twisting them.

questions.q: What do you do to stop her sheering about at anchor?

figure.title: At anchor: ketch, F6 gusting 8
lines: She sheers 40° each way in the gusts
Chain snatches at the end of each sheer
Plenty of chain out, anchor holding

options: Run the engine slow ahead all night
Set a small riding sail on the mizzen
Shorten the chain to hold her tighter
Let out all the remaining chain
questions.why: A riding sail aft acts like a weathervane, holding her head to wind so she stops sheering and snatching.

questions.q: You are preparing your 24 m yacht for offshore anchorages. How should the bitter end of the chain be secured in the locker?
options: By a shackle to an eye, moused with wire
Not at all: the chain's weight holds it
By a lashing you can cut, long enough to reach the deck
By welding it to the bottom of the locker
questions.why: If the windlass fails while she drags, you must be able to slip the chain: a lashing can be cut, and a buoy on the end marks it.

questions.q: You have touched on this bank and will lay the kedge out into deep water with the tender. How do you do it?
options: Warp in the tender, the anchor towed along behind it
Anchor laid first, the warp brought on a second trip
Warp paid out from the yacht, towed behind the tender
Anchor and warp in the tender, warp paid out as you go
questions.why: Pay the warp out from the tender as you go, so you never drag its weight through the water; drop the anchor at full length.

questions.q: You are on a 140 M passage and decide to anchor here until daylight. How do you go in?

figure.title: 0200, off an unlit bay
lines: Crew tired after 30 h; wind W 4 offshore
Bay mouth: sand, the 10 m contour across it
Inner cove 3 m: rocks, old survey
Radar, sounder and plotter all working

options: Slowly on radar and sounder; anchor on the 10 m contour
Along another yacht's plotter track into the cove
Not in at all: anchor outside in 30 m, well clear
Into the inner cove, where the shelter is best
questions.why: In the dark trust what you can measure: radar ranges and the contour lead to charted sand; close in on an old survey is no place at night.
questions.ref: Anchoring — at night on a strange coast

questions.q: At least how far from her anchor do you drop yours, so that your swinging circles can never meet?

figure.title: Anchoring near another yacht
lines: You: 24 m motor yacht, 60 m of chain
Her: 12 m sloop, 45 m of chain
Wind against tide: you will lie differently

options: About 100 m
About 140 m
About 275 m
About 85 m
questions.why: Each radius is the chain's run plus the boat: √(60² − 12²) + 24 ≈ 83 m and √(45² − 11²) + 12 ≈ 56 m; together about 140 m.

questions.q: You are anchoring in this Croatian channel. How do you lower the anchor?
options: In free fall, stopped halfway down
In free fall, with the engines astern
Under power, all the way to the bottom
In free fall, braked hard as it touches
questions.why: In deep water a free-falling anchor and chain gather speed the brake may not hold, and the chain piles on the anchor; power it down.

questions.q: You are writing the anchor-watch orders for tonight. How should the watch check the anchor?

figure.title: Anchor watch 0100, shore unlit
lines: GPS alarm set on the anchor, 90 m radius

options: A torch on the beach ahead, checked now and then
The GPS alarm alone — it covers the whole circle
The chain, felt by hand at the bow each half hour
Radar range and bearing every 15 min, logged, and the alarm
questions.why: With nothing lit ashore, a logged radar range and EBL to the headland plus the GPS alarm show dragging early, even as she swings.

questions.q: Your 22 m motor yacht lies parallel to the pontoon, 4 m off it to starboard. How do you walk her sideways onto it?

figure.note: Twin screws, bow thruster · pontoon to starboard

options: Thruster to starboard; starboard engine ahead, port astern
Thruster to port; starboard engine ahead, port astern
Thruster to starboard; both engines slow ahead
Thruster to starboard; port engine ahead, starboard astern
questions.why: Starboard ahead and port astern swing the stern to starboard; the thruster pushes the bow the same way, so she moves bodily sideways.

questions.q: From rest, you put only the port engine astern, with the starboard one in neutral. What does the stern do?

figure.note: Props turn outwards · port engine astern only

options: Swings to port — as in any boat going astern
Swings to starboard — offset and prop walk add up
Swings to port — the prop walk beats the offset
Goes straight back — the two effects cancel
questions.why: The port shaft's pull aft swings the stern to starboard, and its left-handed prop going astern kicks the stern to starboard too.

questions.q: Your 22 m motor yacht is pinned to this quay with a yacht close ahead. You want to leave bow first. How do you get the bow out?

figure.note: Twin screws · wind E 5, onto the quay

options: Bow spring on, fender forward, port engine ahead
Stern spring on, fender aft, starboard engine astern
Stern spring on, fender aft, port engine astern
Stern spring on, fender aft, both engines ahead
questions.why: Going astern on the stern spring holds the quarter and swings the bow out; the outboard (port) engine astern adds to it.

questions.q: Your 20 m yacht lies alongside this Breton harbour wall for the evening. How much slack must each spring have at HW so it is not bar-taut by LW?

figure.title: Alongside a wall, range 5.0 m
lines: At HW the bollards are level with the deck
Springs: 15 m from cleat to bollard
You will be ashore from HW until LW

options: About 1.7 m
About 15.8 m
About 5.0 m
About 0.8 m
questions.why: At LW the spring runs 15 m along and 5 m down: √(15² + 5²) = 15.8 m, 0.8 m more than at HW. Short lines need far more.

questions.q: You must lie alongside a jetty of wide-spaced timber piles in a swell. Your fenders keep rolling into the gaps. What do you rig?
options: A fender board hung outside the fenders
Breast lines hauled in bar-tight
More fenders, tied closer together
Fenders laid flat along the topsides
questions.why: A plank outside the fenders bridges the piles, so the fenders stay put and press on the board, not into the gaps.

questions.q: Your 24 m yacht is the inside boat of a raft on the town quay. Three more yachts — 11 m, 18 m and 14 m — want to raft out. In what order should they come?
options: 14 m, then 11 m, then 18 m outside
18 m, then 14 m, then 11 m outside
11 m, then 14 m, then 18 m outside
In order of arrival, whatever their size
questions.why: Biggest inside to smallest outside, so each boat's lines and fenders hold a smaller boat, never a larger one.

questions.q: You are stern-to on your own anchor and the passerelle is grinding on the quay. What do you change?

figure.title: Stern-to, 24 m yacht
lines: Wind on the beam, gusting 25 kn
Stern lines run straight back to the bollards
Stern swings 1.5 m sideways in each gust

options: Ease the anchor chain so she lies more freely
Haul both stern lines in until the stern touches
Cross the stern lines: port quarter to starboard bollard
Add a third line straight back from the centre
questions.why: Crossed lines are longer and pull across as well as aft, so they check the sideways swing; the passerelle stays clear of the quay.

questions.q: Your mate wants to lay your own anchor as well, to be safe tonight. What do you decide?

figure.title: Marina berth, 24 m motor yacht
lines: Two lazy lines laid to your berth
Ground chains run across the basin
Meltemi forecast F7 on the beam tonight

options: Yes: lay it ahead to share the lazy lines' load
No, but ease the lazy lines so she rides easier
Yes, but only if the wind really reaches F7
No: it fouls the ground chains; double the lazy lines
questions.why: Where lazy lines are laid, an anchor hooks the ground chains; put both lazy lines on, tight and with chafe gear, and tend them.

questions.q: You are going astern into this slot from rest. What will she try to do, and how do you counter it?

figure.note: 20 m sloop, one RH prop · wind W 5

options: Bow falls to starboard; thruster to port, sternway early
Stern swings to starboard; port helm on early
She tracks straight — wind and prop walk cancel
Bow falls to port; thruster to starboard, go slowly
questions.why: A right-handed prop kicks the stern to port going astern, and the wind on the port beam blows the bow to starboard: both turn her one way.
questions.ref: Boat handling — prop walk and wind

questions.q: You are to moor fore-and-aft between these two piles in a Solent river. How do you make the approach?

figure.note: Fore-and-aft between piles · ebb 2 kn E

options: Head east with the ebb; stern line to the west pile first
Head west into the ebb; bow line to the west pile first
Head east with the ebb; bow line to the east pile first
Head west into the ebb; stern line to the east pile first
questions.why: Stem the stream for control, make the bow fast to the up-tide pile first, then drop back on it and take the stern line to the other.

questions.q: You are towing a dismasted yacht home. How much towline do you let out?

figure.title: Tow 80 M offshore, a long swell
lines: Towline aboard: 150 m of 24 mm nylon

options: About 12 m
About 50 m
About 100 m
About 150 m
questions.why: 1.56 × 8² ≈ 100 m: one wave length keeps both boats on the same part of a wave; at 50 or 150 m one is on a crest, one in a trough.

questions.q: You are towing this yacht towards the harbour entrance over the bar. What do you do before you reach it?
options: Let out more line so that the catenary is deeper
Speed up so that the line lifts clear of the water
Keep 100 m out — the longer tow is always the safer
Shorten the tow, for control and to keep the bight off the bottom
questions.why: A long catenary can drag on a shallow bar and gives no control in a narrow entrance; shorten up in sheltered water, then go alongside.

questions.q: You are taking a disabled yacht in tow offshore with your 20 m yacht. How do you make the towline fast on board?
options: Turns round a strong central point, to ease or cut at will
Round the pushpit, to keep it clear of the rudder
A bowline round a primary winch, tied off hard
Shackled to the stern cleat, so it can never slip
questions.why: Under load you may need to ease or slip the tow at once: turns on a strong central post can be surged, with a knife kept beside it.

questions.q: You are about to take another yacht in tow at dusk, 40 M offshore. What do you agree with her skipper first?
options: A VHF channel; the rest can be sorted as you go
A VHF channel, the speed, and the signals to slow or stop
Only who pays for the tow, before anything else
Nothing: the tow simply follows the towing boat
questions.why: Agree a working channel, the towing speed and back-up signals (torch, horn) for slow, stop and let go before the line takes the strain.

questions.q: What lights do you show at night while you tow her?

figure.title: Night tow, under power
lines: Towline 195 m from your stern to her bow
The towed yacht is 12 m long

options: One masthead light, towing light, sidelights, sternlight
Two masthead lights in a line, towing light, sides, stern
