Three masthead lights in a line, towing light, sides, stern
Two masthead lights in a line, sidelights, sternlight only
questions.why: The length of tow runs from your stern to her stern: 195 + 12 = 207 m, over 200 m, so three masthead lights; a diamond by day too.

questions.q: You are towing this yacht alongside into the marina. Which line takes the load when you go ahead?

figure.title: Towing alongside into the marina
lines: She lies on your port side
Your stern well aft of hers
Bow line, stern line and two springs on

options: The stern line between your two sterns
The bow line between your two bows
The spring led forward from your quarter to her bow
The spring led aft from your bow to her quarter
questions.why: Going ahead you move forward against her, so the line leading aft from your bow tightens; going astern the forward-led spring takes it.

questions.q: You leave at dusk for a 130 M crossing with the RIB tender you have towed between anchorages all week. What do you do with it?
options: Lift it aboard and lash it down for the crossing
Tow it on two painters, the outboard aboard
Tow it on a long painter, riding on a wave
Tow it on a short painter, close up astern
questions.why: Offshore a towed tender can swamp, flip or part its painters, and at night it is a hazard astern; stow it on deck or on the davits.

questions.q: You are being towed home overnight by a fishing boat. What do you do about the towline at your bow?

figure.title: Being towed, 10 h to go
lines: Chafe guard fitted at the start
The line saws on the roller as she pitches

options: Leave it alone — the chafe guard will last all night
Check it hourly and ease it a little to freshen the nip
Lead it over the pulpit, away from the roller
Make it fast tighter, so it can no longer move
questions.why: However good the guard, one spot wears through; easing the line a little each hour moves the wear to fresh rope.

questions.q: In a F9 with breaking seas, a crew member suggests taking all sail down and letting your 20 m yacht lie a-hull for a rest. What do you say?
options: Yes: a big yacht lies a-hull safely in any sea
Yes: with no sail up she cannot be knocked down
No: lying beam-on to breaking seas risks a knockdown
Yes, once the helm is lashed hard to windward
questions.why: A-hull she lies beam-on, and a breaking crest about her beam in height can roll her. Heave to, or run with a drogue.

questions.q: You heave to in your 20 m sloop to wait for daylight, but she forereaches at 3 kn and lies almost beam-on. What do you do?

figure.note: Hove-to: forereaching at 3 kn, nearly beam-on

options: Let the backed jib fly, so it stops driving her
Sheet the main in hard, so that she points higher
Run the engine slow ahead to hold her head up
Ease the main further and lash the helm harder to leeward
questions.why: Forereaching means the main is driving: ease it and add lee helm, so she lies 50° off the wind and drifts, leaving a slick to windward.

questions.q: You have chosen to run off before this gale. What do you do now?

figure.title: Running before a gale, F9
lines: Surfing at 14 kn down the faces
Two near-broaches in the last hour

options: Stream a drogue on a bridle from both quarters
Bear away dead downwind and set more sail
Stream the drogue from the bow, head to sea
Turn beam-on and lie a-hull until it eases
questions.why: A drogue astern slows her to a speed you can steer and holds the stern to the seas; a bridle to both quarters keeps the pull central.

questions.q: Your 20 m yacht must ride out this gale. Which tactic keeps her off the shore?

figure.title: Gale for 18 h, lee shore 30 M
lines: No way can be made to windward
Drift: bare poles 5 kn · drogue 3 kn
Hove-to 2 kn · parachute sea anchor 1 kn

options: Run off under bare poles, steering by hand
Lie to the parachute sea anchor from the bow
Heave to under the trysail and storm jib
Run off slowly, towing the drogue astern
questions.why: In 18 h: 5 kn → 90 M, 3 kn → 54 M, 2 kn → 36 M, all past the 30 M shore; 1 kn → 18 M leaves 12 M in hand.

questions.q: You are setting the trysail in your 20 m sloop for a gale offshore. How is it rigged?
options: On the main track, its clew lashed to the boom
Set flying from a halyard, its tack at the bow
On its own mast track, sheeted to the quarters, boom lashed
On the main track, sheeted to the end of the boom
questions.why: A trysail goes up a separate track over the stowed main and sheets to the quarters, so the boom can be lashed down out of the way.

questions.q: Before a 140 M crossing with a gale possible on the second day, how do you prepare the storm jib?
options: Plan to set it round the furled genoa at sea
Plan to roll the genoa down to its size instead
Leave it bagged in the forepeak until it is needed
Hank it on the inner forestay and hoist it once in harbour
questions.why: Rig and try storm sails before you go: on an inner forestay the storm jib sets low and inboard; set at sea for the first time, it often fails.

questions.q: You will lie to a parachute sea anchor through the night. How do you rig it?
options: From the bow on long nylon, with chafe gear at the roller
From the bow on Dyneema, so the rode never stretches
From the stern, so that she drifts more slowly
From the bow on a short rode, to hold her tight
questions.why: The parachute holds the bow to the seas; a long, stretchy nylon rode absorbs the snatch, and the chafe point is guarded.

questions.q: You must keep heading for port in these seas. How do you drive her?

figure.title: 24 m planing motor yacht, F8
lines: Head seas 4 m, short and steep
At 22 kn she is slamming hard

options: Keep planing, to be in port before it worsens
Slow to displacement speed, seas 20–30° on the bow
Slow to displacement speed, seas dead ahead
Turn beam-on between seas and wait for a lull
questions.why: Off the plane she rides the seas without slamming; taking them a little on the bow eases the pitching and keeps her steering.

questions.q: You are making a soft eye in 10 mm 12-strand Dyneema for a tow pennant. Your crew, used to polyester three-strand, starts to unlay it for tucks. What splice do you tell them to make?

figure.title: Splicing the tow pennant
lines: Crew's habit: tucked splices in polyester

options: Tucks through the braid, each sealed by heat
A short bury, the tail melted to lock it in
A locked bury splice with a long, tapered tail
Four tucks, as they would make in polyester
questions.why: Dyneema is too slippery to hold short tucks: the tail is tapered and buried a long way inside the hollow braid, and heat only weakens it.

questions.q: You are eye-splicing a new length of three-strand nylon for a storm snubber. How many tucks do you make?
options: Two tucks, then heat-seal the strands
Three tucks, as for a natural-fibre rope
Three tucks, with a whipping over them
At least five full tucks, then taper the tails
questions.why: Nylon is slippery and stretches, so a splice needs at least five full tucks to hold; fewer can draw out under repeated load.

questions.q: You are refitting your 22 m yacht for an offshore season and can replace only one set of lines now. Which do you replace?

figure.title: Lines at the end of last season
lines: Nylon dock lines, 6 yrs: hard, stiff, faded
Polyester sheets, 6 yrs: supple, a little fuzzy
Nylon snubber, 2 yrs: supple, slight chafe

options: The nylon dock lines: hard, stiff nylon has lost much strength
The Dyneema halyards: Dyneema ages fastest of the four
The snubber: nylon must be renewed every two years
The polyester sheets: any fuzz means the cover is finished
questions.why: Sun, salt crystals and years of cyclic loading break nylon down from inside; stiff, faded nylon has lost a large part of its strength.

questions.q: Three hours into the tow, you check the pennant at your stern fairlead. What is happening, and what do you do?

figure.title: Towing, 3 h in
lines: Pennant: 12 mm Dyneema through a steel fairlead
It saws 10 cm to and fro as she pitches
Fairlead hot; rope glossy and hard there

options: Normal wear: Dyneema shrugs off any chafe
Friction is melting it: shift the nip and keep it cool
Salt crystals: rinse it in fresh water later
Sun damage from the day: tape over the spot
questions.why: Dyneema weakens when hot and melts near 150 °C; a glossy, hard patch at a hot fairlead is friction heat: move the nip, wet it, or re-lead.

questions.q: You are towing on a bridle from both quarters. What load does each leg carry?

figure.title: Towing bridle
lines: Legs from both quarters to a ring
Angle between the legs at the ring: 90°
Steady pull on the towline: 1.6 t

options: About 2.3 t
About 1.6 t
About 1.1 t
About 0.8 t
questions.why: Each leg = 1.6 ÷ (2 × cos 45°) ≈ 1.1 t: the wider the bridle, the more each leg carries above half the pull.

questions.q: You must join two 24 mm nylon warps end to end for a long tow, with no time to splice, and untie them in port afterwards. Which bend?
options: A reef knot, pulled up hard and taped
A double fisherman's knot, pulled up hard
A single sheet bend, as the warps match
A carrick bend, its ends seized to the standing parts
questions.why: A seized carrick bend holds heavy warps and still comes undone after a hard load; a reef knot capsizes, and a fisherman's jams solid.

questions.q: You are coiling a new right-hand-laid three-strand warp to stow in the lazarette. Which way do you coil it?
options: Clockwise, with the lay
Anticlockwise, against the lay
Round hand and elbow, as it comes
Clockwise and anticlockwise in turn
questions.why: Right-hand-laid rope is coiled clockwise; coiled the other way, each turn adds twist and the warp kinks when it runs out.

questions.q: Your tow bridle's spliced eye goes straight over the pin of a shackle on the towing ring. About what load will break it there?

figure.title: Bridle eye on a shackle
lines: Over a 24 mm pin (D/d 2): about 60% kept

options: About 8.1 t
About 4.9 t
About 5.4 t
About 9.0 t
questions.why: 9.0 × 0.9 × 0.6 ≈ 4.9 t: a tight bend over a thin pin costs more than the splice. A thimble or a fat pin keeps much more.

questions.q: After a night of surge in the harbour, the bowline in the end of your nylon stern line has half shaken loose. What do you do?
options: Replace it with a reef knot round the bollard
Replace it with a clove hitch over the bollard
Replace it with a spliced eye that cannot work loose
Retie it pulled hard: a bowline never shakes loose
questions.why: A bowline can loosen when the load comes on and off again and again, as in a surge; a spliced eye cannot work loose.

questions.q: You must lie to one anchor in this muddy estuary through tonight's gale. Which anchor do you lay?

figure.title: Soft mud, gale load 900 kg
lines: Holding per kg of anchor, sand · mud:

options: The 55 kg Rocna: about 1,650 kg
The 55 kg Rocna: about 2,750 kg
The 40 kg Delta: about 1,400 kg
The 32 kg Danforth: about 960 kg
questions.why: In mud: Rocna 55 × 12 = 660, Delta 40 × 5 = 200, Danforth 32 × 30 = 960 kg. Only the Danforth's wide flukes hold 900 kg there.

questions.q: Your Danforth-type kedge dragged on its first try here. What do you do?

figure.title: Off a shingle beach
lines: Kedge dragged: a pebble jammed in its flukes

options: Lay the heavy bower instead, and load it gently
Leave the pebble in, as weight to help it dig
Clear the pebble and drop the kedge again
Drop the kedge again, faster, to drive it in
questions.why: Light flukes jam on stones and skid over shingle; a heavy anchor with a sharp point gets in, if you load it gradually.

questions.q: You are anchoring for lunch in this Balearic bay. Where do you drop the anchor?

figure.title: Balearic bay, clear water, 8 m
lines: Local rules: no anchoring on sea-grass
Pale sand patches between dark weed

options: On the dark weed, where it is thickest, for holding
In a pale sand patch, then look or dive to check it set
On the weed, with extra chain to drag it through
Anywhere: weed matters only for small anchors
questions.why: Anchors skate over sea-grass, and here it is protected too; drop in clear sand, where the anchor digs, and check it with a look or a dive.

questions.q: You are staying two nights here. How do you rig the chain to stop this?

figure.title: Anchored over boulders, 12 m
lines: Chain grinds and snatches: it has wrapped a rock

options: Let all of it out, so that it lies flat over them
Shorten it, so that less of it can wrap round
Float its middle on a buoy, so it lifts clear of the rocks
Change to the nylon rode, which slides over rock
questions.why: A buoy part way along lifts the chain clear of the rocks, so it cannot wrap and shorten itself; nylon dragged over rock chafes through.

questions.q: You are choosing new chain for your 24 m yacht. What is the smallest size that does the job?

figure.title: 24 m yacht: choosing the chain
lines: Storm load 2.1 t, on a two-leg snubber
Chain: × 4 on its break; 80% left when worn
Break: 10 mm 5.0 t · 12 mm 7.2 t · 13 mm 8.5 t

options: 13 mm
10 mm
12 mm
16 mm
questions.why: 2.1 × 4 = 8.4 t; ÷ 0.8 for wear = 10.5 t: 16 mm. The snubber takes it to the bow, but the chain still carries the whole load.

questions.q: You want the gale's pull to stay horizontal at the anchor, so it cannot lift the shank. How much chain must be out?

figure.title: Exposed roadstead, gale tonight
lines: Depth 12 m; bow roller 2 m up: h = 14 m
13 mm chain: 3.8 kg/m in air, 3.3 in water
Gale pull at the bow: about 1,500 kg

options: About 114 m
About 81 m
About 106 m
About 98 m
questions.why: h = 14 m; 1,500 ÷ 3.3 ≈ 455 m; √(14 × (14 + 909)) ≈ 114 m. Use the chain's weight in water, and the catenary, not 7:1.

questions.q: You are anchored in this open roadstead at 1600. What do you decide?

figure.title: Open roadstead, 1600
lines: Rocks 0.3 M astern; 100 m of chain out

options: Stay, and lay the kedge in tandem with the bower
Weigh and get to sea before dark, while you still can
Stay, and add all the nylon rode to the chain
Stay, and run the engines slow ahead all night
questions.why: An onshore gale makes a roadstead a lee shore: if she drags at night there is no room to recover. Sea room is safer than any extra gear.

questions.q: You will lay a Bahamian moor here, stemming the flood, with 40 m of chain on each anchor. How do you lay it?

figure.note: Bahamian moor · 40 m of chain on each

options: First anchor, then the second across the river from it
First anchor, drop back 40 m, second anchor, stay there
First anchor, drop back 80 m, second anchor, heave back to the middle
Both anchors together, then drop back on both chains
questions.why: Let go the up-stream anchor, drop back twice the scope, let go the second, then heave in on the first: she lies midway, 40 m to each.

questions.q: You lie to a Bahamian moor, riding to the up-stream anchor with the other chain slack. You are leaving. Which anchor do you weigh first?
options: The up-stream one, as it holds the heavier load
Both together, heaving each chain in by turns
The one she rides to, then drop back for the other
The slack down-stream one, then the one she rides to
questions.why: Weigh the slack anchor while she still lies to the other; lift the riding one first and she drifts down over the second chain.

questions.q: A strong wind blows straight across the river. How far off the line of the anchors can your stern be blown?

figure.title: Bahamian moor in a river
lines: Anchors 80 m apart, along the stream
Each leg reaches 45 m from anchor to swivel
Yacht: 20 m from the swivel to her stern

options: About 41 m
About 25 m
About 65 m
About 80 m
questions.why: Both legs taut: √(45² − 40²) ≈ 21 m sideways for the swivel, plus 20 m of yacht downwind of it = about 41 m.
questions.ref: Anchoring — two anchors in a river

questions.q: You have hooked the nylon snubber onto the chain and made it fast. How much chain do you then let out?

figure.title: Snubber rigged, F6 tonight
lines: Made fast to both bow cleats

options: None: keep the chain taut to share the load
Enough to hang in a slack loop below the hook
All the rest, so that it piles up on the anchor
Just enough to bring the chain level with the hook
questions.why: The slack loop means the snubber carries the load and stretches; if the chain is taut, the shocks go straight back to the windlass.

questions.q: Your 24 m motor yacht is sheering wildly at anchor. What do you do?

figure.title: 24 m motor yacht at anchor, F7 gusts
lines: High bow and flybridge catch the wind
She sheers 60° each way, then snatches

options: Rig a riding sail on the bow to hold her head
Run one engine slow ahead to steady her
Drop the second anchor under the bow on a short chain
Shorten the bower's chain to hold her tighter
questions.why: A second anchor under foot, on chain a little longer than the depth, drags as she sheers and damps it; a sail forward only makes it worse.

questions.q: You ran onto this bank on the falling tide, and the wind is pushing her further onto it. When do you lay out the kedge?
options: Not at all: back her off on the engine as she floats
Once she floats, so that the warp does not sit slack
Now, under the bow, on a short warp to steady her
Now, into deep water to windward, taking up slack as she lifts
questions.why: As she lifts the wind will drive her further up the bank; a kedge laid to windward now holds her, and you heave in as the tide comes.

questions.q: You check the plotter's anchor track at 0200. What does it tell you?

figure.title: Anchor track since 2200
lines: 2200–0130: an arc round the anchor, 70 m out
0130: the wind veers 100° in a squall

options: She has dragged since the shift: re-anchor now
The GPS has drifted, so the track means nothing
She is swinging to the new wind, as she should
The chain is still straightening: let it settle
questions.why: Swinging draws an arc about the anchor; a straight run downwind after the shift means the anchor broke out and she is dragging.

questions.q: You are about to back your 24 m motor yacht stern-to in this crosswind. Can the bow thruster alone hold her bow up to windward?

figure.title: Stern-to in a crosswind
lines: Wind 20 kn, gusts 26, on the beam
Side windage 48 m², half of it on the bow
Wind load ≈ V² ÷ 60 kgf per m² (V in kn)

options: Yes: in the gusts the bow takes about 10 kgf
No: in the gusts the bow takes about 270 kgf
Yes: the mean wind puts about 160 kgf on it
No: in the gusts the bow takes about 540 kgf
questions.why: 26² ÷ 60 × 24 m² ≈ 270 kgf on the bow in a gust, against a 160 kgf thruster; it is the gust, not the mean wind, you must hold.

questions.q: Your bow thruster cannot hold the bow in these gusts. How do you go stern-to in your 24 m motor yacht?

figure.title: Stern-to, 24 m motor yacht
lines: Wind 20 kn gusting 26 across the berth
Slot between two yachts, quay astern
Thruster: too weak for the gusts

options: Anchor downwind, chain free, let the wind lay her into the slot
Anchor dead ahead, chain free, hold the bow up on the thruster
Anchor upwind, back in on the engines, brake the chain to hold the bow
No anchor: back in fast and get both stern lines on at once
questions.why: The chain, snubbed as she backs in, holds the bow up to windward where the thruster cannot; the engines steer the stern into the slot.

questions.q: You expect a long, fiddly berthing in a gusty crosswind. How do you plan to use the bow thruster?

figure.title: Bow thruster: maker's notes
lines: Electric, 7 kW, on its own battery
Run time 3 min, then a thermal cut-out
Cool enough to restart after about 15 min

options: Non-stop: it has its own battery to draw on
All the way in, then rest it once she is tied up
Steadily: the cut-out is there only for emergencies
Short bursts at the key moments; chain and engines hold her
questions.why: A thruster that cuts out halfway through the manoeuvre leaves the bow to the wind; save it for short bursts, and hold her on chain and engines.

questions.q: You are stemming this stream in your 23 m twin-screw yacht, stopped over the ground 5 m off your gap on the quay. How do you close the last 5 m?

figure.note: Twin screws · stopped over the ground, 5 m off

options: Both ahead to hold the stream, bow angled in a little
Walk her sideways on split engines and thruster
Both to neutral, and let the crew heave her in
Thruster towards the quay, both slow astern
questions.why: Split engines give little or no thrust ahead, so the stream carries her back; held on both engines, bow angled in, the stream ferries her across.
questions.ref: Twin screws — docking in a stream

questions.q: You are heading downstream to this berth on the quay, and the river is too narrow to turn your 23 m twin-screw yacht. How do you come alongside?

figure.note: River 1.2 lengths wide · 23 m, twin screws

options: Come in fast with the stream, to keep good steering way
Pass the berth, stop, then back up to it against the stream
Drift down beam-on to the stream and land her bodily
Come in bow first with the stream, stopping on the engines
questions.why: Going astern into the stream she is stemming it, slow over the ground and under control; with the stream behind her she cannot stop.
questions.ref: Twin screws — docking in a stream

questions.q: You must leave at 0600. How do you get your 24 m yacht out of this raft?

figure.title: Raft on a tideless quay
lines: Three yachts of 12–15 m outside you
Wind F5 onto the quay; crews aboard

options: Go hard astern and slide out from under the raft
Leave ahead and let the outer boats swing in behind
The outer boats cast off and stand clear; then they re-raft
Spring the stern out with the whole raft still on you
questions.why: With the wind onto the quay the whole raft lies on you, and no spring or engine can move it; the outer boats must stand off while you leave.

questions.q: You will tow this yacht 70 M to port through a moderate sea. What is the fastest you should tow her?

figure.title: Disabled sloop in tow
lines: In a seaway: no more than 2/3 of it

options: About 7.7 kn
About 2.8 kn
About 5.9 kn
About 5.1 kn
questions.why: 10.0 m = 32.8 ft; 1.34 × √32.8 ≈ 7.7 kn hull speed; 2/3 of it ≈ 5.1 kn. Use the waterline length, not the overall length.

questions.q: You hang chain in the middle of the towline to give it spring. Under a steady pull, how deep does it hold the middle of the line?

figure.title: Chain weight on the towline
lines: 100 m of nylon; steady pull 300 kg
20 kg of chain at its middle (17 kg in water)
Dip at the middle ≈ weight × length ÷ (4 × pull)

options: About 1.4 m
About 0.7 m
About 5.7 m
About 1.7 m
questions.why: 17 × 100 ÷ (4 × 300) ≈ 1.4 m: under a hard pull the weight soon lifts; the nylon's stretch, not the dip, is the real spring.

questions.q: Your gearbox has failed 90 M offshore, and this ship will tow your 20 m sloop. How do you make her towline fast?

figure.title: Taking a tow from a ship
lines: She passes over a heavy 48 mm towline
Your sloop: keel-stepped mast, two bow cleats

options: Round the pulpit base, to keep it off the anchor
Spread over the mast foot and both bow cleats, guarded
Round the windlass, with its chain brake hard on
To one bow cleat alone, with a round turn on it
questions.why: A ship's pull can rip out a single cleat or a windlass; share it between the keel-stepped mast and both cleats, with chafe gear at the fairlead.
questions.ref: Towing — being towed by a ship

questions.q: The trawler's skipper wants to get you to port quickly. What do you tell him?

figure.title: Being towed by a trawler
lines: Your yacht's hull speed: about 8.5 kn

options: 8 kn is fine: it is still under her hull speed
As fast as he likes: the faster, the shorter the strain
No more than about 5 kn: near hull speed the loads soar
8 kn is fine, as long as you steer straight behind
questions.why: Towed near her hull speed a yacht squats, sheers and loads her fittings far harder; ask for well under it, however long it takes.
questions.ref: Towing — being towed by a larger vessel

questions.q: You are being towed overnight. What does your helmsman do?
options: Steers only when she sheers more than 30°
Leaves it to the autopilot on a fixed heading
Lashes the helm amidships and keeps a lookout
Steers all the time, keeping her in the towing boat's wake
questions.why: Unsteered, a tow sheers about and snatches the line; steered in the wake, she keeps the pull straight and the load even.

questions.q: You are towing this yacht under power at night. What lights do the two vessels show?

figure.title: Night tow
lines: Towline 110 m from your stern to her bow
She: a 10 m sailing yacht, no engine

options: You: two masthead, sides, stern, towing light · she: sides, stern
You: one masthead, sides, stern, towing light · she: sides, stern
You: two masthead, sides, stern, towing light · she: masthead, sides, stern
You: two masthead, sides, stern · she: sides, stern, towing light
questions.why: Tow 110 + 10 = 120 m, under 200 m: two masthead lights, sidelights, sternlight and the yellow towing light; the tow shows sides and stern.

questions.q: You take a disabled yacht in tow at dusk, motoring. Your yacht has no towing lights. What do you show?

figure.title: Your 20 m sailing yacht
lines: No second masthead light, no towing light

options: The tricolour only, as you have no towing lights
Steaming light, sides and stern, a searchlight on the towline
Your anchor light, to show that you are slow
Tricolour and steaming light, a torch on deck
questions.why: Rule 24(i): a vessel not normally towing that helps one in need may omit the towing lights, but must show the tow, as by lighting the towline.

questions.q: You are towing by day, with 220 m from your stern to the stern of the tow. What shapes are shown?

figure.title: Daylight tow, under power
lines: Your stern to her stern: 220 m

options: A black ball on each vessel
A diamond on your yacht only
A diamond on each vessel, where best seen
A diamond on the tow only, aft
questions.why: Rule 24: when the tow is over 200 m long, the towing vessel and the tow each show a diamond shape where it can best be seen.

questions.q: You are writing the night orders for this tow. Which do you write?

figure.title: Night tow, 12 h to port
lines: Crew of six on your yacht, two on the tow
Towline: 100 m of nylon, chafe gear on

options: Check the line only if your speed over ground drops
No one aft at night; her lights show she is still there
Autopilot on; check the line at each change of watch
A watch aft on the line, knife at hand; chafe and VHF checks hourly
questions.why: A chafing or parted line is caught early only by someone watching it; hourly chafe and radio checks keep both crews on the same plan.

questions.q: At 0300 the towline parts, and its end is trailing astern of your twin-screw yacht. What do you do first?
options: Both engines to neutral, then haul the line aboard
Send a MAYDAY, as the tow is now adrift
Speed up to keep the trailing line taut
Turn back at once to pass her a new line
questions.why: A trailing line soon wraps a propeller and disables you too; stop the props, recover it, then plan the reconnection from upwind.

questions.q: The yacht you are towing has lost her rudder and sheers 30° each way, snatching the line. What do you ask her crew to do?

figure.title: Tow without a rudder
lines: Line snatches at the end of each sheer

options: Ask you to tow faster to straighten her out
Stream a drogue or a bight of warp from her stern
Shorten the towline to 20 m to hold her straight
Move the towline to one of her quarters
questions.why: Drag astern of the tow acts like a tail and keeps her straight; a short line or more speed only makes each snatch harder.

questions.q: You are running your planing motor yacht before these seas. What do you do with the trim tabs?

figure.title: 24 m planing yacht, 16 kn
lines: Seas F7 on the starboard quarter
Bow digs into the back of the wave ahead
She yaws hard each time it does

options: Lower the starboard tab only, against the yaw
Leave them: tabs change nothing at sea
Raise both tabs fully, so the bow rides higher
Lower both tabs fully, to hold the bow down
questions.why: Tabs down push the bow down — right in a head sea, wrong in a following one; raised, the bow stays up off the back of the wave ahead.

questions.q: Could your displacement motor yacht keep pace with these seas and sit on the back of one?

figure.title: 24 m displacement yacht, following seas
lines: Wave speed ≈ 1.56 × period m/s; 1 m/s = 1.94 kn

options: No: the seas run at about 18 kn, she at about 6
Yes: the seas run at about 18 kn, she at about 22
Yes: the seas run at about 9 kn, she at about 11
No: the seas run at about 18 kn, she at about 11
questions.why: 1.56 × 6 = 9.4 m/s ≈ 18 kn; 21.5 m = 70.5 ft, 1.34 × √70.5 ≈ 11 kn. She cannot keep up: slow down and let them pass under her.

questions.q: In following seas your twin-screw displacement yacht yaws to port as each crest lifts her stern. Which engine do you give a burst ahead to check it?

figure.note: Twin screws · following seas · yawing to port

options: The port engine: its thrust swings the bow back to starboard
The port engine astern, to pull the bow back round
The starboard engine: its thrust pushes the bow to starboard
Both engines equally, to drive her straight on
questions.why: Thrust ahead on the port side turns her to starboard about her centre; the port engine astern would turn her further to port.

questions.q: Your motor yacht lists to port in this beam wind. Which trim tab do you lower to level her?

figure.title: Beam wind, F6 from starboard
lines: She lists 4° to port at 18 kn
Both trim tabs now fully up

options: The starboard tab, to push the high side down
The port tab, to lift the low side
Neither: tabs alter only the fore-and-aft trim
Both tabs, by the same amount
questions.why: A lowered tab lifts the stern on its own side, so lowering the port tab raises the low port side and levels her.

questions.q: You must wait 8 hours for daylight off this harbour in your 24 m motor yacht. How do you ride out the gale?

figure.title: Off a harbour, gale SW 8
lines: Sea room: 40 M to the NE

options: Stop the engines and drift beam-on to rest the crew
Run off downwind at speed and come back at dawn
Jog slowly head to sea, the seas fine on the bow
Anchor off the entrance on all of the chain
questions.why: A motor yacht cannot heave to; at steerage way head to sea she rides easily and holds her position, keeping her sea room.

questions.q: Hove-to under the trysail, you see this. What do you change?

figure.title: Trysail set, sheeted to a quarter block
lines: Boom lashed down out of the way

options: Ease the sheet until the flutter stops
Move the sheet lead further aft
Sweat the halyard up harder
Move the sheet lead forward
questions.why: A lead further forward pulls the clew down as well as aft, tightening the leech and easing the foot, as with a jib.

questions.q: You are about to hoist the trysail at the mast in a rising gale at night. How do you rig its sheets beforehand?
options: Two sheets, one to a block on each quarter, both led to winches
One sheet to the leeward quarter; rig the other after a tack
One sheet to the end of the boom, as for the mainsail
Two sheets, both led through the same quarter block
questions.why: With both sheets led before the hoist, you can tack or change tack hove-to from the cockpit, and no one goes back to the clew.

questions.q: You are running off and will stream your drogue astern. How much line do you give it?

figure.title: Running off under a drogue, F9
lines: Want: drogue in a trough as she tops a crest,
and at least one wave length astern

options: About 38 m
About 115 m
About 76 m
About 16 m
questions.why: 1.56 × 7² ≈ 76 m; 1.5 wave lengths ≈ 115 m puts the drogue in a trough, biting hard, just as she starts to surf down a crest.

questions.q: The gale has passed, and you must recover the parachute sea anchor. How do you do it?
options: Winch the rode in from the bow with the canopy still open
Haul in on the rode while motoring slowly away from it
Motor up to its trip-line float and haul it in by the crown
Cut it loose: a parachute cannot be recovered at sea
questions.why: Pulled by the crown on its trip line, the canopy spills its water and comes aboard easily; pulled by the rode, it holds tons of water.

questions.q: You are hanking the storm jib on the inner forestay for a gale. Where do you set its tack?
options: Halfway up the stay, hoisted on a second halyard
Right down on the deck fitting, as low as it goes
Tied to the pulpit, so that it is easy to reach
On a pennant, so the foot sits well clear of the deck
questions.why: Seas breaking over the foredeck fill a low-set storm jib and can tear it; a tack pennant lifts the foot clear of the water on deck.

questions.q: You skipper a 22 m motor yacht on an overnight passage. At 0310 the watch reports a crew member missing. How do you turn to search?

figure.title: Crew missing
lines: Last seen in the cockpit at 0245

options: Williamson turn: hard over, at 60° off hard back to 045°T
Hard over and hold it right round onto 045°T
Anderson turn: hard over and round 250° to the spot
Stop both engines and let him drift down to you
questions.why: Time unknown: the Williamson turn puts you back on your own track, reciprocal 225° − 180° = 045°T, to search along it.

questions.q: Your man overboard is alongside on a line, exhausted, and cannot help himself. Where and how do you get him aboard?

figure.title: Recovery
lines: Sea 2.5 m, the stern rising 2 m
Bathing platform aft, props below it
Recovery net and spare halyard ready

options: Amidships, by two crew pulling him up by the arms
Amidships to leeward, lifted level in the net on a halyard
Up the boarding ladder over the side, by his own effort
At the bathing platform, where the freeboard is lowest
questions.why: In a seaway the stern slams near the props; lift him level amidships to leeward — a vertical lift can make him collapse.

questions.q: At 0140 the engine-room fire alarm sounds on your 24 m motor yacht. Before you pull the fixed system's release, what do you do?

lines: Camera: flames by the starboard engine

options: Keep the engines running to make the nearest port
Open the engine-room door to judge the size of the fire
Stop engines, generator and fans, shut the flaps, count everyone out
Run the extractor fans to clear the smoke for the agent
questions.why: Running engines and fans draw the agent out and feed air in; shut the space tight and make sure nobody is inside.

questions.q: Your fixed system discharged into the engine room at 0144. At 0150 the engineer wants to open the door to see if the fire is out. What do you tell him?

figure.title: After discharge
lines: Now 0150; bulkhead still hot to the touch
System label: keep closed at least 15 min

options: Open it a crack, just enough to look inside
Open it now and start the engines to vent it
Open it now, so the smoke can clear before it spreads
Keep it shut; wait, cool the bulkhead, extinguisher ready
questions.why: Opening early lets air in to hot metal and the fire re-ignites; wait the time on the label and let it cool first.

questions.q: You are holed 110 M from land and estimate the inflow below. With all three pumps running, where do you stand?

figure.title: Damage control
lines: Electric: 3,600 L/h rated, 60 % at this head
Hand pump: 0.7 L a stroke, 40 strokes/min

options: Gaining about 4 L/min — only just
Losing about 55 L/min — fast
Losing about 8 L/min — slowly
Gaining about 28 L/min — comfortably
questions.why: Electric 3600/60 × 0.6 = 36, engine 120, hand 0.7 × 40 = 28: 184 L/min against 180 in — gaining 4.

questions.q: You have hit a submerged object 115 M from land and water is pouring in through the split below. What stops most of it?

figure.title: Damage forward
lines: Can't be reached inside: a tank in the way
Sailcloth, lines and a mattress aboard

options: Speed up so the bow wave keeps the water out
A collision mat over the outside, held on by lines under the hull
A mattress pressed against the tank from inside
Heel her to port with the crew's weight to steady her
questions.why: Outside, the sea pressure pushes the mat into the split; from inside it pushes the patch away.

questions.q: After hitting a log, a hull panel by the forward bulkhead has cracked and bulges inward as each wave strikes. How do you hold it?

figure.title: Forward cabin
lines: Panel cracked, bulging in with each wave
Timber offcuts, wedges, a hatch board

options: Leave it alone — bracing would split it further
Shore it down to the cabin sole, which is closer
Pad and board over it, shored to the bulkhead with wedges
Tape it from inside and keep a watch on it
questions.why: A shore spreads the load through a pad and board to a strong point; wedges tighten it as it settles.

questions.q: Your 24 m motor yacht has run onto a sand bar at the end of a passage. The hull is dry inside. How do you get her off?

figure.title: Aground on sand
lines: Tide rising: HW in 2 h, 0.8 m to come

options: Full ahead to drive her over the bar
Twist her off with the engines and bow thruster
Full astern on both engines at once
Kedge out astern, shift weight aft, haul off near high water
questions.why: Sand drawn into the raw-water intakes can wreck the engines; a kedge and the rising tide get her off safely.

questions.q: You have abandoned to the liferaft 110 M offshore and are clear of the yacht, with the EPIRB transmitting. What do you do in the first hour?

figure.title: In the raft
lines: Raft pack: water, seasick pills, pump

options: Seasick pills for all, inflate the floor, set a lookout rota
Open the canopy wide for air and a better view
Paddle in turns towards the coast, 110 M off
A drink of water for all to keep up strength
questions.why: Seasickness dehydrates fast, the floor insulates against the cold, and a lookout must not miss a rescuer.

questions.q: There are six of you in the liferaft. Following the raft's instructions, how long from abandoning will your water last?

figure.title: Water in the raft
lines: Raft pack 3.0 L, grab bag 4.5 L
Instructions: no water for the first 24 h
Then 0.5 L per person per day

options: About 2.5 days
About 3.5 days
About 2.25 days
About 15 days
questions.why: Day 1 dry; then 7.5 L ÷ (6 × 0.5 L) = 2.5 days: 3.5 days from abandoning.

questions.q: A helicopter is lifting a casualty from your aft deck and has asked you to hold a course and speed. The helmsman keeps looking up at it. What do you tell him?
options: Turn towards the helicopter to keep it in sight
Slow down whenever the winchman nears the deck
Steer by the compass and hold course and speed steady
Follow the helicopter's movements to stay under it
questions.why: The pilot holds station on you; a steady course and speed is what he asked for, and any change upsets the lift.

questions.q: The MRCC will send a helicopter for your injured crew once you are inside its radius of action, and asks you to close its base. When will you be inside it?

figure.title: MRCC
lines: You: 165 M from its base, heading for it

options: About 0700, after 5 h at 9 kn
About 0617, after 4 h 17 min at 10.5 kn
About 0000 tomorrow, after 22 h at 7.5 kn
About 0800, after 6 h at 7.5 kn
questions.why: 165 − 120 = 45 M to go at 9 − 1.5 = 7.5 kn over the ground: 6 h, so 0800.

questions.q: A crew member has had severe abdominal pain for six hours and is getting worse. How do you get a doctor's advice from here?

figure.title: 100 M offshore
lines: Coast station: VHF to about 30 M
MF DSC watch on 2187.5 kHz to 150 M
Yacht has VHF DSC and MF/HF DSC

options: MF DSC urgency call to the coast station, then PAN-PAN on MF
Wait for landfall tomorrow and see a doctor ashore
PAN-PAN on channel 16 to the coast station
VHF DSC distress alert, then MAYDAY on channel 16
questions.why: Medical advice is urgency, not distress; 100 M off only the MF station hears you, and the MRCC links you to a doctor.

questions.q: At night 90 M offshore the mast goes over the side. It lies to leeward, still held by the rigging, and punches the hull on every wave. What do you do?

figure.title: Dismasted
lines: Mast and boom in the water to leeward

options: Haul it back aboard over the side to save the rig
Cut it free; start the engine only once no line is in the water
Leave it alongside as a sea anchor until daylight
Start the engine and motor away to pull clear of it
questions.why: In this sea the spar will hole the hull: knock out the pins, cut the wires, and keep the prop still until every line is aboard.

questions.q: 120 M from land the steering suddenly goes slack. A look over the stern shows the rudder blade has broken off. How do you steer?

figure.title: Steering failure
lines: Sea 2 m, wind F5 on the quarter
Drogue, warps and spare blocks aboard

options: Fit the emergency tiller to the stock and steer
Steer by moving the crew's weight fore and aft
Tow a drogue on a bridle and steer by its two legs
Lash the wheel amidships and sail on as she goes
questions.why: With no blade the stock steers nothing; a drogue on a bridle, one leg shortened, turns her the way you want.

questions.q: On your twin-engine motor yacht the hydraulic steering fails, with the rudders jammed amidships. How do you steer to safety?
options: With the bow thruster alone, at cruising speed
With one engine only, the other one shut down
You cannot steer — anchor and wait for a tow
With the engines: more power on one side than the other
questions.why: Twin screws steer her: ahead harder on the port engine turns her to starboard, and the other way round.

questions.q: At 0130, 110 M offshore, the alternator belt breaks and there is no spare. The engine still runs. What do you keep switched on?
options: Nav lights and the VHF; plot by DR and fixes on paper
The fridge and cabin lights; VHF only to call
The plotter and autopilot, as they navigate for you
Everything until the alarm sounds, then nothing
questions.why: With no charge, save the battery for what keeps you seen and heard — the lights and the radio; a paper plot needs no power.

questions.q: You are 120 M off the coast of a state that publishes this GMDSS coverage. In which sea area are you?

figure.title: Coast state GMDSS notice
lines: VHF DSC watch: to about 30 M
MF DSC watch, 2187.5 kHz: to about 150 M

options: A3 — beyond VHF, so on satellite only
A2 — inside MF DSC cover, outside VHF
A4 — no shore station keeps watch
A1 — still within this state's cover
questions.why: A1 is VHF DSC coverage; A2 is MF DSC coverage beyond it; A3 and A4 lie beyond both.

questions.q: You sent an MF DSC distress alert 140 M offshore and the coast station has acknowledged it by DSC. Where do you now make your MAYDAY call?
options: By voice on VHF channel 16
By voice on 2187.5 kHz
By voice on 2182 kHz
By voice on VHF channel 70
questions.why: The voice call follows on the frequency paired with the DSC one: 2187.5 kHz DSC → 2182 kHz voice.

questions.q: To save paper on a three-day passage you set the NAVTEX to accept the weather forecasts only. What else will it still print?
options: Only gale warnings for the sea area you are in
Everything, once you are within 50 M of a station
Nothing — it prints only the types you pick
Nav warnings, gale warnings and SAR alerts
questions.why: Navigational (A) and meteorological (B) warnings and SAR messages (D) cannot be switched off on a NAVTEX receiver.

questions.q: You bought this yacht last month and leave tomorrow on a 140 M crossing. What do you do about the EPIRB?

figure.title: EPIRB check
lines: Coded for the yacht's flag state

options: Register it in your name on the flag state's beacon register
Re-register it only if you rename the yacht
Nothing — it sends its position whoever owns it
Switch it on briefly to check it reaches a satellite
questions.why: The MRCC calls the registered contacts first, and a stale entry wastes hours. Test it only with the test button.

questions.q: In the liferaft at night your SART's indicator changes as its label describes below. What does it tell you?

figure.title: SART label
lines: Standby: lamp flashes every few seconds
Interrogated: fast flashing and a beeper

options: The MRCC has acknowledged your distress alert
A ship's or aircraft's radar is sweeping you — flares ready
The battery is low — switch it off to save it
A satellite has fixed your position for the MRCC
questions.why: A radar SART answers X-band radar pulses; the change means a radar is in range, so keep a lookout and use flares.

questions.q: At 0220, 90 M offshore, your VHF DSC sounds a distress alert from a yacht 25 M upwind that you cannot reach in this gale. Five minutes on, nobody has acknowledged it. How do you pass it on?
options: VHF DSC relay to all ships, so the nearest one hears
Re-send her alert as your own DSC distress alert
MF DSC relay to the coast station alone, then MAYDAY RELAY to it
Nothing — the coast station must have heard it too
questions.why: Out of VHF range of the shore, relay to the coast station on MF; a DSC relay to all ships only sets off more alarms.

questions.q: A distress has been going on for an hour on channel 16 when you hear the MRCC's broadcast below. What may you now do on 16?

figure.title: Heard on channel 16
lines: ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS

options: Only the vessel in distress may transmit on 16
Nothing at all until the MRCC lifts the silence
Normal working again — the distress is finished
Brief, essential calls only — the distress is not over
questions.why: PRUDONCE allows restricted working while the distress goes on; SEELONCE FEENEE would end it.

questions.q: At 0340, 95 M offshore, you pass a container floating awash. What does the law expect of you?

figure.title: On watch
lines: Shipping lane 10 M to the north
MF/HF DSC and a sat phone aboard

options: SÉCURITÉ to ships near, and report it to the coast station
A MAYDAY, since it endangers every vessel
Nothing — reporting is for merchant ships
Note it in the log; report it at your next port
questions.why: SOLAS V/31: every master reports a direct danger to navigation to ships nearby and to the authorities ashore.

questions.q: At 0500 you hear this MAYDAY. The owner, aboard as a guest, tells you to carry on: he has people to meet at 1800. What do you do?

figure.title: Channel 16
lines: Your ETA at her: about 2 h

options: Stand by on 16 until the MRCC tells you to go
Go to her with all speed and tell her and the MRCC
Go only if the owner agrees — it is his yacht
Carry on — a yacht need only relay the MAYDAY
questions.why: SOLAS V/33: a master able to help must go with all speed; if he does not, the reason goes in the log.

questions.q: At night you collided with a fishing boat; one of your crew is hurt and both vessels are damaged. Once everyone is safe, what do you do about the records?
options: Wait for the fishing boat to report — she was give-way
Report only if your insurer asks you to
Keep the log, plotter track and AIS data as they are, and report
Write a fair copy of the log before you report
questions.why: The investigators need the original records; altering them destroys the evidence, and the report is your duty.

questions.q: The owner wants to sail at 0600 on this 130 M passage to keep to his schedule. Who decides, and what is the decision?
options: The owner — the yacht and the schedule are his
The crew, by a vote at the morning briefing
The insurer, who must be phoned for consent
You do — you wait for the window, whatever the schedule
questions.why: SOLAS V/34-1: no owner may stop the master taking a decision he judges needed for safety.

questions.q: You are buying a 20 m yacht with a loan; the bank lends against a mortgage on her. On which register do you put her?

figure.title: The flag state's rules say
lines: Full register: title and mortgages recorded
Bank: 60 % of price, secured on the yacht

options: The full register, so the mortgage can be recorded
Neither — a mortgage is held at the bank only
Either — the bank keeps the bill of sale instead
The small ships register — cheaper and enough abroad
questions.why: Under these rules only the full register records title and mortgages, which is what a lender needs.

questions.q: You are checking the papers before sailing for a foreign port. What do you sort out before you leave?
options: Nothing — a copy of the registry will do
Bring the original certificate of registry aboard
The surveyor's report from when you bought her
A second insurance certificate for the crew
questions.why: Officials abroad ask for the original certificate of registry as proof of nationality; a copy is often refused.

questions.q: You are about to pay for a used 20 m yacht and the seller hands over the papers below. What must you have before you pay?

figure.title: At completion
lines: Bill of sale signed by the seller

options: A new survey, which clears any debt on her
Only the insurance moved over into your name
The mortgage discharged, so the title comes to you clear
Nothing more — the signed bill of sale is enough
questions.why: A registered mortgage stays on the yacht after a sale; the lender could arrest her from you.

questions.q: The owner lent his yacht to a friend with a coastal certificate, who was dismasted 90 M out on a crossing. Is the claim covered?

figure.title: Policy extract
lines: Warranty: skipper on passages over 60 M
to hold Yachtmaster Offshore or equal
A breach suspends cover while it lasts

options: Yes — warranties only matter for third-party claims
Yes — the dismasting had nothing to do with her skill
Only half — the owner shares the blame with her
No — the skipper warranty was broken on that passage
questions.why: The policy says a breach suspends cover while it lasts; the loss fell inside the breach, whatever caused it.

questions.q: You plan to take the yacht on this passage on 5 November. Are you covered?

figure.title: Policy limits
lines: Mediterranean, within 100 M of the mainland
Planned route: at most 60 M off

options: No — get the insurer to extend the season first
Only for third-party claims, not the hull
Yes — the season matters only for laying up
Yes — inside 100 M is all the policy asks
questions.why: Outside the navigation limits, in area or in time, the yacht is not covered; get a written extension before sailing.

questions.q: At night your 20 m yacht drags her anchor and hits a moored yacht. Both are damaged. What does your insurer pay?
options: Nothing — a dragging anchor is negligence
The other yacht's damage, not your own
Both yachts' damage — it was an accident
Your damage only — she has her own policy
questions.why: Third-party cover pays your liability to others; damage to your own yacht needs hull cover.

questions.q: You are filling in the proposal form to insure your new yacht. How do you answer this question?

figure.title: Proposal form
lines: 'Any losses or claims in the last 5 years?'
Your old yacht grounded 3 years ago

options: Declare it only if the insurer asks again
Leave it out — the claim is paid and closed
Declare it — a hidden material fact can void the policy
Leave it out — it was a different yacht
questions.why: Insurance rests on full disclosure; a past claim is material, and hiding it lets the insurer refuse to pay.

questions.q: The owner's friends offer to pay him €1,500 each for a week's cruise on his yacht, with you as skipper. What does this do to his insurance?
options: Nothing, as long as you hold Offshore
Only the third-party cover is lost; hull stays
Nothing — they are his friends, not customers
No cover for the trip — paying guests are commercial use
questions.why: A private-pleasure policy excludes hire; paying guests make it a charter, and a claim during it would be refused.

questions.q: A charter company offers you a paid job skippering guests on its 18 m yacht for the season. You hold the Yachtmaster Offshore. Can you take it on that certificate?

figure.title: The flag state's rules say
lines: Skippers paid to carry guests need

options: No — the certificate is for recreational use only
Yes, if every trip stays within 150 M of land
Yes, if the guests sign a waiver before sailing
Yes — Offshore covers any yacht up to 24 m
questions.why: The Yachtmaster is a recreational certificate; paid skippering needs the flag state's commercial qualification.

questions.q: You leave tomorrow for a foreign port with the crew below. What papers do you prepare for the crew?

figure.title: Departure tomorrow
lines: Flag state's rules: paid crew sign

options: A crew list only — agreements are for merchant ships
A crew list with passports, and the deckhand's agreement
The crew's sailing certificates and phone numbers
Only your own passport and certificate
questions.why: Arrival clearance goes by a crew list and passports; under these rules the paid hand also needs a signed agreement.

questions.q: You are arriving from outside the customs area after a 140 M crossing. What do you do about the Q flag and going ashore?

figure.title: Pilot book: arrival
lines: Arriving from outside the customs area:
Customs office on the fuel quay

options: All may go ashore; take Q down at the berth
Fly Q only if somebody aboard is ill
Fly Q on arrival; only the skipper goes ashore to report
Fly Q as you leave your port of departure
questions.why: Q asks for free pratique: it flies from arrival until you are cleared, and only the skipper lands to report.

questions.q: You live in the EU and are buying this yacht to keep in the EU. Under the rules below, what must happen?

figure.title: The customs rules say
lines: a non-EU owner, non-EU flag, up to 18 months
Yacht: non-EU flag, VAT never paid
Buyer: you, resident in the EU

options: Sail out of the EU for a day to start a new 18 months
Re-flag her in the EU, which settles the VAT
Nothing — admission runs on until the 18 months end
Import her and pay the VAT: temporary admission ends with you
questions.why: Temporary admission needs a non-EU owner; an EU resident must import her and pay VAT to keep her in the EU.

questions.q: A non-EU crew member rejoins you on 1 July for the rest of the season inside the Schengen area. Until what date may she stay?

figure.title: Visa rule for her (given)
lines: Entry and exit days both count

options: 28 Sep — the Jan–Mar days drop out as she goes
29 Sep — 90 days after the day she arrives
15 Jul — 90 − 75 leaves her only 15 days
8 Jul — 180 days from her first entry
questions.why: As the 180-day window moves on, old days leave it: her count peaks at 83, so she gets 90 days, 1 Jul–28 Sep.

questions.q: You signed Lloyd's Open Form with a tug for your disabled yacht. The tow parts in the storm, and she drives ashore and is lost. What is the salvor owed?
options: A share of the yacht's insured value
Nothing — no useful result, no salvage reward
The fixed fee written into the form
His costs for the nine hours he towed
questions.why: Under 'no cure, no pay' a reward needs a useful result; the yacht was lost, so nothing is owed.

questions.q: Your engine has failed and the mainsail is torn, but you are in no danger. A commercial tug offers help on channel 16. What do you agree?

figure.title: No danger
lines: Port 50 M off; drifting slowly seaward
Tug offers a tow on channel 16

options: Take his line now and settle the bill ashore
Sign LOF — it costs nothing unless he saves you
A towage contract at a price agreed before the line comes over
Refuse, and ask the coastguard for a lifeboat
questions.why: With no danger, agree a towage price first; taking a line with nothing agreed invites a salvage claim on her value.

questions.q: At night your yacht is dragging towards rocks with the engine dead, and a salvage tug offers LOF. The owner is ashore and cannot be reached. Can you sign?
options: Only with the coastguard as a witness on 16
Only once the insurer has agreed by phone
No — only the owner can bind the yacht to a contract
Yes — the master may sign a salvage contract for the owner
questions.why: The 1989 Salvage Convention gives the master authority to make salvage contracts on the owner's behalf.

questions.q: After a fuel-filter change there is diesel in the engine bilge with a sheen on it. What do you do with it?
options: Pads and a container; dispose of it ashore
Add detergent so no sheen shows, then pump
Pump it out once you are 12 M offshore
Pump it out slowly while under way
questions.why: MARPOL Annex I bans oily discharges; a yacht keeps oily bilge water for shore disposal. Detergent only hides it.

questions.q: At 1500 your holding tank is full. Under the rules below, when may you empty it?

figure.title: The flag's sewage rules
lines: Untreated, from the tank: over 12 M off,
under way at 4 kn or more, moderate rate
1500: at anchor, 9 M off the coast
1800: under way, 30 M off at 8 kn

options: Now — 9 M off is well clear of the coast
At 1800, more than 12 M off and under way
Now, if you pump it out slowly enough
Never — a holding tank empties only ashore
questions.why: Both conditions must hold — beyond 12 M from land and under way at 4 kn or more — and only at 1800 do they.

questions.q: You are 60 M offshore in the Mediterranean, under way, with these bags of rubbish. What may go over the side?
options: Glass and tins too, since they sink
Nothing at all — the Med takes no waste
The food waste only; keep the rest for shore
Food waste and cardboard, as both will rot
questions.why: MARPOL Annex V: in a special area like the Med only food waste may go, 12 M or more from land and under way.

questions.q: Reading back the night's log, you find that the 0300 entry gives the wrong course. How do you correct it?
options: Rewrite the night's entries neatly in the morning
Tear out the page and copy it out again fairly
Correction fluid over it and the right course on top
One line through it, the right course beside, initialled
questions.why: The log is evidence in a claim or an inquiry; a correction must leave the original readable and show who made it.

questions.q: You enter a foreign harbour whose pilot book lists these by-laws. Which rules apply to you inside the port limits?

figure.title: Harbour by-laws
lines: Speed limit 5 kn inside the breakwater
Call port control on VHF 12 before entry
No anchoring in the approach channel
Dues payable at the office on arrival

options: The port's by-laws as well as the COLREGs
Only your flag state's rules, as a foreign yacht
Only the COLREGs — by-laws bind merchant ships
Only the by-laws — the COLREGs stop outside
questions.why: Local rules apply alongside the COLREGs to every vessel in the port, foreign yachts included (Rule 1(b)).

questions.q: The owner was skippering his own yacht when she did the damage below, and the claims exceed the limit for a yacht of her size. Can he limit his liability?

figure.title: The flag state applies the LLMC 1976
lines: Owner at the helm after drinking
Entered harbour at night at 12 kn
Quay and two moored yachts damaged

options: Yes, but only for the damage to the yachts
No — loss from his own reckless act cannot be limited
Yes — any owner may limit, whatever the cause
No — limitation is only for commercial ships
questions.why: Under the LLMC the right to limit is lost if the loss came from the owner's own act, done recklessly or with intent.

questions.q: In daylight your deckhand slips off the side deck of your twin-screw 24 m motor yacht at 12 kn. Everyone saw him go and he is in sight astern. Which turn do you make?

figure.title: Man overboard
lines: Fell from the starboard side deck
Seen at once, in sight astern

options: Hard to port first, to swing the stern away from him
Scharnow turn: at 240° off, hard over the other way
Anderson turn: hard to starboard, round about 250°, then stop
Williamson turn: back onto the reciprocal, search the wake
questions.why: Immediate action, casualty in sight, a handy twin-screw yacht: the Anderson turn is quickest; helm to his side swings the props clear.

questions.q: At 0420 a guest tells you she saw a crew member go over the side about five minutes ago. No light or beacon went with him. You want to get back into your own wake in the fewest miles. Which turn?

figure.title: Late report
lines: Seen going over about 5 min ago
No light or beacon on him

options: Williamson turn — the one that covers fewest miles
Anderson turn — the quickest when you act at once
No turn; press MOB now and the waypoint marks him
Scharnow turn — back into your wake in the least distance
questions.why: A late report with the time known: the Scharnow regains your wake in less distance than the Williamson; the Anderson is for immediate action.

questions.q: You start a Scharnow turn to starboard from the heading below. At what heading do you put the wheel hard over the other way, and on what heading do you steady?
options: Reverse at 010°T; steady on 310°T
Reverse at 010°T; steady on 130°T
Reverse at 250°T; steady on 310°T
Reverse at 190°T; steady on 310°T
questions.why: Scharnow: hard over, reverse 240° off the start — 130° + 240° = 010°T — and steady on the reciprocal, 310°T, back in the wake.

questions.q: Your 24 m motor yacht, high-sided with a big flybridge, is coming back to a man in the water in a fresh breeze. How do you make the final approach?

figure.note: Freeboard 2 m, high windage

options: Circle him at speed to flatten the sea around him
Stop upwind of him, beam to the wind, and drift down onto him
Back down on him stern-first so the platform reaches him
Come up from downwind, bow to the wind, as in a small yacht
questions.why: A high-sided yacht drifts faster than a swimmer: stopped to windward she makes a lee and drifts onto him, props clear of him.
questions.ref: MOB — recovery by a motor yacht

questions.q: Your fixed system has fired by itself in the engine room, and both engines and the generator stopped at the same moment. The mate wants to restart the engines at once. What do you say?
options: Yes — but only the engine on the side with no fire
Yes — override the relay; the shutdown is a fault
No — the shutdown is meant; wait the hold time, then check
Yes — engines running will help to clear the gas
questions.why: The system stops engines and fans so they cannot draw the agent out; restart only after the hold time and a check.

questions.q: Under sail in your 23 m ketch, smoke pours from the engine room under the aft cockpit. You have stopped the engine and shut the fuel. How do you put her to the wind while you fight it?

figure.title: Engine-room fire, aft
lines: Engine room under the aft cockpit
Fire port in the engine-room door

options: Keep reaching fast on this tack to make port sooner
Heave to with the fire on the windward side of you
Run off downwind, so the apparent wind is at its least
Bow to wind and slow, so the smoke blows aft, away from you
questions.why: Keep the fire downwind of the crew: with the fire aft, bring her head to wind and slow down so the draught does not fan it.

questions.q: On your 15 m catamaran the port engine-compartment alarm sounds and smoke leaks from round its hatch. How do you deal with it?

figure.title: Catamaran, port hull
lines: Engine under the aft port cabin
Fire port in the compartment lid

options: Stop port engine and fuel, use the fire port, steer on the other
Lift the hatch and empty an extinguisher straight in
Keep the port engine running so its blower clears smoke
Stop both engines and lift the hatch to find the fire
questions.why: Each hull's engine has its own space: keep the hatch shut, attack through the port, and the other engine keeps you manoeuvring.

questions.q: Your 14 m catamaran hits a floating container 100 M offshore. The port bow fills quickly up to the crash bulkhead and she trims down by the head on that side. What do you do?

figure.title: Damage, port bow
lines: Crash bulkhead holding, a slow weep

options: Move the crew forward to port to settle her evenly
Stay aboard, slow down, move weight aft to starboard, watch the bulkhead
Pump the bow dry through the hatch in the bulkhead
Take to the raft — a holed multihull goes down fast
questions.why: The crash bulkhead keeps the rest dry and the other hull floats her: stay aboard, ease the load, take weight off the damaged bow.

questions.q: Two hours after you bounced off a rock ledge, water is seeping round the keel bolts of your 20 m sloop and the floor around them flexes as she pitches. You are 60 M from port, beating in F5. What do you do?

figure.title: Keel area
lines: Keel floor flexing as she pitches
60 M to port, beating in F5

options: Keep beating hard to make port before dark
Tighten the keel nuts hard and sail on as before
Sails down, lifejackets on and raft ready, motor gently to port
Bear away and run under full sail to ease her
questions.why: A working keel can drop off and she then capsizes at once: take the sail load off it, prepare to abandon, motor gently.

questions.q: At 2200 the guests' electric surfboard battery, left charging on the aft deck, starts to hiss and smoke. What do you do?

figure.title: Aft deck
lines: Deck hose rigged; CO2 and powder near

options: A CO2 extinguisher — it starves the fire of air
One powder extinguisher, then carry it below to cool
Cover it with a fire blanket and leave it to burn out
Over the side if it can be done safely; if not, flood it with water
questions.why: A lithium pack in thermal runaway feeds itself, so smothering fails: get it overboard or cool it with plenty of water, upwind of the smoke.

questions.q: On your 24 m motor yacht the engine room is flooding through a split in the plating behind the engine that nobody can reach, faster than the pumps clear it. What do you do first?

figure.title: Engine room
lines: Split in the plating, out of reach
Watertight door to crew mess open

options: Get the engineer out, then shut the watertight door
Send more crew in to hunt for the leak
Shut the door at once with the engineer still inside
Leave the door open so the mess pumps help as well
questions.why: A watertight door stops the flood spreading to the next compartment: count everyone out, then close it and keep it shut.

questions.q: Your yacht is holed 120 M offshore. Her stability notes say she is lost once a further 6 t of water is aboard. How long have you got?

figure.title: Flooding
lines: Stability notes: lost at +6 t (6,000 L)

options: About 24 min
About 15 min
About 9 min
About 7 min
questions.why: Net inflow 650 − 250 = 400 L/min; 6,000 ÷ 400 = 15 min: send the distress alert and ready the rafts now.

questions.q: At 1310, 40 min after high water, your 20 m sloop runs onto a sandbank on the falling tide. You look at the tide table. When is your best chance of getting her off?

figure.title: Tide table
lines: HWs fall to 3.9 m at neaps in 7 days
She floats with 5.3 m of tide here

options: Tonight at 0055 — the next high water will lift her off
Tomorrow at midday, when the tide is back up to 5.4 m
Now, at once — heel, kedge and engine before it falls further
In about 7 days at neaps, when the streams are weakest
questions.why: At the top of springs each following high water is lower — 5.2 m tonight against the 5.3 m she needs — so act before the tide drops.

questions.q: Your 24 m motor yacht is sinking and the raft is inflated alongside the stern. Your crew are mustered on the boat deck. Where do they board it from?

figure.title: Heights above the water
lines: Bathing platform: 0.4 m, clear of fire
Raft on its painter at the stern

options: The boat deck, sliding down the painter into it
The side deck — jump into the sea beside the raft
The boat deck — jump straight down onto the canopy
The bathing platform, stepping in dry one at a time
questions.why: Board dry from the lowest point: a jump into the raft injures those inside, and a jump into the sea brings cold shock.

questions.q: You must abandon your 22 m yacht 130 M offshore with nine aboard. She carries two 8-person rafts. How do you use them?

figure.title: Abandoning
lines: Grab bag, EPIRB, SART, handheld VHF

options: Launch both, share out people and kit, tie them together
Launch one and put all nine in it for warmth
Launch one and keep the other aboard as a spare
Launch both and let them drift apart to widen the search
questions.why: One raft would be over its rating; two tied together share the gear, the warmth and the watch, and make one bigger target.

questions.q: Your yacht went down in seconds and three of you are in the water in lifejackets, with no raft. The water is 12°C and the EPIRB is on. How do you wait?

figure.title: In the water
lines: Three crew, lifejackets on, no raft
EPIRB floating, tied to one of you

options: Take turns treading water to keep the blood moving
Huddle together, chests touching, legs drawn up, and keep still
Swim about to keep warm until the helicopter comes
Spread out in a line to be seen from further away
questions.why: A huddle keeps the heat of chest and groin; swimming or treading water pumps cold water past the skin and cools you faster.

questions.q: You went into the water two minutes ago and your breathing has just settled. The raft is held on its painter to floating wreckage 50 m away. What do you do?

figure.title: In the water
lines: In for 2 min; gasping has eased
Raft on its painter to wreckage, 50 m

options: Take off the lifejacket so you can swim faster
Hold still in the HELP position and wait
Swim for it now, while your arms still work
Wait some more minutes for the cold shock to pass
questions.why: 1-10-1: a minute of cold shock, about ten of useful movement, an hour before hypothermia: use those ten minutes to save yourself now.

questions.q: You have gone over the side alone, in a lifejacket, and the yacht is turning back for you — it may take 20 minutes. How do you hold yourself while you wait?
options: Swimming slowly after the yacht to close the gap
Upright and treading water to keep your head higher
Lying flat on your back, arms and legs spread out
Knees drawn up, arms crossed over the chest, still: the HELP
questions.why: The HELP posture guards the armpits, chest and groin, where most heat is lost; every movement spends heat and strength.

questions.q: The helicopter pilot asks you to hold a steady speed with the wind 30° on your port bow while he winches. What heading do you steer?

figure.title: Winching
lines: Pilot: wind 30° on the port bow
Steady speed 8 kn, hold the heading

questions.why: Port bow means the wind comes from 30° to port of the heading: 040° + 30° = 070°T; 010°T would put it on the starboard bow.

questions.q: Midway across, a crew member who takes insulin turns pale, sweaty, shaky and muddled before lunch. He can still swallow. What do you do first?

figure.title: Crew member
lines: Missed breakfast, seasick in the night

options: Nothing by mouth; lay him down and let him sleep
Sugar now — a sweet drink or glucose — then food and advice
His insulin dose now, to bring his sugar back down
Wait an hour to see whether it passes by itself
questions.why: Low blood sugar: sugar by mouth while he can swallow brings him round fast; more insulin would make it far worse.

questions.q: Dismasted and cut free 120 M from the nearest port, you check the fuel. Keeping the reserve, can you motor all the way in?
options: Yes — exactly 120 M, just enough to arrive
Yes — about 144 M, with some to spare
No — about 96 M; rig a jury sail as well
No — about 54 M; call for a tow at once
questions.why: Usable 90 × 0.8 = 72 L; 72 ÷ 4.5 = 16 h; 16 h × 6 kn = 96 M — short of 120 M, so a jury rig must make up the rest.

questions.q: On your 20 m yacht the wheel turns but the rudder no longer answers: the helm pump has failed. You ship the emergency tiller on the stock, but it will hardly move. What have you missed?

figure.title: Steering
lines: Hydraulic ram on the rudder quadrant
Helm pump failed, no leak found
Emergency tiller fitted on the stock

options: Bleeding the air out of the helm pump first
Lashing the wheel amidships to hold the rudder
Topping up the oil in the helm pump reservoir
Opening the bypass valve on the ram so the oil can pass
questions.why: Oil trapped in the ram locks the rudder; the bypass (crossover) valve lets it flow from side to side so the tiller can work.

questions.q: At 0100 in F6 a guest coming on watch refuses to clip on, saying he has sailed for thirty years. You are the skipper. What do you do?
options: Insist: he clips on or he stays below — your order stands
Let him decide — he is an adult and an experienced sailor
Ask the owner aboard to settle it in the morning
Note his refusal in the log and let him go up
questions.why: The skipper answers for the safety of everyone aboard, and his safety orders bind guests and crew alike.

questions.q: Your yacht is sinking 120 M offshore. A ship shows on AIS 8 M away, and you have a VHF DSC set and a satellite phone with the MRCC's number. What do you do first?

figure.title: Your kit
lines: Satellite phone, MRCC number in it
Ship on AIS 8 M away, closing
No coast station in VHF range

options: Phone the MRCC first: it can task the ship itself
VHF DSC alert and MAYDAY on 16, then phone the MRCC
DSC individual call to the ship, then talk on 72
Call the ship on 16 by name, without a MAYDAY
questions.why: A DSC alert and a MAYDAY reach every ship in range at once; a phone call reaches only the MRCC, and the ship 8 M off hears nothing.

questions.q: At 1300 you are calling a distant coast station on your HF set, and on 4 MHz it is faint and broken. What do you try next?
options: VHF channel 16, which carries further by day
4 MHz again at full power until it clears
A higher band, such as 8 or 12 MHz
A lower band, such as 2 MHz on MF
questions.why: By day the sky wave carries the higher HF bands further: over a long distance in daylight move up a band, at night move down.

questions.q: At 0300 you must send an HF DSC urgency call to the coast station below for medical advice. Following its guide, on which frequency do you call?

figure.title: Coast station guide (HF DSC)
lines: Day: 4 MHz to 300 M, 8 to 800 M, 12 beyond
Night: 4 MHz to 500 M, 6 to 1,000 M, 8 beyond
You are 650 M from the station

options: 6312 kHz
questions.why: 0300 is night: 650 M falls in the 6 MHz band (500–1,000 M), so 6312 kHz; the day table would give 8 MHz.

questions.q: In the raft, your grab bag holds an AIS-SART, not a radar SART. A ship is closing at night. Where will her watchkeeper see you?

figure.title: Grab bag
lines: AIS-SART switched on, up on its pole

options: As a SART target with your position on her AIS display
Only on the MRCC's screen, through the satellites
Nowhere until she comes within about a mile
As a line of 12 dots on her radar screen
questions.why: An AIS-SART sends its GPS position as an AIS message: it shows on AIS displays and plotters, not on radar like a radar SART.

questions.q: You are standing by a yacht in distress 3 M away. On 16 two other yachts keep chatting over her calls, and no coast station is in range. What may you say?

figure.title: Channel 16
lines: MAYDAY from a yacht 3 M off, ongoing
You are not controlling the traffic

options: SEELONCE FEENEE, then your yacht's name
SEELONCE DISTRESS, then your yacht's name
SEELONCE MAYDAY, then your yacht's name
PRUDONCE, then your yacht's name
questions.why: Only the casualty or the station controlling the traffic says SEELONCE MAYDAY; another station near her imposes silence with SEELONCE DISTRESS.

questions.q: Alongside after the passage, you notice the EPIRB in its bracket flashing: it has been transmitting for an hour. Nothing is wrong. What do you do?
options: Take the battery out so it cannot happen again
Switch it off and say nothing — no harm was done
Switch it off and tell the nearest MRCC it was a false alert
Leave it on until the MRCC calls you about it
questions.why: A 406 MHz alert has started a search somewhere; switch off and tell the MRCC at once so that they can stand it down.

questions.q: At 0400, 140 M offshore, your MF DSC set receives a distress alert from a vessel 380 M away. A minute later a coast station acknowledges it by DSC. What do you do?
options: Send a DSC relay to all ships to spread the word
Acknowledge it by DSC so she knows she was heard
Turn and head for her at your best speed now
Listen on 2182 kHz and log it; help only if asked
questions.why: Once a coast station has acknowledged, the alert is in hand: watch the voice frequency, log it, and stand by to help if asked.

questions.q: You are 2 h into a 40 M run towards a liferaft when the MRCC calls you with the message below. What do you do?

figure.title: MRCC on channel 16
lines: Ship 'Nordic Star' 4 M from the raft
She has been tasked and is proceeding
You are released from the search

options: Resume your passage and log the release with the time
Resume your passage; there is nothing to log
Carry on to the raft — only her crew can release you
Carry on until you see the ship take them aboard
questions.why: SOLAS V/33: once told that other ships have been requisitioned and are complying, you are released; record it in the log.

questions.q: The MRCC asks ships near a sinking fishing boat 70 M away to go to her. By your figures you can reach her, but then no port with the fuel left. What does SOLAS require of you?

figure.title: Your position
lines: Nearest fuel after her: 110 M on

options: Go anyway — the duty to assist comes before your safety
Tell the MRCC you cannot go, and log the reason
Log the call, but there is no need to answer the MRCC
Say nothing on the radio; others will answer the call
questions.why: V/33.1: a master who is unable to assist must enter the reason in the log and inform the SAR service — never just stay silent.

questions.q: At 0200, 130 M offshore, the wind rises to a steady force 10. The last forecast, two hours ago, gave force 6 to 7 with no gale warning. What does SOLAS V/31 ask of you?
options: Nothing — reports are for ice and derelicts only
Record it in your log; report it at your next port
Report it to the coast station and to ships nearby
Report it only if the yacht is damaged by it
questions.why: V/31: a master who meets winds of force 10 or more with no storm warning received must pass it on to ships near and the coast.

questions.q: At night you collide with a sailing yacht. Nobody is hurt and your own damage is above the waterline. Before you go on, what must you do for her?

figure.title: After the collision
lines: Crew of four, no injuries reported
Your bow damaged above the waterline

options: Stand by only if she was the stand-on vessel
Exchange insurers' names, then continue at once
Nothing more — nobody was hurt in the collision
Stand by until she needs no help, and give your yacht's details
questions.why: After a collision the master must help the other vessel and her people, so far as he safely can, and give his ship's name and port of registry.

questions.q: You are moving your yacht from one flag to another. Before the new registry will enter her, what does it want from the old one?

figure.title: Change of flag
lines: Registered on flag A, mortgage paid off
Flag B's form asks for an old-register paper

options: A deletion certificate: closed, with no mortgage left on it
A letter from the builder confirming her hull number
Nothing — she may stay on both registers for a year
A copy of her current certificate of registry
questions.why: A ship may fly one flag only: the new register needs proof the old registration is closed and no mortgage is still recorded on it.

questions.q: The owner has gone bankrupt and the yacht is sold for less than her debts. In what order are the three lenders paid from the sale?

figure.title: Mortgages on the register
lines: Rule: by date entered; unregistered last

options: C, then A, then B
B, then A, then C
B, then C, then A
A, then B, then C
questions.why: Registered mortgages rank by date of entry, not of signing — B (12 Mar) before A (20 Mar) — and the unregistered C comes last.
