questions.q: You bought this registered yacht 40 days ago and have sent nothing to the registry yet. You plan to sail for a foreign port tomorrow. Where do you stand?

figure.title: Flag's registry rules
lines: On a sale, registration lapses in 30 days
unless the buyer applies with the bill of sale
Certificate aboard: in the seller's name
Bought 40 days ago, no application yet

options: Fine — the bill of sale aboard proves her nationality
Fine — the seller's certificate covers her until renewal
She is unregistered — apply and get papers before you sail
Fine — the registry is needed only for a new name
questions.why: Past the 30 days her registration has lapsed: without a valid certificate she has no proven nationality abroad.

questions.q: Your employer has taken this yacht on a bareboat charter for the summer and you are her skipper. The owner, aboard as a guest for a weekend, orders you to change the passage plan. Whose instructions do you follow?

figure.title: Charter
lines: Owner aboard as a guest this weekend
He wants to go to a different island

options: Whoever is aboard — the owner, since he is here
The insurer's — the policy names the owner
The owner's — the yacht is his, charter or not
The charterer's — the owner gave up control for the charter
questions.why: Under a bareboat charter the charterer takes possession and control and engages the skipper; the owner aboard is only a guest.

questions.q: Your flag applies the MLC rest rules to your paid deckhands. Looking at their last 24 hours below, who has broken them?

figure.title: Deckhands' rest, last 24 h
lines: MLC: 10 h rest/24 h, ≤2 spells, one ≥6 h

options: Ben and Carl — no 6 h spell
Nobody — all three had 10 h
Ben only — he has three spells
All three — rest must be unbroken
questions.why: All had 10 h, but Ben's comes in three spells and neither of Carl's two reaches 6 h; only Anna's 6 + 4 meets the rule.

questions.q: Your paid deckhand breaks his wrist in a foreign port and is signed off to fly home. Under your flag's rules below, who pays for his flight?

figure.title: Flag: paid crew (MLC 2006)
lines: Written agreement for every paid crew
if sick or injured in service

options: You, as the skipper who signed him on
The owner, as his employer
The deckhand himself
The port's health authority
questions.why: MLC: a seafarer signed off sick or injured in service is repatriated at the employer's cost — here the owner.

questions.q: Under Lloyd's Open Form a salvor towed your disabled yacht off a lee shore. As saved she is worth €380,000, and he claims €420,000 for a hard job. What can the award be?

figure.title: Salvage claim
lines: Danger high, skill and effort great

options: The full €420,000 — he decides what the job was worth
A fixed tariff by length, whatever he claims
Some part of the €380,000 — never more than that
€380,000, plus his costs over and above it
questions.why: Salvage Convention art. 13: the award is fixed on the listed factors but may not exceed the value of the property salved.

questions.q: In a storm a fishing boat took your crew off your sinking yacht. Next day a tug found her still afloat and saved her under LOF. The fishermen ask whether they are owed anything. What is the answer?

figure.title: Two rescues
lines: Day 1: fishing boat saves the crew
Day 2: tug salves the yacht under LOF

options: The whole award — they were on the scene first
Nothing — saving lives earns no payment at all
Their own award, paid by your crew for saving them
A fair share of the tug's award, as they saved the lives
questions.why: Art. 16: the people saved owe nothing, but a life salvor in the same casualty shares fairly in the award for saving the yacht.

questions.q: Your disabled yacht is being towed in under LOF and the salvage master asks you to keep a bilge pump running and a lookout aft. What is your duty?

figure.title: Under LOF
lines: Asks: bilge pump on, lookout aft
You are still aboard with 3 crew

options: Co-operate fully and do what he reasonably asks
Only what your insurer has approved in writing
Refuse — as skipper you take orders from nobody
None — the salvor now answers for everything
questions.why: Salvage Convention art. 8: the owner and master must co-operate fully with the salvor and take the yacht back once she is safe.

questions.q: You agreed a fixed price for a tug to tow your yacht, engine dead, 40 M to port. Halfway a gale gets up, she starts to flood, and the tug's crew come aboard and pump for six hours to save her. What can the tug claim?

figure.title: The tow
lines: Tug's crew pump for 6 h and save her
No danger when the tow was agreed

options: Only the €4,000 — the price was fixed in advance
Salvage for the extra work, beyond the towage price
Double the price, as the job was harder than agreed
Nothing — salvage needs LOF signed at the time
questions.why: Art. 17: work under a contract earns salvage only when it goes beyond the contract's due performance — as when a new danger arises.

questions.q: Becalmed and in no danger, you clearly refuse a fishing boat's offer of a tow, and say so on 16. She makes fast to your bow anyway, tows you in and claims salvage. What is she owed?

figure.title: On channel 16, 1420
lines: You: no danger, no tow wanted, thanks

options: A salvage reward, which any towed vessel owes
A reward, but halved as you did not ask for it
Nothing — you refused her clearly and with good reason
Her fuel only, since she did save you time
questions.why: No danger, no salvage; and art. 19 gives nothing for services forced on you against an express and reasonable refusal.

questions.q: While you take on fuel alongside, the nozzle sticks open and about 20 L of diesel goes over the side into the harbour. Once the flow is stopped, what do you do?

figure.title: Fuel berth
lines: About 20 L of diesel in the water
Absorbent boom at the fuel kiosk

options: Spray detergent on it so it breaks up quickly
Say nothing — 20 L will be gone within the hour
Hose it away from the pontoon with deck water
Report it to the harbour office and help contain it
questions.why: An oil spill must be reported to the port or coastal authority at once; detergent only sinks it and makes the harm worse.

questions.q: At 1530, 80 M offshore, you pass through a long, fresh oil slick with a tanker on AIS steaming away from its end. What do you do?

figure.title: Slick
lines: Slick 2 M long, fresh and dark
Tanker on AIS at its end, 3 M off
Your position, time and her name noted

options: Report it to the coast station: position, extent, ship
Call the tanker on 16 and tell her to stop it
Photograph it and post it online for the authorities
Nothing — reporting pollution is the tanker's own duty
questions.why: Coastal states rely on sightings: give the coast station or MRCC the slick's position and size and the ship suspected.

questions.q: Your yacht's particulars are below. What does MARPOL Annex V require of her about garbage?
options: Nothing — Annex V does not apply to yachts
Placards on the discharge rules, displayed aboard
A garbage record book with every disposal in it
A garbage management plan and a record book
questions.why: Annex V: every ship of 12 m or more shows the placards; the plan starts at 100 GT or 15 persons, the record book at 400 GT.

questions.q: Your 15.4 m catamaran, six aboard, stays three nights in this harbour. What do you pay?

figure.title: Harbour dues
lines: LOA rounded up to the next whole metre
Tourist tax €1.50 per person per night

questions.q: You arrive at a bay inside a marine reserve, and the pilot book prints the notice below. Where do you anchor your 22 m yacht?

figure.title: Marine reserve notice
lines: Yachts over 20 m: mooring buoys only

options: Anywhere — the rule is for local boats only
On the seagrass, which holds well, with plenty of chain
In sand beside the seagrass, the chain lying over it
You don't: you pick up one of the reserve's buoys
questions.why: Local rules bind visiting yachts too: over 20 m this reserve wants you on a buoy, and its posidonia is protected.
